en: Salutation to Śrī.
Salutation to Śrī Rāmacandra.
Salutation to the great preceptor, the venerable Vighneśvara.
Salutations to the venerable Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, and Kaśyapa.
This [work] is composed by the great sage, the venerable Bhṛgu, in the Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavat-śāstra.
The Authority on Sacrifice:
Now begins the first chapter, by which every ritual action— whether pertaining to the Śruti, the Smṛti, or otherwise— is succinctly set forth.
Salutation to that Vikhanas, the knower of the meaning of all the Vedas;
[this is] the dialogue between the sages and the questions and answers concerning Bhṛgu, the most excellent and best of sages, who dwells in various worlds.
Having approached and bowed down to him who was seated upon a grass mat, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, and whose mind was fixed on the Blessed One, those of restrained senses asked:
"By what path, by which mantras, and to which deity [should we pray]? (1-2)
O Sage, best among those who speak, tell us all that so that, by worshipping it, they may attain the supreme, unsurpassed state. (3) [The Praise of Worship]
Bhṛgu said:
"Everything that has been requested by you, I shall explain well and in its entirety;
listen with a focused mind, having remembered the supreme deity Nārāyaṇa. (4)
One should worship Hari, the imperishable Lord of all worlds, with mantras originating from the four Vedas according to the path consistent with the Śruti;
by that very devotion, he [the Lord] himself will swiftly [reveal] Vaikuṇṭha.
One attains that state; there is no destiny higher than Keśava.
One should constantly worship that Viṣṇu, the means of all means, who eternally bestows liberation upon all and grants the fruits of all desires.
The proper worship of the village deity and the one who receives offerings brings constant bestowal of all perfections to its inhabitants and increases sons and grandsons;
O ascetics rich in austerity, this is the common *agnihotra* for those who maintain no sacred fires.
For those who maintain the sacred fires, this second [form] is for the sake of pacification and bestows all accomplishments.
Indeed, there are two kinds of worship;
that worship is declared to be twofold: with form (mūrta) and without form (amūrta).
An offering made in the fire is formless, whereas the worship of the image is with form.
Indeed, the formless [offering] perishes in the absence of the sacrificer;
however, the supreme worship of the image is unbroken, eternal, and constant. 10–11.

In the Sūtra, Vikhanas has declared that everything from the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) onwards, including the pouring of the oblation into the fire (agnyāghāra) and concluding with the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, should be performed in its entirety; likewise,
one should act according to the prescribed path even in the worship of an image.
O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall explain in due order the path for propitiating Ālaya—
the entire craft, beginning with the examination of the ground and ending with the ritual of expiation,
straight and clear, for the purpose of mantra-rites.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Inquiry of the Sages," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the second chapter:
henceforth, I shall proclaim the sequential procedure for the examination of the ground (*bhūparīkṣā*).
Prior to the time of commencement, the sacrificer should choose a preceptor who is a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), devoted to austerity and virtuous conduct, dedicated to daily fire-offerings,
one who has reached the further shore of learning, disciplined, and free from other defects.
Having invited that Brahmin who is learned in the scriptures and endowed with kinsmen, and having honored him, one should again summon the master builder (sthapati) in the month of Caitra—
or in any other auspicious remaining month— on a favorable day.
On an auspicious day favorable to the village and the patron,
having reached a sacred Vaiṣṇava site and performed purification as prescribed,
one should commence the rite of sowing the sprouts on the preceding night.
If the Brahmin is the sacrificer, the offering of the sprouts (aṅkura) should take place in his house;

if it is someone else, it may be done there or elsewhere. In that case, however, it should be done immediately. On an auspicious moment, the preceptor (ācārya), facing either east or north, [should perform the rite].
Then, having made [the child] lie down, he should touch him with his two hands while reciting the Bhūsūkta.
Having dug a square pit measuring two *tala*s in width and depth, and having removed the earth, the Guru should cast that soil back [into the pit].
If [the soil] is superior, one should know there will be great increase; if inferior, an inferior yield; if equal, a similar yield.
Alternatively, having observed other signs, one may begin [the work].
If it is in a village, one should plow only after examining the site of the assembly hall.
First, one should plow for the sake of the village once the center of the site has been established. Then, having entered the dwelling, one should perform the examination of the ground;
thereafter, according to the prescribed rite, one should arrange the cattle and other livestock.
Having determined the site according to the prescribed rules, one should mark out the divisions;
having had it consecrated with mantras and worshipped thoroughly, one should present the sacrificial offering (bali). 12.
The layout of the site (vāstuvinyāsa).
In the village, having divided the portion for Brahman into four parts, one should worship the five forms in the portion intended for recitation;
in that same area, the temple of the worshipper should be situated either to the south or to the north.

Or he should construct it in the western direction or in a nearby intermediate region; likewise, he should cause the bedchamber to be built in the north, the cow-pen in the southeast, and the marketplace in the southwest, according to the prescribed rules.

In villages with fewer than a thousand Brahmins, or even in those of middling size, one should worship this form [of the deity] with a hundred, two hundred, or more [Brahmins]. Furthermore, [the offerings should include] a seat, a standing posture, a bed, and indeed objects of enjoyment.

One should arrange for the prosperity of the village, or alternatively for Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. To the north, in the middle path, lies the temple of Hari in the western quarter; or else, as prescribed, there may be a standing shrine or a seated one to the south.
In the Vaiśānya [corner], one should place the abode of Hara facing east;
in the Agni corner, the house of Gaṇeśa facing west; likewise, in the Saumya [corner], Durgā facing east; in the Paiśāca [corner], the Six-faced One [Kārttikeya]; and in the Yama [corner]...
To the northwest of Vighneśa is the cell of the Mothers and that of Guha.

(20) The aspect of Venus and Mercury is favorable for the Sun, while the aspect of Vighneśa and Guha is unfavorable; the aspect of Bṛhaspati bestows happiness, whereas the aspect of Śiva brings misfortune. (21)
This [image] of Viṣṇu, which bestows all prosperity especially in villages and other settlements,
should be viewed from the front as having a gentle form, and likewise from the back.
In the same manner, one should worship five images outside the sacrificial site (vāstu).
One should especially perform the worship of Dhruva in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
A wise man should likewise provide for his enjoyment; however, in the Paiśāca [direction], one should exclude the middle [deity].
Similarly, outside the village boundary, there is the worship of Dhruva at the junctions of paths.
If that enjoyment is indeed permanent, one should arrange it upon the site; otherwise, near water, in a forest, or elsewhere, one should establish it permanently or perform the permanent worship.
A wise man should install it facing east or as is appropriate, according to what has been prescribed.
One should not worship Viṣṇu in the center of a city or in any other direction [than the west].
One should worship the auspicious Viṣṇu together with Śrī and Bhūmi in the western direction.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Examination of the Ground and Other Matters," in the section on Sacrificial Rites within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the latter part of the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the third chapter: Ploughing.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the excellent and supreme procedure for ploughing.
On a favorable day within the auspicious months, and when the builder is likewise well-disposed,
one should determine the boundaries for where the temple with its enclosure wall on all four sides shall be built, and then clear away the grass and other debris from that auspicious site.
One should make the *arka* twelve *tālas* long, the *yuga* sixteen *tālas*, and the *hala* twenty *tālas*. The *ṛṣi* should be twenty-four *tālas*, and the *kṣiṇī* twelve *tālas*.
The shaft (*vaṃśada*) should have a circumference of eight *aṅgulas*, and the goad (*pratoda*) should be six *prādeśas* in length.
One should employ the remaining rites according to logic, endowed with these characteristics.
Having taken a rope made of muñja grass, one should firmly bind two white bulls;
having bound their hooves and horns with gold, one should give them grass to eat.
The patron and likewise the preceptor, equipped with all musical instruments,
should cause the Vaiṣṇavas to enter the ground preceded by lamps;
there, having constructed a water-shed (prapā) on the western side according to the prescribed characteristics.
Having made a covering all around, one should decorate it with canopies and other ornaments.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) of rice grains in the center of the Vaṣva-stena [mandala],
one should likewise place [the deity] there in the western part, specifically to the north of the *cakra*.

Having fashioned the pedestal according to the rule for the Viśas, with its dimensions and height increased by one part, and having placed a seat-grass (kūrca) facing east upon it, one should worship above it; indeed,
the sacrificial oblation should be properly offered to the Sudarśanas of the Viśas.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited at the end, he should again bind two bulls.
The preceptor, having been given [the fee] by the sacrificer, should take up the Muñja-grass cord and, reciting the "Rudra" [mantra], bind it around his waist. 10–11.
Having likewise fastened the pair of oxen, the wise man, reciting "Tryambaka" and uttering the Vaiṣṇava mantra, should pull the plough until the end.
Afterwards, having summoned a ploughman who is well-prepared and pleasing to the mind...

The wise preceptor, having restrained [the disciple] with the utterance "viśvataḥ karṣa yā," should collect seeds such as those of the *kaṅgu* millet and, having cast them into water until they show signs of sprouting, should cause them to be sown with the *Viṣṇu-sūkta*. 13–14.
Having offered water with the Vāruṇa mantra, performed the protection rite according to the rules,
duly worshipped those deities, and performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana), the preceptor should, once the sprouts have fully grown, present them to the herds of cows.
Now, if one wishes to perform it immediately, one should spread *dūrvā* grass and fasten [the image]. 16.

Having performed purification in the area of the womb-chamber (*garbhālaya*), one should prepare a beautiful sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains, measuring two cubits in length and breadth. 17.
Likewise, draw the lines for the sections (varga-rekhā) with their tips pointing east and north;
then, provided with two diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) and endowed with four corners,
[construct] the crossroads (catuṣpatha) joined by eight fingers from the square (veda), and likewise by nine.

Having worshipped the eight guardians of the quarters (lokapālas) at the junctions of the eight threads, as well as the supporter (dhātṛ), the directions, and the tridents of stone; and having offered an oblation (bali) with milk-rice (pāyasa), the preceptor himself—previously indeed without the artisan—[should proceed]. 19–20.
Afterwards, one should worship those deities here with the artisan;
having thoroughly cleansed [the site] and collected the [remnants], let it be given to the crows.
Having firmly established the ritual stake (śaṅku) here, the Guru, together with that artisan, [should proceed].
"Having determined the directions for the sake of the sacred abode, one should begin according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Section on Sacrifices, in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu, within the Section on Sacrifices.
Now begins the fourth chapter:
the Installation of the Gnomon.
O you whose wealth is penance, I shall explain the method for the installation of the gnomon.
Having leveled the surface of the ground at the site for the construction of the palace, one should smear it with cow dung to the extent of a *gocarma*. Then,
one should stretch a cord from the eastern end to the northern end across the middle.
In the middle of that [altar], one should fashion a sacrificial stake (śaṅku) in the shape of a spike using sacrificial wood according to the prescribed rule; its height shall be one span (vitasti),
the circumference at its base one span, and the circumference at its tip nine finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Gradually tapering and straight, such is the characteristic of the gnomon (śaṅku).
In the middle of that, one should draw a circle with a measurement double that of the gnomon; one should place it to the east of sunrise, accompanied by the sound of a conch shell.
In that [mandala], one should worship the Sun as the presiding deity and Indra and the others around him;
one should place a dot on the western shadow falling upon the line.
Likewise, in the afternoon, one should place a dot on the eastern part of the line.
That [measurement] divided by ninety-six, with one part subtracted, is the *aṅgula* for that [month].
In Aries and Taurus it is zero; in the month of Libra it is two *aṅgulas*;
in Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces, it is four *aṅgulas* by that same [calculation].

In the months of Cāpa (Sagittarius) and Kumbha (Aquarius), [the increase] is six fingers, and in Makara (Capricorn), it is eight fingers; thus, the fingers are stated for each month respectively. Having divided [the elapsed days] by thirty parts, one should add those portions corresponding to the elapsed constellations according to the proper method and take the remainder.
Having moved the thread from the northern point to the southern point, one should fix the mark;
the wise man should then stretch the cord through the center and to the eastern end.
Then, the learned one should rotate the thread from the north and south points like a fish to form a circle.
Then, having stretched a cord between the tail and the mouth,
and thus having determined the directions, one should determine the location of the base. Once this has been constructed, it should be equal to half the height of the vimāna.

A wise person should have a pit dug reaching either to the edge of the inhabited area or to the edge of a stone, as is appropriate. Having dug that pit to the extent of the width and length of the seat for its firm foundation,
it should be five cubits, four cubits, or three cubits deep, respectively.
The wise man, having first filled it entirely with sand mixed with water and made it firm with *ativṛkṣya* plants or by trampling with the feet of elephants,
should then gradually divide that dug-out pit into five parts at intervals of ten cubits.
When [the structure] has been bent down by one-third, the wise man, using either stone or brick—
whichever material the temple was built with— and likewise sand,
should skillfully make it very firm, little by little. 16–17.
Having first determined the division into even and odd parts,
the learned [architect] should lay down the first brick according to the aforementioned rule.
They know that a temple constructed from a single material is the most excellent.
That which is not made with bricks above the plastering there is the middle; when the floor-panels are covered with young [grass], one should know that to be the inferior;
the wise should recognize that which is made with these mixed as the mixed type. 19–20.

Regarding the characteristics of stone for the purpose of constructing a *vimāna*: I shall now describe the classification of stones for the sake of the *vimāna*. The best [stones] are of four kinds: white, black, red, and mixed. 21.
One may bring forth that which is produced from the earth, from a mountain, or from water;
among these, that from a mountain is superior to that from water, and likewise, that from the earth is superior to that from a mountain.
O Lord, if the abode of the Master is constructed with even a single stone, it is most excellent.
That which is made with two stones and three bricks together should be known as the middle;
one should know that to be the smallest, whether it be mixed or unmixed.
A wise man, most learned in the scriptures, should have it constructed according to the prescribed characteristics. 23–24.
Bricks should be fashioned from stone; one should not work upon bricks [if they are already there], nor should one cause that which is contrary to those stones to be done. 25.
That which is born of white [clay] should be placed above; that which is born of ploughed earth, or mixed with red, [should be below].
A wise person should apply either a mixture or white over red;
over black, white should be applied, but one should avoid both red and mixed colors [over it].
A discerning person should not employ those two as primary colors when mixed with red.

In the construction of a dwelling for Viṣṇu, one should use either white stone or black stone; the white stone should be placed upon the black. In other dwellings, however, one may act in all ways, except that stone must not be placed above brick in temples and the like. 28.

One should have the end of a group (varga) made with a single substance, provided there is no confusion [of materials]. (29) In the case of items such as sandals that are counted as pairs, one should not have them made with two substances; if they were so made, it would result in malevolent magic (ābhicāra), therefore one should certainly not have them made in that way. (30)
Having understood this, the wise preceptor, endowed with the strength of the patron, having determined the matter together with the patron and the artisans,
should deposit those bricks on an auspicious day of pure rising.
The mantra-knower who understands the scriptures should commence the meditation according to the method stated by [his] hand.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Section on Sacrifice," in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium spoken by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now, hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the construction of a Bālā temple, whether it be in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure. 1.
One should construct the abode for the young [deity] specifically in the northeast, the east, or the north of the primary site, or alternatively in the northwest or the west;
beginning with a measurement of five cubits and increasing by two cubits at each step.
The extension of the Bālāhāra should end at nine cubits and be threefold;
its width from the base of the wall should be four tālas or three tālas, while the remaining interior width should be five or seven cubits.
The wise one should desire the face-pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) to be equal [in size] to the main hall, or three-quarters, or half;
just as it is for the original sanctuary (mūlalaya), so it should be for the new sanctuary (taruṇālaya).
The wall should be constructed by the wise one using either earth, bricks, or stone.

In the case of a small temple (*taruṇālaya*), one should perform the rites for the first offering, the consecration of the womb (*garbha*), and the installation of the door, as prescribed by the rules, even without [the full construction of] the hall of the deity (*bālāgāra*). For the sake of protection, one should install the doorposts and the door-leaf in the small temple.
One should establish the jewels with mantras, even without [the usual materials] such as the floor slabs; above that, it may be covered with grass or even covered with clods of earth.
If it is a multi-storied celestial mansion (*vimāna*), the wise one should follow the sequence for breaking through the floors.
The wise one should divide the intermediate portion of the elements in the middle;
having conceived the first ground for the divine and human [mandalas] in the middle, the intelligent one [should likewise do so] for the two-storeyed [Paiśāca] and the three-storeyed [Paiśāca]. 9–10.
In the human [scale], the pair should be two stories high, especially for the five-fold form (pañcamūrti);
in the piśāca [scale], the wise one should install the Puruṣa and others around the center. Each one of those should be two stories high, especially for the five-fold form.
The wise man should perform the "Single-Step" (ekapada) rite for Brahmā;
having fashioned an image made of gold, silver, copper, or wood according to his means, the learned one should then install it. 12–13.

If that which was worshipped in another temple becomes empty and is subsequently requested [to be moved] there, the wise man, filled with haste, should perform the rite for its transfer. Alternatively, he may install the image in the house of the donor or in a temple for children.

At the time of the installation of the original deity (mūlasthāpana), one should relinquish a domestic image that was borrowed. At the time of the installation of the original deity, the wise man should install a statue after having it fashioned for the temple; otherwise, he may perform the rite of "removal" (hāraka).
On an auspicious day favorable to both the village and the sacrificer, one should perform the installation of the auspicious [image] on the day prior to that; thereafter,
having performed the "opening of the eyes," [one should immerse it] in milk, cow's urine, and likewise water.
Having accepted [the invitation] and having praised [the deity] again in the sacrificial hall, one should adorn it.

In the center, at the place of the bed, one should arrange five fires; one should purify [the area] on all sides in due order with the circumambulation of fire and the five products of the cow. 18–19.
The Guru, having cast two full *droṇas* of [grain]— free from broken or cracked pieces— and having placed the weapons, insignia, and other items [within], should consecrate the jar; then,
having properly set it upon a pedestal of grain, he should indeed perform the installation according to the sequence prescribed for the *pratiṣṭhā*.

Meditating, one should invoke [the deity] into the pitcher and perform the ritual bathing correctly. Having likewise spread out the bedding on the altar, one should place the cosmic egg and other items in their proper order; then, having placed the Lord of Gods upon them, one should lay him down together with the pitcher.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there and likewise tie the protective amulet (*kautuka*).
Having uttered the "Oṃ Vaiṣṇava" mantra, one should lay Hari down with his head toward the east;
then, having provided a northern covering and properly praised the *hautra* ritual, [one should proceed].
One should perform the invocation of the form, the fire-oblation, and so forth, as prescribed in the *Pratiṣṭhā* [text].
Having passed the remainder of the night and bathed according to the rules for bathing, one should enter the sacrificial site and invoke the imperishable Hari.
Having given the teacher's fee (dakṣiṇā) when an auspicious rising occurs in the movable zodiac sign,
and taking up the pitcher and the image preceded by a stream of water,
one should perform the circumambulation of the temple while reciting "apratadviṣṇu".
Having installed the Lord of Gods upon the altar together with the two Goddesses during the festival of his sleep (svapanotsava),
one should mutter the Ātma-sūkta and then mutter the Viṣṇu-sūkta and other hymns; then, taking the Śakti residing in the water-pot, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu through these various forms.

Having invoked [the deity] residing in the *kumbha* onto the head, and having invoked the Goddess and the other members of the retinue for the festival, the worship, and the sacrificial offering (*balibimba*) out of devotion;
having invoked them like one lamp from another, he should worship them in due order.

He should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited there and offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and other such foods. The wise man should perform the invocation and dismissal according to the prescribed rule, even in the case of obligatory and occasional rites, honoring [the deity] strictly according to the injunctions.

If one desires to perform the permanent worship (dhruvārcā) in the childhood temple (bālālaya), one should likewise construct the childhood temple; then, on a level ground within the ritual hall (karbhageha), one should not use a foundation stone, as it has been made firm with bricks. 32.
For the purpose of support, no stone is used once it is consolidated with bricks.
Then, without that [central image], one should likewise install the jewels and so forth, as well as the mobile [deities].

Due to their mobility, the wise one should install the mountains and so forth together with the earth that constitutes their life-force, according to the procedure prescribed for the *kautuka* (auspicious image). 33–34.
Thereafter, having constructed that abode with its defining characteristics at the aforementioned location,
the wise one should cause it to be completed, ending with the pinnacle and the trident;
just as the image, together with its festive thread, is brought in from the place of the child.
One should perform the worship of Dhruva at the primary site exactly as prescribed. Having first placed the jewels during the auspicious moment (muhūrta), one should perform the worship of Dhruva;
having established [the deity] upon that, one should carry out the eight-fold binding (aṣṭabandha).
If the preceptor is unable to carry the large-bodied image himself, the architect, having brought the image to its appropriate place by means of a mechanical device without a jar,
should establish it, perform the purification, and then bring the jar before it.
"In the same manner, one should worship the external [deities]; the distinction is that the others are as before.
Thus ends the fifth chapter on the section concerning sacrifice in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Laying of Bricks.
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme sequence of bricks:
in the months beginning with Caitra, on an auspicious day when the moon is waxing.
Having properly gathered stable (sthira) signs and avoiding mobile (cara) signs,
one should perform the rite in a location favorable to both the village and the patron.
One should fill it with water and very smooth sand.
Having leveled that [foundation], one should enjoy it until the completion of the palace;
then, whether it be a stone or brick, the wise man should have the first brick laid, using brick against brick and stone against stone.
One should increase the three [measures] beginning with the *dhātṛ* up to twenty-three using the *mānāṅgula*;
it should be joined according to one's wealth. This is called "long.
Its width is said to be half of that, and its thickness should be half the width.
Having identified the face and the foot, and having applied the designation to that which is formless,
the wise one should offer the auspicious [materials] as prescribed for the purpose of installation; then, after performing the consecration (adhivāsa), he should prepare the sacrificial hall.
In the middle of that, there should be a place for the bed, two cubits in length and breadth, and one cubit in height;

to the east of that, there should likewise be a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and a domestic fire-hearth (aupāsana). Having adorned it with clay, the wise man should perform the earth-sacrifice (bhūmi-yajña).
Having established the fire according to the rules, he should bathe [the image] in succession with seven jars;
having bathed it and covered it with a new cloth upon the bed, and having performed the auspicious lustration (kautuka), he should cover it with a new cloth. 9–10.
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava mantra, and thereafter the Viṣṇusūkta,
the mantras beginning with those of the four Vedas, the Śrīsūkta, the Bhūsūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta,
together with the vyāhṛtis, and having bowed down to the fire; 11.
One should not spend the night listening to or watching instrumental music, dance, or song.

Having bathed in the morning during the auspicious hour (muhūrta), one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains on the ground to the south of the entrance to the inner chamber, while standing upon sandals.
Having divided this [space] into nine parts, the Guru should deposit the wall in sequence;
having taken three parts on the exterior, the remaining interior portions are left.
From east to west and from north to south, he proceeds in order starting from the east.
The Guru should install [the vessel] with its opening intact while reciting the *caturvoda* mantra and others.
He should then thoroughly fill that opening in the middle with gold, gems, earth, and so forth.
Having invoked it with the *stham* mantra and made it firm, he should indeed offer it.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, concerning the section on Sacrifice, in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the seventh chapter: the Deposition of the Embryo (*garbhanyāsa*).
Henceforth, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa),
which is proclaimed as the abode of the deities and their head.
[It is performed] at the end of the *masūra*, at the end of the *cāra*, at the end of the *prastara*, and within the *gala*.
The inner sanctum (garbha) is praised when it measures five units at the end of the spire (śikhara) and below the pinnacle (stūpikā).
Alternatively, one may place it in an assembly hall (āsthānamaṇḍapa), or likewise in a bathing pavilion (snapanamaṇḍapa),
in a city gate (gopura), in a kitchen (pacanagāra), or in any other pleasing location.
In the middle of the residential quarters, to the south of the gatehouse (gopura) from the exit,
or even to the south of the entrance;
the wise one [should place it] within the wall of all the gatehouses.
At the end of the site, one should deposit the embryo in the pavilion or the bathing hall;
if he is a twice-born (Brahmin), it should be on two lintels, a Kṣatriya on a kumuda moulding,
a Vaiśya above the jagatī, and a Śūdra upon the stairs.

In a palace, however, one should especially place [the image] within a separate chamber for all [deities], or otherwise have it placed inside the door; at night, one should cause the embryo to be deposited.
It should be as wide as the base of the temple, or even less by a quarter or a half.
Then, the *phelā* (pedestal) is said to be one-quarter less than the width;
it should be equal in height to its width, or even eight parts less.
A wise man should place it on the right pillar of the door, equal in extent to the thickness of the wall.
Then, having divided [the area] into eight parts, one should place four parts on the outside and bring three parts into the interior; in that location, one should perform the rite,
having worshipped Pauṣṇī and mentally recollecting the Lord of Gods.
Having recited "viṣṇur yonim," one should place the embryo right there. Then, having strewn grass around the fire and offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation together with the Vaiṣṇava mantra,
the performer should dismiss the fire and honor the preceptor.
Afterwards, having summoned craftsmen and commissioned them to make it very firm,
one should honor them and then have the celestial chariot (vimāna) constructed; its size may be slightly less than the prescribed measure, or even much smaller.
One should make a solid casket provided with nine compartments and a lid, fashioned from gold, silver, or even copper;
it should be carried along the same path by which one is to ascend to the summit. 14–15.
One should fashion the womb-vessel (garbhabhājana) as an octagon, an eight-sided figure, or circular; likewise,
one should fashion auspicious mountains, trees, conchs, and other weapons,
as well as earthen clods, bulbs, gems, and their respective colors and marks.
One should likewise bring materials made of musical instruments, as well as gold and other such substances;
one should also fetch the barks of the Plakṣa and other trees, as well as other flowing waters, and all other things originating from sacred fords (tīrtha). 17–18.
On an auspicious day, under a constellation favorable to the performer, and especially in a fixed zodiac sign,
one should offer the ritual sprouts (aṅkura) on the previous day and likewise on that very day;
having properly prepared the site in the hall as described and having performed the nourishing rites thoroughly.
Having constructed a sacrificial altar (vedi) two cubits in width and one cubit in height at its center, one should prepare the domestic fire-pit (aupāsana-kuṇḍa) to the east of it,
facing the temple, in a pure place, especially during the evening.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound with rice grains, one should spread a cloth across it from east to west; having placed a basket in the center, one should collect all the ritual materials. Then the preceptor, with a serene mind, should likewise face the north.

Having sprinkled the materials with the Gāyatrī mantra, he should also show that vessel (phelā). Having purified it by means of the Bhūmi-yajña, he should perform the Āghāra oblation according to the rules.
Then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), he should spread [the grass] upon the altar as before.
In the center of that, one should place the *svastisūkta* and the *pheṣas*;
upon the altar, one should worship the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*) as well as the lord of the *nāgas*.
Having wrapped [the image] with a new cloth, one should place flowers upon it.
Having kindled the fire and strewn the sacred grass, one should thereafter recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta;
then, having offered oblations with the Śrī-sūkta and the Vaiṣṇava mantra ending in "svāhā," one should likewise offer to the King of Serpents and to the Guardians of the Quarters.
Having uttered "from all jewels" (sarvaratnebhyaḥ), and likewise "from all minerals" (sarvadhātubhyaḥ), "svāhā from all seeds" (sarvabījebhyaḥ svāhā), and also "from all worlds" (sarvalokebhyaḥ);
[and] "from rivers" (nadībhyaḥ), "from the netherworlds" (pātālebhyaḥ), and also "from trees" (vṛkṣebhyaḥ) and "from mountains" (nagebhyaḥ).
"Let it be well-offered, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*, [with the mantras] 'to the elephants' and 'to Viṣṇu.
Having offered the oblations and having properly worshipped the Sādhyas at the conclusion, the wise preceptor should install that [image], accompanied by all musical instruments, during that night."
"The womb [of the image] and those two jewels are thus fully adorned.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, concerning the section on sacrifice, in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The Procedure for Vimānas: Hereafter, all the various types of vimānas have been described; now, within the section on dwellings, the one-story type shall be explained. 1.
Beginning from one cubit and increasing by two cubits at a time,
up to nine cubits, the single-storey temple is specifically of four types.
Its height is three parts, or one and a half, or three-quarters, or double that [of the base].
It is known by the names Triguṇa, Pauṣṭika, Jaya, and Adbhuta.
The width of the house's foundation is said to have two types of measurement: four parts, two parts, five parts, or three parts. 3–4.
Having divided that height into eight parts, one part shall be for the plinth (samūrakam);
two parts shall be for the foot-height (pādottuṅgam), and one part for the entablature (prastaram). The elevation of the neck (grīvodaya) shall be one part, and two parts for the spire (śikhara).

The portion for the height of the *sthūpikā* (finial) shall be one part, especially for a single-storeyed temple. One-third of that is the height of the neck (*grīvā*), and it is said that the height of the pedestal (*vedikā*) is likewise.
I shall now describe the various components of the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the plinth (*pāda*) individually.
Having divided [the height] into twenty-four parts, one should recite the following:

the portion for the Nāgas is the measure of the *jagatī*; the portion for the *dhātu* (foundation) and for the *kumuda* (fillet); the portion for the *ambara* (coping); the portion for the *kumbha* (pitcher), which is the foremost; and the portion for the neck (*kaṇṭha*).
The portion for the other tremor (kampa) should be one part, and the horse (vājina) should be three parts. 9.

Likewise, the wise man [should fashion] the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭa), its projection (nirgama), and the fringe (daṃśaka); first, the height of the base (upāna) should be one standard finger-breadth (jātyaṅguli). 10.
One should construct a railing, or a double railing, or an exit for the feet,
or a niche for those others, with whatever artistry ensures beauty as appropriate; or there may be a water-channel toward the north or the west, as is fitting.
One who possesses wisdom should first perform the division of the *jagatī* and other parts;
the width of the temple (*prāsāda*) should be divided into twenty-four parts,
or twenty-five parts, or indeed twenty-six parts.
The half-portion of the wall-pillar base is considered to be one part divided into three:
namely, three measures (vahni), four measures (veda), or six measures (ṣaṇmātra), or else the width of the foot (pādaviṣkambha).
The projection (nirgama) of the wall and the pillars should be one-quarter, or one-and-a-half, or three-quarters of that measure.
The height of the pillar may be equal to the height of the elephant's ear, or mixed, or unmixed.

According to the eighth part of the Dharmananda, its width at the base increases toward the top; thus, the wise have stated that it extends to the tip of the upper foot, and therefore it is not a mere staff (daṇḍaka). 15–16.
The wise one should determine the height of its base (pādodaya) as six, seven, or eight parts;
having thus established the height of the pedestal (vedikā), he should further proceed with [the plinth] up to six parts.
Then, one part should be for the neck (kaṇṭha), one part for the pitcher (kumbha), and likewise a lotus (padma) above that.
The portion with an upward vibration at the top is excellent; that should have paired walls. An odd number is uneven and not desired for the wall-crests (śālākūṭa) and walls.
At the conclusion, one should construct that; its placement in the divisions is thus prescribed. 18–19.
The width of the archway pillar is declared for all to be one-fourth the width of the wall or pillar;
above the *vīrakāṇḍa* is placed the upper *vājana* and the lotus.
The *kṣepaṇa* and *nimnakampa* should be below that, and above them, the *vallikāntaka*.
One should cause the auspicious *vadarīdarśana* to be made with various and diverse leaves;
and at the very top of this pillar (*stambha*), there should be the *bodikā*, *vīra*, and *kāṇṭaka*.
On top of the base (phalaka), a height equal to one staff (daṇḍa) for each is recommended;
the height of the pitcher (kumbha) should be the same as the elevation of the pedestal (podana), while the height of the nose (nāsī) should be half of that.
The staff for the two necks (kaṇṭha) should be one-quarter of a staff, and it should be fashioned with a creeper-staff (vallī-daṇḍa).
Likewise, that which is called the "small staff" (kṣudradaṇḍa) is prescribed as being one-quarter [of the height].
24. And its foot, its neck, and the length of the nose above [the neck]—the *pālikā* is joined to the neck of the *kumbha* by means of the neck of the *nāsī*. 25.
One should divide the *bodhikā* and the *phalakā* equally;
from the *phalakā*, one should set aside one cubit for a *vetra* and fashion the remainder as a *padma*.
Nevertheless, the *toraṇas*, the bathing slab (*snānaphalaka*), and so forth, are especially [to be fashioned] in that manner.
The door should generally be wide, or its width may equal the thickness of the wall.
It is taught that the height of the door should be one-quarter greater than its width, or even half as much;
furthermore, having divided the height into eighteen, eight, nine, or ten parts, the rise of the door [is determined] again.
The portion consisting of six mānas and eight vavas is known as the *śuddhadvārodaya*.

One should divide the remaining portion—consisting of half an *utsaṅga* and half a *pataṅga*—into two parts. Each of those two parts should have a pillar projection (*stambhanirgama*) equal to its own measure. 29–30.

An intelligent person should have the door-panel (kavāṭa) made there according to what has been stated in the definition: it may be said to be one-quarter greater than the width (bahula), or even half greater, or said to be one-and-a-half times, or twice the width of the two door-posts (pāda). Then, the wise one should construct the door-panel as described in the specific rules.
Joined with the aforementioned tree and bound with a copper plate,
having made the emergence of the stone twenty-one parts,
the upper portion is said to be three parts, and likewise the base (vājana) one part.
Its projection is said to be equal to that; likewise, one should perform the *valabhī* as three parts, and the *vājana* above it as one part each.
The *kapota* should consist of two parts, or half of that, with its projection being the same.
Some say one should suspend either a staff or half a staff;

others say one should have it made with a staff and a half, or two staffs, broad, with a sunken nose, according to its height and beauty, and adorned with a sacrificial offering (bali) and a hook (haka). 35–36.
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) is one-eighth of the width of the base, less one unit; having divided that [height] into four parts, the width of the neck (grīvā) is said to be one part.
The height of the shoulder (skandha) is one-third [of the total], and the height of the pedestal is desired to be one-third.
It may be quadrangular, octagonal, or mixed, according to the desire of the builder.
(38) It should be spacious, with its height equal to the width of the altar-base;
its middle portion should be reduced by one-eighth, and above that, it should gradually expand. (39)
A wise man should construct the spire (śikhara), making it gradually slender for the sake of beauty, with its width at the base of the altar (vedi) reduced by one-sixteenth part.
The length of the cornice (vāpālikā) should extend to five parts or three parts from the edge of the lip (oṣṭha).
The opening [of the lotus] should be five parts wider than the *pālikā*;
it should be joined with eight petals, and at the tip, the stalk should have a height equal to the petals.
The construction of the *śikhara* (spire) should be lofty; the remainder should then be executed according to the rules of proportion. 41–42.
The width of the great nose (mahānāsa) shall be one-third of the śikhara;
the wise say the projection of the nose (nāsikā-nirgama) should be equal to three-quarters or half of that.
There, the height up to the shoulder (skandhānta) should be one-fourth of the width.
One should have that Śakti-banner raised up, or else one should have it made with three legs.
Having fashioned a wheel on the back of the Śakti-banner according to the proper measurement,
the wise man should install it very firmly for the sake of causing auspiciousness.
One-third of the lotus is praised as the height of the pitcher (kumbha);
one-third of the pitcher's height is the cavity (kandara) above the pitcher.
There, the rim (pālikā), the pollen (reṇuka), and the bud (mukula) are each three times [the preceding]. 46.
Furthermore, having divided the lofty dome (stūpikā) of the temple into eight parts,
one part shall be the *valagna*, a fourth part the *kumbha*,
five parts the *kaṇṭhara* (neck), and one part the *pālikā*, so says the wise one. 47–48.
The bud-shaped [pedestal] is said to consist of three parts; one should have it made of gold or other materials.
One should construct a pavilion in front, equal in size and measuring three-quarters [of the main structure].
If the pavilion has perfectly aligned lines, the inner chamber should be situated within it.
The width of the intermediate space (antarāla) is prescribed for all temples as one and a half cubits, two cubits, or even three cubits; or it may be one *daṇḍa*,
one and a half *daṇḍas*, two *daṇḍas*, or three *daṇḍas*.
A wise architect should know that the inner chamber within the palace pavilion should be situated in the middle of the intermediate space, provided with walls, pitchers, and creepers,
or else featuring pillars and arches, or even pillar-cages. 52.
In this manner, either a pillar-base (stambhasauṣṭika) or a gateway (toraṇa) is constructed.
If it is a Vimāna temple on the central path, its projection (nirgama) beyond the measurement-line (mānasūtra) shall be one daṇḍa,
or one and a half daṇḍas, or three daṇḍas.
It is of three kinds: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Visa-ra.
That which is composed of squares (jāti) and lacks triangles (śrama) is called Nāgara.
The wise declare that a structure joined with circles (vṛtta) is called Dvyaśravṛtta.
The neck, joined with the middle and the Bhadraka, is an octagon and is called Svastibandhana.

From the base (upāna) up to the pinnacle (sthūpī), that which has the proportions of the castes (varṇa) is known as Nāgara; and from the neck (kaṇṭha) upwards, that which is octagonal is called Drāviḍa.
One should perform the rites beginning with the *nṛkanda*, as well as what is recited as the *veśara*; one should practice the rules of ornamentation and the discourse mentioned in the *Nirukta*.
On the great altar above the platforms in the eastern directions, [one should proceed].
Having caused the figures of Puruṣa and others to be made, one should likewise cause those of Kāla and others to be made.

In a two-storied temple, however, one should fashion the figures of Candra and the rest above the main hall; in temples with three stories and more, one should fashion them in this manner according to the sequence.
Above the *prati* (pedestal), at the corners and especially at the location of the neck, the wise man should have a golden lion fashioned, or according to some, [another figure].
Alternatively, he may sit with one knee bent, or on the seat of Brahmā (*brahmasana*). 61.
The wise man should cause it to be made according to the specific logic of movement and posture.
Furthermore, for the deities among the Puruṣas and others, the measurement may be equal to the base, or half the height of the pillar, or one-quarter, or three-quarters. 62–63.
Starting from twenty-five finger-breadths (*mātrā*) and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step,
the height (*udaya*) likewise becomes sixfold, ending at thirty finger-breadths.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Section on Sacrifice," in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavat-śāstra*, the compendium spoken by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the ninth chapter, on the rules for the enclosure wall.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the enclosure walls.
The first enclosure is said to be half the height of the temple, or equal to it, or one and a half times, or likewise double; the second is likewise double,
the third is said to be triple, and the fourth is likewise equal to that.
The wise state that the fifth, sixth, and seventh [measures] are equal to the third;
alternatively, the measurement of the *hasta* may be threefold, being superior in sequence.
Or else, half of the *ālaya* (the main hall) is considered equal; this is known as the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*).
The second, consisting of the embryo (garbha), is nine cubits plus one cubit in height; the third, consisting of the elements (bhūtadhātu), is nine cubits plus nine cubits, O wise ones;
and the fourth is seven, nine, and eleven cubits respectively. 4–5.
The fifth [mandala] consists of nine Rudras (nine squares) plus thirteen additional hands;
it is equal to the Mahāmaryādā [mandala] in every other respect, specifically.
When that [area] has been made square, it may also be increased by one quarter.
The width of the gateway of the ramparts should be made one and a half times, or one and three-quarter times, or twice, thrice,
or even four times the length of the inner enclosure (antarmaṇḍala), extending from the south or the north.

For the purpose of bathing, for the purpose of the hall, for the purpose of the assembly area, for the purpose of expansion, for the purpose of recreation, and for the measurement of the garland-path, the pure architect should increase the pavilions for the sake of the devotees performing circumambulation. 9-10.
Beginning from three cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time, it should reach a measurement of fifty cubits; thus there are eleven stages of increase.
As previously described, this expansion is made outwardly for the sake of auspiciousness.

If there is an increase in its defect, there will likewise be a defect in its destruction. If there is another dwelling situated within the enclosure wall, one should begin the construction from that temple and have it completed at the end of the year.
Whether it be Śambhu, Śaṅkara, Hari, or any others, they are like deities who have taken refuge in the assembly; one should not act without those who have taken refuge.
14. The measurement of the wall-support (bhittiviṣkambha) shall first be one cubit (hasta).

Then, O wise one, knowing the divisions, one should gradually increase the width at the base and the tip by one part in each successive stage; likewise, the diameter, the circumference, the width, and the height should be increased respectively by three parts, one part, one part, and one part. 15–16.
Then, the foremost [measurement] is eight parts less than that, located inside the wall;
the middling is in the middle of the wall; and the lowest is outside the wall.
Having abandoned the first category, [it may be placed] either to the south or to the north.

The door for the kitchen (kṣudhra) should be made in the southwest, the northeast, or the west, according to the specific requirements; however, it is never desirable [to place it] in the [other] inferior directions. One should act such that whichever direction the palace faces, its door faces that same direction. 18–19.
A wise person should perform [the rites] starting from the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) specifically in the second and subsequent ones,
either in the cardinal directions, the intermediate corners, or in the middle of the directions. Some say it should be done in the direction where the path to the door lies.
Some learned ones maintain that this [practice] is not desired in the first [case], nor in the other two;
(21) even in the first case, if it is performed in this manner, there will be strife within the kingdom; the heads of those two should be fashioned in succession like the shape of a sword. (22)

The best type of enclosure wall has a prominent foundation and so forth, while the inferior type has straight walls; these should be situated to the north, east, or south of the rampart. Furthermore, a water channel should be constructed appropriately beneath the plinth.

Whether it be joined with walls or not, or even provided with many stories, the wise should construct the first enclosure equal to the length of the entrance; just as it stands in relation to the wall, so should one cause that wall to be made. 24–25.

One should construct a pillar with its wall in the middle of the surrounding vimāna; that should be slightly distinct or entirely uniform on all sides. According to the prescribed rule, one should have the thickness of the wall made as described therein.
Starting from the base of the palace steps up to the northern end according to the rise [of the structure],
the height of the plinth (pāda) in the portion of the elements (dhātu-aṃśa) should be two *masūra* units or five (*bhūta*) units;
beginning from sixty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), it increases by six finger-breadths at each step.
The width of the foot is said to be ninefold, ranging from eight to eleven finger-breadths;
this is measured by the specific *dhātu-aṅgula* starting from the *dhātu-aṅgula* and increasing up to the *ambara-aṅgula*,
ending at fifteen finger-breadths.
One should construct the pillars situated at the sides of the wall, provided with the necessary materials for the plastering (30).
One should then gradually lay down the beams (uttara) pointing northward and extending from east to west;
having performed the work of joining according to rule, one should likewise apply the wooden coverings (vājana) in their proper order (31).
"And the wise one should place [the image] on its proper spot using a balance.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, concerning the section on sacrifice, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu within the venerable *Vaikhānasa-śāstra*,
in the tradition of the illustrious Vaikhānasa Bhārgava.
Now begins the tenth chapter:
on the characteristics and construction of gate-towers (gopura).
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the gate-towers.
First is the door-decorative ornament (*dvāraśobhā*), and the second is the door-hall (*dvāraśālā*). The third is the door-palace (*dvāraprāsāda*), and the fourth is the door-mansion (*dvāraharmya*).
Another is the gate-tower (*dvāragopura*); thus, there are indeed five types in their respective order.
Having divided the width of the Tribhūta, Vinirvāṇa, Rudrahasta, and so forth, in sequence into three parts, one should extend it with that [width] increased or decreased;
likewise, by increasing [the measurement] by one cubit starting from two or four cubits.
Likewise, the measurement in cubits is ninefold, up to sixteen cubits;
then, in sequence, it is one and a quarter cubits, two and a half cubits, and finally three cubits less a quarter, as the projection [nirgama] increases by three cubits respectively. 4–5.
Having taken one-third, one-fifth, and two-fifths of half the width, outside that wall, the remainder is as prescribed for the residence;
this is the characteristic of the mandala, beginning with its construction.
O best of sages, listen as I describe the pavilions and other structures: first, in the front of the first enclosure (āvaraṇa), one should construct a face-pavilion (mukha-maṇḍapa) to the east;
or alternatively, one may construct a bathing pavilion (snāna-maṇḍapa) in the second enclosure.
One should cause the bathing hall to be constructed in the northeast and the north at the front;
in the southeast, the kitchen; in the south, the sacrificial pavilion (yāga-maṇḍapa); and one should perform the dance pavilion (nṛtta-maṇḍapa) in the southwest and the northwest.
One should place upon that pavilion the vessels prescribed for worship, those made of metal, mother-of-pearl, and so forth, as well as those of gold;
in the middle of the southern wing, the location for the bed is recommended.
Between Yama and Nairṛta, one should place the water reservoir;
between Nīla and Varuṇa, one should install the worldly image;
and between Varuṇa and Uda, the flower-pile pavilion.
Between Kubera and Īśāna, one should construct the pavilion for the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
On the northern side of the temple, the wise man should construct a pit;
there he should perform the daily and occasional bathing rites and the ceremonial ablution (snapana).
On the western side of the Soma [mandala], one should arrange the attendants such as Cāmara and others; between Īśāna and Śakra, one should establish the place for the garments and other items.
This is the location for the deities of the retinue.
I shall describe the inner sanctum and other features of the surrounding enclosure in due order:
on the southern side of the wall is Brahmā, and on the northern side is Hara;
likewise, between the wall and the entrance arch (kautuka), there are Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhṛgu.
One should place Dhātṛ on the southern door-panel of the main entrance;
Kīnāśa on the lower lintel, Bhṛti on the upper, and Pataṅgaka on the northern lintel;
likewise, one should place Pati and Varuṇa on the pillars to the south and north.
Outside that, on the side of the wall, one should worship Maṇika and Prabhāvatī; or else, at the door of the pavilion, one should worship Dhātṛ and the others as well.
On both sides of that door, one should worship Tāpana, which bestows success.
In the center is Nakṣatrapāla, and to his east are Śrī and Bhūtagaruḍa (18).
On the ground in the middle of the south of the vimāna is Mitra, and Viṣvaksena and Kṣattṛ are on the pedestal in the north (19).
One should worship Viśvāvasu in the middle of the southern side of the celestial chariot;
one should place Mitra in the west, or alternatively, Kṣattṛ in the north;
and one should worship Vīśa at the entrance of the first [section].
Outside the south and north [squares] is the Kiṣkindhā Tīrtha.
To the south of Kiṣkindhā is Indra; in the southeast is Agni;
in the south is Yama; in the southwest is Nirṛti; and likewise Varuṇa [is in the west]. 21–22.

Having worshipped Vāyu in the northwest, Soma in the north, and Īśāna in that direction (the northeast) during the second round, or else [worshipping them] in the first round when those [deities] are omitted;
then [one worships] the Discus, the Banner, the Conch, Bhūta, and indeed Bhūtanāyaka.
The wise, having worshipped each [deity] in its respective place within each respective enclosure (āvaraṇa),

should worship them according to the sequence stated in the Nirukta; or else, in the first [enclosure], they should worship the guardians of the temple (vimānapāla) and the world-protectors (dikpāla), while in the lower [enclosures], they should worship others in the first [enclosure].
One should worship the retinue exactly according to the sequence stated in the Nirukta;
the abode of the retinue is said to be half the size of the vimāna, or equal to it, or even one-quarter less, provided it is joined with a front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa). 26.
One should have a retinue fashioned, joined with the permanent *kautuka* (sacred thread).
That *kautuka* is indeed the best; one should not [place it] upon a pedestal in that location.
Having invoked [the deity], the daily worship is the lowest and devoid of color. 27-28.
If one is unable [to move] the image from its respective location,
one should construct a pedestal using stones or bricks and perform worship there. If the shrine is situated within a wall, the pedestal should be supported by the temple structure itself.
One should arrange those things not explicitly mentioned according to the sequence stated in the *Nirukta*.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Section on Sacrifice," in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The Collection of Stones.
Now, hereafter I shall explain the sequence for the collection of stones; they are of three classes: those from mountains, those born of the earth, and those born of water. 1.
A stone produced from a mountain (giraja) is said to have its face upward, one from the earth (bhūmija) downward-facing, and one from water (jalaja) facing toward the water; likewise,
stones are classified as male, female, or neuter according to whether their base and tip are level.
A male [liṅga] should be of this description: dense, smooth, and resonant with the sound of a bell;
it should be thick at the top, whereas a female [liṅga] is thick at the base, and a neuter one is neither.
One should properly fashion the Lord of Gods with a female stone; by what other means could one do so?

One should have that [foundation] prepared with care, and one should have the mandalas of the respective deities prepared there where it is visible; if a wise person perceives a fissure, knowing it to be a "stone-womb" (a flaw within the stone), he should avoid it with great effort. 5.
Then, on the day of Kṛttikā, the wise and discerning Karṇa, together with his artisans, prepared the site in the forest along with the dwellings and the materials for the fire-offerings;
having examined that ground and cleared it of all grass, he made it ready.

One should perform the ritual of circumambulation with fire (paryagni) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and here one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made.
On the right side of that stone, one should worship Vanarāja;
on its left, one should worship the Lord of the Gods (Indra), and one should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in their respective directions.
One should offer oblations by name to all the deities, as well as to the Vidyādharas, the Yakṣas, the Piśācas, and also the Nāgas and Gandharvas;
one should worship these eighteen classes.
Having said, "Go quickly to that place," and having bowed down properly,
the wise man should take hold of the *dṛḍhakārī* [stone] with the *vaiṣṇava* mantra and the *hulikā* along with the *gāyatrī*, and then split that stone with the *viṣṇugāyatrī*. 10–11.
One should fetch [the image] for both the goddesses and all the sages with their respective mantras;
having given the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā), one should honor the artisan. Having placed it upon a cart, one should transport it to the temple without negligence.

Having caused [the deity] to enter and having established [it], the wise man should have an image fashioned according to the measurements of height, width, and circumference, including the limbs and minor parts, whether it be fully painted, half-painted, or otherwise. 13–14.
A wise person should make the *srava* [spout] the size of a barley grain and ensure it is not deficient in the *dhruva* [fixed vessel];
if the worship of the *dhruva* is to be performed very clearly, one should have it made so that it is beautiful.
If it is made of wood, one should procure it and have it fashioned just as if it were stone.
Among stationary images, one made of wood is best; likewise, an earthen image is superior to a wooden one.
An image fashioned from clay is better than one made of stone, and one made of copper is superior to a stone image.
If the stationary image is to be of stone, one should make it of solid stone and avoid any other material.
One should have it made either variegated or half-variegated; that is the worship of the *dhruva*.
Now I shall describe the measurements and the characteristics of the *dhruva* as well:
that which is half the width of the temple is declared to be the best.
One should take half of that [measurement] as the middle portion, and one-fifth of it as the smallest;
having divided the exterior wall-width into two parts and further into twenty-six parts, one should arrange the other portions in sequence upon them. 19–20.
By increasing each part by one, the wise one should divide the inner [circle] into twenty-seven parts; having divided the other into twenty-six parts,
he should join it with one [part], so that there shall be a half-part as the rising point.
The height of the door should be equal to the measurement of the foot (pāda), or likewise the height of the door;
or it may be increased by one quarter, or even decreased by one quarter; or it may be half of that, or less by a finger-breadth (aṅgula) according to the measurement of the doorkeeper's foot. 22–23.
In the *masūra* portion, one should increase by a quarter, a half, or three-quarters [of the width], starting from one cubit and increasing by six, six, or half-a-finger [at each step].
Thus, nine types of height are prescribed, ranging up to three cubits in due order. 24.
Beginning with one *tāla* and increasing by one *tāla* at a time,
there are nine types of measurement according to the *tāla* scale, ending at nine *tālas*.
Subsequently, the height of the patron (*yajamāna*) is divided into eight, seven, and six parts.

Having performed the division and so forth as prescribed, until that auspicious vision [is reached], the heights for the maker are sevenfold, extending from the eyes, face, nose, and the boundary of the mouth, to the heart, the end of the breasts, and the navel. 27. These are their respective measurements.
By increasing the height of the base and other parts by two finger-breadths according to the *mānāṅgula*, the height reaches twenty-six [units], fifty, or ninety-five *aṅgulas*.
By increasing the *golaka-aṅgula* of the pedestal and other parts according to the *mātrāṅgula*, [the proportions are established]. 28–29.

The measurements from the setting [of the base] are sixty-one, and from the rising [point] they are twenty-seven; having thus determined these measurements for the feet, the pedestal, and the *kāñcaka*,
the wise and learned one should fashion the fixed image (*dhruvabera*) according to his desire for the sacrifice.
Next, the emergence of the pedestal (pīṭhodaya) should be described specifically for the standing posture (sthānaka).
It may be equal to, one and a half times, or twice the height of the serpent’s body (bhujaṅga). Having taken one part of an angula from all around its feet, 32.

It should be either square or perfectly circular, endowed with sixteen petals; its measurement should be equal, extending from the base of the *kautuka* (the central auspicious mark) to the edge of the wall.
Furthermore, having made a sturdy vessel (*sthāla*) with a height equal to that of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
In the worship of a fixed image (drūvārcā), it should specifically be one-third, one-fourth, or even one-eighth [of the size]; it may be either polygonal or circular.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Section on Sacrifice," in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the twelfth chapter: the collection of timber.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the collection of timber.
The Khadira, Āsana, Candana,
Campaka, Madhūka, and Jāti trees, as well as other glossy and auspicious trees, are prescribed;
one should fetch them from pure locations such as ponds containing lotuses and water-lilies.

One should avoid those trees that have been burnt by fire, those that are naturally decayed, those infested with holes from worms, those broken by other defects, and those possessed of other maladies.
Wise men know that trees are of three kinds: male, female, and neuter.
Likewise, one should have the other [objects] made from male trees according to their respective characteristics.
One should recognize that as a male tree which possesses many branches, is well-rounded, endowed with straightness, has a thick root, and a slender tip.

A tree that is female (strīvṛkṣa), thin at the root, and not designated as male (puṃśaka)—the sacrificer, having gathered the materials for the oblation along with all musical instruments, should have it removed by means of [auspicious] implements under a constellation favorable to the performer.
6. Having collected the requisites for the fire-offering together with all the musical instruments...
Having carefully observed the signs in the forest,
the craftsman should approach a beautiful tree, clear away the grass, shrubs, and creepers surrounding it, and having selected the spot, he should remove the old dwellings from that place.
Having performed the sacrifice to the Earth on the northern side and having purified the ground with cow dung,
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made and offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with pure food.
Having said, "To the King of the Forest," one should offer the oblation at the foot of the tree.
Speaking "O Forest Lord" (vanaspate) toward the directions starting with the east for the tree;
[he offers] to the forest deities, to the spirits (bhūtas), to the yakṣas, and also to the nāgas,
to the piśācas and vidyādharas, and to the group of eighteen.

Having offered the bali-oblation in sequence with each respective name followed by "namaḥ," and having praised [the deity] saying "May there be satisfaction," he should uncover the body [of the image], prostrate,
and touch that tree while reciting "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakre."
Taking an axe with both hands, the wise one, reciting the *Viṣṇukāyatri*, says,
"O King Soma," and having split [the wood] starting from the east,
he should then summon Takṣaka and cause him to cut and join it. 13–14.
Having caused it to fall toward the eastern directions, having split the front portion and divided it as appropriate, one should join it to the south of the Guru.
Having placed it upon a cart and entered that abode, [one should proceed].
Once it has been dried within a short time, the wise man should have the beloved image made;
likewise, having had the spear fashioned according to the rules, the learned one should again have the two goddesses made according to the rules, until an auspicious day arrives. 16–17.
I shall describe the measurement for the two goddesses: one may have it made up to the ears, to the tip of the nose, to the jaw, to the limit of the arms, or to the navel.
The measurement for all the attendant deities should be equal to that of the goddesses.
Likewise, one should make the measurement of the outline (uddeśa) half [the size] of those two;
or it may be equal to the *dhruvabera*, or even eight *aṃśas* less.
One should likewise fashion Brahmā and Śaṅkara on the wall with the same proportions. 19–20.
One should likewise fashion the two worshippers as appearing in a painting upon the wall; for Brahmā and Īśa, one should arrange them in the eastern direction according to the aforementioned colors.
Having divided that space between the wall and the kautuka into six parts, [one should proceed].

Having taken one part from the wall, the wise man should place the sage (the *muni* mark) there on the second [line], whether to the south or north; if it is entirely horizontal, he should [adjust it] according to rule to the west of that *brahmasūtra*.

One should cause the deities, such as the Goddesses and the members of the assembly, to be represented by those respective substances; indeed, by means of those substances, according to the sequence of their respective *tālas*.
I shall now describe specifically the arrangement of the steps within the inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*).
One should lay down seventeen threads with their tips pointing east and north;
having divided [the area] into two hundred and fifty-six parts, sixteen are in the center—
that is the Brahma-square— and thereafter, surrounding it, there are sixteen squares for the feet.
Its divine portion is ninety-six parts all around;
the human portion outside is sixty, and the piśāca portion is likewise in sequence.
Having divided that kautuka-sthāna of the Brāhma [mandala] into three, the divine portion is [thus established]. 26–27.
On its western side, or in the middle, one should prepare a seat for the standing posture; and for the sitting posture, one should prepare a seat between the divine and human [spaces].
The most learned in the scriptures should establish the lying-down seat among the human [spaces].
Having offered the permanent image (dhruvārcā) in the inner sanctum according to the Nāgasūtra,
there are forty-nine squares in the central space;
that is the Brahma-square, and surrounding it is the Naga-portion as well as the divine portion.
Outside, the remaining sixteen parts should be assigned in sequence as follows: the Paiśāca, the Mānuṣa, the Śāntika, the Pauṣṭika, and the Daivika.
One should especially install the Yogavīras and Brahmā in the Brahma-sthāna.

Between the divine and the human [forms], the wise one should gradually install the image for the sake of enjoyment alone; this is the procedure for the installation of the stone [liṅga] in the Paiśāca [form]. 32.
The procedure for the installation of the stone.
O ascetics, I shall now describe the procedure for the installation of the stone slab.
The months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Māgha, and Vaiśākha— whether during the northern or southern solstice— are especially suitable, provided they are favorable to the performer of the rite.

On an auspicious and stable day, the wise one should establish [the image] according to the prescribed ritual; having performed the rite of offering the finger-measure on the aforementioned day as before,
and having first stayed in the water at a river or the like, or else in a pit.

To the south or the east of the Ālaya, one should have a sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) constructed as before and adorn it with archways (toraṇas). In its center, there should be a bed-altar (śayyāvedi), extending in length equal to the width of the wall. 36–37.

To the east of that [main hall], one should prepare the assembly fire-pit (sabhyāgnikuṇḍa), measuring either one and a half times the size of the image or with a height equal to one-fourth [of its width]; this may be done together with or without the lotus-fire-pit (padmāgni).
Then, having constructed the bathing altar (snānavedi) to the north, one should perform the purification of that ground.
Having performed the sacrifice of the ground, one should then carry out the ritual circumambulation with fire in due order.
Having sprinkled [the site] with water from jars and other vessels, one should subsequently perform the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) rite and the pouring of the libation.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should install Hari upon the altar using five jars.
Having spread a bed upon the altar as described, one should place [the image] upon it,
cover it with a new cloth, and likewise tie the *kautuka* (wedding/garland).
One should then lay Hari down in such a way that his head is directed toward whichever direction the door faces, following the proper sequence.

Then, for the sake of great purification, the wise man, having performed the ritual procedure according to the tantras, should sprinkle [the image] with the Pavamāna and other mantras; the remainder shall be the same as before.
Having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest, he should place the image ending with Gaṅgādhara into the Sabhyāgni fire.
Having invoked [the deity], one should perform the *juṣṭākāra* and the *svāhākāra* offerings;
then the *vaiṣṇava-sūkta*, the *puruṣa-sūkta*, and thereafter the *viṣṇu-sūkta*;
then the *ekākṣara-ādi-sūkta* and thereafter the *śrī-bhūsūkta*.
Having offered oblations to Brahmā and Rudra, he should spend the remainder of the night in due order.
45. Having bathed at dawn, the preceptor, having entered the place of the bed, should raise the deity, worship him, and lead him into the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra). 46.
Then the wise one, having divided the space from the center (garbha) to the door into seven parts, should divide the middle portion into six parts;
from that, the thread for the left side of Viṣṇu should be established by the learned one within that [space] of Hari. 47.
The secondary cord should be suspended and fixed at the opposite point. 48.
Having placed the pedestal in its center, the preceptor, together with the artisan, should gradually place the gem and other materials, and then set the image upon the machine. 49.
Having recited "Pratadviṣṇustave," one should firmly install the image (bera);
having likewise specifically installed the Goddess and the other deities with their respective mantras, one should perform the eightfold binding (aṣṭabandha) according to the prescribed ritual.
In a temple made of stone, some say there should be an image of stone; in one made of brick, some say it may be made of copper.
In a temple made of wood, one should not have an image made of stone or clay; however, if there is a gap in the wooden floor, one should place light materials upon it.
In the first [case], one made of stone is prescribed; in the second, one made of wood;
in the third, one made of a trident (śūla); or in the fourth, one made of metal.
Alternatively, it may be made of clay, or it may have spikes on all sides.
Having established it according to the rite, the mantra-practitioner should gradually smear it with sugar.
Afterwards, having dismissed the fire, the sacrificer, as well as the preceptor, should worship them, give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and duly honor the Vaiṣṇavas.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, concerning the section on Sacrifice, in the Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra, the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter:
the ritual procedure for the installation of the Śūla.

Henceforth, I shall explain the procedure for the pacification of the *śūla* (the "thorn" or obstacle), as prescribed: when the asterism of the seat (*āsana-kṣatra*) has arisen, during a fixed zodiacal sign (*sthira-rāśi*), and at an auspicious rising (*śubha-udaya*).
Having offered the sprouts (*aṅkura*) and likewise performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in water, [one should proceed].
Having constructed the sacrificial hall and adorned it appropriately,
and having fashioned the altar with its characteristic marks according to the measurement of the wall's width,
he should then prepare the assembly hall (sabhya) and likewise dig a pit to its east and another to its north.
Having purified the trident with the *paryagni* rite and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) as before,
and having installed the *sabhyāgni* fire according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should duly deposit the trident upon the altar together with the two goddesses.
Having bathed [the image] according to the rules with mantras, either with its own [mantra] or with a new one,
one should spread out separate cloths and place it upon them;
above that, one should set a bamboo staff, and on its two sides, two side-staffs.
Above that, one should place the thunderbolt-staff (vajradaṇḍa), and likewise the tree-staff (vṛkṣadaṇḍa) below;
then the hip-staff (kaṭidaṇḍa) on the right side,
the right limb on the right, the left limb on the left side, and finally the crown (mauli) at the top, in due order.
Having installed the Goddess and the others on their respective sides in due order,
the wise knower of mantras, having recited "asthibhyaḥ sama" and performed worship, should bind the marriage-thread (kautuka) at the conclusion of the Puṇyāha rite in the proper sequence.

Having recited the Vaiṣṇava [mantra] and laid [the deity] down in due order, having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest, and having performed the invocation and other rites with that form in the Sabhya fire,
one should thereafter recite the Vaiṣṇava mantra and the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Having offered the Narasūkta at the end, one should thereafter offer the Śrī Bhūsūkta;

then, having offered the "Atvāha" verse along with its ṛṣi and other details, as well as the Sarvadaivatyamantra, one should likewise sacrifice one hundred and eight oblations ending with "svāhā" to the bones with the mantra "asthibhyaḥ. 11-12.
