Having offered oblations with all the *vyāhṛtis*, he should pass the night amidst the chanting of the Vedas;
then, having bathed at dawn, the righteous one, during an auspicious moment when favorable stars have risen,
should take up the spikes and enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) carrying them upon his head.
Having prepared a pedestal upon the jewels, the preceptor, while reciting the Viṣṇu-sūkta,
should install the Brahma-staff and then install the Goddesses and the others in their proper sequence.
One should place the bamboo staff against the side of the hip and the thigh-staff in sequence. 15.
Below the hip-staff, one should fix it to the wall with a support; having established everything according to the proper method in its position for standing, sitting, or reclining. 16.
The wise and learned man, together with the master builder, should firmly establish the immovable [pillar];
furthermore, for the sake of strengthening the joint, he should bind it with copper rings and with ropes, accompanied by the eight verses spoken in the Nirukta. 17.

Having wrapped it with a copper plate, one should fashion it through skill and intelligence. 18. Preparation of the Clay: I shall now describe the preparation of the clay specifically for the purpose of a permanent image (dhruvabera).

A wise and intelligent person should not take the delightful mud from a field near a river, nor from a pond that bestows the merit of lotuses; rather, on an auspicious day, he should bring earth possessing the proper characteristics from another holy site to the front of the temple.
Having placed it either in a cloth or on a mat,
and having dried it, one should take it in an earthen vessel and deposit it in a pure place along with *sattva*, *kaṣāya*, fragrant substances, and sand. 21.
Having stirred it together for one month, one should let it steep in water.
Having sprinkled it with water from the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha trees for half a month, and having let it remain for half a month in water infused with Triphalā; 22–23.
Having stirred that clay with a fourth part of powdered stone and having let it sit for a day along with powdered black gram (māṣa),
[one should add] śrīvaiṣṭaka, guggulu, saffron, and resin (sajjara).
Having added sixteen parts of honey, curd, and ghee,
as well as the essence of bilva fruit, one should grind them with water and let them sit for half a month with gold and silver.
Having infused three vessels with the powder of *kapittha* resin for a moment during an auspicious hour, the wise practitioner should begin the mantra-consecration;
he should offer his fingers [as a pledge] on that very day, or even prior to it.

Having performed the pouring of the libation (āghāra) into the Gārhapatya fire according to the prescribed rule, one should place earth upon the rice grains in the western part of the fire and worship it with the mantra: "Obeisance to the shoulders" (aṃsebhyaḥ namaḥ). 28–29.
Having kindled and strewn the sacred fire, being intent on meditation,
he [recited] the Śrīsūkta, the Mahīsūkta, and thereafter the Viṣṇusūkta,
the Vaiṣṇava, and the Narasūkta, along with the mantras of the two sages.
One should worship one hundred and eight times with the mantra ending in "māṃsebhyaścaiva.

Having meditated upon the imperishable Lord of Gods with the "Ekākṣara" and other mantras, and having recited [the names] beginning with Medinī, one should proceed in order over the binding of the cords.
Having worshipped the Guru, the artisan, and the Vaiṣṇavas and others in due order, one should gradually apply clay to the major limbs, beginning with the head; then,
having dried every limb, one should slowly apply the clay again.
Having placed the jewels on top, the knower of mantras should, in due order,
apply a plaster of sugar mixed with a paste for more than a month, using the mantra;
[this is] the taking up of the sugar.
Having gathered sugar in a pure place within a sacred field,
having washed it with pure water and ground it into an extremely fine powder, one should rub it with the decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and dry it very slowly. 35–36.
Having repeatedly stirred it with the liquid extract of *kapittha* fruit,
one should combine it with cotton wool so that it becomes very smooth and beautiful; having stirred it until it is extremely fine, one should place it in a golden vessel.
Having fully prepared the fire and offered oblations into the *sabhyāgni* with the Vaiṣṇava mantra (38),

as well as the Śrībhūsūkta, ending each with "svāhā," and finally offering a thousand oblations with the mantra "to Rudhira," the practitioner of mantras should place [the materials] upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). 39.

Having worshipped [the deity] with the mantra "to Rudhira," and having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) at the end of the word "namas," one should worship Viṣṇu, Śrī, Pūṣan, Khyāti, Cirāyus,
Garuḍa, the two Cakras, all beings, and the Vaiṣṇava.
Having offered oblations ending with "svāhā" and having dismissed the fire,
the Guru should take sugar with his head, enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), and while reciting the Narasūkta, he should apply it [to the image] in due order. 41-42.

Having consecrated the goddesses and others with their respective mantras, the Guru again summons the architect (sthapati), worships him, and— having presented that [image] which possesses the primary and secondary limbs and the correct characteristics,
and having had it fashioned— he should begin the covering of it with cloth.
Having gathered together the cloth for covering and fine cotton fabric as before,
one should then perform a fire-oblation (homa) in the Sabhyāgni fire as previously described, with the mantra "tvace svāhā."

Having placed [the vessel] upon a seat of grain and worshipped it with the mantra "Obeisance to Tattvacā," and having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), he should dismiss the fire and take the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, taking [the vessel] with the Vaiṣṇava mantras and with the mantra beginning "Of Soma," [he should proceed].

Having joined the limbs together, the artisan should subsequently cover them very firmly, evenly, and without gaps, and then adorn them with ornaments. (47) However, in the case of images made of stone or wood, there should be no cloth or clay.
Having smeared the clay, the wise one should apply pigments of those colors in sequence (verse 48). Then, having likewise taken the clay ending with pearl-white,
he should perform the previously mentioned oblation in the aupāsana fire upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) (verse 49).
Having worshipped [the image] in a golden vessel with the mantra "Oṃ,
salutation to those who dwell in the bark," and having taken it at an auspicious moment while reciting the Viṣṇu-sūkta,
one should have the artisan anoint the Goddess and the others with that respective mantra.
Then, having anointed [the disciple] everywhere, he should bestow the sacrificial fee upon the Guru.
(51) I shall now describe the refinement of the castes on an auspicious day when favorable results arise;
having taken all the caste-classes individually, one should place them in a golden vessel. (52)
Having ground [the ingredients] with resin-powder and water as appropriate,
and having prepared the Pauṇḍarīka fire and performed the Āghāra libation as before,
the wise one should cause a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be made in the western part of the fire.
Having spread out a new cloth, one should carefully place it upon that;
having said "Obeisance to Jīva," and having worshipped and performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa),
one should indeed spread out the Vaiṣṇava mantra joined with the Supreme Self.

One should worship one hundred and eight times with the mantra ending in *svāhā*, beginning with "O Jīva," and while touching that [image], one should recite "Hiraṇyagarbha" three times. Then, taking those [materials] of the same color, one should enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*).
Taking up red lead (hematūli), the Guru, facing north,
should recite the Viṣṇusūkta and smear the dark-colored [image] with the mantra "bhūto bhūte" upon the crown and other parts, as well as on the garment. 57–58.
Having said, "Tejo vatsava," and having anointed [the image], the knower of mantras,
having anointed the Goddess and the others with their respective mantras, and having subsequently anointed its golden and dark [parts] according to the rule— 59.
Having smeared [the image] upwards for the purpose of that consecration and having marked its characteristics (lakṣaṇa),
he should afterwards dismiss the artisan and begin the installation.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Section on Sacrifice," in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now I shall fully explain the procedure for the *iṣṭakā* (bricks) at the conclusion [of the rite]: having taken a straight, sound, and flawless piece of *khadira* wood. 1.
The artisan, having fashioned the pinnacle-shaft (sthūpiśūla) according to the rules and characteristics as declared in the Nirukta, should thereafter cause the brick-work to be constructed;
he should proceed according to that very same rule which was prescribed for the first brick.
One should worship the stūpa, the śūla, the deity, the pedestal, and the earth; then, one should worship Puruṣa and the others, as well as Nyakṣa and the rest, in order around them.
Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites as prescribed for the first brick.
At dawn, the knower of excellent mantras, having placed the pinnacle-pin and the bricks upon the chariot, facing either east or north,
should take hold of the stones and other materials while mentally recollecting the Lord of Gods.
One should install the four Vedic mantras in the directions starting from the east;
having recited the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should firmly install the pinnacle-stake.
Afterwards, having summoned a craftsman and honored him according to one's heart's desire, [one should proceed].

One should perform the consolidation (dṛḍhīkaraṇa) endowed with all the characteristic marks; here too, whatever has not been mentioned, the wise one should carry out according to the method stated in the Khila. After completing the pinnacle (śikhara), one should subsequently coat it with excellent pigment.
O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall now describe the consecration of the gatekeepers.
Having properly taken up the stone slab, one should have it fashioned according to the prescribed rite, [placing it] at the base of the wall in the various courtyards of the temple.
In the pavilions and other structures, one should construct [the door] according to the measurement of the base;
having divided [the height] into seven, eight, nine, or ten parts, and having set aside one part,
the remaining portion shall be the height of the door, while its width shall be half of that height, increasing gradually.
The wise man, having divided the remaining one part into two equal halves,
should likewise cause the half of the serpent and the half of the bird to be drawn;
and having divided each of those respective parts into sixteen portions, he should fashion the elevation of the wall-base.
Starting from one-thirteenth part, it becomes the *tuṅga* (ascendant) of that fixed point;
or [starting] from one-seventh, or one-eighth, or one-ninth, according to those respective parts.
Then, having divided the earth-limbs (*bhuvaṅga*) and so forth by three, one should act accordingly.
In each case, that respective portion shall generally be one-quarter more, or one-and-a-half times, or three-quarters less, or double, in sequence;
or else, the wise man [should calculate] the breadth of the earth's circumference in sequence as double. 15–16.

One should fashion flower creepers and the like with a thickness equal to the width of the two pillars; having divided the width of the wall into five parts, the wise know the best [measurement] to be one part. They know that the midpoint of the heart is where the three-quarter line of the foundation (avasthāna) lies.
Alternatively, having established the solar [line] or that [central] line externally in sequence,
the wise one, having correctly prepared the cord characterized by five parts at the interval and the very center of the earth-limbs, [should proceed] in the proper place. 18–19.

Having performed purification with products of the cow and other materials, one should properly carry out the installation during another auspicious month, avoiding the months of Pitṛ and Māsa, and on an auspicious day; likewise, having performed the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).

Having filled a jar with products of the cow and other substances, and having performed the grand consecration, one should perform the ritual sprinkling from the pitcher and the binding of the protective thread (kautuka). Then, having spread out the beds, one should have them lie down upon the bed.
If the object to be consecrated is large, one should not invoke [the deity] but should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).

Having established the *aupāsana* fire, one should offer oblations ten times for each door-deity, beginning with the *vaiṣṇava* mantra ending in the *vyāhṛtis*. 23. One should offer those [oblations] in sequence.
He should spend the remainder of the night with the recitation of the Vedas and other such sounds.
Then, at dawn, having cast out the fire and during an auspicious moment when favorable stars have risen,
the wise man should take up a piece of earth and place it to the east.
Above that, having placed the jewels according to the ritual rule on the southern and northern sides,
as well as on the pedestal and in front, while recollecting their respective mantras,
one should install Pātāla and Varuṇa above with their own individual mantras.
Having bound it very firmly with lime, one should place gold upon the two tips.
Then, with the mantra, one should place a golden bird (pataṅga) over those two;
the serpent should face downward and the bird should face upward. 27–28.
Facing each other, they should likewise honor their respective husbands and Varuṇa;
then, having dismissed the artisan, one should properly perform the purification here.
Then, taking up the water-pot and invoking [the deities] as before, one should proceed.
Having performed a special worship, one should then carry out the ritual action;
having likewise honored the astrologer, the artisan, and again the preceptor,
and having prepared the door-panels according to the rules, one should join them in sequence once the work is completed.
O God of gods, one should have the consecration of the door-panels performed; otherwise, destruction would occur, therefore one should act in this manner. 32.
The ritual for the installation of the pedestal and other components.
I shall explain in detail the specific characteristics of Pādabodhika as well as Uttarā, Tulā, and the others;
I shall describe them individually, especially regarding the forenoon.
Having established the *aupāsana* fire, one should bathe [the image] in sequence with water-pots;
having worshipped the *Ṛgveda* at the eastern foot, the *Yajurveda* at the southern, and the *Sāmaveda* at the northern, in due order.
Having placed all the coverings and other items upon the scales, one should worship the Atharvaveda and perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) as previously described; thereafter,
having sprinkled water around the fire, one should proceed with the mantra that is the first of the Vedas.
Meditating upon the fire while reciting those Vaiṣṇava mūrti-mantras, one should offer oblations; then,
at an auspicious moment, the wise man should place a supporting stone below and smear it with lime mixed with gems or gold.
Having recited "agnim īḷe" and established the foot according to the mantra,
one should smear it with sudhā and place gold and jewels well upon it.
Reciting "iṣe tvorje" and so forth, one should [place] that Bodhigā facing north.
Having properly placed [the vessel] facing east, upon it he should, according to the mantra,
place gold and jewels while recollecting the Sāmaveda; he should place them at either the eastern end or the northern end, and place them in the north.

Having properly placed the jewel and gold upon it, specifically above that, the wise man, reciting "aśnō devī," should gradually cover either the scale or the stone slab from the eastern edge to the northern edge.
First, the wise man should fill the hollows with lime,
and afterwards, he should set down the joined pieces and coat them with a mixture of oil and sugar;
if there are other houses that are covered with grass, he should do the same for those.
Having worshipped Atharvan, one should gradually cover [the structure] with straw,
or having constructed a wall with characteristic marks using either earth or bricks; then, placing the hand upon it while reciting the Atharva-mantra, together with musicians...

The edge [of the structure] should be joined with cloth-bands, pegs, and iron bolts (46). A wise person should gradually cover it from above with clods of earth everywhere on the palaces and so forth, and in all directions on the pavilions and so forth (47).
The ritual procedure must be performed with all these mantras in their proper sequence;
otherwise, there would be destruction, and that site would become unstable.
Therefore, one should indeed perform the consecration of the mantras at that site for the sake of protection.

In this regard as well, whatever has not been mentioned, the wise man should perform all those rites according to the procedure stated in the *Khila*, as is appropriate. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Section on Sacrifices," in the *Bhṛgusaṃhitā*, the sacred scripture (*bhagavacchāstra*) of the Vāsiṣṭhas.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter: the classification of the places of articulation (sthāna) and so forth.
Hereafter, I shall explain the classification of the places of articulation and other factors in their proper order.
The Lord has dark-blue limbs, four arms, and holds a conch and a discus;
his right hand is in the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhaya) and his left is in the gesture of granting boons (varada),
with either the left ear of a lion or [the left hand] hanging down to the hip.
Seated alone, with Bhṛgu likewise on the right and Mārkaṇḍeya on the left, or alternatively, with both Bhūmi and Puṇya as the worshippers;
whether complete or partial, and with both Bhūmi and Puṇya as the two worshippers.
One should have the entire [deity] well-inscribed with its respective materials.
On the southern side of the wall, one should depict Brahmā, who has four arms, faces the north, and holds a rosary and a water-pot. 4–5.
The first [hand] grants fearlessness; the left is resting on the hip.
Śaṅkara is white-complexioned, four-armed, and wears matted locks;
in his left hands he holds a deer, an axe, and another [hand] granting fearlessness resting on the hip.
A wise person should cause the best [image] to be made facing south;
for the two sages (the conch and discus), there should be no wine at all, especially not for the lowest [type].
One should never perform [the rite] for the two sages with wine, nor ever with the conch and discus [as the objects of worship]. 8.
Likewise, on the lower [seat], the second Brahmā, and similarly on the Śarṇābha [seat],
she stands with her right foot placed upon the right side of Lakṣmī;
her left [foot] is bent, and in her right hand she holds a slightly curved lotus.
With her left hand extended and gazing slightly upward toward the gods, she is dark-complexioned;
in the northern direction is Pauṣṇī, holding a blue lotus in her right hand, standing with her left foot extended. 10–11.

One should cause her other [hand] to be slightly contracted, with eyes wide open in wonder, and perform the *viparīta* (reversed) gesture on both the right and left sides. Likewise, one should place the *bhṛgu* (the little finger) between the wall and the object of curiosity on the right.
He was seated with one knee raised, while the other was likewise drawn up in the *utkuṭika* posture;
his left hand, bearing a lotus, rested upon his thigh, while his right foot was likewise drawn up in the *utkuṭika* position, the left being the other. 13–14.
In this very manner, having seated those two worshippers with their palms joined in reverence,
one should likewise cause the manifestation of Brahmā and Īśa in the eastern direction;
and above, on the upper and side walls, [one should place] Māyā and Saṃhlādinī.
Tumburu and Nārada, as well as the Kinnara couple, the Yakṣa and Vidyādhara, Sanaka and Sanātana,
and both Āditya and Candra— Vidhu considered them all to be of the highest order.
Tumburu, Nārada, and the Kinnara couple are said to constitute the middle quality; it is inferior when devoid of Sanāgī and others.
In the third position, Virasthāna, it resembles grain and is yellowish-green.
O wise ones, that which is joined with Brahmā, Īśa, and the two Munis, as well as Kiṣkindha and Sundara, and further endowed with the two Sanakas, is known as the Uttama Sthānaka.
That which is devoid of these four, beginning with Kiṣkindha, they know to be Madhyama.
When diminished by two, one, and zero [units], it is the lowest;
the deity of the station of separation has two arms, smoky-colored garments, is dark-complexioned with white limbs, looks upward, and possesses the quality of darkness (tamas). 21.
One should likewise place Vimalākṣa in the Pauṣa-cakra at the station of Brahmā and others;
and one should establish the god Viraha in the night-time yoga-posture (yogāsana) starting from Ārdrā, having a white body, yellow garments, and four arms.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, endowed with the Brahma-seat,
with matted locks and a crown, and with two hands holding sprouts placed behind [the ears],
[he is] white, without the conch and discus, and possesses an upper garment and a sacred thread. 24.
With eyes opening wide, adorned with earrings, armlets, and necklaces—
thus the Lord [was worshipped] in the yoga-posture together with the eight deities beginning with Dhātṛ;
that [worship] is the best when performed in union, while that without the two worshippers is middling.
But without the four [deities] beginning with Candra, the yoga-seat is inferior.
[The deity] is seated upon a lion-throne (siṃhāsana), dark-limbed, and four-armed;
he holds the conch and discus in the front [hands], while the [other] two grant fearlessness and boons. 27.
Having fashioned that left [face] as a lion’s ear on both sides of the deity,
one should have Śrī Devī placed on the right side and Mahī on the left, with the right foot extended and the left foot drawn up. 28–29.
A lotus is in his right hand, while the left rests upon his thigh;
having drawn up the right leg and extended the left, there is a blue lotus in the right hand and likewise the Earth-goddess in the left. 30.
In the same manner, on the side of the wall, the wise one should have Brahmā and Śaṅkara depicted seated as before,
along with the two attendants Māyā and Saṃhlādinī, and likewise the two Vyājanyas. 31–32.
Likewise, it is specifically declared that the most excellent [seat] is the Bhogāsana, occupied by the Gandharvas Candra and Sūrya, as well as Tumburu and Nārada, together with the Kalpa-tree. 33.
In that same manner, O Lord of the Gods, the two Ṛṣis who are the worshippers should indeed station themselves in their place;

likewise, one should properly arrange Sītā and Dhṛti, the daughter of Pūṣan, for the purpose of worship, as well as Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and the others, along with the Ṛṣis who are the worshippers, up to Manu. (34–35)
The Guru should sit in the vīrāsana posture together with the eight deities beginning with Sanaka.
The six intervals from Brahmā to Sanaka constitute the kanyasa (lowest) [level].
According to the specific requirements of each of the two goddesses, the procedure for the vīrāsana posture is as follows.
Likewise, having fashioned an image in the midst of the Piśācas— that heroic seat—
one should establish that deity facing eastward, with all his attendants, beginning with Brahmā, residing within the womb-chamber (garbhagṛha). 37–38.

Some say one should cause a reflection to appear on a wall or as a half-painting; with whatever materials the original image was made, with those same materials [the image] of the one dwelling in the womb should be made.
If one is capable, one should have it made with those [materials], and one should not practice with anything else.

For the sake of removing spatial constraints or specifically for the sake of strength, one should have it constructed according to the prescribed rules, even if it appears to be impossible; I shall now describe the height of the lion-throne separately—listen! 40-41.
Having divided the height of the entrance to the sanctum (garbhadvāra) into twelve parts, one-sixth is declared the best, one-fifth the middling, and one-fourth the lowest;
one should have it constructed accordingly. 42.
"In that [Garbhālaya], all ten thousand characteristics have been fully described by me.
As stated in the section on measurement and so forth, one should likewise fashion the lion-throne.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, concerning the section on sacrifice, in the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā* of the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*.
In the Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavat-śāstra of Bhṛgu,
this is the sixteenth chapter: the procedure for the Yoga-sleep.
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence for the yoga of reclining:
the Lord of Gods is said to be twice [the standard size], and likewise half of that half.
His right hand is dark-blue in luster; its ring finger and tip are raised up.
The left leg, adorned with all ornaments, is fully extended;
the right leg is likewise extended, joined at the ankle and toes, or it may be extended upon that [left] thigh, while the eyes are slightly upturned. 3.

The wise one should likewise cause the entire posture of Madhu and Kaiṭabha to be performed, with the right foot extended and the left slightly contracted, resting upon the earth or upon the sacrificial altar (puṇyā). 4.
Beside the feet, one should especially depict two fanged beings of terrifying form.
Seated upon the navel-lotus is the Creator (Brahmā); one should represent all five weapons together, or perhaps only half of them in a variegated manner.
One should place Viśāmitra and Paripṛthi on the upper part of the enclosure, with palms joined and well-positioned; likewise for Brahmā and Īśa.
Thus is that supreme yoga [performed] by the two sages and Amita.
The medium [form] is without the inferior [element], being devoid of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
On the couch, however, one should meditate on the Lord with dark-blue limbs, four-armed, reclining upon the serpent Śeṣa, his body adorned with all ornaments.

Having extended the right hand placed in the *upādāna* gesture, another [hand] holds the crown; the left hand is extended upon the thigh, while another hand forms the *kaṭaka* gesture, and the left foot is extended. 10.
The wise one should slightly bend one foot and place it between the two feet; likewise, the distance from the heel to the end [of the other foot] should be twenty finger-breadths,
and from that point, fourteen finger-breadths to the right of the Brahma-thread.
The face should be three finger-breadths wide at the back, beautiful up to its lateral edges; likewise, one should place Śrī Devī at the side of the head and Mahī at the side of the foot,
touching them with both left hands, and in that same manner, one should arrange the seat.
Brahmā and Īśa are the two worshippers; one should likewise place them to the south and north.
Similarly, at the side of the feet, one should have Vikaṭa and Kātyāyanī fashioned, as well as Madhu and Kaiṭabha, blazing with poison-flames and being consumed by fire. 14–15.
One should likewise depict Brahmā seated upon a lotus throne at the side of the wall, as well as the five weapons, Viṣṇu, and Mitra;
and also Āditya, Bhāskara, Tumburu, and Nārada.
He worshipped the two Aśvins, the eight guardians of the quarters, and likewise the hosts of Apsarases.
Among them, he offered the best portion of enjoyments to Tumburu along with Nārada and the Aśvins;
he did not offer such to the guardians of the quarters, nor to Kanyā, nor to the other sages.
I shall describe the Hero lying upon his bed— dark-limbed, four-armed, bearing the conch and discus, and specifically resting with his head upon a pillow.
His left hand is extended, and the two Goddesses are at the side of his feet.

And while it was being churned, Mārkaṇḍeya, Bhṛgu, as well as Brahmā and Śaṅkara, the twelve Ādityas, the Ṛṣis, the Rudras, along with the Apsarases, and Nārada appeared together with Madhu and Kaiṭabha. (20–21)

The highest couch is together with the Kinnaras; likewise, that without the Rudras, Ādityas, and Apsarases is middling; and lower than that is [the one] without the Kinnaras, Sanaka and the others, and the two worshippers.
22. And likewise [the one] without the Kinnaras, Sanaka and the others, and the two worshippers.
In the absence [of the full form], there should be a single hood; without the entire body,
one should perform the *abhicāra* rite upon the pedestal, and carry out the remainder of the ritual according to the rules,
extending as far as the height of Ananta’s bed and making it likewise vast.
O Brahmins, in that radiant [mandala], one should depict in sequence the curved hoods, the five excellent weapons, the navel-lotus, its stalk, Brahmā, and the other deities,
ending with the letter *va* (varṇānta) and the *makula* (the point).

In that same manner, the wise man should cause [the image] to be made so that it is pleasing to the maker. In the celestial chariots (vimānas) mentioned above, one should perform the installation and other rites;
however, in the case of the permanent image (dhruvārcā), one should perform them especially without the ritual of the reclining image (śayana). 26–27.
Four [stones] should be equal for the standing posture, and likewise four for the reclining posture;
some say these should especially be made of stone or copper.
The wise man should make all the attendant figures equal, as previously described.

If capable, one should always have all the images fashioned out of stone (29). A wise person should not perform the worship of the retinue merely by means of light; nor should one ever perform the worship of the inferior together with the principal attendants (30).
"In the ritual of the retinue, however, there is no fault in the worship of the fixed [deities].
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Section on Sacrifice, in the *Śrī Vaiśaṇasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, within the Section on Sacrifice.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter:
The Rules for Vimānas. Next, the characteristics of kautukas, ātukas, and so forth, shall now be described.
Wood, stone, copper, silver, and gold,
as well as gems— each of these is excellent for the materials of worship among the fruits [of offerings].
One should not have a festival image or an object of worship made from stone, wood, or gems.
The wise declare that when [the deity] is standing, it is called *sthitam*; when seated, *āsīnam*;

when lying down, *sthānakam* or *āsīnam*; and when in the marriage ceremony (*kautuka*), it is likewise. Afterward, there is the festival (*utsava*) and the ceremonial bathing (*snāpana*), especially the offering of the *baliberam*.
In all cases, one should arrange the standing posture for the two goddesses just as it is for the god;
during a festival, whether the god is seated or standing, and especially during the rite of *kautuka*, one should proceed exactly as for the god. 4–5.
In all the incarnations, a wise person should have that specific form made as a curiosity, except for the Fish and Tortoise incarnations; however,
for the festive image among the incarnations, one should have it made with four arms.

Or, during the Rāmakṛṣṭi festival, the wise man should have an image made of whatever form the Lord Dhruva possesses; or he may have an image of Viṣṇu made for the processions during the various incarnations.
During the invocations and the worship, he should worship him using the name "Dhruva."
Otherwise, a wise person should not perform the bathing, festivals, or auspicious rites;
for they know each one of these to be equal to the three sacred fires (tretāgni) for the performer. Therefore, having meditated upon each of them with a steady mind, one should worship them properly.

Because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is one within the body, one should likewise behave toward others as toward oneself. Since even a mere form is desired as being half of Śaṅkara’s essence, one should therefore worship it during its incarnations, and also those of the other two.

O Lord of Devas, with whatever material [is used for] the Lord of Devas, the knower of the scriptures should likewise have the pedestal, the radiance, and other items made from that same material. Having divided that form into nine parts, one part is indeed the best.
Having divided the first part into three, the wise should likewise make one part the middle;
having divided that [middle] part into three, one part is the lowest. One should make the *dhruva* a portion of that row, and the *tāla* should consist of a portion of the *ambara*.
Having made the *tāla* and its solar portion (*bhānubhāga*) equal to one part, that [unit] is a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
By increasing [the height] by two or three finger-breadths starting from Rudra [eleven], there are twenty-seven heights specifically for the *kautuka* and other [images]. 15.
Or one may perform it using another measure, provided there is no cutting of fingers;

(16) furthermore, regarding the two other rites—the ritual bathing and the festival—a wise person should thoroughly examine their auspicious or inauspicious nature by means of the arrival of that [deity] and other such signs. (17)
The characteristics of income and so forth:

one should increase the height by fire (three); the income (āya) divided by the Vasus (eight) is multiplied by the hermitages (three), and the expenditure (vyaya) is again divided by the elephants (eight). 18.
Multiply the [remaining] sūtras by four; the remainder is the *aṃśaka*. Multiply that by three and divide by eight; that is called the *yoni*.
Having multiplied by eight, one should subtract that from the day by means of the eight.
That [number] multiplied by seven and divided by seven gives the day; likewise, the lunar date (tithi) is determined.
If the income (āya) is greater, it is auspicious and brings all prosperity;
if the expenditure (vyaya) is greater, it leads to misfortune. Some say that when they are equal, it is neutral. (20–21)
They know that on the Nandā tithis, there is a thief, the power of enjoyment, wealth, a ruler of the earth, a eunuch, fear, poverty, and one who has gone abroad; these are considered inauspicious.
Having abandoned poverty, theft, impotence, and being abroad, [the remaining] brings about auspiciousness.
The banner, smoke, lion, dog, bull, donkey,
elephant, and crow— these are the eight origins in sequence;
each preceding one is said to be auspicious, while each subsequent one is likewise inauspicious.
On a banner, a bull, or a lion, it shall bring about great accomplishment;
one should count from the day of the maker until the end of the day of the image. Or, conversely, [the asterisms] beginning with Vipata, Pratyak, and Naidhana [are unfavorable].
If the days of Saturday, Sunday, and Tuesday bring about an auspicious conjunction, one should act;
otherwise, one should not perform anything for the sake of auspiciousness—rather, one should practice what is truly auspicious.
I shall now describe the sacred seats (pīṭhas) of Kāñcī and the others according to their nature.
The foundations for the fire-altars (agniveda) are measured by six, six, eight, and nine [units];

the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭa) should consist of one part, and it may be either distinct or not distinct [from the base]. O wise ones, the upward projection of the petal (dalamūrdhvodaya) should be half less than that [fillet]. 28.

Below the lotus, the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be reduced by five parts from its width. Its height may be equal to its width, or twice its height, or one and a half times, or less by a quarter; the remainder should be determined according to aesthetic propriety. 29–30.
If there is an *upapīṭha*, having divided it into twelve parts,
one part shall indeed be for the pedestal (*pādukā*), two parts for the lotus (*padmaka*),
one part for the fillet (*kampa*), and three parts for the neck (*kaṇṭha*).
One part is for the *kampam*, one part for the lotus (*padma*), and two parts for the upper fillet (*uparipaṭṭikā*).
The base (*pīṭa*) of the seat (*āsana*) should be three, eight, or more than eight parts; the wise say its height may also be less than that. 32–33.
Some say it should be twice or thrice as long as its height;
one should construct a very firm support for the halo on both sides.
One should have the halo made according to the measurements specified in the section on proportions, suitable for the image.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, concerning the section on Sacrifice, in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for the application of beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*).
One should travel during either the northern or the southern solstice;
when the Sun is in Aquarius, Virgo, or Cancer— excluding the Sun in Sagittarius or Cancer— one should select other months and likewise choose an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).

Either in the house of the sacrificer or in a delightful temple, having adorned it with canopies and other ornaments, and having likewise prepared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the domestic fire (aupāsana),
one should establish the Vaiṣṇava fire and offer oblations well.
Having offered oblations with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, as well as the Brahma- and Raudra-sūktas (4), and having properly offered to Vīśa, Śaiṣika, Cakra, and Vighneśa,
one should likewise prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains to the south of that fire (5).
Having spread out a square cloth as is auspicious,
one should direct it toward the west for the Cakra, toward the north for the Śaiṣika,
toward the east for the Viśeṣika, and toward the south for the Viśveśa.

The wise one should cause altars (sthaṇḍila) to be made with rice grains beneath the wheel. Having placed bundles of grass (kūrca) upon those two with their tips pointing eastward, the knower of mantras should likewise properly worship Jayā and the others, as well as Indra and the others, all around them.
Having fully worshipped Vighneśa, one should offer the oblations; then,
taking that purified beeswax and placing it in a metal vessel with the syllable Om (praṇava),
one should set it upon the mandala.

One should prepare the primary constituent part with the mantra "iṣe tvorje tvā," and having arranged the ten syllables, one should also cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made;
then, having recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra, performed worship, and touched [the object], [one should proceed].
Then, having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava and having dismissed the other deities,
he should dismiss the fire; thereafter, taking that [fire] over the head of the sacrificer amidst the sounds of the branches in the sacrificial pavilion, he should perform that rite.
Having properly dismissed the artisan after honoring him with what is pleasing to his heart,
and having worshipped the master builder there, the one learned in the scriptures, together with the preceptor, fashioned that auspicious image upon it.
Having smeared [the image] slowly with soft [pigment] and dried it, having bound it with cloths in the sunlight according to the ritual procedure, and having smeared and dried it again,
one should perform the fire-oblation as before, desiring what is favorable for the patron.
Likewise, having thoroughly purified the iron, one should place it in iron vessels;
at night, one should cook it with fire using water in the proper proportions, and once it is prepared according to the method, having drained it, one should heat the embryo within it. 16–18.
Then, one should fill it with heated iron;
thereafter, at dawn, the artisan and the patron, together with the preceptor,
should slowly break open the clay and thoroughly examine for defects.
If the image becomes defiled by defects such as being cracked or broken, the preceptor, having considered that the defect is minor, may perform the rite again as before; or,
having brought back the original image, he should act exactly as previously done.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, concerning the section on Sacrifice, in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter:
On the Signs of the Fingers.

Henceforth, I shall explain the characteristics of measurement by the finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). There are three kinds: the measured finger-breadth (*mānāṅgula*), the conventional finger-breadth (*mātrāṅgula*), and the body-proportional finger-breadth (*dehalabdha-aṅgula*).
Eight *paramāṇus* (atoms) constitute one *rathareṇu* (dust mote on a chariot wheel).
A chariot-dust particle multiplied eight times is a hair-tip;
likewise, a hair-tip multiplied by eight is a *likhya*; eight *likhyas* are a nit (*yūka*);
and eight nits are a barley-corn (*yava*). Eight barley-corns constitute a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). 3.
After that, the *mānāṅgula* (measurement finger) shall be the width or length of the middle phalanx of the middle finger of an average-sized man; or else,
it may be the *mātrāṅgula* (measure finger), which is derived from the proportions of the image.
And the designation of the elements for three fingers shall be declared:
Mātrā, Mokṣa, Ambara, Viṣṇu, and Eka-saṅkhyā are proclaimed [as the five];
O twice-born ones, [the others] are Pakṣa, Akṣi, Golaka, Aśvinī, Vibhāga, and Kalā. 5–6.
A pair of lice is called one *pāda* of two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*);
fire, the Rudrākṣa varieties, and the qualities (*guṇas*) constitute a bond of three finger-breadths (*triyaṅgula*).
The castes, colors, and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), as well as the Vedas, the ages (*yugas*), and the four lotus-born faces [of Brahmā], are likewise measured in these units.
The divisions for the establishment [of the altar] are designated as four finger-breadths (catur-aṅguli).

The objects of the senses, the sense organs, and the elements—earth and the arrow (five)—constitute the five parts; these are the six finger-breadths for the limbs of the rite of the performer and the Kumāras. 8–9.
The elements, the netherworlds, the continents, the Sage, and the seven fingers;
the serpents multiplied by eight, and the guardians of the directions numbering eight; the nine Nandas, the planets, Indra, and the threads, [all] measuring nine fingers.
The Dharmanāḍī direction, the row, the descent, and ten finger-breadths; 11.
The Triṣṭubh meter, the hair-tufts, and the Rudras are designated as eleven; Yama, the zodiac sign, the face, and the Tāla measure are known by the designation of twelve finger-breadths. 12.

One should identify measurement (māna), standard measure (pramāṇa), height (unmāna), circumference (parimāṇa), comparison (upamānaka), and likewise hanging measurement (lambamāna) by their respective designations.
Among these, māna refers to the length of the image, while pramāṇa refers to its transverse dimension.
It would be dense with thick foliage and visible by its height;
that height is the elevation of the site, and the desired lofty dwelling is said to be measured by its dimensions, and dimension refers to the measurement of its breadth.
For the comparison is indeed between two; when it has reached its limit, that surface and the hanging cord are described as being like a statue. This is the measurement of the *tāla*.

I shall describe the sequence of the number of tālas, beginning with Dharma and ending with Ākāśa. The supreme [form] consists of ten tālas for Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara; Śrī, Bhūmi, Umā, and Vāṇī are [represented by] ten tālas in the medium [measure].
Indra, Arka, Janendra, Rudra, and others; the sages, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins;
Viśākha, Śaiṣika, Durgā, the Ṛṣis, and likewise Guha—one should have these members of the other assembly made with a height of ten tālas. 18–19.
The Lord of Yakṣas and the planets and so forth [should be made] with a measurement of nine *tālas*;
the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others are best when measured by nine *tālas*.
Humans are [measured] by eight *tālas*, and Pretas and others by the number of the *rasas* (six).
One should have the Vetālas made seven tālas high, the Kubjakas five tālas; the Vāmana with four tālas, the Kinnaras with three tālas,
the Kūśmāṇḍas with two tālas, and the Kabandhas with one tāla.
For each of these, there are three types; the best, in order, is twenty-four hundred finger-breadths, which is the supreme ten-tāla measure (2400 aṅgulas).
The middle one is proclaimed to be one hundred and twenty finger-breadths (1200 aṅgulas). 23.
One hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula) is declared to be the minimum [length].
That measured from the thumb to the forefinger is indeed a *prādeśa*; that measured by the middle finger is a *tāla*, and with the ring finger it is a *vitasti*. 24–25.
With the little finger [extended], the gokarṇa is ten fingers; with the hand [palm] having ten fingers, the kiṣku is twenty-four fingers; the prajāpati is twenty-five;
the dhanurgrāha is twenty-six; and the dhanurmuṣṭi is twenty-seven.

For these [offenses], one should impose a fourfold fine; or, in the case of houses and such, one should cause them to be dismantled; or else, except for the cutting of the staff, one should always [destroy] the dwelling of a deity or the residence of a human with one's own hand.

In the worship of the house, the bed and other items are measured by the span (vitasti) and the finger-breadth (aṅguli), while the chariot is measured by the three-finger-breadth (tridaśa) and so forth, as well as by the sesame-seed (tila). The temple of the deity is prescribed to be measured by the *prājāpatya* cubit (*hasta*).
I shall now describe the measurements for the bow, the fist of the bow,
the cubit (*kiṣku*) of a human, or the span (*viśveṣa*) of a human,
as well as the proportions for the standing postures (*sthānaka*) and so forth of Hari. (30–31)
From the end of the shoulder to the wrist, it should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas), or even [six]; now I shall describe the measurement of the face up to the ears, conch, and discus.
From the middle of the belly to the elbow, it is desired to be six finger-breadths.
For Abhaya, [the distance] between the nipples is specifically said to be thirteen finger-breadths; for Svāgata,
the abdomen extends from the middle finger to the navel, measuring ten finger-breadths.
The wise one [should mark] from the middle of the face to the edge of the hips with nine finger-breadths;
likewise, from that [middle] to the root of the left vulva and similarly to the line of the navel, and to the edge of the side and to the end of the wrist with nine lines. 35. Thus.
The space between the knees is declared to be one *bhāga*; the space between the hips is one *bhūta*.
The space between the ankles is six *aṅgulas*, and the space between the wrists is one *bhūta*.
The space from the wrist to the end of the forearm is declared to be one *āśrama*, and the space between the middle fingers is six *rasas*.

The Vasus [should be placed] between the two thumbs; what is not mentioned here should be done as in the Khilokta [tradition]. One should have a long plank made behind according to the previously mentioned tree [measurement]. Having determined the cavity, one should likewise fashion it so that it hangs down.
Then, that thread of the thighs [is to be placed] on the crest-lock, in the middle of the jewel; 40.
and in the middle between the meeting of the eyebrows, in the middle of the tip of the nose, in the throat, in the heart, in the belly, in the navel, in the anus, and in the two feet. 41.

One should suspend the thread through the middle so that it touches the tip of the nose and the navel; the distance from the thread to the edge of the crown-ribbon is declared to be one *samayāṅgula*.
The center of the jaw is said to be greater by one *yava* than the *āśrama*.
The end of the *hikkā* (the epiglottis) should be thus; the middle of the thighs is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
At the navel, it is said to be eight barley-corns (*yava*), and the root of the womb (*yonimūla*) is two finger-breadths.
The middle of the thighs should be one *varga* (four finger-breadths), and the distance between the knees is six finger-breadths.

The space between the shanks and the nāgas, starting from the front of the *nalaka*, should be eight and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in sequence; thus it should be, O wise one, from the tip of the big toe forward.
One should then hang down another line measuring two and a half finger-breadths.
In this manner, one should suspend the *pārśvasūtra* (side-measure line) as far as the ends of the arms;

that [line] lies between the arm and the elbow, in the middle of the crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*) of the head, and likewise for the two neck-creepers (*kaṇṭhavallī*), the neck, the knees, and the shanks. 46–47.
One should not allow the mind to become lax regarding the middle of the throat,
the crown of the head, the nape of the neck, the hump, and likewise the shoulder-blade.
One should then suspend the plumb-line over the buttocks, the sides, and the middle of the back.

On the side of the head, on the outer part of the cheek, and on the outer part of the temple, as well as at the nipple—[these are the points]. (49) One should hang the central thread down from the hips to the thighs and down to the knees; indeed, the lotus and other seats are suspended there among them. (50)

Upon contact with that limb, one should cause it to hang down in this manner by means of a technique; likewise, one should suspend the six lines, beginning with the middle one, over the seat and the upper body.
Above the seat, one should perform everything exactly as previously described. 51.
From the edge of the left knee to the top of the body, it should touch [the ground] up to half the height;
at the right knee, it should be reduced by one final finger-breadth.
Whatever else has not been stated should all be understood according to the rules for measurement previously explained.
In the same manner, the wise one should fashion the image (bhāva) so that it appears beautiful.

53. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Sequence of Finger-Measures and Proportions," in the section on Sacrifice within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.

Henceforth, O twice-born ones, I shall explain the sequence of measurements for the most excellent [image]: from the crown of the head to the feet it is one hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
At the crown, the space to the end of the hair is one and a half aṅgulas, and that [space] to the end of the hair is two aṅgulas.
Therefore, that [measurement] up to the end of the eye-line is the Veda (four units) or more than the Veda;
therefore, up to the end of the line of the nostril-passage, make it equal to that as appropriate.
They declare the length of the face to be thirteen and a half finger-breadths.
In the same manner, the wise artisan should fashion [the image] up to the jaw; the neck is said to be half an aṅgula, and the height of the shoulder-blade (kandharā) is one part.
From the base of the throat to the end of the heart, it measures thirteen and a half aṅgulas.

From the heart to the seat of the navel, and likewise from the navel to the genitals; from there, the space to the knees is declared, and it is said to extend to the end of the constellations (the feet). One should make the hermitage (the body) the measure of the knees, and the shank should be equal to the thigh.
The height of the palm-portion (*tālabhāga*) is very lofty; the length is suspended, and from the top of the face to the hairline, they declare it to be nine threads (*navasūtra*).
From the crown of the head to the end of the hair on the back, the face itself is distinguished.
From the uṣṇīṣa to the end of the hair at the side of the head, including the crown, it measures twelve aṅgulas;
the circumference of both ears together is thirty-nine aṅgulas;
the jaw is two aṅgulas in length, and its height above is one yava.
The width at the neck-joint is half a rasa (three finger-breadths) and half a kalā (one finger-breadth); this is prescribed as the width of the entrance to the neck.
The width at the front of the neck is proclaimed to be half of one-eighth [of the total height], while the width at the base of the neck should be eight finger-breadths. 9–10.
The neck is said to be well-rounded and encircled by three lines;
rising gradually from the line of the *hikkā*, it measures one-fourth of a *veda* (one-sixteenth) [of the total height] therefrom.
It then decreases by half a finger-width (*ardhāṅgula*) successively until the end of the arms, and likewise [the rest].

The *hikkā* (neckline) is two finger-breadths wide; below the collarbone (*jatru*), the *nimna* (depression) is one finger-breadth; the *kalaṃśaka* (shoulder-blade area) is broad up to the ends of the arms and is known to be four and a half finger-breadths;
the width at the front of the hips (*kaṭyagra*) is considered to extend for four finger-breadths.
This base of the hips is considered to be twenty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in width;
one should fashion the body above the hips in the shape of a cow’s mouth.
It is said that the remaining height should be increased by five finger-breadths and one barley-corn (yava).

The width and length of the scrotum should be desired at one *āśrama-aṅgula*. (15) The measurement of the root of the knee and that which is above it, the binding of the thigh, and the width of the base of the thigh and the measurement of its opening are now described. (16)
The surface of the middle of the thigh is said to be twelve *aṅgulas* in measure;
the width at the top of the thigh is said to be one and a half *paṅktis*,
and the circumference of the knee-joint (*jānu-maṇḍala*) should be five and a half *aṅgulas*.
The width of the base of the shank is said to be eight finger-breadths (yava);
the width of the middle of the shank is provided with seven mātrās;
and the width of the forehead (alaka) is likewise declared to be one and a half āśramas.
The width at the ankles is eight *aṅgulas*, and likewise the width between the two feet;

the measurement of the middle breadth of the feet is stated in sequence [as follows]. The width at the tips of the feet should be known as six and a half *aṅgulas*. 20. Thus the measurements are declared.
The distance from the axle to the edge of the felloe is known as the *veda*, and they consider its rising height to be equal to that.
From the axle to the base of the thumb [of the wheel] is desired to be half a *mātrā* in extension;
that measurement of the *aṅgula* for the *āśrama* is extended with a length equal to the big toe of the foot. 21–22.
Its *tāla* measure, including the *yava*, shall be two parts; half of that is said to be the *nakhatāra*. Half of that again should be the circular base of the foot.
The height of the mouth is one finger-breadth, and the mouth is fleshy on both sides. 23.
Endowed with two quarters of an *āśrama*, and twenty-nine and a half *śakas*; then a quarter of an *agni* with a *yava*, and a half-*kalā* finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
These are extended by the measures of the index finger and the others, beginning with nine, eight, four and a half, and eight. 24–25.

Half of one's own *tārā* plus a *nakha* is the remainder, as prescribed in the section on measurements; below the *dhikkā*-line, the length of the forearm (*bāhu*) is measured in *dinas*, while the span from the elbow (*kūrpara*) and the forearm (*prakoṣṭha*) are both twenty-one [units].
Therefore, the measurement of its tip is praised as being half a finger-breadth (27).

In the width of the palm, the remaining middle portion is one part of the metal (dhātu) and one finger-breadth in length; the height of the ring finger is said to be six parts (rasa) plus two barley-corns (yava) (28).
The length of the index finger is said to be five and one-fourth parts of a finger-breadth;
the little finger is four and one-quarter parts long.
I shall now describe its breadth from the thumb to the little finger.
The remaining portion, increased by two *pādas* in length, is placed on both sides of that [central part]. The measurement for the emergence of the front joint is likewise two *nakhās* in length;
the joint at the base of the thumb is the measure for the body of the toes of the foot. (30–31)

The root-joint of the index finger (tarjanī) should be two barley-corns; the length of the middle finger (madhyamā) should be three and one-quarter digits (aṅgulas), and its root-joint should be three and five-sixteenths of a digit, augmented by four barley-corns.
The root-joint of the little finger (kanīyasī) should be [the same].
Between the two [sections] at the tip and the root, the remaining joint is situated in the middle.
On the thumb, however, one joint is a *kalā*; it is taught that the fingers have three joints each.
Half a *bhūta* (one-quarter) is the portion of the width of the *kalā*, and from that, the middle [portion] is extended by a sixth part (*rasāṃśaka*). 33–34.
Of that *tāra* root, [the measurement] is one and a half *kauśikas*; above the base of three and a half thumbs is the middle of the base of the index finger;
from below the base of the thumb to the wrist is the *sānaka*.
The portion at the belly of the thumb should be like that of the Śuka; its thickness should be two and a half aṅgulas (36).
The thickness of the heel of the hand should be one and a half [aṅgulas], and the tip of the fingers should be one aṅgula.
Below the fingers, each part should likewise be thick with a thickness of two and a half [aṅgulas] (37).
The sole is as broad as a parrot’s belly, measuring two-and-a-half digits in width, with the heel and the forepart of the hand [of the foot] being depressed;
its center is fleshy, exceeding two digits in thickness, and the subtle lines on the sole, such as those of the conch and the discus, are described. 38.
The width at the base of the arm is traditionally held to be nine *mātrā*-aṅgulas;
specifically for the middle [finger-width], it should be eight and a half *aṅgulas*,
and then for the elbow, it is again one and a half *munyaṅgulas*.
The *kauśika* [measurement] is for that forearm; half of that [plus] a quarter is for the middle [of the hand].
They know its wrist-width to be one and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The width of the ear is two finger-breadths, and its length is remembered as eight.

The distance between the two eyebrows is said to be equal to a thread [one finger-breadth], and the height of the two ears is one digit (vidhu). Likewise, the distance between the back of the neck and the nape is thirteen finger-breadths, and the width of the face is also thirteen finger-breadths. 42–43.
Below the end of the *pippalī* [tube], that stalk should hang down by two parts;

the interval between the stalks should be half a measure, and the nine stalks should be one *yava* [in thickness]. The *pippalī* should be one and a half measures, and the hollow should be according to the sequence.
The ear is described as being shaped like a pericarp, and its stalk-like part is proclaimed to be two *yavas* in length;
the ear-lobe (*karṇapālī*) is equal to that, while the ear-flap (*karṇapaṭṭikā*) is half a *mātrā*, and the ear-stalk (*karṇanāla*) is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). 45–46.
In the middle, shaped like the letter *la*, with a *picu* and an *uṣṇīṣa*, and with a crest (*cūlikā*) at the base of the ear,
a measurement of eight *aṅgulas* from the root of the ear to the outer corner of the eye is recommended.
The eye should be two *aṅgulas* larger, or even four *aṅgulas* larger.
Its width should be six barleycorns, and one should divide its length into three parts.

In the middle of that black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) and on its two sides, there should be white circles; in the middle of the black [circle], however, there is a light (jyotis) the size of a single barleycorn. 48–49.
In the center of the circle of vision (dṛṣṭimaṇḍala), there is a drop (bindu) measuring eight parts of a barleycorn (nāgāṃśaka).
At the edge of the eye (akṣānta), it is two barleycorns wide and red; at the portion of the pupil (kanyakāṃśa), it is likewise one barleycorn.
Above that, there are the protective stars (varmatārāḥ); one should proceed with half a barleycorn and then one barleycorn.
The eyelashes consist of ninety hairs, possessing a luster like black collyrium (kṛṣṇāñjana).

The measurement for the two eyes and eyebrows is one and three-quarter yavas; the pupil of the eye is the middle part of the two [parts] of the body of Kāma, and the line of the eye is the space between the two. 51–52.
The midpoint of the eye-line is situated between the eyebrows; from its base to its tip, the form is like a bow, gradually becoming slender.
The globular part [of the eye] exceeds [the length] by one barleycorn (*yava*) at the lines of the eyebrows and the eyes.
From the line of the eyebrows to the end of the hair on the crown, that [distance] is equal to two and a half units (dvyardha-mātraka).

The space between the two eyebrows is half a unit (ardha-mātra). The length of the eyebrows should extend as far as the nose. The midpoint of the eyebrows should be as wide as the breadth of the eyebrows themselves. 54–55.
O wise one, the distance between the two eyes should be two mātrās plus a barley-corn (yava);
likewise, the distance between the two nostrils is desired to be two aṅgulas.
Half of that [two-aṅgula measure] would be the middle [measurement], and half of that again is the rule for the base.
The portion for the *golaka* (the spherical part) is five [units], while the tip of the nose (*nāsikāgra*) and its elevation (*udaya*) are six and seven [units] respectively.
The tip of the nose (*nāsikāgra*) is above the two nostrils (*puṭa*), and the opening (*randhra*) of the two is considered to be one *tāra*.
The opening of the three-fold *tāṭikā* is one *tāra* and seven and a half *yava*s.
The elevated part of the ear is like a grain of barley,
while the cavity of the nostril is like a *niṣpāva* seed;
thus, the shape of that nostril is like the form of a sesame flower.
The height of the Puṣkara (the central top ornament) should be one part; its middle portion should be two yavas thick;
it should have a projection of one and a half [parts] hanging from the tip of the nose, which is very beautiful;
and the globular part (golaka) extending to the edge of the side compartments should be two yavas larger.
Half a *bhāga* is the height of the *yavala*; half of that is its pupil (*tāraka*).
The *bhaga* is two *yavas* greater; the moon is as long as the upper lip. The width of the upper lip is three and a half *yavas*.
The northern edge should be one barley-corn [in width], and the wise man should make the heart [of the stone] half a barley-corn.
It should gradually diminish in thickness from the edge of the lip to the end of the tongue,
being extended in length by six and a half barley-corns, and raised by one barley-corn.
The lower part, together with the *pālikā*, extends downward for one and a half *māyavāra*s;
this is declared to be thirty-two *paricakṣas* in circumference.
Its width is two *yavas*, and its height is known to be equal to that.
The length of the fang should exceed [the base] by one *yava*, and it should be like a bud together with its bite-mark (66).
Above that, the wise say there should be sixteen teeth;
for the lower row, the width and height of the lower tooth should be half a *yava* more than the upper one (67).

The length of the tongue should be six finger-breadths, and its width half of that; the neck should be equal in length to the vulva (bhaga) and likewise heavy. The nape of the neck (kṛkaṭikā) and the joint should each be twenty-seven mātrās in measure.
It should be thirteen and a half parts due to the entry of the neck below that;
the measurement below that, from the body of the back, is one and a half finger-breadths;
and the measurement below that, extending further, is twenty-two and a half finger-breadths.
The portion of the thigh (vedāṃśa) should be one-fourth [of the body] and the knee [height] should be one-fourth; the shank (jaṅghā) should be thirty finger-breadths, or not less than that.

The heel (pārṣṇi) is declared to be equal in length to the height of the body, and the length of the back (pṛṣṭha) is likewise proclaimed. The distance between the two armpits across the back should measure twenty-seven units.
Starting from the back of the neck and extending ten units upward, one should form the buttocks; thereafter, from the base of the thighs, the height should be increased.
Between the large breasts, the thickness at the collarbone should be one unit.
The hip-projection (kaṭyakānti) shall be one part, and its width half a part;
its thickness shall be one-sixteenth of a part, and likewise one part above that.
The width of the hip-staff (kaṭidaṇḍa) shall be nine and a half parts.
The two buttocks (sphik-piṇḍau) should have a width of nine and a half parts and possess their proper characteristics.
The waistband (nīvī) behind should be five and a half parts, and its fastening (bandha) four parts.
Whatever else has not been mentioned here, the carpenter should understand and fashion it through his own ingenuity.
One should have [the image] fashioned together with the preceptor according to the methods prescribed in the treatises on arts and weaponry.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Tenfold Supreme Proportion (daśatāla)," in the section concerning the construction of sacrificial altars and so forth, within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
The Procedure for Vimānas.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of rules for the deities and others.
They declare that the measurement of the two goddesses is ten *tāla*s in the middle [scale]. 1.
From the feet to the crown of the head, the height is one hundred and twenty finger-breadths;
it is described as having three curves and two arms, being either very graceful, symmetrical, or both. The shoulders should be level and elevated, and both [the arms] should be equal.
The beautiful right hand of the Goddess Śrī is extended,
resting upon the root of her thigh and reaching toward her side with its fingers slightly bent; likewise, her right hand on the ground holds a blue lotus as before.
Likewise, their left hands are extended, joined with a basket and a crown;
they have pure golden bodies and are adorned with all ornaments.
Their feet stand beside the god, while the other two [feet] remain bent.

From the crown of the head to the hairline is the *bhaga* (the face), extending to the corners of the eyes by six *yavas*. From the corner of the eye to the edge of the eyelid it is four *yavas* more; likewise, the space from the eyelid to the bridge of the nose is three *mātras* and six *yavas*.
The distance from the bridge of the nose to the chin is said to be one *dhanus*, and from there to the throat is two *golakas*.
From the throat to the end of the heart, and from the heart to the end of the navel,
and from there to the end of the root of the yoni— therein it measures sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
From there to the end of the root of the wood, they know it to be twenty-six finger-breadths.

Two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) are prescribed for the ankle, and the shank is said to be equal to the thigh. One part is the length of the sole, and four parts are declared for the foot; one part is the length of the big toe, and the index toe is considered to be equal to that.
The remaining fingers are characterized by being successively diminished by half a finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgula*).
The length of the thumb and the others is declared by Kalānāga and Muni to be as follows:
the length of the nails is praised as being seven, five, and six barley-corns (*yava*) respectively.
The width of the forepart of the foot is six fingers;
the heel is twice that, and the eye [of the foot] is five fingers up to the ankle.
The breadth of the *nalakā* (the lower leg bone) is one part, and the upper part of the calf is three *golaka*s (twelve fingers). 12–13.

The *dhātu* (pedestal) arising from that should be broad, starting from the base of the thighs; it should be as thick as an elephant’s trunk, circular at the top of the thighs, and its legs should be like reeds.
The *vimukha* (faceless) pedestal should have a width equal to the hip and a length of one *dhātu*-finger. 14.
It is four *mātrās* in length, shaped like the leaf of a *nyagrodha* tree;
the secret region is broad and fleshy, with the width of the hips being one-sixteenth part [of the total] and the length of the hip-sockets being declared to be seven finger-breadths in width. 15–16.

The navel is six barley-corns in width; its depth is one finger-breadth. The middle part between the breasts is as wide as a serpent (one finger-breadth), and the distance from the heart to the breasts is said to be thirteen finger-breadths; the width of the breasts is nine finger-breadths.
The nipple should be one *tala* in measure, and the *tārāducca* (the height of the star) should be half of that.
One should fashion it joined with a waist-band (*kakṣyābandha*) according to what is beautiful.
Subsequently, the distance between the two armpits (*kakṣa*) should be seventeen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). 18–19.
The wise state that the span of the forearm is four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) in length;
the elbow should be two mātrās, the forearm (prakoṣṭha) nine finger-breadths (randhrakāṅgula), and the palm seven finger-breadths; therein, the middle finger is considered to be one kalā.
One should fashion the ring finger with its natural proportions and the little finger broad;
likewise, one should make each finger beautiful with its ring.
One should also fashion the wrist, the forearm, and the space between the middle of the elbow and the hand.
The base of the neck and the neck itself should be raised by seven finger-breadths each in succession;
the mouth should be eleven finger-breadths wide, shaped like a hen’s egg, symmetrical, and as bright as the light of the moon.
23. Having made it joined with half-and-half [proportions], it should be gentle and equal in luster to the moon.
From the hairline, [the distance to the end of the nose] is two-and-a-half measures; from there, the eye is successively two akṣas and two yavas.
For a man, it is equal with six yavas. The fire [of the forehead] is one aṅgula in length. The remainder is the half-arch of the ear, which is two-and-a-half measures in height.

From the wrist to the end of the ring-finger, the height is twelve fingers; from the navel to the wrist, it is thirteen and a half fingers. When extended, the distance between the sides and the arms consists of seven cubits.
An expert in the arts should skillfully fashion the hermitage (āśrama) from the wrist to the base of the thighs, including the forearms and the fingers as parts of that aesthetic form;
likewise, on the left side of the head, the left eye should be white.
One should hang the thread from the fold at the lower lip, then from the jaw, the breast, the navel, likewise the middle of the thigh, and finally the edge of the heel;
this is the procedure for the hanging [of the thread] in the case of the *samabhaṅga* and *tribhaṅga* postures, as previously described in the supplementary section.
Having performed exactly as prescribed until it is pleasing to the eyes and mind—
specifically including the retinues from Dhātṛ down to the bhūtas,
their colors, vehicles, banners, and so forth, as well as their asterisms and names— 30–31.
I have already clearly explained, along with their defining characteristics, the procedure for worship within my treatise on ritual authority;
likewise, a wise man should fashion all the attendants in due order.
Furthermore, whatever has not been mentioned here regarding images and so forth, that too [should be done] in sequence.
The wise and intelligent preceptor should perform [the rite] according to the procedure stated in the *Khila*;
furthermore, the specific details for the installation of Viṣvaksena will be explained.
Having performed very severe austerity for half the duration of that for Vāsudeva, [he should proceed].
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, concerning the qualification for sacrifice, in the *Vaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu. Furthermore,
having previously attained *sārūpya* and *sāmīpya*,
he cast off his material body here through the grace of the God of gods.
Having attained that which is extraordinary, inconceivable, and difficult even for the gods to obtain,
Viṣṭaraśravā was pleased by his well-performed austerity and said:
"O Dharmavit, my devotee shall worship me constantly along with him."
"Mādhava has said that for one who performs sacrifice according to the injunctions, his act of offering the used flower garland (vimālya) shall lead him to the state of Viṣvaksena;
whether for his own sake or for the sake of others, [this should be done] in the presence of the God of gods."
In that temple, one should worship Viṣvaksena either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),

or in water, or on a bundle of grass (kūrca), or on a pedestal (pīṭha), or on an image (bera), or in a shrine (vimānaka), or in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa), or even in the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa).
Between Kubera and Īśāna, on the northern side of the wall,
the wise one, having constructed its temple, should install [the image] according to the prescribed rite;
or alternatively, he may install it facing south at the pinnacle (cūlikā).

In the temple, the width of the base should be one-eighth or one-seventh of the total area; its height is likewise prescribed in successive proportions. One should fashion the permanent image (dhruvabera) according to the measurements of that temple.
The height of the principal image (mūlabera) is said to extend from the base to the end of the penis as the smallest;
to the limit of the arms is the best; and in the intermediate [category], it is twenty-six parts.
By increasing by one part each time, there are twenty-seven varieties.
Based on the principal image (mūlabera), one should perform the rites for the preliminary image (kautuka) and so forth as previously described;
one should fashion it with two arms, nine tālas in height, and red complexion, or with four arms, four and a half tālas in measurement, and dark complexion.
Whether joined with the goddess Jayā or separated from her, he should indeed make him two-armed if seeking liberation, four-armed if seeking victory,
joined with Jayā if desiring a son, and likewise devoid of her if seeking knowledge.
Alternatively, ten thousand images for the festival may be made, accompanied by either of those two [types of deities]; or else, a single image (ekabera) should be used.
Having first prepared the image for the festival, one should worship it seated in all instances.
Furthermore, if there is the capacity, one should fashion a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and so forth, beginning with the *dhruva* [pole];
one should perform the measurements for its festive procession (*kautuka*), festival (*utsava*), and worship (*arcā*) as being identical [to those of the deity].
It should have the luster of a *palāśa* flower garland and be adorned with excellent yellow garments.

If one should fashion [the deity] with four arms, the right hand should display the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the left should hold a bracelet; the other two hands should hold a conch and a discus.
One should visualize [the deity] as being of dark complexion, with the first pair of hands displaying the gestures of fearlessness and the bracelet.

One should fashion everything as peaceful and similar to the God of gods, even without the Śrīvatsa, the sacred thread, and the Kaustubha gem; the goddess Jayā, resembling molten gold, should be fashioned in a state of great intoxication.
Having contracted the right foot and extended the left foot, one should place her, seated with hands at the knees, on one's immeasurable side;
[the practitioner] should gaze calmly at her while she stands amidst gods and humans.
One should establish [the image] under an auspicious lunar mansion, at a favorable moment, and during a rising of good fortune;
having placed the right foot upon the seat and extended the left,
one should hold a vajra with the right hand, or an *abja* (lotus) with the left, or else a mace.
One should represent him seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), adorned with a crown and other ornaments,
or else endowed with a discus and a conch in his hands; or alternatively, having offered the ritual sprouts (aṅkura), one may place them on the right side like a sword.
In the main pavilion or at a water-stall (prapā), like unto Vāsudeva,
one should perform the "unveiling of the eyes" (akṣimocana) on the second day in the forenoon;
having performed the *āghāra* oblation according to the rules, let the *vāstuhoma* be well-offered.
Having offered oblations with "Svāhā to the teeth" and so forth, and likewise with the mantras beginning with "Svāhā to the head," as well as with the two pacifying mantras of the five elements,
the Vaiṣṇava mantra, and similarly having offered the Jaya and other oblations;
Having offered oblations ending with the *vyāhṛtis* while mentally recollecting the Lord of Gods,
and having recited the *Śānti-mantra*, one should perform the opening of the eyes;
then, having released the cloth, one should show the cow, the clarified butter, the heap of grain, and so forth.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and subsequently established the sacred fire,
one should again perform the three-fold preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for the purification of the image; having adorned the sacrificial hall, one should prepare a couch-altar in its center.

One should perform [the rite] either at three sacred fire-chambers or at the domestic fire; having performed the evening twilight worship, one should take the city that has undergone the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa),
accompanied by musical instruments and adorned with all ornaments.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should enter the temple;
then, having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should perform the Āghāra libation in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having taken up a water-pot filled with a *droṇa* measure, one should perform the worship.
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra, one should again mutter the Ātmasūkta; then,
