having muttered the Śānti mantra, one should place its seed-syllable (bījākṣara) and worship that deity in the pitcher according to the prescribed rite.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should consecrate [the image] with water-pots; having placed it upon the altar, one should indeed perform the tying of the protective thread (*kautuka*) thereon.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should then lay the immeasurable [Lord] upon the bed.
Having offered the *uttarācchādana* oblation and praised the *hautra* ritual, the Hotṛ priest,
while reciting "May the divine Lord come, peaceful... and so forth,
as well as "The Person with his retinue" and "Accompanied by victory," [performs the rite].
After the words "May he be approved by the deities," one should then recite:
"He who is ever devoted to dharma, followed by the ṛṣis, peaceful, and blessed—Oṃ! and so forth.
Then [he gave] Viṣvaksena, Śānta, Hara, and likewise Amita; Jayā, Suṅaprādā, Bhadrā, and likewise Samṛddhinī,
Puṇyā, Puruhūta, and the high-minded Syandana.
"Aghakarmā, Viśvāṃśa, Viśvākṣa, and Viśvasūdana— one should worship these,
who are the embodied forms stationed at the doors, as well as Dhātṛ and the others, as before;
and [one should worship] Dharma, Vṛṣan, Bhūta, and Gati, which are indeed the mounts."
To Carakī, Devatārī, and Pūtanā— in that same sequence—
and likewise to Pāparākṣasī; having thus invoked these four forms and offered clarified butter, one should perform oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle.

Then, having offered oblations to Citta and the others, and thereafter to Āvāruṇa, and next to Āgneya, Prekṣāma, Dhī, and Viṣvaksena— having recited these with the Vyāhṛtis, one should sacrifice one hundred and eight times with clarified butter (ājya).

Having offered oblations of sprouts of *dūrvā* grass combined with cakes, parched rice, and barley flour, one should worship the deity of Viṣṇu with sixteen rounds of clarified butter; thus the installation,
together with the deity, will be accomplished if one performs everything in this manner.
Or one may perform all rites for this [deity] by means of its forms or two mantras;
having passed the remainder of the night, one should bathe in the morning according to the rules and perform the ritual placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) at the time prior to the installation.
Having extinguished the fire at that time, he should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with water;
when the auspicious moment has arrived, he should install Hara according to the prescribed rite, while touching the feet of the image and reciting the Puruṣasūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymns.
Having uttered "Suvaḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Bhūḥ," the wise one should perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*. Having placed the syllable "Aya" on the seat (*pīṭha*), he should place the syllable "Sha" in the heart;
having placed the syllables of the five elements, the wise one should place them in their respective locations.
One should encircle all the inscribed syllables with the *praṇava* alone;
thereafter, one should invoke [the deity] and worship her with the seat and other offerings.
However, one should never perform this for the festival image of the Goddess.
Having invoked the deities of the auspicious day and the [deities] of the rites for averting misfortune at the right and left sides of the entrance,
one should likewise worship Dhātṛ and the others in the first position as before; then,
either behind that temple or behind the image, in due order.
Having invoked the four goddesses beginning with Carakī, one should worship them;

then, having bathed the image again with pure water from jars or otherwise, and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should adorn it with new garments and other ornaments.
Having honored [the preceptor], one should perform all ritual acts as if for Viṣṇu;
having worshipped the teacher, and likewise other devotees according to one's desire, one should then, with a concentrated mind, honor all the devotees.
Whether seeking a kingdom, wealth, knowledge, or desiring a son—
whosoever performs this with devotion shall attain all their desires; this is the worship of Viṣvaksena.
Hereafter, I shall explain the worship of Viṣvaksena;
one should not perform it as a primary rite, especially for one who is merely seeking peace.
One should worship him with the remnants of the offerings to the Lord of Gods, even using materials made of clay.
One should perform the consecration at dawn and at midday;
one should worship the Lord of Gods three times a day with the twenty-seven-fold ritual, especially adorning Him with the remains of His offerings (nirmālya).
Having taken the portion already offered as the fourth part, one should offer it;
or else, having cooked it, one should offer two *prasthas*, or double that amount,
or even whatever remains in the vessel according to the custom.
Some wise men say that one should give that *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering) to cows or to a Śūdra, and it may be eaten by his devotees;
or else, at the end of the worship performed during half a watch (*ardhayāma*), the wise man should offer this prayer to the Infinite One.
Having said, "O Viṣvaksena, forgive whatever was deficient in the worship of the devotee of Hari," he should again cause [the devotee] to perform a prostration.
This is the procedure for the installation of the master.
Henceforth, I shall explain in due order the characteristics of devotees,

specifically of the Brahmins and others who are patrons and sacrificers; thus the patron, desiring to act as the performer, should indeed employ the measurement of the standard finger-breadth (mānāṅgula).

One should fashion it according to the measurement of a finger-breadth or by the sequence of the *nāgatāla*; one may employ a trident made of stone, wood, or metal in the case of a stationary [liṅga],
while for a mobile one, it should be made of iron, gold, or silver.
The height of the deity should be measured from the armpits, between the breasts, or up to the navel;
if it is stationary, it is declared to be fixed, whereas for a mobile image during a festival,
one may perform [the measurement] by increasing the length in increments of two finger-breadths starting from seven *mātrā* finger-breadths.
One should perform its measurements in nine ways, or employ other measurements; one may have a seat or a standing platform constructed according to the desire of the patron,
or one may establish it in the pavilion and so forth during the first consecration.
The Brāhmaṇa [form] is described as having a topknot (*śikhā*), with palms joined in *añjali* at the heart, two arms, very steady, gazing slightly toward the reality (*tattva*),
seated on a pedestal that is one-fourth of a *bherī*, and wearing three sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*).
One should fashion a captivating image (bera) upon the Brahma-seat;

one should have the Brāhmaṇas wear a topknot (namauli), the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas likewise, while for the Śūdras one should have them shaven (mauṇḍa), or else one may arrange their hair in a manner that is pleasing to the eyes and mind.
One should have [the image] made standing, or seated in a comfortable posture,
without Brahmā, or with another [deity], or even with only the hand holding the weapon— having done so according to the donor's preference, it possesses the required characteristics.
The vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), when properly applied, is always a characteristic of the *sāttvika* nature; it is yellow, according to the venerable *Vaikhānasa-bhagavac-chāstra* of Bhārgava.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
The consecration of the Blessed One... [and] the offering of sprouts.
Now, therefore, O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall explain the ritual beginning with the examination of the ground for the God of Gods, as well as the method for the offering of sprouts. 1.
One should perform the rite of sowing the seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) seven, nine, five, or three days prior [to the main ceremony].
The height of the *pālikā* vessels should be one span (*vitasti*), their width half of that, and their opening [of equal measure].
Below, the width is extensive; the middle width is ten finger-breadths (daśāṅgula).
The emergence of the pitcher (kumbha) is equal to that, and its mouth is one rasa (six) finger-breadths in length.
The face should be like the lip of a pitcher, and the belly of the pitcher is ten finger-breadths.
The remainder, joined with the door of the hermitage, should be equal to the *pālikā*;
the height of the *tāla* should be like a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), and the openings and so forth should be equal to the *pālikā*.
One should construct it either with gold or, according to some, even with clay.
If it is made of clay, it should be fired and free from other defects.
One should also procure śāli rice, vrīhi rice, priyaṅgu, mūga beans, niṣpāva beans, mustard seeds, chickpeas, sesame, tilva, and kuludha.
According to what is available, one should bring either mung beans along with the necessary materials;
having cast them well into water specifically in the forenoon,
one should keep them in a secret place until a sprout is seen.
Alternatively, one should perform [the rite] for a peaceful person facing the Ālaya, or in the northeast, or in the north;
or in his own sleeping chamber, or in the north, having decorated it with canopies and the like, and having smeared it with cow dung. 9–10.
Having adorned it with five colors until it is pleasing to the eye and mind,
one should fashion it as a square measuring nine cubits, seven cubits, or even five cubits in both width and length.
Having first drawn twenty-five squares with threads extending east-west and north-south,
one should designate a single square in the center as the pedestal (pīṭha) of the Creator (Brahmā),
and eight surrounding squares for the purpose of the wandering deities.

The wise and discerning one should leave four openings in the four directions for exit; the intelligent one should then construct separate fire-altars (sthaṇḍilas) for each of the remaining positions of the sun, measuring the length and breadth of those very positions.
Those who proclaim vast meanings shall each individually be the foremost of their age.
In this manner, there shall be a pedestal (pīṭha) with a bowl (pālikā), made either of grain or of rice;
the sacrificial priest (ṛtvij) shall have a vast extent, while the height shall be proportionate to the wealth [of the patron], increasing in due order.

The pedestal for those [deities] such as Jaya and the others, as well as for Śeṣa and the rest, should likewise be made respectively from one āḍhaka, half of that, or a quarter of that, of rice grains; it may be square,
perfectly circular, triangular, or shaped like a bow.
The pedestal for Jayā and the others should be shaped like a staff, marked with a lotus, triangular,
and circular respectively; thereafter, the Śārja and Daṇḍa [deities] should be placed one finger-breadth to the right of these doors.
Having always provided peaceful seats for Śeṣa and the others, as well as for Śambhu, one should proceed outside the *pālikās* for Śeṣa, Jayā, and the rest;
if capable, one should likewise have altars (*sthaṇḍilas*) prepared for the guardians of those respective directions. 20.
Or likewise, one should worship that sacred thread (pavitra) upon the ground as the respective seat.
Having tied an aśvattha sprout, dūrvā grass, and kuśa grass to the middle [of the thread], one should diligently fill the *pālikā* vessels and so forth with clay in due order. 21–22.

Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra and taken up [the materials] with the Praṇava, the knower of mantras should recite the Medinī mantra and place the earthen vessels (pālikās) in the northeast and other directions;
then he should place the water-pots (kumbhas) to the left of the door.
Having recited "rākām ahaṃ," one should again place the Śarīra on the right side of the door; then, with the mantra "sinīvāli pṛthuṣṭuke," one should deposit it in sequence,
one by one, according to the order of the castes, in each of the positions for the Pālikās.
On the right side of Brahmā, the preceptor (ācārya),

facing north and seated upon the seat of Brahmā, should meditate upon the God of gods; having first mentally offered Brahmā and the others from his heart, he should establish the sacred syllable *praṇava*.
Upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), on the grass mats (kūrca) and in the vessels and so forth, one should invoke [the deity] in due order:
four-faced and four-armed, adorned with all ornaments, with the right hand in the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and the left resting upon the thigh. 27–28.
Holding a water-pot and a rosary in his hands respectively,
one should place Brahmā, who is golden-hued, wears dark garments, and is seated upon a lotus,
at the eastern gate facing east, or likewise at the southern gate.
In the vimāna with the western door, and likewise in that with the northern door,
one should likewise meditate upon Aja facing east, as well as the others according to the rule—
[Aja] having a golden body, yellow garments, two arms, and holding a lotus. 30–31.

The Lord stands with a basket upon his head; Śeṣa is behind him facing west, and the elephant-faced one, glowing like coral, sits facing north, holding a plantain, a mango, and a breadfruit, as well as a noose and a goad. 32.
The wise one should meditate upon Ekadaṃṣṭra, who has four arms and a curved trunk;
he is clad in yellow garments, his body is dark-hued, and he holds a sword and a shield.
One should worship Paṅktīśa, who has two arms, wears a crown-box, and faces the east. (33-34)
White, clad in dark blue garments, gentle, with two arms and holding a staff,
adorned with a crown and a casket, well-established and facing south;
[the directions] behind are red-hued like gold, green, and indeed blue.
Resembling the *dhātakī* leaf, with the luster of the white water-lily and the blue lotus,
and with a radiance like the sky— these [goddesses] are successively two-armed, holding lotuses, wearing sacred threads and garments, seated comfortably, and facing that [deity]. 36–37.

Having visualized Jayā and the others as possessing all ornaments and limbs, the wise practitioner himself, facing the direction, should meditate upon Medinī, Rākā, and Sinīvālī. (38) He should contemplate Medinī as wearing yellow garments, with a dark-complexioned body, standing with two arms.
Holding a *pālikā* vessel in her two hands, she has beautiful hair and a face turned toward that direction;
she is the goddess beloved by the full moon, with a countenance resembling the full moon, golden-limbed, clad in white garments, standing like the full moon itself while holding a water-pot. 39-40.

The remainder is the same: having meditated upon Chinīvalī—white-limbed, with dark blue garments, holding a shallow cup (śarāva), and likewise resembling the earth—one should worship her seated in her respective place, or otherwise [worship] the attendants. 41.
Having likewise visualized Soma within the seed-syllable, holding the seed in his two hands—
whether standing or seated, facing north on the right—
having thus meditated and having worshipped the deities with seats and other offerings, [one should proceed].

Having properly offered the oblation with the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles, one should cause the sacrificial food to be offered, or duly present the *bali* offering to Śeṣa and the others in their proper order;
then, while recollecting the mantra, one should offer water for drinking and mouth-freshener.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should at the end collect the seed from the Soma plant (45).

Having chanted the Viṣṇu-hymn (*viṣṇusūkta*), one should sow [the seed] starting from the northeast; having offered water with the Varuṇa-mantra, the officiant should cause the sacrificer to sow it (46).
If he is a Śūdra, he should cover the preceptor with a cloth once more, worship him, and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he should collect the barley seeds from the Soma water.
Having worshipped those [seeds] for three nights, he should then win them back again.
If sprouts appear immediately, one should perform the rite either at night or even during the day (48).
Having likewise performed all the preliminary actions, one should sow with flowers or with rice grains; one should cause that ritual act to be performed immediately (49).
One should sow [the seeds] in a vessel or a shallow dish, according to what is available;
the characteristics and colors of the sprouts have been described by me in the *Khila*.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Offering of Sprouts," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Vaikhānasas.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter:
The Procedure for the Installation of the Lord.
Now I shall describe the supreme method for the installation of the Deity.
One should perform [the rite] during either the northern or the southern course of the sun;
among the months— excluding Mārgaśīrṣa, Āṣāḍha, Māgha, and Bhādrapada—
the month of Phālguna is best, as are Caitra and Vaiśākha.
The month of Kṛttikā is the lowest, and the remaining months are middling;
even during those censured months, one should perform expiatory rites and other duties.
[One should also avoid] Śravaṇa, Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Hasta, Revatī, and Punarvasū.
One should especially accept Svāti, Mṛgaśiras, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Citrā, Aśvinī,
the three Uttaras, and Rohiṇī; particularly during the bright fortnight, or at the time when the moon has reached the fifth lunar day.

The sixth and fifth [tithis] should be taken, excluding the portion of Viṣṭi; a fixed (sthira) zodiacal sign is well-suited for collection, whereas a movable (cara) sign is not to be taken. Some say that in an urgent matter, even a dual (ubhaya) sign may be used when there is an auspicious conjunction.
One should select an auspicious weekday belonging to Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, or the Moon.
As before, one should likewise avoid the three [nakṣatras] beginning with Ārdrā, as well as Maghā, Mūla, Kṛttikā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Āśleṣā; Saturn and Mars are also to be avoided.
One should avoid the fourth, eighth, ninth, fourteenth, new moon, and full moon days, as well as the evening and the afternoon;
however, avoiding the night, one should properly perform [the rite] during the forenoon.
On the occurrence of a falling meteor, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, during an earthquake, or when there is a stroke of lightning—
on any such day associated with other defects, a wise person should strictly avoid it.
[This concludes] the selection of the preceptor (ācāryavaraṇa).

He [sought] Brahmins who were pure and devoted to knowledge, followers of the Vaiṣṇava path, learned in the Vedas, and engaged in the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti according to the Vaikhānasa Sūtra;
they were disciplined, descended through an unbroken lineage, and dedicated to the daily fire-oblation.
Having summoned those who are well-disposed, who know the application of ritual mantras, and who are free from other defects, one should inform them of all that is to be done;
likewise, one should select officiating priests and worshippers endowed with such virtues.
One should choose as a teacher a single person who possesses preeminent knowledge, is skillful, is esteemed by all, and is endowed with every auspicious mark.
The teacher is the protector, the teacher is the sustainer, the teacher is the mother, and the teacher is the father.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa is the Guru; his acceptance [of disciples] excludes those who are deaf, those with deformed nails, the blind, those afflicted by leprosy, insanity, or other diseases,
as well as those with missing limbs, those with redundant limbs, and those characterized as "śipiviṣṭa" and so forth.

A wise man should, at the outset, avoid those who are without a wife, offspring, or sacred fire; those who are excessively old or very young; those who are deformed; and those who have already been initiated by another.
Then the preceptor, restrained by the gravity of his serene disposition, [should proceed].
Having understood the ritual procedure with his mind, being intent on favoring the learned,
he should bathe, perform the daily obligatory rites, and gather the necessary materials. (19) *Kriyāsaralī*
I shall describe, in due order, the opening of the eyes for the nine images on the ninth,
seventh, fifth, third, or second day prior to the day of consecration; or it may be done without mantras.
Having had it fashioned by a craftsman, one should indeed perform the purification rite there;
avoiding the rising of the Sun, Mars, Rāhu, and Saturn, and during an auspicious lunar mansion, the wise man should have the right eye fashioned with the recitation of mantras. 21–22.
Then, on the previous day or on that very day, the wise one should perform the assembly of the pedestal (pīṭhasaṅghāta) for the red images, such as those used for festive occasions (kautuka),
either facing the temple or in the house of the patron. 23.23-24a.
Either in the middle of the ritual pavilion (karmamaṇḍapa) or in another temple, having smeared the ground with cow dung and decorated it with five colors,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with grain and place a pedestal (pīṭha) well-settled in its center.
The wise man should cause a pit to be made, starting from the Dhātrī tree and extending as far as the Bhūta tree;
on the southern side of the pedestal, the performer of the rite (ācārya) should face north,
remaining with his head slightly inclined at a short distance to the west of that spot.

Having applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and the sacred thread (upavīta), the master architect (sthapati), standing facing east, meditates mentally upon the purifier and the Lord of Gods; then, seated with one knee bent, he should visualize [the deity] and cause [the disciple] to face east. 27–28.
Then, having taken up gems, one should remember their presiding deities;
one should worship the guardians of the directions upon the pedestal and Dhātṛ in due order.
One should place the Brahma-gem in the station of Brahmā and the Vajra-gem in the station of Indra.
The wise practitioner of mantras should place a pearl in the southeast, lapis lazuli in the south, conch-shell in the southwest, crystal in the west, moonstone in the northwest,
sapphire in the north, and above that, an emerald.
Having whispered the mantras dedicated to the deities of those directions, the Guru should settle [the gems];
or, in the absence of gems, he should deposit gold according to what is available.
Thereafter, having worshipped the deity while reciting the mantra "Bhūrasi," the Guru [proceeds].
Having established and consecrated [the image], and having summoned the master architect (sthapati) once again, the master architect should worship the Lord of Gods upon the pedestal once more; then,
having stretched the measuring lines, he should place the images back in their respective positions.
The wise preceptor, having thoroughly tested [the image] and secured it with a mechanical device,
and having honored the artisan, should dismiss him; then the preceptor, having consecrated the image with products of the cow and other substances, should bring the image back again.

On a seat facing the Ālaya, the preceptor, with a serene mind, should place Hari facing the east (verse 36). Having bathed according to the rules along with the sacrificer and the officiating priests, he should perform the Brahma-sacrifice.
Either facing the Ālaya, or to the south, in a pleasing place,
having constructed a water-shed or a pavilion and decorated it as before, one should prepare a pit for the aupāsana fire with its characteristic marks in the center.
On its northern side, one should perform the Bhūmi-yajña in due order;

having caused the circumambulation with fire (paryagni) to be performed, one should sprinkle water mixed with kusha grass around the image of that [deity], using the Hiraṇya-pavamāna and other mantras.
Having established and adorned it with new and excellent garments,
and having duly installed the sacred fire (pāvaka) upon the aupāsana hearth, he should offer the āghāra oblation dedicated to Viṣṇu on its western side.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should spread a new cloth over it; then,
taking the deity and establishing the Lord facing east upon the mound,
the wise practitioner should recite the Vaiṣṇava, Viṣṇu-sūkta, Brāhma, and Raudra hymns in their proper order.

Having offered the Śrīsūkta at the end, the wise preceptor should, in due order, offer the crest-jewel, the garland, and so forth; having offered these at the conclusion of the mantras, he should touch each respective limb. Then, having bound a horn of a donkey with gold, together with its calf— 43–44.
Having properly established the village [of the image], one should place auspicious offerings—
ghee, honey, curd, and milk, not less than a *prastha* each— in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or brass, facing the deity. 45.
Then the mantra-practitioner should sequentially place [the syllables] from *samā* up to the end of *uttara*.
Having duly worshipped the *Samaveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Rgveda*, and the *Atharvaveda* in those [sections] respectively, he should collect eight kinds of grain. 46–47.
One should bring one *droṇa* each of the grains: *śāli*, *vrīhi*, *priyaṅgu*, *māṣa*, *niṣpāva*, *sarṣapa*, sesame, and *mudga*;
or else, one may take an equal amount of *vrīhi*, or even just one kind alone. 48.
Half of that [measure] is said to be rice, and half of that again one should take sesame.
Having worshipped Vāyu therein, one should perform the recitation of the Vedas,
accompanied by the sound of conchs and kettledrums and joined with the resonance of the Vedas.
Having covered his face with a new cloth before the deity and turned his face upward, the wise one stands inside facing north;
having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), he should remember the Lord of Devas in his mind.
One should obtain an auspicious *tāḍanī* (hammer) made of gold and silver, ten fingers in length, tapering from the base to the tip, and circular in shape; likewise,
one should obtain a needle (*sūcī*) measuring one finger in width, nine-folds thick, and provided with a handle.
Taking hold of those two with both hands while reciting "pra tad viṣṇu" and the Viṣṇusūkta,
the wise preceptor should release the eyes, whether in the *savya* (leftward) or *apasavya* (rightward) manner, while reciting the Narasūkta. 54.

Having meditated in his mind upon the eyelashes as armor, the blood, and the white [sclera] as immeasurable splendor (55), and having sequentially recollected Earth and the other elements as its presiding deities within that [eye],
he beheld the Lord of the God of Gods, bowed down, and sought His permission (56).
Having uncovered the concealed cloth, the wise one should show the cow while reciting that specific hymn,
and he should perform the meditation with the mantra "The Maruts are the Supreme Self," as well as showing the sesame seeds and rice grains (57),
and the clarified butter and other items with their respective Vedic mantras and so forth.
Having recited the verse "brahma jajñānam," he should likewise show [the image] to the Brahmins.

If it is wise, he should perform everything in the same manner together with the two goddesses; however, if they are separate from the bathing festival and the main image (bera), he should do so for each individually.
Having gathered [the materials], the wise one should display them and have that temple constructed; if it is new, he should have it built according to what has been declared as pleasing.
At the opening of the eyes of the *dhruva* [image], the wise one [should perform the rite] with gold of the respective color.
Having worshipped the goddess Mahī in the vessel, one should likewise release the eyelashes and other parts;
one should release the attendant deities, such as Dhātṛ and others, with their respective mantras.
This is the specific distinction; otherwise, everything else is the same, and one should commence the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).

If one performs the permanent worship (dhruvārcā) specifically in the house at the site described for the marriage-thread ceremony (kautuka), having established it upon a jeweled pedestal like a collection of thrones,
one should then perform the "unveiling of the eyes" (akṣimocana) there, especially within the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
Then, one should also perform the rites of consecration (*adhivāsana*) and so forth by means of the *yantra* itself.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for Opening the Eyes," in the section on Sacrifice within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, in the venerable *Vaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
[End of] the venerable *Vaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra* in the lineage of Bhṛgu.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter: The Ritual of Consecration (Adhivāsa).
Now follows the consecration for the purpose of purifying the wooden image.
I shall explain in detail the ritual for the worship of Dhruva along with his retinue:
(1) taking thirty-two full *prastha* measures of [grain], free from broken or cracked pieces, and having taken each individual vessel and wrapped it with thread; (2) [one should proceed].
Having washed it and placed the pitcher facing forward upon a heap of one *droṇa* of grain, one should fill it with water in due order, cast into it gold, gems, and other such items,
and having added bundles of *kuśa* grass, wrap it with a fine cloth.
Having assumed the Brahma-posture, facing north with his right side toward the north,
he should meditate upon the sacred fords (tīrthas), invoke them into the water within the pitcher, and then,
having worshipped the presiding deity in due order, prostrate and offer obeisance.
Having worshipped Dhruva afterwards and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited,
the wise knower of mantras, having uttered "This is conjoined," should place the *kūrca* of the relationship together with the water-pot using that very same water.
Having sprinkled water and perceived the deities as being present, one should cause them to enter into that [vessel].
Having meditated upon it as the "Cold Ocean," one should perform the rite for the two goddesses separately from the God of Gods, or else one may do so in a single pitcher.
One should cause the attendant deities, such as Dhātṛ and others, to reside separately or together for three days, two days, one day, or even overnight.
If there is a permanent image (dhruvārcā) for the household ritual offering (gṛhapiṇḍa), one should perform the "unveiling of the eyes" (netravimocana).
Below that, having fashioned a sacrificial post (yaṣṭi) from trees suitable for sacrifice according to the prescribed characteristics,

and having prepared its base (pādān) according to the sequence of trees as required for the emergence of the image (berodaya), one should [place them] in the corners starting from the southeast with the first mantra of the Vedas.
Having placed it upon the staff above that, and having worshipped the remainder,
one should again place the staff with its top pointing north while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
Right there, one should especially take hold of the water-pot (kumbha) at the side of Brahmā.
Having made a very fine hole, one should gradually wind the thread around it;
having filled it with pure water, one should place the jewels and other items therein in sequence.
Having worshipped [the deity] in that water, one should place it upon the staff.

Having recited the Vāruṇa mantra, if [the deity] is separate from the two goddesses, one should sprinkle it together with the gods upon the crown of the head and perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) without interruption in a pleasant place such as Nandā for the purpose of the consecration with water and other substances. 15.
Having adorned [the deity] with flower garlands and spread out new cloths,
and having likewise decorated the Lord of Gods, one should then circumambulate him in either a village or a temple; thereafter, having entered that very bank, one should proceed.

Having bathed [the image], covered it with a new cloth, and worshipped it, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; at the conclusion, one should properly honor the preceptor.
Then, taking the deity with both hands, one should circumambulate the site in a clockwise direction.
Having gone there and entered, one should place it facing west.
Then, having bowed to Varuṇa with the mantra "hiraṇyaśṛṅga," one should worship that Lord of Waters with concentration, beginning with the offering of *arghya*. 19–20.
Having recited the "vaiṣṇava" mantra and joined it with the two goddesses, the wise one should cause the Lord to lie upon the bed with his head toward the east;
having placed a pillow at the head, he should cover each separately with a cloth.
Having covered that [area] below the neck, one should worship them in sequence on the ground.
(22) Having worshipped the Commander-in-Chief, one should worship the conch in the east;
having worshipped the mace in the south, one should worship the Śārṅga bow in the west. (23)
Having worshipped the sword on the left, one should worship the parasol above;
having kindled a perpetual lamp, one should perform the surrounding covering.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) for three days, two days, or even for a single day.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, he should likewise enter the temple;
[he should also place] the fire-drills, the garland of darbha grass, the archways, the cloth,
the sacrificial vessels such as the *sruva* ladle, and the water-pots and so forth, in their proper order.
As stated by Vikhanas in the Sūtra, a learned man should likewise cause it to be constructed in the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices in their proper sequence;
it should be fashioned from sacrificial trees, elevated by one vitasti and one aṅgula.
One should gradually fashion a broad forehead with the *nāgāṅgula* measure, dense with hair reaching to the eyes;

having formed the frontal plate (*phalaka*) in the middle of that, one should make it elevated by a *dhātvaṅgula*, and likewise cause the *śrīvatsa* and other marks, as well as a half-design (*ardhacitra*), to be fashioned upon it. 28–29.
The Śrīvatsa, the full pitcher, the kettle-drum, the mirror, the pair of fish, the goad, the conch, and the whirlpool are the eight auspicious signs in sequence;
likewise, the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the sword.
One should have this made within a palaka; this shall be the half-citraka.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Section on Sacrifice," in the venerable Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now, hereafter I shall explain the sequence of rules for the sacrificial hall (yāgāśālā).

Having constructed either a pavilion (maṇḍapa) or a gabled structure (kūṭa) to the east or the south of the temple, in a pleasing location, according to the requirements for the residence; ||| 1 ||| [end of verse] ||| having constructed either a pavilion (maṇḍapa) or a gabled structure (kūṭa), as if it were the primary dwelling.

One should have it constructed as beautiful, provided with four doors. It should be square, level, and shaped like a shallow bowl, measuring one *prādeśa*, one *kiṣku*, or one cubit (*hasta*) in width, and joined with a base of *nandadhātu* stone.
Having made a straight, level line with a cord of *darbha* grass or *muñja* grass,
and having fixed a *bilva*-wood peg at its center, one should extend a ten-fold cord [from that point].
If the eastern ends and the western ends of the cord are both provided with two loops (*raṇṭha*), [the measurement is complete].
Having firmly fixed the stakes upon the stake, making it immovable and very secure,
one should first extend [the cord] from east to west; thereafter,
one should likewise extend it from north to south in the middle, and by that same means, one should count the steps.
One should install pillars in sequence on the four-spoked, four-cornered, and eight-jointed [structures] respectively, using pleasing materials such as betel-nut wood;
the height of the pillars should be ten *tālas* or twelve *tālas*.

One should sequentially place the wooden strips (paṭṭikās) starting from the eastern end and extending to the northern end. Having covered the holes with *nālikāra* leaves, some say that the *varṣavāraṇa-kūṭa* (the roof-structure for warding off rain) should be omitted.
If one should cause it to be made with straw, one should make it seamless in due order;
in the center, the Brahmā-pada consisting of nine squares is declared to be the place for the bed.
Its measurement may be one and a half times that of the image, or else according to the measurement of the wall.
One should lay out the divisions starting from the east and extending all around for the purpose of the doors.
In the third part of the Brahma-line, one should cause the Sabhyāgni fire-altar to be constructed, as in the case of the Śrāmaṇaka fire;
and prior to that square, one should construct the Āvāhanīya sacrificial pit.
Like the *aupāsana* fire, the wise one should fashion the *pauṇḍarīka* fire-pit in the middle square toward the southeast; it should be twelve finger-breadths in height,
formed by rotating a circle with a radius of eighteen and a half finger-breadths.
That [altar] should be circular, with an upper altar (ūrdhvavedi) where each part is raised by one unit;
its height and middle width should be exactly one āśrama finger, while its lower base should be six fingers wide—such is the characteristic of the altar. 14–15.

Having made the depression sixteen digits deep and ten digits wide, the wise man should, according to the rules stated for the *sūtra*, fashion the *anvāhāryapacana* fire-altar in the western portion of that square;
then, he should again fashion the *āhavanīya* altar in the [northeastern] corner.
Having constructed a level ground with a height of four palm trees and a width of one palm tree,
there should be a sacrificial altar for the materials in the northern part of the hermitage site; then,
the wise man, having established the Gārhapatya fire according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtras, [proceeds].
Therefore, one should directly designate the birth-place for the worship of the jar;
then, in the eastern portion consisting of four parts,
that wise man, having constructed the *āvasathya* fire-pit according to the characteristics prescribed in the Sūtras, should perform the excavation in the northeast.
When the foot has gone outside, that wise one [should know] that among the twenty-eight positions, the remaining ones are indeed for the movement of the attendants of the gods;
[therein is] the archway, the full water-jar, and the sprout of the lamp. 21.
Having adorned each and every door, one should further decorate it with canopies and the like;
it should be provided with a garland of *darbha* grass and equipped with a small banner.
It should be made beautiful by adorning it with flower garlands and other such items. 22.
Having smeared it all over with cow dung and decorated it beautifully,
and having adorned it with five colors and scattered rice grains, [he should place them] in the vicinity of each of the respective shrines for all the attendants. 23–24.
They should perform the preparation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the domestic fire-ritual (aupāsana), the laying out of the altar (śayana), and the recitation for the Hotṛ priest;
or else, at the proper time for Viṣṇu's rite, they should indeed perform the recitation for the Hotṛ priest.
Then, either at the conclusion of the invocation (āvāhana) or otherwise, one should invoke all the retinue.
The wise know that in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice there are five fires:
the Gārhapatya to the east, the Ānvāhāryapacana thereafter, and the Aupāsana fire-pit in the middle among them. 26–27.

The Gārhapatya fire should be the principal one, while the Sabhya fire is used for the recitation of the Hotṛ priest's praises; however, some consider the Sabhya fire to be the lowest, being merely an adjunct of the single fire.
Along with the Pauṇḍarīka fire, these were used in the sacrifice of the Lord Hari.
If the consecration of five images is performed here specifically together,
one should likewise place the water-pot (kumbha) upon a single altar during the meditation;
otherwise, they will become agitated and manifest worldly appearances.
If one should perform the ritual separately according to one's own rule,
then all those seeking the goal, having bathed and performed the evening *saṃdhyā* worship,
should enter the sacrificial hall and, facing north, stand on the southern side.
Having saluted the teacher, he should occupy the seat of Brahman (brahmasana),
apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
then he should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Śiras and the Vyāhṛtis in their proper order.
One should recite [the mantra] with the breath suspended; that is called *prāṇāyāma*.

O twice-born one, if the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is a Brahmin, he should perform it thus in the presence of the preceptor (34). Others, however, desiring the fruit of the rite, should perform it with the permission of the Brahmins.
In the same way, the wise [disciple] should especially cause the Adhvaryu priests to perform the rites during the forenoon; thereafter,
having prostrated before the deity who has been consecrated through the preliminary rite (*adhivāsa*), he should carry out the ritual action in the afternoon.
Having raised it up, one should place it on its bank in due order;
having consecrated it with pure waters, one should also adorn it with garments and other ornaments.
Then, having mounted it upon a palanquin or a chariot, that [image] possessing the auspicious marks—
Having circumambulated the village and entered the sacrificial hall (38),
the wise one should place the Lord, facing eastward, upon a consecrated seat in the western part; having thus prostrated, he should thereafter commence the ritual action (39).
Then, after the offering of the seed-syllables (aṅkura), having bathed according to the prescribed rules for bathing,
and having recited in due order the Vaiṣṇava hymns, the Narasūkta, and the mantras beginning with the four Vedas, one should finally perform the Brahmayajña.
Or a three-night fast, or even a quarter-kṛcchra;
or a one-day fast for the removal of all sins—
having performed this, the wise preceptor should remain until the very end of the ritual.
Especially for his preceptor, as long as the ritual action is not completed, he is not defiled by the two-fold impurity beginning from the birth of the child;
likewise also for the officiating priests, the sacrificer, and his [preceptor].
As long as the end of their karma has not been reached, so long does their sin persist.
(44) One should cause the feeding of Brahmins to be performed before the day of the consecration;
one hundred and eight is the primary number, while half of that would be the middling. (45)
At the conclusion of that meal, the wise and righteous-souled man should, according to his capacity and strength, kindle the fire— the lowest being twenty-seven [strokes]—
On the following night, one should especially commence the Vāstuhoma sacrifice. 47.
Having prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the north of the temple or to the north of the hall, one should perform the Āghāra libation as previously described. 48.

With the two mantras beginning with "vastoṣpate," the two earth-sacrifices (bhūmiyajña) are performed; subsequently, the deity of the earth is invoked, and the oblation is offered intensely. With the mantra "aham agniḥ," the fire is taken up using a torch.
The wise man should perform the *paryagni* rite with the mantra "adabdhāyo'śītatano," and he should especially cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed on all sides.
Then, having strewn grass around the fire, he should offer oblations to Viṣṇu ending with those to Varuṇa.

Having offered oblations with the *sahavyāhṛti* mantras, the wise one should likewise perform the internal homa (*antahoma*). Then, having established the sacrificial fire in the *gārhapatya* hearth according to the previously mentioned procedure, he should enlarge the preceptor’s dwelling.
Having been honored by the Guru, the officiating priests (ṛtvijas) were then summoned;
they prostrated themselves before the Gārhapatya and other sacred fires,
which were established with their respective mantras in the directions between Yama, Indra, Kubera, and Varuṇa.

O best of the twice-born, having introduced the general rules for all oblations, I shall now specifically describe the presiding deities of the various types of fire-offerings, beginning with the *āghāra* libations,
as well as those for the ground, sand, the lunar altar (*sthaṇḍila*), and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). (56–57)

The sages [are assigned] to Varuṇa, Vāyu to the water, and likewise the Vedas to the *kūrca* grasses at the front; Hari is in the knot, and Hara likewise. Hari is the presiding deity of the four types of strewing (*paristaraṇa*) in due order.
The northern edge of the enclosing sticks (paridhi) extends toward the south and west;
[therein dwell] the Gandharvas, Indra, Varuṇa, and Īśāna. In the water-vessel (karaka) is the five-elemental [deity].
For the libation (tarpaṇa), Anala is to be known [as the deity]; for the two upper [vessels], Agni and Veda.

Īśa and Indu are the presiding deities over the two most excellent [blades]; the three [deities] are on the head; Bhūmi is declared to be the deity of the two strainers (pavitra), the vessels for curd and clarified butter, and the juhū-ladle.
Atharvan is the lord of the sruva-spoon, and Vāsuki is remembered as the deity of the other vessels.
Brahmā and Soma are the presiding deities of the two *praṇītā* vessels, those on the south and north respectively;

Agni is the lord of the clarified butter (*ājya*), Īśa of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and likewise all the gods are the lords of the other oblation materials in their respective order; that Grandfather (Brahmā) is the sovereign of them all.
It is traditionally taught that all the gods are present in twenty-one fuel-sticks (*samidh*);
the *palāśa*, *bilva*, *nyagrodha*, *śamī*, *audumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *khadira* are proclaimed as the seven types of fuel-sticks in their respective order. (64)
For those for whom Agni, Śrī, and Samayā are [the deities], and the Moon and Sun are the presiding lords of the Vedhas [square],
[one should worship] Prajāpati at the top and bottom of a fire-pit marked with two lines, and then the Vasus starting from the southeast in the Sabhya and other fires. 65–66.
The pit-moon, the six-faced one, and the line— especially in the rite of fire-oblation (homa)—
the mantra-practitioner, having understood the presiding deity, should cause each respective ritual to be performed;
if it were otherwise, there would be destruction, and both the rite and the performer would perish.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Sacrificial Hall," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter in the *Bhārgava* [recension] of the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*.
The Specific Āghāra Oblations:
Now, O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall explain the specific āghāra oblations;
having placed two praṇidhis in the water of the northern praṇidhi. (1)
Having first invoked the deities of the assembly, beginning with Agni, one should then perform the Gārhapatya sacrifice in the Gārhapatya fire, which has the Lord of Sacrifice as its presiding deity.
Then, in due order, one should recite: "Oṃ Bhūḥ Puruṣa," and "Acyuta."
Having said "Anvāhāryakam," he should likewise [invoke] him in the Anvāhārya [fire] with "Yajñadaivata Viśve" and "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ Puruṣaḥ" in sequence,
and having invoked Satya, he should likewise worship with the *juṣṭākāra* formula.
Having uttered "Āhavanīya" and also "Yajñadaivata," he should invoke the deity Puruṣa with "Oṃ Suvaḥ Puruṣaḥ. Thereafter,
he should likewise invoke the Gārhapatya fire (Avasathyāgni) and also "Yajñadaivata."
Oṃ, having sequentially invoked Mahat-Puruṣa and Aniruddha behind [the fire], as well as Sabhyāgni and Yajñadeva;
and likewise, having invoked Jana-Puruṣa and Viṣṇu in the Sabhya fire according to the proper order—Oṃ. 6–7.
In the lotus-fire, one should worship Pauṇḍarīka, who is also the deity of that sacrifice.
Then, saying "Oṃ Tapaḥ Puruṣa," one worships Vāsudeva;
thereafter, saying "Oṃ Satyaḥ Puruṣaḥ," one worships Nārāyaṇa.
Having invoked [the deity] and offered that clarified butter (ājya), one should perform the oblation in due order. Now,

I shall describe the meditation upon the great-souled purifying fire for the sake of the offering to the deity, according to tradition, according to one's capacity, and according to the prescribed rule.
Then, with a buffalo’s face, he praised that Jātavedas, who resembled a *kiṃśuka* flower, was clothed in peacock feathers,
adorned with all ornaments,
and enveloped in garlands of flames.
It had two heads, four horns, two ears, and two nostrils;
it possessed four eyes, seven hands, and a single seat for its mind;
it had three feet, was adorned with a girdle, and was equipped with a staff and a black antelope skin.
He was wearing an extremely fine lotus-fiber sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
seated upon a seat of darbha grass with *svāhā* and *svadhā*, possessing a monkey-banner, mounted on a ram, and surrounded by hosts of all the gods. 14.
Seated likewise in the middle of the pit, comfortably established in the Brahma-posture,
seven cubits tall and with matted hair, he is stationed facing the western direction;
in his right hand he holds a spear, and he grants boons while also holding the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

Having meditated thus upon him holding, with devotion, the *juhū*, the *upajuhū*, and the mace in his left hands, I shall now describe, according to my ability, the characteristics of the tongues [of fire]:
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and Vasuprabhā.
Atiraktā, and likewise Bahurūpā—thus [the goddesses] are sevenfold.
Hiraṇyā, Śyāmaraktā, Kṛṣṇapītā, Atiraktakā, and Śaṅkhābhavarṇā are the [goddesses]; their locations are also those of Īśa, Indra, Agni, and Yama. 18–19.
Vāruṇa, Māruta, Madhya, Jihvāna, Niyata, Krama, Agni, Vaiśvānara, Hutāśa, Hutavarcas, Jātavedas, Kṛṣṇavartman, Deva, and so forth are its designations. 20.

Having meditated upon the places of worship and the deities in their proper order, the wise man, endowed with concentration, should offer oblations at each respective spot using sacrificial fuel-sticks, all the sages say, along with parched grain, cakes, sesame seeds, and boiled rice. 21–22.

Īśa is the deity of the cake and the fuel-stick, Ravi (the Sun) is the deity of the parched grain, Agni is the deity of the clarified butter and the mustard seed, and the Pitṛs are the deities of the sesame seed;
[these are the presiding deities] for the sacrificial porridge and for the act of creation of all living beings.
The Creator is the deity manifest; the two-staffed ascetic (Dvijaṇḍa) can easily accomplish [the goal].
(24) If the oblation is offered in the ear, there is disease; if in the nose, great fear; if in the eye, blindness; but if on the head, there is total destruction. (25)

Poverty results from other [factors] such as the hands; therefore, having reflected on this, the wise man should consecrate an arrow with the *aṅgāra* mantra and offer it into the fire at the tip of his tongue (26).
When the *idhma* is offered, he should remain standing; when the *caru* is offered, he should be seated.

The wise man, meditating thus upon the God—who, when offerings of fuel-wood and clarified butter are made, lies with His splendor stilled; and who, when offerings such as sesame and cakes are made, sits comfortably—should perform the oblations of ghee and other substances according to the prescribed rule. 27–28.
The preceptor should perform the offering of fuel-sticks into the fire according to the prescribed rite, [placing them] between the ring finger and the thumb;
having set aside those dedicated to Indra and the Maruts, he should place the clarified butter in the middle of the *sruva* ladle.
Taking four finger-breadths [of the material] while meditating, one should cast it into the fire.
For the oblation of sesame and mustard seeds, the wise man, omitting the "Indra-finger" (the thumb), should offer the food in the manner of a single pearl-shell measure, just like an akṣa fruit.
The wise practitioner, repeatedly recollecting the Lord, should offer oblations of parched grain (*lāja*) in the measure of a handful upon the tongue at each respective spot, ending with *svāhā*.
First, how should it be done? With the mantra: "O Aditi, give your consent. (32)
The determination established in the scriptures is for the sake of ensuring the health of the fire:
"O Aditi, may you follow after me. When this oblation has been offered, one should perform the final dismissal (visarjana) for the purpose of restoring the fire's well-being.
That which is placed upon the tongue is here called "leavings" (ucchiṣṭa);
the exponents of Brahman say that in this matter, what fault could there be?
The Vedas declare that fire is the mouth of the gods and is auspicious.
"‘We choose Agni as our messenger’—with these words, [the verses] beginning thus occurred many times (36).
Wherever there were logs of wood, the wise knew that to be Karṇa; and wherever the smoke was very slight, they knew that to be Nisikāma (37)."
Where the fire burns only slightly, there you should observe the eye; the wise declare that a mass of glowing embers is the head of Agni.
Where the fire blazes intensely, there the mouth is distinguished.
Meditating thus upon her who possesses a hundred tongues of flame, the wise one should perform the oblation. 39.
The knower of mantras should meditate on Svāhā as another goddess, like Lakṣmī herself, dwelling in dark-blue silk and radiant with molten gold. 40.
One should thus meditate upon one's own deity as dark as a fresh blade of dūrvā grass, clothed in red garments, seated upon a comfortable *bhogāsana*.
In the forenoon, the preceptor should especially summon the disciple.
For the purpose of worshipping the principal pitcher, he should take up a site at that location.
Then, accompanied by all musical instruments and adorned with all ornaments, [he should proceed] especially to holy bathing places such as rivers and the like. 42–43.
Having gone there and turned toward the north, holding the jar with his head,
he should take up the water prescribed for worship while reciting "dhārāsu sapta" (44).
Having taken it, the disciple previously instructed should set it down facing north.

In the center of the sacrificial ground (*sambhāra-vedī*), having purified [the site] with *kuśa* grass according to the mantra (45), the wise one should place cardamom, sandalwood, incense, and so forth upon it; then,
having covered that with a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) and wrapped it with cloth (46).
Then, having gathered the ritual materials, the wise preceptor, with a serene mind, should arrange them in order according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtra;
he should be dressed in two white garments as upper and lower robes and adorned with golden flowers and other ornaments. (47)

Having adorned [the deity] with rings, sacred threads, and the like, and with anointing of white fragrances, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should thereafter practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the section on Sacrifice within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Chapter 27:
The Ritual for the Worship of the Pitcher (Kumbhapūjāvidhi).
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
The knower of mantras, having taken a jar filled with thirty-two *prasthas*,
[should take] that earthen jar if it is free from all defects, shaped like a ripe *bimba* fruit, and properly fired. 1–2.
In the sacrificial hall, in the north-western direction, the wise man, facing north,
having wound [the cord] at intervals of one barley grain with a threefold thread according to the mantra beginning with "yajurvedādi," while reciting, "O pure one, carry the oblation."
Having washed it with pure water, one should bring it back together with its lid. Then,
having placed in front of the Guru either a full load of rice, or half of that, or a quarter, respectively, one should set the pitcher upon it.
Having recited "idam āpaḥ śivatamaḥ," one should strain that water with a new cloth and fill the pitcher while reciting the mantra "dhārāḥ.
Then, having touched it with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should add scented water.
The knower of mantras, having wrapped the pitcher with two cloths— one of silk and one of linen—
should place upon it, in every respect, bundles of kuśa grass, unbroken grains of rice, sprouts of the aśvattha tree, and auspicious flowers such as tulasī, along with pure water.

Auspicious objects and jewels, along with elephants and Garuḍas, a golden tortoise, especially the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, umbrellas, banners, lamps, scales and the like, as well as pairs of ploughs; 9.
Having inserted [the image] made of gold, which is one finger-breadth less than the body of Viṣṇu, the wise man,
having prostrated before and obtained the permission of the Lord of the gods, and having performed the propitiatory rite with the mantra "śanno mitra," should begin the meditation. 10–11.
The wise practitioner should assume the posture by placing the right foot above and the left foot below, with the knees separated; then,
having firmly grasped both big toes, he should likewise hold his penis and testicles.
Pressing [the tongue against the palate], remaining as motionless as a lamp placed in a windless spot, with the face slightly upturned, the teeth touching the teeth,
and the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose— the wise one should maintain the posture for a month.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), which is threefold by name:
exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka).
Among these, that which consists of emitting the exhaled breath is called exhalation (recaka).
The wise know that exhalation which fills the self is *pūraka* (inhalation).
The restraint of that exhalation is traditionally called *kumbhaka* (retention).
Having performed *prāṇāyāma* according to one's capacity and strength, [one should proceed]. 16–17.

Having placed that seed-syllable in the heart, one should envelop it with the *praṇava*; the letter *a* is its initial seed, while the letter *u* becomes curved (*kuṭila*). The letter *m*, ending with the *nāda*, is thus called the *praṇava*.
Having formed the Varuṇa-maṇḍala within the water-pot,
one should properly place the primordial seed-syllable in the center of the water and surround it with *praṇavas*.
Then, having touched oneself, one should subsequently mutter the *ātmasūkta*.
Then, having recited the "Sahasraśīrṣa," the Nārāyaṇīya section, the Śrīsūkta, the Mahīsūkta, and hundreds of Praṇavas, one should,
with a concentrated mind, perform meditation properly.
Immeasurable, unborn, eternal, the support of all, and ancient;
devoid of qualities, partless, perpetual, the supreme self, and imperishable—
like ghee in milk, oil in sesame seeds, fragrance in a flower, and juice in a fruit.
Having meditated with the mind upon the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who pervades everything like fire within wood, as being entirely present in the center of the lotus in the heart;
then, having thus meditated there, the practitioner of mantra [should contemplate] Hari within the water of the pitcher.

One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who is golden-hued, with his face, eyes, hands, and feet likewise red; who wears garments of white and peacock feathers; who is the essence of the syllable Om (praṇava);
and who is adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and a long sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
Having meditated upon the four-armed Lord who bears the conch and discus, who possesses the *śrīvatsa* mark,
the God who is higher than the highest, together with the assembly of goddesses and others,
the Guru should properly invoke the flowers into the pitcher.
Because he is all-pervading, the wise say that this invocation from the universe into one place is merely a partial resonance;
therefore, having invoked him into the jar and worshipped him with the eight forms, [one should proceed].
If the installation is to be performed in this manner specifically in the abode of a child,
one should enter that abode of the child, bow down to that God of gods,
bathe him well with pure waters, and properly install [the deity] in the seat of life (jīvasthāna).
Having worshipped [the deity] with special care, one should properly offer the oblation (havis).
Having prostrated and said, "Forgive me," one should perform the worship of the water-pot (kumbha),
facing north, to the south of the marriage canopy (kautuka).

Having placed a water-pot before the heap of grain, the knower of mantras consecrates that pot with mantras; then, having installed the Śakti in the *kautuka* (auspicious thread) during both the sleep-rite and the festival, he subsequently bows to the Deity.
Having placed the deity endowed with the [auspicious] marks upon a water-vessel or a lotus,
and having placed the mandalas above it, one should sequentially invoke the immutable Lord of Devas and the Śakti residing within that image by means of mantra. 34–35.
Then, having meditated upon Hari within the water of the pitcher, one should worship Him up to the offering of *arghya*.
If the image should become possessed of defects such as being scorched by that [fire] or other flaws,
one should subsequently discard it according to the rite and procure a new image.
If an image worshipped in the temple of the ignorant (the *bālālaya*) is requested for the worldly [temple],
the knower of mantras, having installed that image in the primary temple (*mūlālaya*) with the *mūrti-mantra*, should worship it according to his capacity using the *mūrti-mantra*. 37–38.

If that image [of the deity] has become worn out, one should not [discard it]; rather, having invoked the Śakti into the image for the sake of ritual curiosity (kautuka) and so forth, one should gradually discard that image during the months beginning with Caitra.
If that image is endowed with the proper characteristics and adorned by the two goddesses...
Having first performed the ritual according to the rules, and subsequently having had the eyes opened and so forth, one should install [the image] exactly as prescribed by the injunctions;
there is no fault in this, because the continuity of power is one and the same. 40–41.
If the image worshipped in the Bālālaya, which is worthy of the primary abode, cannot be abandoned, one who knows the mantras should take it and install it in the primary abode.
Then, having taken the Lord of Devas along with the water-pot, the knower of mantras [should proceed].

Equipped with the Śakuna-sūkta and adorned with all ornaments, one should enter the sacrificial hall and place it there in the center; having consecrated the water-pot (kumbha) with mantras upon a pedestal of grain to the south, one should establish it. 43–44.

Having properly installed the God and the two Goddesses, one should perform the ritual bathing correctly; having established the connection with the water-pot (kumbha) and placed the kūrca-grass bundle there according to the mantra,
one should then form a row with rice or paddy grains, arranged like a staff.

Whether together with the two goddesses, or together [with others], or even separately—46—the row [of vessels] should be with jars; if it is separate there, they know the best [arrangement] to be milk, ghee, honey, water with white mustard seeds, and unbroken rice. 47
One should fill the hands separately with fruit, water, and kuśa grass; then, having taken the subsidiary bathing waters (upasnāna),
one should place them upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) starting from the north, and arrange the subsidiary bathing waters on the south side.
Adhipa [received] the Atharvaveda, the two Aśvins the Sāmaveda; Vatsara the Yajurveda; the Apsarases [received] Vāyu and Āditya;
and afterwards Kaśyapa, Maruta, the Munis, Takṣaka, and Vāsuki.
During the preliminary bath (upasnāna), one who knows the mantras should worship the seasons in their proper sequence; having bathed the Lord of the gods and worshipped him,
he should recite "aśanno devīr" and the mantra "agna āyāhi."

Having recited "Agnim īḷe," and then saying "Pūtas tasya," (52) having said "Imā oṣadhayaḥ" and also "Abhi tvā śūra," and having recited "Catvāri vāk," he should perform the ritual bathing with the accompanying mantras in their proper order. (53)
Having recited "The four waters," the knower of mantras, having worshipped each substance in turn and sprinkled the pitcher,
should bathe Hari in sequence and then wipe Him with a cloth after bathing Him again with scented water.
Having taken the Lord of Gods from the pit and placed him upon a seat in the northwest,
he adorned the Lord of Gods— the imperishable Master residing in the pitcher— with new garments, upper cloths, and other ornaments, and worshipped him thoroughly.
Then, having said "I have known," the knower of mantras sprinkles the bed;

he then spreads out six *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, half that amount of husked rice, and sesame seeds, and above those, in successive layers, half the amount again. 57. Having spread them out one upon the other in order, [he proceeds].
The first bed is born from an egg; likewise, the second is born from a shaven head. The third bed is born from hair, and the fourth is born from skin.
The fifth bed is born from the left side, each situated successively above the other.
Having spread the seat and wrapped it with a white cloth, the wise and intelligent preceptor should then place two pillows upon it; thereafter,
having scattered flowers and unbroken rice grains while reciting the mantra "vedāham," he should proceed.
Thereafter, having taken the deity along with the water-pot in due order,
and having recited the Śakuna-sūkta, he should place the Vaiṣṇava deity together with the two goddesses upon the bed-altar in the center, while speaking auspicious words.
Having established auspicious weapons all around, the wise one should likewise place them down and worship them in a clockwise sequence; then,
having properly settled [the deity] upon the ground like a water-pot, he should worship it thoroughly with flowers and other offerings.
Alternatively, having spread out beds and taken [the image] from the pit, the knower of mantras should place it upon the bed and worship it along with the water-pot; likewise,
he should worship the crest [of the image] with a golden vessel and one āḍhaka of rice.

Having filled [the vessel] and placed it at the head, having covered it with a golden or woven cloth, and having circumambulated that abode, one should place it facing [the deity] and cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made. 66.

The learned preceptor, reciting according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtras, saying "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ," and having said "mahāṃ indro nṛvad," as well as the mantra "trātāram," and likewise saying "agnirāyasmā," then again [the Guru]. 67–68.
With the mantra "Svasti dā," he should bind [the thread] clockwise around the right hand;
then, with the respective mantras of the two goddesses, he should likewise bind it on the left hand and on the water-pot in due order. 69.
He should bind it on the left hand and likewise on the pot with the mantra.
The preceptor, together with the officiating priests, shall enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha);

having removed the pitchers that were placed there and having properly worshipped Dhruva, he shall, along with the installers, cause the proclamation of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) as prescribed for the festival.

Then, having entered the hall and bowed to the God of gods, one should have him lie down with the two goddesses while reciting the mantra "Yad vaiṣṇavam. Whichever direction the door of the temple faces, that same direction shall be the direction of the head.
Having provided an upper covering, especially beneath the *kalā*,
one should likewise place the *bali-bera* (the offering image) together with the two side-images of the deity on the altar for the bathing festival, using the previously mentioned mantra. 74–75.
Then, the learned one, having spread the well-adorned upper garment over the sacrificial altar of materials, should sequentially place the grains upon the cloth,
and having arranged gems and other items in vessels of gold and so forth, [he should worship] their presiding deities.
Having accepted the invitation and worshipped Viṣṇu, one should cover [the image] with a new cloth (77).
Then, one should perform the teaching of the Vedas, the Sūtras, the Purāṇas, and so forth, around the sacrificial hall, starting from the east and proceeding in due order (78).

The wise one should cause hymns, praises, and various other musical instruments to be performed, as well as songs and dances before [the deity], according to the prescribed rite. (79) Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of the Vessel," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter:
Worship of All Deities.
Now, furthermore, [the procedure] for all the attendants in their proper sequence.
The wise man should perform the oblations and other rites according to the prescribed method.
Thereafter, the learned one should worship Śiva upon the great altar;
the intelligent one should place Brahmā to the south and likewise Śaṅkara to the north.
The wise man, having meditated according to the previously mentioned method, should worship Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhṛgu in the south and north respectively;
and at each door, he should worship the six deities, beginning with Yama in the east.
One should properly worship Maṇika and Sandhyā at the eastern gate.
Then, in the southeast, one should worship Īśa, Balīśa, Vāgdevī, Arka, Śakra, and Śrī; and in the east, Pāvaka, along with Īśa and the others, all facing westward.
One should worship Bauma, Jagadbhū, Durgā, Dharma, Manda, and Rohiṇī, as well as the Mothers, on the right side, facing north. Then,
one should worship Nīla, Mahākālī, Puruṣa, and Varuṇa in succession.
Budha, Jyeṣṭhā, Pulla, and Vāyu— these he should place facing the east; Śukra, the sages beginning with Bhṛgu, Gaṅgā, Dhanya, and the Lord of Night (the Moon),
as well as the five elements and Śānta— he should place these at the eastern end facing the south.
Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Nyakṣa and ending with Uttara in the east and so forth,
one should worship Vikaṭa and the Nāga king at the eastern gate in succession. Outside, facing the gate, one should worship the Anapāyi-gaṇas in order.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the ancient lute with the eight forms.
In whichever direction the celestial chariot (vimāna) may be, the door is conceived there; that very direction shall be the final resting place, the abode of those who do not depart from it.

There, endowed with the respective meditations, one should worship Bhūtādi and the others, ending in their respective directions by name, for they are indeed imperishable. Afterwards, having summoned the Hotṛ priest and honored him with garments and other offerings, [one should proceed].
The Adhvaryu likewise performs the sprinkling around the Sabhya fire as before (verse 13).
Having offered the oblation to Viṣṇu, he then says, "O Hotṛ, come to the mouth [of the sacrifice]. Standing facing west, the Hotṛ remains to the east of the Sabhya fire (verse 14).
Having said, "O divine Adhvaryu," and having sipped water again as before,

he should recite the previously mentioned praise beginning with "Salutation to the Proclaimer" (namaḥ pravaktre) up to the end of "O Brahmin, O Burden-bearer" (brāhmaṇa bhāra), and having thus gratified the fire.
If the Brahmin is the sacrificer, one should recite his *pravara*;
if he is a Kṣatriya, one should recite the *pravara* of his domestic priest (*purohita*) in the proper order,
or else the *pravara* of the domestic priest, or indeed the *pravara* of his teacher (*guru*).
For a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, in that same order, if it is the village of Kaśyapa,
a learned man should praise the *hautra* or indeed the *guru-pravara*.
At the end of the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame," he should face the west.
"May the Blessed One come," [saying this] with the Mūrti-mantras in sequence (19),
and likewise, the Hotṛ priest should invoke [Viṣṇu] up to the element of earth with the four Mūrtis in order, saying, "I invoke Viṣṇu. (20)

The Adhvaryu priest should likewise perform the extinguishing of the fire and cause the utterance of "Svāhā" and "Hā"; then, having kindled it, he should subsequently sacrifice to Vaiṣṇava together with the Vyāhṛtis.
First, having determined the worship according to the ninefold method as prescribed, one should proceed according to one's capacity.
Likewise, he should praise some of those present in the assembly at the appropriate time (verse 22).
Having sprinkled water as before, he should offer oblations into the fire using fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood soaked in clarified butter,
reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra "Nārāyaṇāya vidmahe" in due order (verse 23).
One should worship with the six mantras beginning with "viṣṇornuka," along with those belonging to Viṣṇu,
as well as the Śrīsūkta and Mahīsūkta, in their proper sequence; and with the six [mantras] beginning with "tat savituḥ" and "svasti caiva," together with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One should offer oblations with the five Vāruṇa mantras and likewise with the Jaya mantras; having offered the Abhyātāna mantras, at the end one should offer the Rāṣṭrabhṛt mantras,
as well as those beginning with "yad devāḥ" and the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, while recollecting each respective deity.
One should offer oblations with the mantras beginning with "brahma jñānam" and ending with "ye bhūtāḥ," as stated in the Khila section, which are dedicated to all deities (verse 27).
Alternatively, one may offer to the attendants stationed on the ninth path, as described in the Vimāna [section].
The mantra-practitioner should offer those mantras with clarified butter according to the prescribed rite and in due order.
(28) In this rite, for whichever deity no specific mantra is known, one should offer oblations to that very deity while recollecting Nārāyaṇa. (29)
Having sprinkled water around the Āhavanīya fire, the knower of mantras,
while recollecting the deity, should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn and the Narasūkta;
likewise, he should especially offer the Brāhma and Viṣṇu-sūktas during the Anvāhārya rite.
In the center, however, one should offer oblations into the Gārhapatya fire with two divine mantras and a Vaiṣṇava mantra;
furthermore, one should offer them ten times into the Āvasathya fire with two Raudra mantras and a Kaubera mantra as well. 31–32.
The wise man should also offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire in due order, using milk, curd, and ghee mixed with parched grain (lāja), in portions of one handful each.
Then, he should offer the Pauṇḍarīka oblation into the Vaiṣṇava fire for the sake of the gods and others.

The wise knower of mantras, having soaked white lotus petals in clarified butter and meditated upon the Lord in his mind, should offer them into the fire in sequence, reciting the Narasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pāramātmika hymn. 34–35.
In the oblations for Indra and the other deities, the practitioner of mantras should offer ghee separately with their respective mantras, while recollecting each particular deity.
A wise person should perform the *sabhyāgni* and *pauṇḍarīkāgni* rites in all the fires.
The wise man should perform the mantra-homa as prescribed in the Sūtras in the proper sequence (37).
He should keep the fire unextinguished and pass the remainder of the night in due order with songs, dances, and so forth, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas (38).

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of the Retinue," in the section on Sacrificial Duties within the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra* as proclaimed by Bhṛgu in its compendium.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter:
"The Deposition of Jewels" (*Ratnanyāsa*).
Therefore, at dawn, the righteous-souled one, having bathed according to the prescribed rules for bathing,
performed the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) and libations (*tarpaṇa*) as taught in the *Sūtras* beginning with the single [verse],
and having performed the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), he entered the sacrificial hall.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the gods of gods, one should awaken Him with the *praṇava*.
Having recited the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should gradually cause Hari to rise;
then, having removed His garments, garlands, and so forth, one should adorn Him with new garments and ornaments.
Afterward, having taken the jewels and entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha),
the wise and learned one should deposit them into that pit as prescribed in the Vedas and the Khila texts.
Then, having leveled the ground there and strewn grain over it with the recitation of mantras, [he should proceed].
One should spread a new cloth with its fringes pointing upward over that [altar].
Then, having entered the sacrificial hall in the presence of the God of gods,
the sacrificer shall give the prescribed sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests.
Having honored the preceptor like a deity with bracelets, rings, and various garments,
the patron should then offer ten *niṣkas* along with water in the presence of the deity.
Having touched the feet of the Lord, they should recite [mantras], intent on meditation (8).
Thereafter, while touching his feet, they should recite the Śrīsūkta;
then, to the right side of the deity, facing north (9).
A sacrifice performed with meager sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) leads to the ruin of that sacrificer;
therefore, one should give as prescribed and worship him according to the injunctions. [One should honor] astrologers, Vaiṣṇavas, and other scholars learned in the study of the Vedas.
One should especially worship all others according to their respective status.
Afterwards, at the muhūrta, the righteous-souled patron, accompanied by his ministers and the officiating priests (sthāpaka), [should perform the rite] with the mantra "Bhūḥ Pra-padye. 11–12.

"O Moment, grasp all that is other than [the self] as complete! Having thus prostrated, one should offer a handful of flowers along with various sounds and all manner of banners, peacock feathers, and the like. (13)
Accompanied by weapons, other auspicious items, incense, and lamps;
joined with the chanting of the Vedas and the Śakuna Sūkta, one should take a water-pot upon one's head and proceed in front. 14–15.
Taking the *kautuka* (sacred thread) and other items, he should lead them in sequence behind the pitcher;
