having performed a circumambulation of the temple, he should enter the sanctuary again.
Having established the *kautuka* in the station of Brahmā with the Vaiṣṇava mantra, [he should proceed].

On both sides are the two goddesses; then, on the right, the bathing ceremony (snāpana), and likewise on the left, one should establish the festival image (utsava-bali-bera). Furthermore, he should place the ritual jar (kumbha) marked with auspicious signs upon a heap of grain at the front of the marriage-thread (kautuka). 17–18.
Having renounced [all else] on his right side, the wise man, facing north and assuming the svastika posture, should again perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and recite [the mantra].
Having recited the Ātmasūkta at the end, he should duly install the Mātṛkās.
Then they should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta and the Nara-sūkta (20). Having touched the feet of the deity, they should chant while absorbed in meditation;
thereafter, they should recite the Śrī-sūkta while touching his respective feet (21).
Standing on the southern side of the Dhruva pole and facing north, the Guru,
having touched the feet of the Dhruva pole, should likewise recite the Dhruva-sūkta,
as well as the Narasūkta, the Vaiṣṇava-sūkta, and those of the two goddesses.
The Guru, while meditating upon each respective mantra for the various assemblies, should perform the recitation (japa).
Having taken up a bundle of kuśa grass (kūrca), the wise one, facing north,
should place the syllable *A* between the feet and the syllable *Ā* on the two ankles.
The letter *i* is said to be between the knees, and another, *u*, is in the secret place;
thereafter, *ū* is in the belly, and *ṛ* is also in the heart.
*Ṛ* is at the root of the throat, and another is at the tip of the throat.
One should place the syllable *ai* on the right arm and the other, *au*, on the left; thereafter,
having placed *e* on the two lips and *ai* on the teeth,
one should place *o* on the tip of the nose and *au* in the middle of the eyes.

Having placed the letter *aṃ* in the middle and the letter *visarga* on the head, one should properly place it joined with the *nāda*, and then encircle it with the royal mantra (*rājamantra*). After that, one should place the letter *ā* on the head and the letter *ā* on the orb of the face.
The letter *i* is in the right eye, and the letter *i* is in the left eye; 29.
the letter *u* is in the right ear, and likewise the other (*ū*) in the left;
the letter *ṛ* is in the right nostril, and [the letter *ṝ*] on the left. 30.
Then, one should place the letter *e* sequentially on the two cheeks behind those [syllables], the letter *ai* on the belly, and likewise the letter *ai* on the head;
similarly, the letters *e* and *o* are placed on the sides of both rows of teeth.
The syllable *śi* with the letter *ṅ* should be placed on the tongue, and that same syllable with the visarga (*śiḥ*) should likewise be placed;
having thus deposited all the vowels in sequence, one should afterwards place the *ka*-group on the right hand, the *ca*-group on the other hand, and [the remaining groups] at the joints. 32–33.
The *ṭa*-group [of consonants] is on the right foot, and the *ta*-group on the left foot;
the two *pa* syllables are on both sides and at the back;
the *ba* syllable is on the spine, the *ra* syllable on the belly, and then the *bha* syllable in the heart.
The letter *ma* is in the middle of the belly, the letter *ya* at the base of the arm;
the letter *ra* is in the throat, and the letter *va* on the left arm. One should touch with the hand below [the navel] the letter *śa*, and the letter *ka* on the right side. 35–36.
On the left side, the letter *ṣa* should be [visualized] above the heart in sequence;
specifically, the letter *sa* on the right hand, and the letter *ha* on the other hand, while the wise practitioner touches with his hand. 37.
One should place the letter *la* on the abdomen with the tip of the *kūrca* [mudrā];
having placed the letter *kṣa* on the head, one should then place the others in sequence on the crown of the head.
Having meditated upon those lords of the letters together with the resonance (*nāda*) and joined with the *praṇava*, [one should proceed]. 38–39.
Thereafter, one should arrange [the syllables] in sequence and bind the limbs with mantras;
having uttered the single-syllable [mantra], one should especially place it on the crown and in the center.
Then, in order: "viśve" on the forehead, "nima" on the right eye, and "prāṇa" on the eyebrows.
Having said, "Speak, spreading [yourself]," over the two eyes and also the two ears;

having said, "Thou hast become the wielder of the thunderbolt," over the two nostrils; having said, "The Dhātṛ," over the two nostrils; having said, "The Ṛcs and the Yajus," over the tongue; and having said, "He is this," over the two teeth. (41–42)
At the two jaws, "Thou art Sarva";

at the lips, "And by the Sāmans, Thou art Am"; at the heart, "Thou art Tvaṣṭṛ"; at the navel, "And Mitra"—and thereafter, at the secret parts, "Thou art Viṣṇu"; and at the knees, "Thou art Bhūr-bhuvaḥ."

Having recited "ya evaṃ nityam," one should place the verses in sequence upon the two ankles, the middle of the feet, and the two knees; thereafter, O Lord of Gods, one should meditate upon Him in the head, the navel, and the feet.
Having recited "suvarbhu vardhu," the knower of mantras should sequentially deposit the worlds; then, having meditated upon the universal form (viśvarūpa) by means of the seed-syllable of Vāyu,
he should sequentially bind the worlds together and deposit the primordial seed-syllable in the heart.

Having properly placed there the primordial seed-syllable, which consists of all the gods, possesses a golden body, and is the cause of all, one should encircle it with the Praṇava; likewise, having assigned the Mātṛkā to both sides, one should place the two goddesses there. 47–48.
Having properly deposited each respective seed-syllable in the heart and likewise encircled it,
one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), gaze upon the God of gods,
offer a handful of flowers, prostrate, and seek permission.

Having prostrated before the Śakti situated in the pitcher while reciting "Idaṃ Viṣṇur," and saying "May the Blessed One come," the knower of mantras should take the Śakti from the pitcher with the *kūrca* grass and first invoke Viṣṇu into the *dhruva* vessel. 50–51.
The wise preceptor should cause this water to flow over the head;
around that pedestal—in the east, Puruṣa;
in the south, Satya; in the west, Acyuta as previously mentioned; and [in the north], Niruddhaka.

Having correctly invoked [the deities] in the north, the wise one should invoke Kapila and the others in due order, as prescribed for the placement of flowers (puṣpanyāsa), and then invoke the Mūrtis in sequence.
Then, on its right side, he should say, "I invoke Śrī. 53–54.
Having invoked Mahī on the left, having prostrated and obtained her permission,
and having placed the syllable *ma* in the heart, one should likewise invoke Brahmā as before; then,
having placed the syllable *śa* in the heart, one should invoke Rudra in due order.
Having placed the syllable *ma* and the syllable *bhṛ* in the hearts of the two sages respectively (56),
and having indeed performed the placement with their forms on the head, one should invoke them in sequence.
Having said, "This is united," one should place the *kūrca* of the connection (57).

Having uttered the syllables previously mentioned for this [deity], and having placed the *kūrca* grass with its tips pointing eastward while saying "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," one should place it between the *dhruva* and *kautuka* vessels;
and from the *kautuka* vessel, one should place it with its tips pointing north in the space between the *kautuka* and the *snāna* (ablution) vessels on the right.
With the tip pointing north and ending toward the north, one should place the *kūrca* in the center of the festival pavilion;
thus it is prescribed for the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), but not for the other two.
Likewise, from the permanent image (*dhruvabera*) one should draw forth power (*śakti*), just as light is drawn from one lamp to another in succession. 59–60.
Having correctly invoked [the deity] into the *kautuka* (protective thread) and then during the bath,
the wise and learned practitioner should meditate and invoke [the deities] from the *dhruva* vessel in their proper sequence;
or alternatively, just as [the fire] is led from the *gārhapatya* fire to the *anvāhārya*.
Therefore, the fire is always brought forward into the Āhavanīya; likewise, one should properly invoke [the deities] from the Dhruva fire into the Kautuka and other [fires],
starting from the east and proceeding around the altar for Indra and the others by their respective names.
Having thus invoked and worshipped the attendants (pārṣadas) beginning with Dhātṛ in their proper order,
and having correctly deposited their respective seed-syllables (bījas) up to the great elements (mahābhūtas),
the wise Guru should perform the invocation; however, he must not place the seed-syllable in the vessel itself.
Having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), he should gaze upon the Lord of the lords of gods and perform prostration. Then,
having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made, he should finally perform worship as prescribed for the visualization (darśana).
Furthermore, he should teach the Vedas, the Sūtras, the Purāṇas, and so forth, in their proper sequence.
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) and performed the fire-oblation (homa), he should present the sacrificial offering (bali).
After worshipping the image of the deity, he should circumambulate the temple.

Having praised the deity and bowed to the preceptor, one should subsequently perform worship according to the sequence prescribed for the ritual bathing; that night, one should carry out the bathing ceremony.
Then, following the conclusion of the installation, the festival should take place during the afternoon of that same day.
And during the consecration, one should give all the ritual requisites to the preceptor;
otherwise, they will perish and become fruitless, of this there is no doubt.
A wise person should bury unused materials in a pit.
"It is possible for me, and even for the immortals, to describe that fruit: having become the lord of Vaikuṇṭha, one shall personally attain the same form as Him.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Fixed Image," in the section on Sacrifice within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā* of the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*.
In the Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra of Bhārgava,
this is the thirtieth chapter: The Installation of Śrī and Bhūmi.

Now I shall describe separately the supreme procedure for the installation of the two goddesses, Śrī and Bhūmi, once the deity has first been established. A wise person should install the marriage-thread (kautuka) of the goddess, whether it has been previously applied or not.
One should especially establish the festival together with the two goddesses.
For the sake of the prosperity of that village and particularly for the sake of the festival,
one should have the deity and the two goddesses fashioned using the very same materials with which they were originally made.
In some cases, there are two goddesses at each station (*sthānaka*) or on the seat (*āsana*);
in that case, it should certainly be the *dhruva-āsana*, and likewise the *cauda-sotsava-sthānaka*.
Here, one should perform the rite for the two goddesses, and the *dhruva* seat as previously described shall be used.
The wise one should perform the ritual according to the very same procedure mentioned previously (verse 5).
Having offered the sprouts either in front or to the south,
and having designated the sacrificial hall, he should decorate it so that it is well-adorned.
Having placed the *sabhyāgni* in the middle row, and the *śrāmaṇakāgni* like fire on the right,

one should then construct an altar (*vedi*) in the eastern direction from that, and subsequently a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the *aupāsana* fire according to the sequence. The measure of the image (*bimba*) is one and a half [units] in the row of the Dharma.
Having constructed a pit to the east of that according to the previously mentioned measurements (verse 8),
the wise man should have a bed made for the purpose of the Soma-cooking on the ground;
likewise, he should perform the *aupāsana* rite to the east, and he should carry out that pit to the east.
Having taken the two goddesses who have entered [the state of] acceptance as before,
one should place them in order in the western sacrificial hall facing east;
and having performed the previously mentioned *vāstuhoma* and purification as before.
Having sprinkled water over all [the vessels], the wise one should prepare the fire in sequence;
having collected [the fire] as before into the pitcher and prepared it separately in each of the seven jars, he should perform the ceremonial bath (saṃsnāpya) just as previously described.
Having likewise spread out separate beds on the bed-altar for the two of them, and having bathed the two goddesses as previously described along with the water-pot (kumbha),
one should finally tie the protective cord (pratisara) and then have them lie down in succession from east to west.
Having made an upper covering, one should perform the surrounding enclosure;
having worshipped upon the altar, the wise one should successively worship Jaya and the others, praising the previously mentioned *hautra* rite in each of the two *aupāsana* fires. 14–15.
One should invoke the goddesses, Jayā and the others, in sequence with their respective mūrti-mantras; having extinguished them in due order, one should cause the utterance of "svāhā" to be made.
Then, in the southern fire-pit, one should worship with the Śrīsūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymns.
Having offered oblations with the Jayā and other Mūrti-mantras, one should provide thorough protection.
In the northern fire-pit, having offered oblations with the Mahīsūkta, the Vaiṣṇava [mantras], the Jayā and other Mūrti-mantras, and together with the Vyāhṛtis; 17–18.
Having pacified all the Daityas in the assembly fire as before, he should protect the assembly like a god and pass the remainder of the night in due order.
Having bathed at dawn and entered the sacrificial hall as previously described, he should proceed.
Having raised [the fires] and adorned them with other cloths as before,
he should worship the Guru as previously described and likewise dismiss the fire. Then,
having properly taken those two fires, he should join them into the Sabhya fire in due order.
Having performed the concluding oblation (antahoma) and properly maintained the fire at the end,
one should join it with the aupāsana fire, and here peace (śānti) is well-offered.
At an auspicious moment when a favorable hour has arisen, one should take up the water-pot as before.
After following behind the two goddesses and entering the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha),
one should place them upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) facing the marriage canopy (kautuka),
using their respective mantras; and the two goddesses should be placed at the right and left sides.
The Guru should recite the respective hymns previously mentioned for the Kautuka;
having performed the placement of the syllables (nyāsa) as before, he should likewise do so for the two goddesses in the Acala [mandala],
having first properly invoked them in sequence, like one lamp from another lamp.
One should thus invoke [the deity] in the proper sequence and also cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made.
Having worshipped the Imperishable One together with the two goddesses according to the very sequence prescribed for worship, one should duly offer the previously mentioned oblation (havis).

Whether accompanied or unaccompanied by the two goddesses, one should perform the bathing and the offering of the *baliberam* (food-offering vessel) for the immutable Lord, according to the desire of the patron.
This should be done if defects such as decay have occurred in the *kautuka* image.
Having abandoned that [image] even without [formally dismissing] the Goddess, and having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the Śakti as before;
29. the best of those learned in the scriptures, having observed the gravity or lightness of the faults, if the fault is grave, the wise man should likewise abandon the image. 30.
One should not abandon an image suitable for ritual union (sandhāna), nor likewise should one abandon the mental image;
if one abandons the image out of delusion, one certainly becomes more sinful.
Having fashioned the physical form (bera), thereafter, in the case of fixed images (dhruva) and so forth, it is the same.
The wise knower of mantras, beginning with the opening of the eyes, should have the image fashioned from the same materials as those used previously; and in this matter,
the wise one should establish the marriage ritual together with the two goddesses just as before.
Among all images that have become damaged, one should abandon that which has arisen from a defect;
having made a new image, one should worship it together with the remaining [deities].
If an image should be stolen by thieves, then [one should act] oneself.

The wise one should not abandon [the previous deities] as before; rather, once others have been established, having installed them in another location, he should worship them according to his means. This applies unless those two goddesses are the *kautuka* (auspicious marriage-thread) itself. 35–36.
Having had [the image] made, the wise man should not install the two goddesses as previously described;
however, if the two goddesses have been thus installed and are free from defects, he should worship them together with those [other deities]. 37.
In all respects, the primary importance of those two is equal, each being singular in its own right.
O wise ones, one should worship with them, along with those aforementioned goddesses, in a state of joyful wonder; and I shall now describe the manner of Hari’s taking of a wife.
At the conclusion of the evening worship, having prostrated correctly before the two goddesses, if the Brahmin is the patron, he should likewise bring the two goddesses to his own home,
install them well, and perform their worship there together with the preceptor.
Either in a separate house or in a delightful pavilion,
having decorated the sacrificial hall as before with auspicious rites, and having purified the side-entrances and the pathways leading to it; 41–42.
One should fashion the height of the swing (ḍolā) to be one and a half times the length of a staff, using beautiful wood from the *kramuka*, *nālikera*, or sacrificial trees.
Having placed it specifically for the sake of the Goddess Śrī on the right side of the swing—
Having placed the tips to the left for my sake, one should firmly bind them;
the wise person, having bound the tips together with a cord, a noose of *kuśa* grass, or one made from coconut fiber, [should proceed]. 44–45.
Having worshipped Śeṣa in that [image] according to the prescribed method,
one should join him with the *lamba* (the cord) and bind those two very firmly with the mantra "Obeisance to Śrī" (*śriye jāta*).
One should then lead [the deity] and worship Śeṣa upon his seat, adorning him fully.
One should wrap a garland of *darbha* grass around the pillars in a clockwise direction (47).
One should then wrap that [garland] with a moving cord made of *campaka* and *utpala* flowers in sequence;
having smeared [the area] with cow dung, it should be adorned with five colors (48).
Having performed these, one should worship Jayā and the others around them in sequence;
then, when an auspicious moment has arrived, having prostrated before the God of Gods,
one should bathe him thoroughly with scented water and adorn him with ornaments.
Having worshipped him and bound the protective thread (*kautuka*), and having prostrated before the God of gods,
the wise one should place Him— adorned with all ornaments— as before, upon a chariot, a palanquin, a horse, or a swing.
Accompanied by conch shells and kahalas, joined with dance and song, accompanied by the sound of hymns and joined with the resonance of auspicious cries (svasti),
together with all ceremonial offerings and accompanied by a rain of flowers. 52.
Accompanied by horses, elephants, and other mounts, and surrounded by lamps,
one should bring the deity like a king and cause him to enter the swing;
thereafter, having taken up the two goddesses, one should install them in their former place.
The sacrificer, together with his wives, should bow down to the deity from behind,
wash the deity's feet with milk, and offer a handful of flowers (kusumāñjali).
Having offered the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) here, and having bowed and obtained permission, [he should proceed].
Together with all the devotees, he should cause him to enter that house.
Having brought [the image] and placed the Lord of the gods upon a well-adorned seat on the right side, facing east, the preceptor should attend to him like a king.
The sacrificer, together with his wives, having prostrated and obtained their permission,
should cause the *madhuparka* as prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* to be offered;
this begins from the offering of water and continues until the sight of the *dhruva*.
One should perform all the rites in every respect according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtras.
Having determined the lineage (gotra) of that God of gods by means of the lineage of the Guru,
one should cause it to be bestowed upon the two Goddesses and the patron (yajamāna) by means of that very lineage.
If the king is the sacrificer, one who knows the mantras should cause [the gift] to be given by means of the master’s lineage;
if a Vaiśya or a Śūdra is the sacrificer, one should cause it to be given by the master’s hand. This specific rule has been declared; the remainder is according to the path stated in the Sūtras.

Thereafter, one should have [the image] fashioned according to the rules and worship the Guru properly. Then, having taken the fire of Viṣṇu’s installation with the mantra and having divided it into two parts, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) upon all the limbs for the sake of prosperity.
For my sake, he should take [the fire] from the left and place it here in this house;
at the conclusion of the rite, having properly grasped the previously mentioned fire,
he should establish it in the aforementioned kitchen and guard the fire well.
From that time forward, one should perform the previously mentioned oblation in the perpetual fire (nityāgni).
Having completed the ritual actions here up to the point of the observation of the Pole Star (dhruva),
and having given the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā), one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.

In the marriage chamber, one should likewise consecrate the Lord of Gods together with the two goddesses using abundant waters, according to the path prescribed for the pure ablution (śuddhasnāna). Then,
having seated him upon another throne and adorned him with garments and other ornaments, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped with the eight services (aṣṭopacāra) and even with the royal forms [of ritual],

the rice cooked by the officiating priests (ṛtvij) according to the path prescribed for the oblation (havis)— the nectar (naivedya) here should be prepared according to one's capacity, but not exceeding six droṇas at most. 68–69.
Having offered abundant mouth-perfume here in the house,
and having properly fanned the fire with composure along with the hosts of Śrī, [the worshipper], adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by all musical instruments, [should proceed].
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, he should enter his own abode.

If, during the rite of taking the hand in marriage, the path of the gods has been touched by twice-born men, and if there is a fault because of that, then [the rite] arises through that very [act]. 71–71.
Having entered the temple and performed the ritual ablution as before,
one should install the deity in the seat of life (jīvasthāna) and properly offer the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Thus is the marriage festival performed by him according to the prescribed characteristics.
The sin committed during his lifetime perishes at that very moment.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of Śrī-Bhūmi," within the section on Sacrifice (Yajñādhikāra) in the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Vaikhānasas. This concludes the section on Sacrifice.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter: the separate consecration of the sleeping [idol] and other [rituals],
the method for separate consecration, and also [the rules for] the bathing and festival ceremonies.
I shall describe the procedure for the image; listen, O best of sages!

Having fashioned the image with all its characteristics according to the previously stated rules, and having ensured the astrological signs are favorable for the maker, one should do so even before that day.
Having offered the sprouts, one should also gather the ritual requisites;
having likewise prepared the sacrificial hall, one should adorn it as prescribed by the rules.
O wise ones, if the installation of all three images is performed together—
Likewise, one should perform two fire-offerings (homa) for the "untying of the eyes" in a single fire;
having separately shown the substances for the vision of the cow and so forth, one should carry out the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) as prescribed for the sake of purifying that image. 4–5.
Having likewise prepared the worship of the three deities together in a single water-pot as before,
the wise one should perform the constant worship in the water of the pot according to the path of the guru’s instruction, like a lamp from a lamp in succession.
Having invoked [the deities] and worshipped them, one should also cause [the disciple] to perform prostration (7).
Having established the five fires together with the lotus [vessel] according to the previously mentioned method,
the wise one should likewise have the fire-sacrifice (homa) performed and other rites as before (8).
Having bathed the deities individually with seven jars, one should likewise place them individually upon the aforementioned grains on the altar (vedī),
having spread out [seats] such as those made of eggs and so forth, and install the deities in their proper order.
Together with the water-pot, one should worship the lamps with the eight forms;
likewise, having bound the protective thread (pratisara) and laid [the image] down in due order,
one should praise the fire-sacrifice (hotra) as previously described, specifically reciting the mantras of the forms.
Having invoked [the deity] as far as Gaṅgādhara, he should likewise offer the *juṣṭākāra* oblations;
then, at the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), he should spend the remainder of the night in the sequence previously described.
Having bathed in the morning, the righteous one, without waking the deity, should proceed as before.
Having removed the withered offerings, one should worship with the eight forms.

Having entered the inner sanctum and placed the gems upon the pedestal as before, the wise one, having likewise dismissed the sacrificial fire, should establish it in the perpetual fire (nityāgni) in due order. 13–14.
The patron, having honored the preceptor, should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with water;
then, having prostrated before the preceptor, he should indeed request him for the installation.
Thereafter, the preceptor, taking up the pitcher and carrying it upon his head himself, [should proceed].
Then, having led the presiding deities clockwise around the temple in that manner, those whose wealth is austerity (the officiants) entered the sanctum and,
placing the ritual pitcher upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the Dhruva pole.
They should specifically install the deities in their respective places as before;
having taken the Śakti from the pitcher, they should likewise [install it] in the permanent image (dhruvabera).
Then, having invoked the Śakti from the permanent image into the bathing vessel and the sacrificial fire, [they should proceed].
Having invoked [the deity] into the *balibera*, one should worship it in that same sequence. 19.

All else is as previously stated; this is the specific distinction according to the sequence: the wise one should perform the bathing during the *snāpana* rite and the festival during the *autsava* rite. 20.
At that time, one should perform the daily festival (nityotsava) at the *balibera*. He who performs this with devotion goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
This is the procedure for the five types of installation (*pañcapratiṣṭhā-vidhi*).
O ascetics rich in austerity, I shall now declare the five types of consecrations and their proper times;
one should cause the ground to be ploughed only after having thoroughly examined it. Having constructed the temple there, [one should perform the rites] to the south of the location of the door.

O wise ones, this is the time and location for the specific placement of the first bricks on the ground below according to the prescribed rule; thereafter, the knower of mantras, having prepared the foundation (garbha) according to the stated injunction, [should proceed]. 23–24.
One should place the vessel within the womb [of the altar] either at the end of the neck, within the band, or at the time of establishing the door; thereafter,
the wise one [should do so] at the conclusion of the temple.

Then, having sequentially observed and properly established the remaining divine limbs, the wise one should then install the *sthūpī* and the *śūla*, and having set them according to the rule, he should coat them with lime and paint. 26–27.
First, one should perform the laying of the bricks for the foundation, and after that, the laying of the core;

then, having properly installed the trident (śūla), one should again perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā). O best of the twice-born, having thus performed the laying of the head-bricks (mūrdheṣṭakā), [the rite is complete].
The sequence is as follows in the *Pañcapratiṣṭhā*, especially regarding the *sāmṛta* [rite]:

29. If it is specifically the *hāraka* [type], then having first placed the *iṣṭakā* (brick) in order, one should thereafter place the *garbha* (inner sanctum), and then again the *mūrdheṣṭakā* (topmost brick). 30.
Then, having properly established the trident and smeared it with its respective color,
the wise one should install the *dhruva* [liṅga] along with the *kautuka* and other items upon the support (*dhāraka*).
Furthermore, he should perform the worship of the *dhruva* at the beginning, middle, and end.
One should establish [the deity] at the end of the *dhruva* and at the end of the class (*jātivarga*) together with the *kautuka*.

Having first determined the temple according to the prescribed rite, and having constructed it with its proper characteristics in the location desired for the child’s station as previously stated, one should proceed. 32–33.
Having taken up the clay image and installed it according to the ritual procedure,
and having performed the consecration at the end, the Guru should then quickly [remove] the image from the house of offerings to the primary abode as before.
That which is established after having been prepared as "with nectar" (sāmṛta), they know that as such.
When one is unable [to perform the full rite], the installation performed in the primary abode with auspicious items and so forth, as before, is called "the remover" (hāraka). 35–36.

Of these two, they know that which possesses nectar (sāmṛta) to be primary, while that which merely bears it is secondary; therefore, even the distinction between the *dhruvārcā* and the other is common in general, yet specific in particular cases.
In all scriptures, in every way, the desire of the sacrificer and his consort is paramount.

O you whose wealth is austerity, having first grasped the treatise alone (verse 38), I shall explain the method for establishing a temple two stories high (verse 39); having constructed the abode according to the rules for the qualification of the resident, it should be endowed with ornaments.

First, having established the seat of enjoyment (bhogāsana), and then establishing the second position in the second [place], one who knows the mantra should worship according to the will of the practitioner, following either the path of yoga, the path of enjoyment, and so forth, or by means of a single path. 40.

One should have stationary images (dhruvaberas) made as previously described, according to the requirements of each respective floor; however, because they are measured across many stories, this is especially true for the *sāmṛta* type.
The conclusion of one story and the beginning of the next should coincide with the end of the stone slab (prastara). 41–42.
Therefore, in each respective house, the wise man, having fixed those various *dhruvas* at their proper times, should have another floor constructed once it has been covered;
such *dhruvas* are to be placed within those palaces on every successive floor.
One should install the smaller members especially one above the other;
for if it is done otherwise, there will be misfortune. At the very beginning, one should place a stone [pedestal]; in the second stage, wood; and in the third, the *śūla* (spike) itself.

In the fourth [case], it is declared that [the image] should be made of clay; in other cases, it should be made of metal. Alternatively, one should install a trident (śūla) everywhere as prescribed by the ritual rules (46), having smeared it with the appropriate color according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The wise one should commence the consecration in due order according to the prescribed rite (47). On the day specified, having offered the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) for each successive level,
he should gather the necessary materials (48).
Likewise, having performed the rite of opening the eyes and having consecrated [the image] in that same manner,
one should act as before in front of the sacrificial hall and at the primary ground; furthermore,
on its western side, one should perform the rites for the sake of the two stories.

To its western side, likewise for the three-tiered [structure], one should cause a sacrificial hall (yāgaśālā) and its ornaments to be constructed as before; and likewise, one should cause an altar (vedi) to be made in their centers as before. 50–51.

Having observed fire-pits for each of the deities as before, the wise one should choose them on all sides according to their respective requirements; likewise, he should do so for the officiating priests (ṛtvij) to the north of the temple.
Likewise, having performed the Vāstuhoma in a single fire for all mobile [deities] in every respect (53),

and having likewise purified them, one should perform the oblation in the universal fire (sarvāgni). Then the preceptor, having prepared the water-pots according to the ritual rule (54), [should proceed].
Having bathed the deities with water-pots, he should likewise tie the protective thread (kautuka);
having praised the previously mentioned *hotṛ* priest specifically on the primary ground,
he should invoke all the attendants (*pārṣada*) and likewise offer an oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*).
Together with Viśvāmitra and the others, one should invoke the two remaining [deities] up to Mukhapālī; this is the specific distinction, while the rest should be performed as before.
In the morning, having raised the deities at an auspicious moment when a favorable conjunction arises, [one should proceed].
Having fully honored the teachers, one should likewise worship the Vaiṣṇavas;
having installed the deities in their respective inner sanctums as before,
and having invoked them as previously described, one should worship them and present the offerings.

In the second story and above, one should specifically worship those beginning with Brahmā and ending with Vaiṣṇava—seventeen in number—from the first story up to the top. The wise man should first worship all the attendants on that [first] story. 59–60.
One should perform all occasional rites (naimittika), such as sleeping festivals and the like, or indeed the extraction of the offering (bali-uddharaṇa), on the first floor; likewise,
one should perform the daily rites (nitya-karma) on the other floors as previously described.
When there are multiple stories, from the third story onwards, one should perform the ritual for each floor (*talaṃ prati talam*).
A wise man should perform the daily bath (*nityasnāna*) at the beginning of each [floor], or he may perform it only once at the very beginning.
However, when the builder is in a hurry and measuring many floors, [the rule as stated above applies]. 62–63.
Whether on land or in water, one should install each [deity] together with the *kautuka* [thread];

then, designating another [deity], one should worship it in the place of the Child (*bāla*). And if the place of the Child has not been prepared for any reason whatsoever, [one should proceed accordingly].
Some say that one should install [the image] on the left side of the portico (mukhamaṇḍapa).

If it has been installed in another location, then the initial rite (kriyā) should likewise be performed in the primary temple (mūlālaya); however, if the patron (yajamāna) is in a hurry, [the procedure] is as previously stated. 65–66.
Without regard for time, the wise one should indeed install each of these as far as the edge of the site; there is no doubt that no fault arises.
In all the scriptures, whatever is pleasing to the patron is for the sake of the deity.
Indeed, by speaking what is pleasing to him, the Guru does not incur any fault.

(68) As long as there is a dome (śikhara), one should likewise install a pinnacle-stone (iṣṭakā), a finial (stūpī), and a central shaft (śūla) upon the head, and then have the excellent rites performed. (69)

Then, one should install [the image] as previously described for the installation in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*). Having first established the fixed stars (*dhruva*), one should subsequently place the head-bricks (*mūrdheṣṭakā*) upon it.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Separate Installation of the Bathing and Other Rites," in the section on Sacrificial Rituals within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence for the worship of the Lord of Gods.
Having risen at dawn, the worshipper, while mentally recollecting the Lord of Gods, [should proceed].

Having bathed according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtras and performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), and having recited "pra tad viṣṇu stavate," one should go again to the temple and first perform a prostration toward the vimāna with the aforementioned mantra.

Having circumambulated the celestial palace (vimāna) clockwise, there are two [options] in the first enclosure: if there is a desire for a stable abode, the worshiper should perform the circumambulation within the inner mandala; if not, one may or may not do so. 3–4.

Except at the time of twilight, neither the worshipper nor any other devotee should cross the shadow of the temple; if they do so, it brings about misfortune. At twilight, both in the evening and in the morning, one should perform circumambulation of Hari’s abode.
The fruit of that is impossible to describe, even by me or by Brahmā himself.
Having performed two circumambulations and having prostrated before Vimala,
he took up the yantra and said, "May the Rakṣas be driven away!"
Having uttered "hiraṇyapāṇi," one should join the door-panels in sequence;
then, with the mantra "divaṃ vivṛṇu," one should perform the opening.
Having entered within by that same [mantra], one should prostrate before the immutable Lord.
Having struck [the drum] with both hands while reciting the mantra "May [the Lord] come," and having said "With devotion,
to the Blessed One," he should pray to the Son of Devakī;
likewise, the disciple, having bathed and bowed to the God of gods, should do the same.
Having recited "duhataṃ diva," the devoted one takes up the water-pot;
having recited "toya ādyam" for the sake of prosperity, he draws water from the river, and having recited "somaṃ rājānam," he enters the temple once again.
Having placed [the water] in a reservoir for collecting water and purified it with a mantra,

having scented it with usīra and other fragrant substances, and having sprinkled it with the *mārjanī* while reciting the mantra "Idam āpaḥ śivāḥ" and "Avadhūta," one should perform the purification. 12–13.
Having said, "Āśāsustava," one should sprinkle with cow-dung water everywhere,
especially at the womb, the doors, and so forth, at every door;
one should smear [the area] shaped like a half-moon with cow-dung.

Having washed all the vessels around the sacrificial ground (bhūtapīṭha) to the extent of a cow-hide, the wise man, reciting "O raw grains, O strength," should cook the oblations and side-dishes according to the prescribed rule. 15–16.

Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should honor the Lord of Gods with the mantra "pūtastasya. Then, having removed the remains of the offering (nirmālya) and wiped [the deity],
and having thoroughly worshipped Viṣvaksena, he should worship the other attendants (varṣada).
Thereafter, the wise worshiper should likewise wear the sacred thread (pavitra).

Then, having prostrated before the presiding deities of the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), such as Keśava and the others, he should apply the vertical marks with either sandalwood paste or clay. 18–19.
Having performed the nyāsa of the *mātṛkā* as before, one should meditate upon oneself as Hari; then,
touching the heart while reciting "Brahma, O Brahman, the Self," and saying "The sky, the sky you are" for the head, and "O tuft" for the tuft.
One should personally perform the rite of armor (*kavaca*) with the mantra "sa vedā";
then, one should meditate upon the discus and conch on the right and left arms respectively,
and thereafter, for the sake of self-protection, one should clearly meditate upon the bow in the east.
The wise one should visualize the Śakti on the right side, the mace (gadā) on the other [the left], the sword (khaḍga) well-placed on the left, and the discus (cakra) above;
and Vāsuki in the intermediate directions, as well as the other weapons as before.
One should remember the Lord ending with *phaṭ* while touching [the head] with the right hand (24).
Or, one should likewise remember the protection with the Vedic mantra "O Viṣṇu, protect you," and with "You are the Sun" on the left side, and "You are the Moon" on the left. (25)
Having renounced [the senses], the wise man should place the seed-syllable *ā* at the beginning in his heart, as well as the deities of the directions:
"Agni, Aśvin, Vidhi, Yajña, Brahmā, and Indra.
Then, touching from the thumb to the little finger, he should likewise [place] the presiding deities.
Having remembered the two palms of the hands as the mandalas of the Sun and the Moon (27), one should touch the forearms with the mantra "In this [space] is this"; then,
having said "Become Brahman," one should personally contemplate oneself as that Deity (28).
Then, following the path of the guru’s instruction, that righteous soul should perform *prāṇāyāma*;
having risen from that state, he should again [worship] with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī and with the five form-mantras (*mūrti-mantra*) between the feet of Dhruva.
Having offered a flower at the feet and finally prostrated with the *kautuka*,
and having brought the *kautuka* while reciting the mantra "Bhūḥ prapadye," he should place the imperishable [deity] together with the two goddesses in the northeast of the root abode.
Having placed [the deity] upon the bathing throne while reciting "pari raṃha," and having bathed [him] according to the ritual procedure, one should wipe [him] there with a cloth alone; then,
having placed [him] upon the worship throne, one should adorn [him] with garments and other ornaments.

Having sprinkled the seat with the *Āyatri* mantra while reciting "asaṃyuktam," the wise and intelligent practitioner should cast down the *kūrca* grass—connected to the *dhruva* and *kautuka* mantras—at the eastern door; at the western door, he should place it with its tips pointing eastward. 33–34.
To the south or the north, one should place a kūrca-grass seat facing north between the feet of Dhruva, saying "Obeisance to Viṣṇu. Then,
one should offer flowers and other offerings in the directions starting from the east, beginning with Puruṣa and the others.
One should first properly place the eight [deities] beginning with Kapila in the corners;
in the second [circle], one should place the [deities] beginning with Vārāha in the four cardinal directions in sequence;
and in the intermediate directions, one should place those beginning with Subhadrā, as well as the flowers. 36–37.
In the third [stage], one should indeed place flowers here for the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in their proper order;
while remaining steady, one performs this especially upon the seat.
Likewise, one should place them all around the extended foot.
Then, for one lying with their head toward the north, [the thread] should be placed between the two feet;

or else, with the mantra of the forms of the two goddesses ending in "namaḥ," one should offer it at the edge of the pedestal, starting from the east and extending to the northeast for the *kautuka* as well. 39–40.
Likewise, one should worship Subhadrā and the eight deities, as well as Mitra and the others;
furthermore, one should worship Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhṛgu on the south and north [sides].
Similarly, one should worship Brahmā and Śaṅkara at the entrance of the marriage pavilion (kautuka).

Thereafter, the wise disciple should worship Dhātṛ and the others, as well as the nine attendants (pārṣadas) mentioned previously. Having performed the worship up to the offering of the *arghya*, he should worship Dhātṛ and the others in sequence from the main door using the *mūrti-mantras* ending with "namaḥ. 42–43.
One should worship only those respective door-keepers and not others; all the attendants of the Vedas and so forth would become twice as many, O ascetics.
Some desire worship, while others indeed desire offerings.
At dawn itself, one should worship all members of both types of assemblies.
At that time, the wise man should offer a bali-oblation to those who desire strength, and likewise cause a bali-oblation to be performed for others who desire power.

Even if [the ritual] is inverted, misfortune will occur; therefore, one should also perform worship for those two with due regard. Prior to the worship of the God of Gods, at the conclusion of the offering, one should cast the *bali* for those dear to the God.
That worship is of two kinds: daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika). (48) One should offer the oblation (bali) for them when the sacrificial food (havis) has been presented during the daily rite;
however, one should not offer the oblation at other times, except during festivals and the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice. (49)
Having gathered all the vessels for the worship, as if in a state of exhaustion,
one should place a seamless, concealed cloth at the inner door for the purpose of the worshiper’s vision during the midday rite. 50.
[One should avoid] those who revile the Vedas, heretics, initiated persons, the deaf, and so forth.
Seated on the right side of the deity, facing east,
the worshipper should sit with one knee bent, facing either east or north.
Having sat upon a cloth, a wooden plank, or in a forest suitable for a seat,
and having recited the *ātmasūkta* while remembering the Deity,
one should say "Suvar, Bhuvar, Bhūḥ" over the head, the navel, and the feet. (53)
Having placed the seed-syllable *ya* in the heart within the sandals,
and having encircled those two with *praṇavas* joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*,
one should likewise meditate upon the syllables while recollecting the God of gods.
Having bowed and extracted the aspiration (praṇidhi), just as one lamp is lit from another lamp,

the righteous-souled one, with devotion, invoked it through the aspiration along with the two goddesses into that water; then, having meditated upon it in the same manner, he placed it upon the head of the auspicious image.
"Invoke Viṣṇu," saying this, one should cause [the deity] to flow through the forms in sequence.
The wise one should likewise invoke Śrī on the right side and Mahī on the left; some do so both in the ritual image and during the festival. 57–58.
One should perform both the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the dismissal (*visarga*), as well as the bathing (*snāpana*) and the festival (*autsava*).

Furthermore, in the daily worship (*nityārcanā*), one may perform these either at the beginning or likewise at the end. When [the deity] has been installed in that house, one should indeed perform the rite with the sacred thread (*kautuka*) upon a single altar (*vedī*).
If one performs the invocation and dismissal with the *balā* flower during worship—
having thus invoked [the deity] at the edge of the pedestal and prepared a seat with flowers, *darbha*, or *kuśa* grass, while saying, "May the Lord accept this seat"— 60–61.

Having said, "O you who are superior to all," and having uttered, "Welcome to the presence" and "The mind is directed toward you," one should request the water for washing the feet with the mantra beginning with "anumadānaṃ.
Then, with the mantra beginning with "trīṇi padā," one should offer water for the feet at the [deity's] feet.
With the mantra "śanno devī," he should likewise offer the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka);
then, reciting "tad viṣṇoḥ paramam," "tad viprāsaḥ," and "varo mātre," he should likewise [offer] the hand-washing water (karman) for Viṣṇu according to the mantras.
The wise one should offer flowers, incense, perfume, lamps, and the water-offering (arghya) in due order with those same mantras, reciting "Trirdehi" three times as before,
while remembering the presiding deities of the substances along with those aforementioned mantras.
The wise know that among all ritual offerings, that which is dear to Hari is most worthy of honor;
therefore, the intelligent devotee should present what is auspicious and comparable to the madhuparka offering.
Consequently, at the conclusion, he should first cause the guest to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed mantras.
If no material substance is available, one should offer water; if water is unavailable at dawn, one should offer unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
At the conclusion of the bath, as well as for the water for washing the feet (pādya), one may offer water using a kūrca.
This applies especially at the end of the water-offering (arghya) and at the beginning and end of the sacrificial oblation (havis).
In that same manner, there shall be water for sipping; one should not perform this elsewhere.
One should offer the bath, the towel, the garment, the upper cloth, the ornament, and the sacred thread in due order with the appropriate mantras according to the prescribed characteristics.
Reciting the mantra "āpo mitraśca tejaśca bhūto bhūta," and at the conclusion of the mantra "agnim dūtam," one should again remember the presiding deities;
thereafter, one should offer the items from the foot-water (pādya) up to the lamp, using the previously mentioned mantras.

But in the absence of material offerings, the wise one should worship the two goddesses together with the Lord in sequence using flowers and the *mūrti-mantras*, each according to their respective mantras (70). Afterwards,
he should perform the ceremonial bathing (*snāpana*), the festival (*autsava*), and worship the *baliberam* (the offering image) (73).
Having smeared the mandala with cow dung in front of me,
the disciple, having received permission from the Guru, should take a vessel of sacrificial oblation and worship the Sun in due order while reciting the mantra "adhāvanī."

With the mantra "devasya tvā," he should sprinkle [the offering] with ghee alone. Then, having divided the food in the vessel into four parts, the wise man, chanting Vaiṣṇava mantras, should place one portion into the vessel while mentally recollecting the deity.
Regarding the side-dishes: one should first place them into the vessel with the mantra;
having composed oneself with the Gāyatrī, one should take them and place them upon the maṇḍala, on a tripod made of gold or the like, or upon a cloth over the maṇḍala. 77.
Having placed [the vessel] and poured clarified butter into it, one should place a flower upon it.
Having touched it while reciting "I am He," and saying "Subhūḥ svayam" (The auspicious one himself), one should subsequently offer the oblation with the five Mūrti-mantras.
The two goddesses likewise, either after the bathing and other rites or even from them,
whether seated or standing, should perform what is fitting for that image. Then the Guru, having taken a second portion for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), [proceeds further].
Having performed the oblation as previously described, the wise man should again offer the *bali* offering.
Then, saying "This is sweet, cool water for Viṣṇu," he should subsequently give water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), followed by a cloth scented with perfumes.

Having separated the root and the tip of the betel leaf and having perfumed it, one should divide four areca nuts and likewise two more; then one should give that [betel] together with the lime powder, or even separately from the ghee. 83.
"From the ghee," so it is said. Or else, one may give it combined with the powder.
The younger [disciple] should receive this in nine ways as described;
having worshipped the bali offering according to the prescribed rite, or by means of the bali-bera itself,
he should thereafter perform circumambulation according to the method stated for all cases.
The knower of mantras should perform prostrations according to the prescribed rite with the Viṣṇu-sūkta;
having offered a handful of flowers, he should request, "Forgive me.
Having likewise prostrated before the lords of the gates, he should do so with the mantra beginning with "Sūrya."
One should bolt the door afterwards and release it before the appointed time.
If, out of delusion, Hari becomes angry at an improper time, quarrels will break out in that village, and the people will depart hither and thither, clad in their clothes.
The worshipper, having taken for himself a fourth part and half of the Vaiśvadeva offering,
should eat the remaining portion after the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite;
this includes the remnants of the Bali offering, the remnants of the Homa, and the remnants of the Vaiśvadeva itself.
The worshipper should take [the food] for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva offering and for his own meal (90). Having taken the portion offered and divided it into four parts,
O wise ones, one part should be given to Senaśa (91).
The food offered to Viṣṇusena becomes *nirmālya*; therefore, a wise man, having taken that offering, should give it to cows or to a Śūdra.
Taking two parts of what remains, it should be given to the twice-born.
All the twice-born should partake [of the food] like the remains of the guru’s meal;
for Viṣṇu is the father of all. Therefore, that which has been offered should be eaten by the Brahmins who are the refuge, as well as by the officiating priests and the worshipper. 93–94.
One should not give [food] especially to Caṇḍālas, outcasts, and others, nor even to other heretics; for if one were to sacrifice [for them], it would become a source of fault.
An expiation for this is impossible for me to declare, nor even for Brahmā.
Therefore, a wise man should not cause those who are excluded from the lineage of the thread (tantu) to offer [the oblation].
As I have previously declared in the Khila section, one should perform it according to that very rule; likewise, at midday, one should worship according to the procedure stated in the Khila. 96–97.

The rules for the preparation of oblations, all other constant rites in every respect, the rules for side-dishes such as those made from cow products, and likewise the rules for the daily festivals and the offering of sacrificial oblations (bali). 98.
One should perform all the secondary services according to the procedure prescribed in the *Khila*.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Daily Worship," in the section on Sacrifice within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[End of] the *Bhārgava* [portion] of the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*.
In the lunar mansions of the month, or in other auspicious asterisms, there is authority for sacrifice in those auspicious asterisms.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
The Occasional Worship. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain; listen, O best of sages!
I shall describe the occasional worship which bestows the fruits of all desires. 1.

Wise scholars who have mastered the Vedas declare that worship on the new moon and full moon days, as well as on the twelfth lunar day and during the Śravaṇa asterism, is the primary form of worship. They also state that the Viṣṇu-pañcarakṣā constitutes occasional (naimittika) worship.
If, during the regular daily worship in that month, there is indeed a fault due to ignorance—
whatever is deficient or in excess becomes complete through worship on those [specified] lunar months, asterisms, other auspicious asterisms, and likewise on the five days of Viṣṇu.
Midday is said to be the time for the worship of the God during the equinoxes,
solstices, transits, and the *vyatīpāta* yoga, in due order;
and at those respective times, one should worship the Lord of Gods according to the prescribed injunctions.
The wise sages declare that Jayā and Jayantī are meritorious lunar days that bestow the fruits of all desires and remove all sins; specifically,
when Punarvasu occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha.
Whether joined [with the asterism] or not, it is likewise recited as "Jayantī.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, when it is joined with Rohiṇī or even without it,
it is proclaimed as "Jayantī" by those who have mastered the Vedas.
The wise know that *Jayantī* is joined with either the *Saumya* (Monday) or the *Āgneya* (Sunday).
*Jayā* shall be the foremost day, and *Jayantī* likewise follows the rule;
the wise should perform the worship of *Jayā* at midday and honor Rāghava.
One should worship Kṛṣṇa on the day of Candrodayā and likewise on Jayantī;

one should worship Him on both Jayā and Jayantī for the pacification of faults. One should also perform worship during the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of the month of the year, as well as for the peace of that specific month.
In all cases, at the end, one should offer a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for the sake of peace.

A wise man should perform worship during the five asterisms of Viṣṇu for the sake of stability and prosperity; he should perform the ritual bathing during the *snāpana* [nakṣatra] and the festival during the *autsava* [nakṣatra].

O ascetics, at each respective time, I shall describe the method of worship for both [the disciple and the preceptor] toward the Lord of Gods, according to their means and in detail. Having prostrated before the God together with the patron (yajamāna), the preceptor—

Then, at midday, having taken the Lord of Devas from the sleeping chamber and having properly installed the Master in the middle of the decorated pit, one should perform the ceremonial bath (svapana) as prescribed, in accordance with the specific desire. 15–16.
Thereafter, one should properly place [the deity] in the seat of life (jīvasthāna) at the site of worship;
likewise, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) prior to the midday worship.
At its conclusion, one should perform a festival (utsava), for the sake of universal peace during the festival.
At the conclusion of the midday worship, having again prostrated before the Lord of the gods, one should place the festival image upon an auspicious vehicle; then,
reciting the Svasti-sūkta, one should circumambulate that temple.
Having adorned him with all ornaments, he should place him in the pavilion at the site of the rite,
either accompanied by the two goddesses or alone, according to his desire;
this is the supreme application for the sake of the patron and the fourfold assembly.
The fourth [element] is the seat for the purpose of honoring the assembly.
O twice-born ones, if the ascetic, the asura, the yoga, and the supreme [state] are out of place, there will be misfortune; indeed, the seat must be in its proper position.

If [the number] is greater, there will be an increase of enemies; if less, there will be a decrease. I have likewise explained those respective measurements and the trees in the section on waste land (khila). Having fashioned the arches (toraṇas), one should properly install them in their respective places.
Having meditated upon those forms of the gods, one should worship them according to the procedure mentioned previously.
Having decorated the assembly pavilion everywhere with plantains, areca nuts, and other such items, one should divide it into nine sections. 24-25.

O ascetics rich in penance, one should fashion an ascetic (tāpasa) in the eastern quarter, and an asura in the quarter of Kubera (Dhanada). In the western quarter, one should fashion the seat of Yoga belonging to Varuṇa;
and in the northern quarter, the supreme seat served by Brahmā and the other gods.

One should gather all the delightful materials for the ritual requisites (sambhāra). 27. This treasure-trove [should be placed] appropriately before the Lord of Dharma (Dharmeśa) or the Lord of Water (Nīreśa), at whichever spot the Lord of the Gods of Gods resides; at that very spot, the worshipper should remain. 28.

If he stands on another foot, the worship becomes fruitless; therefore, the wise man should offer a welcome and a respectful greeting to the ascetic. He should also offer water for the feet (pādya) for the purification of the palate and tongue, as well as water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Next, one should offer a handful of flowers, perform prostrations, and provide mouth-freshener; likewise, one should apply a cloth to cover the neck and perform anointing.
Furthermore, one should rub the body with sandalwood paste as a king would. 30–31.
One should provide mouth-freshener and diversion as appropriate here;
having taken up the deity like a king, one should place him upon the throne of the Asura.
Then, having performed the *pravaramaṇa* rite, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*).
Having first performed the cleansing of the *ālaka* with *āmalaka*,
and having bound it with a cloth, one should then thoroughly cleanse the limbs;
having sprinkled [the body] below the throat with delightful substances such as sandalwood and the like.
The wise one should smear the Lord with fragrant, purified, and pure substances, as well as with turmeric, from the neck downwards according to what is aesthetically pleasing; then,
he should bathe him comfortably with pure coconut water.
Then, having released the hair-tie and sprinkled him with scented water,
the wise one should provide a covering garment, and offer water for the feet, water for sipping, an upper cloth, a purifying thread, and likewise a sacred thread.

The wise one should likewise offer water for the feet and so forth, and worship as before; that arghya-water should be used for touching, as well as for bathing and washing. Furthermore, it should be offered elsewhere during daily and occasional worship.
Having offered a handful of flowers, bowed down, and sought permission,
the preceptor should take up the thousand-streamed vessel and worship the Moon;
standing therein facing north, he should hold it in succession above his crown.
The preceptor must perform the bathing of the principal limb;
therefore, the preceptor should proceed with the consecration by means of a thousandfold stream.
In this manner, it should likewise be performed for all [limbs] by the preceptor.
If it is obstructed by others, that worship shall become fruitless.
With conch and lotus [vessels] held by those who are certain [of their purity], he should perform the consecration upon that very [image].
He should cause the learned Brahmins to teach the Vedas to him in due order, surrounded on all sides.
At that time, the preceptor should likewise recite the Narasūkta;
then, after the ritual bath with a thousand streams, having consecrated [the image] with the waters from the jars,
and having offered a cloth, he should place Hari upon the yogic seat.
Having performed the *pravaraṇa* ceremony, one should thereafter fumigate [the image] like a king (45).
Having scattered flowers with both hands, one should likewise perform the auspicious binding (*maṅgalabandhana*).
Having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should clothe it in beautiful garments (46).

Having adorned [the deity] with fine silk garments, waist-cloths, and so forth—whatever is pleasing to the devotees—and having decorated [him] with perfumes and garlands, one should worship [him] with offerings beginning with water for the feet and ending with the arghya offering;
then, having drawn aside the curtain, one should even cause [the devotee] to perform prostration. 47.
Having taken dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains at midday, and likewise a lustration (nīrājana) ceremony in the evening, one should show them to the Lord of Gods while reciting the Praṇava;
then, for the sake of protection, one should scatter flowers and unbroken rice grains in the cardinal directions. 48–49.
Having circumambulated [the deity] clockwise while recollecting the presiding deities of those directions,

one should apply an upright sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍraka*) on the forehead for protection with the mantra "Viṣṇus tvām," and then show the mirror, as well as the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the vehicle.
Having thus displayed the Vedas in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
he should sequentially teach the Purāṇas, Stotras, Sūtras, and Kalpas;
and in front [of him], there should be singing and dancing accompanied by all musical instruments.
One should cause a proclamation to be made; the Lord is praised with hymns of praise.
There should be one *āḍhaka* of rice, one *prastha* of sesame, and again one *kuḍuba* of ghee, as well as mouth-perfume;
these should be brought separately into the vessel.
Having worshipped the Vedas in that [place], he should then give them to those who are learned in the Vedas. First, he should offer *dūrvā* grass to the cows in the presence of the God of gods;
then, having performed a prostration to his guru, he should finally say "Forgive me" to Janārdana.

Then, one should give abundant [food] according to the previously mentioned procedure; subsequently, when the great oblation (mahāhavis) has been obtained, one should offer it according to the procedure stated for the *khila* [supplementary rites].
Having given water for drinking and sipping, as well as a cloth and perfume for the hands, [one should proceed].
Then, having offered mouth-perfume and bowed to the God of gods, one should place the deity upon a supreme seat made of *rājavarta* stone;
[one should offer] all kinds of various foods, such as cakes and the like. 57–58.
One should offer coconut water according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should give water for sipping (ācamana) and present mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa). Having performed a dance for diversion at the end, one should bow down to the God of gods.
Having placed the deity upon a vehicle, adorned with all ornaments,
one should perform circumambulation either in a village or at a temple; indeed, one should especially perform circumambulation within the temple itself.
Having established the Imperishable One in the place of the Jīva along with the two Goddesses,
one should worship him especially and also cause prostrations to be made.
The mantra for all these ritual services was previously proclaimed in the Khila.
Thus should the wise one perform the daily and occasional worship (nitya-naimittika-arcana).
If there should be any lapse in the mantras, some [remedy it] with the syllable *Ṭā*;
he who performs this occasional worship (naimittika-arcana) with such devotion—63–64.
"His self liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

(65) Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Occasional Worship," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu. [End of] the Section on Sacrifices.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the procedure for the bathing of the Deity on the occasion of the consecration,
at the conclusion of a festival, during the two solstices, and at the two equinoxes.
During a solar or lunar eclipse, one should diligently perform the ritual bath;
likewise when there is wealth available, during the five asterisms, during the asterism of the month, at other transits,
for the sake of pacifying ill omens and the like, and even upon seeing an unfavorable sign.

One should perform the ceremonial bathing of the deity specifically at the time of the patron’s birth asterism, or the king’s birth-protecting asterism (janmarakṣa), or during the two solstices, or during an eclipse of the sun or moon. 3–4.
When the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa) has passed and the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana) has likewise begun,
or at midday on other days when two days have elapsed— if [the conjunction] occurs during those two periods, it is even more excellent and superior, being doubled by the lunar mansion and the month.
If the most excellent conjunction should occur, especially during the ritual bathing;
if there is a full conjunction on the previous day, then likewise on that very same subsequent day,
one should offer the sprouts on the prescribed date.
For the purpose of bathing, one should collect all the materials such as clay and the rest,
either from a river, or from a lake, or from a field at the root of *darbha* grass (8),
or even that which has been dug up by an elephant's tusk or by a cow's horn.
One should likewise collect pure clay from an ant-hill inhabited by crabs or from the root of a *tulasī* plant on the day preceding [the ritual]; furthermore,
there are the Himavat, Ūrja, Vindhya, and the distant Vedaparvata mountains.

Mahendra, Hariścandra, and the mountain named Śataṛṅga are situated in the east and other directions respectively; they are white, yellow, black, and red in appearance, each measuring one hundred yojanas in height, having their roots in the ocean, and extending for a hundred yojanas.
And all those [seeds] sown there first spread out over the temple grounds:
rice, paddy, barley, mung beans, likewise black gram, millet, wheat, sesame, and lentils.
One should collect mustard seeds and grains for the sake of the sprouts,
and likewise take the other eight auspicious items previously mentioned; some also say one should prepare a base and a pedestal from mountains and such materials.
Then there is the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as ghee, honey, and curd;

likewise milk, scented water, thereafter water with unbroken rice grains, water with fruits, water with kuśa grass and gems, and again water with all medicinal herbs over which mantras have been recited.
One should take these twelve substances, one āḍhaka of each,
and should also collect bilva leaves, auspicious flowers,
nutmeg, camphor, śrīkhaṇḍa, and uśīra.
Masūra, damana, mudga, and chickpeas for the sake of the powder;
likewise, [the wood] of aśvattha, vaṭa, pitṛdruma, and arjuna, as well as that of khadira, madhūka, vañjula, and asana. 18–19.
One should collect bark, wool, and earth from bathing places such as rivers for the purpose of medicinal decoctions;
likewise, *siṃhī*, *nakulī*, *vyāghrī*, *nandā*, *aditi*, *sāhvayā*, *pāṭhā*, *sahadevī*, and *durvā*— these are the nine medicinal herbs.
One should also bring turmeric that has the luster of gold,
as well as its powder; furthermore, a wise person should take six parts of rice powder, along with *hareṇu*, *sthauṇeyaka*, leaves, and other such ingredients.
One should collect all kinds of fragrances, such as cardamom, cloves, camphor, sandalwood, and uśīra, as well as the breath of living beings,
and other flowers, perfumes, cloths, and ornaments. (23)
Furthermore, the wise man should acquire what is prescribed for worship according to the path;
then, the learned one should gradually procure realgar, red arsenic, antimony, yellow pigment, and the metals, in accordance with the ritual injunctions. 24–25.
Jars filled with an *āḍhaka*, bowls filled with a *prastha*,
water-pots filled with half a *droṇa*, and even jars filled with a *droṇa*— as well as all other various vessels, provided they are free from cracks and brokenness. (26)

Having brought other auspicious items, the wise and intelligent man should likewise gather other *kūrca* grasses; following the procedure prescribed for the *khila*, he should perform worship during the first part of the night and offer them outside the house.
In the first enclosure on the left, the wise one,
having spread bedding upon grain and established the Imperishable One (Viṣṇu) upon it,
should likewise tie a *prītisara* cord and have [the deity] lie down as prescribed for the installation.

One should perform the bathing of the image during the festival; in its absence, however, one should do so during the festival. If the two goddesses are absent during the festival, one should bind the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon Hari.
In the absence of both, one should perform the rite at that time or upon the *kautuka*.
Having first taken up the two goddesses, one should immediately perform the protection and other rites;
likewise, one should never move the seat of the vital breath (prāṇa) while it remains in the void.
Therefore, one should not move the deity without the two goddesses, nor even with the hotṛ priest.

Without performing the daily bath, one should not move the two goddesses from their place of life; the fire-chamber should not be left empty, just as the wife of a Yajurvedic priest [does not leave her husband].
The wife should not go from the fire-sacrifice house to another village.
In the same way, one should not worship the Goddess on a seat other than [the prescribed one];
this is always the specific distinction for the wise regarding the two goddesses and the *kautuka*. Because others are subject to movement, one should move them for that reason.
Then, when the time of twilight has arrived, if one desires to sleep,
one should first complete the ritual bathing and afterwards properly perform the daily rites; if it should be the morning time, one should proceed until the completion of the worship on the seat.

Having performed that bathing, one should subsequently perform it for the *kautuka* (the protective thread), especially during the first part of the night; however, there is no dismissal (*udvāsana*) for the other two.
Having tied the *kautuka*, one should perform those respective rites at their appropriate times.
When the invocation and dismissal are performed at their respective times,
even if the auspicious thread (*kautuka*) is specifically misplaced, no harm is done by the performer;
provided, however, that the ritual bathing takes place during the fourth watch of the night.
One should likewise project the *śakti* from the *kautuka* onto the *dhruva*;
then, at that time, having taken the *kautuka* [thread] from the middle of the pit and having bound the *kautuka*, one should bathe it as prescribed for the ritual bathing (*snapana*).
Even in the case of the *dhruva* [liṅga], the invocation (*āropaṇa*) is prescribed at the conclusion of the night worship;
because the power (*śakti*) is eternally present within that *dhruva*, the invocation is always declared to be unnecessary.
Furthermore, in the case of the *kautuka* [liṅga], one should perform that same ritual action as in the *kautuka*. 42–43.
There is no fault in this; there is always a power for that curiosity.
Because of its state as Vāsudeva, it is like the lighting of a lamp from another lamp. Therefore, one should perform the ceremonial bath, the oblation, and the food offering for the deity Kautuka.
At the conclusion of the bath, having worshipped him thoroughly, one should properly install him in the seat of the living soul (jīvasthāna).
Likewise, at sunrise, having invoked him and worshipped him again as before,
one should first offer the occasional oblation (naimittika-havis) and afterwards present the daily offering (nitya).
If the ritual bath (snapana) occurs between the two twilights during the *kautuka* ceremony,
one should take the *sambandha-kūrca*, bow down, and then have [the deity] follow;
having subsequently tied the protective cord (*pratisara*), one should bathe according to the procedure for the ritual bath.
Having worshipped the Lord in the pavilion and offered the oblation,
the wise one should then take the deity and install Him upon the altar with the mantra beginning "abhūrasi," accompanied by the Praṇavas. 48–49.
Then, having placed the *sambandhaka* beard [of the deity] in that manner, one should worship it; furthermore,
the bathing chamber (*āsnapanāgāra*) should be situated toward the northeast,
the north, or specifically the northeast, or else within a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).

One should have that constructed according to what is stated in the *Nirukta* and adorn it as prescribed for the ritual bathing (51). Having made a pit with the proper characteristics in the central row of Brahmā, one should surround it with a row [of cells] provided with four gates (52).
The wise one should have the seats for Paṅktīśa and Amita made with rice grains, or he should worship the seats of the guardians of the directions upon the ground;
having sprinkled the row [of seats] with the Gāyatrī mantra, he should do so with the mantra "sumitrā naḥ."
Having recited "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," one should spread darbha grass there;
likewise, having taken up water with the mantra "dhārāḥ" and performed the purification with a cloth, [one should do so] if it is at night, in the presence of the fire.
Having gathered the jars and subsequently wound them with thread for auspiciousness,

one should wash them with water and fill them well with the previously mentioned substances. In the place as prescribed, one should arrange them in rows, placing the earth and other materials in their proper sequence.

Having taken eight portions of clay in separate vessels with the mantra "udutya," he should place them between Indra and Īśāna on the left side of the doors; then, in the corners starting from the east, he should place stones with the Viṣṇu-sūkta. 57–58.
