Having placed rice and other grains between Yama and Agni with the mantra "śukrantā," one should place sprouts in the middle of the two abodes of Yama and Agni with the mantra "soma oṣadhīḥ," and on the right side of the doors of Indra and the others.
And in the intermediate directions, one should place the "auspicious signs," such as the Śrīvatsa and the other eight auspicious marks (60).

Stating that "one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth," [he says] that the pañcagavya is in the northeast, and its clarified butter is also in the corners of Īśāna and Indra (61).
One should place honey in the fire between Indra and Agni;
curd between Yama and Agni; Śrīraṃ between Yama and Nairṛta; and scented water as well as unbroken rice-water in the south-west (Nairṛta) direction.
One should indeed place the water with fruits between Nīla and Vāruṇa;
likewise, one should place the Kuśa-water between Varuṇa and Udāna;
and the jewel-water in the northwest (Vāyavyā), between Soma and Vāyu.
Likewise, one should place the water for recitation (japyodaka) between Kubera and Īśāna,
and the water with all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhyaudaka) to the left of these; one should then sequentially deposit the subsidiary baths (upasnāna) with the mantra "Sādhiṣṭha."

Having uttered "imāḥ sumanasaḥ," the best of mantra-knowers should offer meritorious flowers such as bilva and the like, as well as the powder of nutmeg and other spices, between Yama and Nila, and between Varuna and Nairṛti. 66–67.
Having said, "This [place] is not barren," one should deposit the presiding deities while recollecting them;
between Varuṇa and Udāna, one should deposit the decoction-powder and the water from the various tīrthas using the Vāruṇa mantra itself. 68.
Having said, "The four waters," one should indeed place the forest herbs with the mantra "Rudramanya" in the middle between Vāyu and Someśa; thereafter,
one should place yellow turmeric powder in the middle between Nīla and Paṅktīśa.
With the mantra "sinīvālī" and with the mantra "ime gandhāḥ," one should offer flowing perfumes and *hareṇuka* between Īśāna and Soma;
[one should offer] white garments and upper cloths with the mantra "tatpuruṣāya."

Between Īśāna and Soma, the wise and intelligent practitioner should place all fragrances and *hareṇuka* with the mantra "Tatpuruṣa," and in the northeast, he should sequentially deposit clay and other materials, along with mats, cloths, and upper garments. 62–63.

O ascetics rich in austerity, some learned ones, having specifically set aside substances such as clay and so forth, cover all these with new cloths using the *praṇava* in the event of a lapse in the mantras; thus says the knower of mantras. (63)
On the second altar, one should worship Jaya and the others of the chasm in their proper sequence (64).
Having worshipped Vīśāmitra, Paṅktīśa, and the guardians of the directions with their respective forms in their respective places, one should perform a prostration to Hari (65).
Then, having taken the deity from the bed and placed it in the center of the pit like a king,

the wise one should subsequently worship it in due order, ending with the *arghya* offering. Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Depositing the Materials," in the section on bathing within the *Yajñādhikāra* (Chapter on Sacrificial Rites) of the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The Section on Sacrificial Authority.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter:
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence for the worship of the ritual substances.
Having worshipped Mahī on the eight types of soil, one should worship Indra on the mountains;
having worshipped Vāyu among the grains with the aforementioned forms in due order,
one should worship Tārkṣya on the sprouts and the guardians of the quarters on the auspicious objects.

One should worship Śiva in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), Viśve-devas during the secondary ablution (upasnāna), and likewise in the clarified butter (ghṛta); one should worship the Sāmaveda during the secondary ablution for a year in due order.
One should worship the Ṛgveda in the honey, and [the deity] Prāṇa during its secondary ablution.
One should worship Rudra with the *yajus* mantra during the curd bath;
then one should worship the Atharvans during the milk bath, and thereafter the Aśvins during its supplementary bath.
Then, during the bath with scented water, one should worship the Seasons (*ṛtus*), and subsequently the Maruts during its supplementary bath.
Having worshipped Kāśyapa with *tvakṣatoda* and likewise the Guru with *upasnāna*,
one should worship Soma with *phalodaka*; then, during the *upasnāna*, one should worship Vāsuki,
and during the *upasnāna*, one should worship the Munis with *kuśa* grass and the King of Serpents.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu with water containing gems, and likewise Soma with his [own] water;
[one should worship] Pavitra with *jūpya* water, and with the water for the secondary bath (*upasnāna*), flowers;
and with water containing all medicinal herbs, Arka, and likewise the Apsarases with the secondary bath water.

One should worship Dhātṛ upon the flowers of merit (puṇya), Cakra upon the powder, and the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) upon the decoction; furthermore, one should worship Kumāra at the bathing place (tīrtha) in due order.
Wise men likewise establish the Rudras upon the medicinal herbs and Haridrā.
Having worshipped Sinīvālī, one should likewise worship Indra among the fragrances (gandhas).
Having worshipped Tvaṣṭṛ on the cloth (plota), one should worship Prajāpati on the root-fragrance (mūlagandha).
And having worshipped Durgā among the constituent elements (dhātus) with the [divine] forms (mūrtis) in the same sequence as before.

Then, having honored the guru along with his disciples, he should present the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); likewise, having performed the tasting of curd (dadhiprāśa), he should perform ācamana and then perform ācamana again.
Afterward, he should likewise hold the pavitra strainers on both hands.

The Guru, wearing a white upper garment and adorned with bracelets and other ornaments, should again worship the Lord of Gods with offerings beginning with water for the feet (pādya) and ending with the arghya offering;
having gathered the materials for worship, he should sprinkle them with water from his ritual hand (karaka). 13–14.
Saying "Please protect [this]," the student, having bowed to the deity of the substance and taken it, should place it in the hands of the guru while remaining with his body bowed low.
The guru, having sprinkled it with the *praṇava* (Om) and taken it with both hands, [should proceed].
Having raised [the vessel] up to the top of the head, and having caused it to circumambulate the Lord of Gods three times or once, the Guru,
the knower of mantras, should then join the name of that substance in due order with the mantra itself.
Saying, "I shall bathe Viṣṇu with this," one should sprinkle Him with those substances;

then, taking that vessel again, one should place it back in its former position. Regarding each substance, having removed the previous offerings (nirmālya) and worshipped with the mantra, [one should proceed].
Having uttered "Ekākṣara," he should bathe him again with clay (19).
Having said "Viśve nimagna," and having caused [the image] to be circumambulated by mountains,
he should [bathe it] again with grains using the mantra "Praṇaprasūti" (20).

Thereafter, one should bathe [the image] with sprouts while reciting the mantra beginning with "vita," and having said, "Thou hast become the wielder of the thunderbolt," one should perform a circumambulation with auspicious items.
Then, having recited "vasoḥ pavitram," one should bathe the Imperishable One with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
With ghee, he should say, "O Agni, come hither" (*ghṛtena 'cāgna āyāhi*); with honey, "Agni we kindle" (*madhunā 'cāgnimīl̥ataḥ*);

with curd, saying "For food, for strength" (*iṣe tvorje tvā*); and afterwards, with milk, he should bathe him while reciting the mantra "May the divine waters be auspicious to us" (*śanno devīḥ*) and "Thee, O hero, we have not harmed" (*adabhyā śūra*).

Having performed the ritual with scented water according to the rule, and having recited "These herbs," as well as the water with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and the water with *utpala* flowers, the wise man, while muttering [the mantra], should offer water with fruit, using the *Viṣṇu-gāyatrī* and the *kuśādbhida* verse beginning with "Four."
He should bathe [the deity] with water containing gems and water consecrated by recitation, using the mantra "apūta stasya" (25);

and having uttered the mantra "catvāri śṛṅgā," he should perform the respective secondary ablutions (upasnāna) with water containing all medicinal herbs and various other substances in their proper sequence (26).
Having said, "The four waters," one should bathe [the deity] with a steady mind and worship with meritorious flowers while reciting, "O Creator, O Ordainer. Then,
having recited, "The Ṛg verses and the Yajus formulas," one should bathe [the deity] in sequence with powders.
Having said, "This is that very God," one should rub Lord Hari with unguents;
then, saying, "He is all-knowing," one should bathe Him with holy waters;
and saying, "The limbs of Him who is the Sāman," one should cleanse Him with forest herbs.
The wise man, saying "namo devā," should bathe [the image] with turmeric;
then, saying "thou art a woman," he should bathe it in due order with fragrant powder. Having bathed it with scented water, he should then wipe it dry with a cloth.
Having adorned [the image] with garments and other ornaments, [one should worship it] with the mantra "tvaṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.

Then, having thoroughly anointed it with the root-fragrances (mūlagandha), the wise one should next adorn it with pigments (dhātu) and worship it with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings. 31–33.
Having again taken up the Lord Hari from the pit onto the yoga-seat,
one should firmly resolve upon the yoga-seat and install Him specifically in the southwest or the west of the pavilion, reciting the mantra "adbhyaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ".
Having performed all the ritual services prescribed for his seat, one should properly offer the oblation (havis) to the Lord of Gods here;
thereafter, taking the deity, one should circumambulate that temple.
Having performed [the rite] three times or once,
the Guru, being composed, places the Lord of Devas in the seat of the *jīva*, and having prostrated with the words "Forgive me," he remains concentrated in the seat of the *jīva* three times or once.

The Guru, having established the Lord of Devas and bowed while saying "Forgive me," should thereafter properly worship the deities of the daily rite (nityārcana) and those that have dissolved [into the main deity] during the fixed worship (dhruvārcā), following the sequence as in the pavilion (maṇḍapa). 36-37.
Having set aside the clay and other materials, one should worship the deities in their proper sequence;
then, having entered the inner sanctum and taken up the ritual substances as before,
the practitioner of mantras should bathe [the image] as previously described and likewise worship the permanent icon (dhruvārcā).

During famines caused by droughts and other calamities, inauspicious effects are destroyed through the ritual bathing [of the deity]; therefore, O Lord, one should perform the bathing with great effort.
Regarding these substances as well, there is a prescribed measure, a specific application, and a remedial procedure. (39–40)
The origin and the nine divisions have been proclaimed by me previously in the Khila;
likewise, one should perform those things not mentioned through the mantra. At the conclusion of the rite, some say that one should bathe the two goddesses of that [deity].
If the first name [of the deity] should be on the same pedestal within the interval of the ritual action, one should bathe me, the Lord, along with the Earth, using pure baths;
and if it is the permanent image (dhruvārcā) accompanied by the Goddess, then one should bathe the two Goddesses during that interval of bathing. 42–43.
"Having bathed [the deity] with pure water, one should perform the remaining rites together with Śeṣa.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing Substances," within the section on Sacrifice (*yajñādhikāra*) in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium (*saṃhitā*) proclaimed by Bhṛgu. This concludes the section on Sacrifice.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter:
The Varieties of Ablution. Hereafter, I shall explain the lowest of the low types of ablution.
For devotees, for those who are weak, and even for those of small means, [these rites] are of great significance;
they are common to all during ablutions. Therefore, with substances such as cow-products, ending with water containing all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhī), [the bath is performed].
The twelve principal vessels are filled with substances and all their parts; likewise, there are twelve subsidiary bathing jars (upasnāna-kalaśas) filled with water in due order,
together with water mixed with turmeric powder.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, on the aforementioned day, one should especially prepare twenty-five water-pots for the purpose of the ceremonial bath; likewise,
having offered the sprouts, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) for the sake of protection.
In the previously described pavilion, having laid out twenty-five squares on level ground according to the ritual lines, one should specifically determine the measurement of the walls;
here, in the central square, one should leave eight squares vacant all around for the pit.
For the purpose of circulation, four [vessels] are for the sake of the gates in the directions respectively;
likewise, for the purpose of installing the jars,
one should place a jar of one *āḍhaka*, half of that, or one *prastha* for each remaining solar square (*arkapada*).
Having gathered rice, one should prepare a seat for that [deity] with a width equal to the [length of the] foot; according to availability, one should arrange the materials separately for each.
On the seat, after sprinkling and drawing lines, there should be a separate layering of *darbha* grass.
Having prepared them, one should collect the pitchers and fill them thoroughly with ritual substances (10).
Having cast *kūrca* grasses into each with the *praṇava*,
and having provided lids for each, one should place them down while reciting the *Viṣṇu-gāyatrī* (11).

One should then place curd from a cow, unbroken rice with water flowing upward, and water containing gems in the intermediate directions (vidiśās); starting with the northeast (īśa), these are placed on the left side of the doors.
On the other side, starting from the east, one should place clarified butter, milk, fruit, and the object of recitation (japyam).

One should place honey-scented water, kusa-grass water, and water with all medicinal herbs (13). According to the prescribed rule and in that same sequence, one should set down the waters for the secondary bath (upasnapana) to the left of these, from the blue lotus up to the interval between the lords of the directions (14).
Having set aside the turmeric, one should wrap [the image] with a cloth;
then, taking the consecrated deity and placing it in the middle of the pit,
one should arrange kūrca-grasses all around, with some pointing eastward and others pointing northward.
Upon the altar, one should worship in sequence up to the *arghya* offering, beginning with Jaya and the others (16).

Having worshipped Paṅktīśa, Amita, Vīśa, and the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*) outside the pitcher using their respective form-mantras (*mūrti-mantras*), one should then worship the Lord of the Pitcher (*kalaśeśa*). (17)
Śiva, Viśvasūnu, the Sāmaveda, the Vatsaras, Ṛta, Prāma, Yajus, Rudra, Atharvan, and the two Aśvins; then the Tīrthas, Lokanātha, Viṣṇumūrti, and Garuḍa. 18.

Then Soma, the Nāga king, the Sage (Brahmā), Takṣaka, Puruṣa, the Gandharvas, the Mantras, the Vidyādharas in succession, Arka, and the Apsarases— these are the presiding deities there, each in a single form. 19–20.

Having meditated upon Sinīvālī in the yellow [quarter] and having offered the seat and other honors up to the *arghya*, one should worship her through the [divine] forms, using mantras beginning with *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Afterwards, having bowed to the Deity and worshipped him with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, one should proceed.

The Guru should stand facing north, to the right of the deity. Then, having prostrated before him, the disciple should take the products of the cow and other materials and, while reciting the mantra "Protect me," offer them into the hand of the Guru in the proper sequence.
Then, having sprinkled it again with the *praṇava* alone and taken it up with meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
and holding it in the left hand while grasping the *kūrca* placed there with the other hand, he should praise the name of the substance.
At the end of the mantra, one should pour [the water] once upon the crown of the head with the tip of the *kūrca* grass.
Then, having moved that substance three times clockwise together with the *kūrca*, one should bathe Viṣṇu with that substance while reciting: "I bathe Viṣṇu. Thus, one should perform the bathing.

Furthermore, having poured five handfuls of water for the feet—which yield fruit—into the feet again, one should bathe Hari with the remnants as if he were a king; then the disciple, taking that jar from the hand of the preceptor, [should proceed]. 27.
Then the disciple, taking that jar from the hand of the preceptor...
Having properly placed his hands in the previous position, he should likewise wash them.
Having recited "avasoḥ pavitram," then by the mantra "agna āyāhi," then "agnim īḷe," then "iṣe tvā," and then "śanno devīḥ" in sequence— 28–29.

Reciting "Abhitvā" and "Imā oṣadhīḥ," and with the four verses beginning with "Catvāri vāk," "Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe," and "Kramāt," as well as "Catvāri śṛṅgā," the wise man should then bathe the Lord with the primary and secondary bathing waters.
Having recited "The four waters," one should likewise bathe [the deity] with water-pots (kalaśas).

Then, having adorned each ritual substance with garments and other offerings, and having worshipped up to the arghya offering, one should recite "For the sake of Śrī, born... and finally bathe [the deity] with turmeric-water in the same manner.

Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods and having dismissed the lords of the pitchers, one should perform the consecration with oil according to the procedure prescribed for the pure bath; then,
having wiped [the deity] with a cloth and having taken the Imperishable One out from the pit.
Having properly seated [the deity] in the yoga posture, one should likewise honor him with garments and other offerings;
having worshipped him and offered the arghya and so forth, one should then give a gift as before,
and here itself present a great oblation or an abundant, imperishable offering.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground while reciting the mantra of supplication,
and having performed the ritual of diversion (vinoda) there at the end, one should thereafter worship the Guru.
Then, taking up the Lord of Devas once more, one should perform a circumambulation of the abode.
Having established it in the *jīvasthāna*, one should worship it here as previously described (37). Or, if the *kautuka* was taken from the pit at the conclusion of the rite,
the wise one, having properly placed it in the *jīvasthāna*, should worship it with mantras (38).
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The General Procedure for the Ritual Bath," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter of the section on Sacrifices.

The characteristics of the wheel for the purpose of the festival—the specific measurement of the wheel—will now be explained; its measurement may be according to the *mānāṅgula* or according to the *mātrāṅgula*. 1.
Or else, Dhruva should have it made with a finger or a tool such as a *ghāṭaka*, with a width and depth of one *yava*;
having made it perfectly round with that very [measure], the wise man should proceed thereafter.

Whose foot is it? The *varga* [is determined] by the *aśvinī* finger in sequence. 3. Ten thousand spokes are seen behind by the twice-born; likewise, the heart is on both sides of that central thread. 4.

The middle part of the outer cloth-band on both sides should be one finger-width thick; it should be long and thick at the ends, gradually tapered for aesthetic effect, and made smooth. Furthermore, there should be two heavy lines (gurukās) separated by two finger-widths, with a pair of rows in the space between them.
Likewise, those sixteen spokes are slightly curved like bamboo leaves.
At their tips and on their sides, there are flames joined by another finger’s breadth;
they should be known as equal to the radiance of the flames, threefold and sharp in appearance.
The Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) is in his heart, measuring nine tālas;
[his height] is thirteen aṅgulas, or alternatively, eleven or seven aṅgulas. With those fingers of Indra (śakrāṅguli), the two-armed deity is joined with palms pressed together in reverence.
Whether seated or standing, and in whatever manner the curiosity [of the form] may arise—

whether endowed with flowing ornaments or joined with the recollection of reality, whether accompanied by a pedestal or devoid of one— one should cause the Lord to be fashioned within the heart. 9–10.
One should likewise visualize the Lord Anapāyin in front, possessing a basket-shaped crown (*karaṇḍakuṭa*), joined with the half-moon ornament (*ardhacandrāṅga*), and having a beautiful face;
or else, another [form] with a lion’s face or the bud of a lotus.
Alternatively, the wise one should have [the image] made on both sides;
or indeed the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) accompanied by the flames of the wheel, or else a lotus, or a lion-faced [deity], or even a crocodile-faced [deity]. 12–13.
Or one should place it very firmly upon a wooden plank in the yoga position;
or alternatively, one should place it upon the heads of two lions on top of a plank.
That [plank] should be equal to, or twice, or even three times the size of that wheel.
The length of the mace is said to be equal to that of the discus-master (cakreśa).
It should be fashioned according to one's capacity, symmetrical, straight, and adorned with a blade, a bulbous end, and a pommel. 15–16.
Then the wise one should firmly install the discus or the mace, endowed with its characteristic marks, upon a lotus pedestal according to the prescribed rite;
the pedestal should likewise be four finger-breadths high and eight finger-breadths in width. 17.

Having fashioned that [pedestal] as square or circular and surrounded by eight petals, one should, as before, apply [the ornaments] in sequence at the base of the mace (gadā). One should make the height of the serpent [coil] equal to one finger-breadth (aṅgula), or if the mace is smaller, then accordingly.
Whatever else has not been mentioned here, the wise one should have it all performed according to the treatises on the arts (*śilpa-śāstra*);
he should have all the rites for the worship of the Siddhas and so forth performed as previously described. (20) This concludes the section on the types of locations for the *cakra*.
O ascetics rich in austerity, I shall now describe the procedure for the installation of the wheel.
On an auspicious day favorable to both the village and the patron,
one should first perform the rite of offering the germinating seeds on that very day.
Having gathered the necessary materials, one should have the sacrificial pit (dakṣiṇocana) prepared;

likewise, having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) by a river or similar site as described for the marriage ceremony, and having constructed the sacrificial hall, one should adorn it with arches and other decorations.
In the middle of that, one should construct a square altar (vedi) measuring one and a half [units] in length and width, and rising by a fourth part;
and to the east, the Āhavanīya pit and the Aupāsana fire-pit.
Having constructed its bathing altar in the east according to the previously mentioned measurements (25), and then having taken up the consecrated discus and sprinkled it with water,
one should circumambulate the village and likewise install it in the hall (26).
Having established the fire as previously described, one should again prepare the pitcher; then, taking the *sumbha* vessel as before, filling it with water as previously done,
and wrapping it with two cloths, one should likewise place the gems and other items therein.

One should place a water-pot upon a pedestal of grain facing the wheel (28). Worshipped by the patron, the Guru should meditate upon himself as the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) in the center of the heart-lotus, two-armed and with hands joined in *añjali* (29).
Having meditated upon [the deity] as having a reddish luster with yellow garments and limbs, and having worshipped him perfectly,
one should invoke him into the pitcher (kumbha), worship him as previously described,
place that wheel (cakra) upon the altar, and bathe it in succession with the ritual jars (kalaśas).
Having adorned [the image] with garments and other ornaments, and having placed it sequentially upon a pedestal of grain (31),
one should likewise fasten a protective cord (pratisara) to it together with the water-pot (kumbha). Then,
having laid the discus down and properly praised the office of the Hotṛ priest (32), [one should proceed].
One should praise the other weapons, such as the discus and others, which are the personified mantras;
then, having strewn grass around the fire while reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra,
one should offer two oblations of "abhūmāna" and "vandhya," joined with the Gāyatrī.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations and passed the remainder of the night,
he should bathe in abundant water, take up the previously described wheel as before, and,
knowing the mantra, perform a circumambulation of the abode together with the wheel.
On the southern side of the pavilion, having specially prepared a pedestal,
one should deposit the previously mentioned jewel and install it with the mantra. Then,
having thoroughly kindled the two rotating wheels, one should project the seed-syllables as before.
Having likewise invoked Śakti from the pitcher, one should worship her with incense and other offerings;
then, having presented milk-rice and other foods, one should properly worship the Guru.
He who performs this with devotion shall conquer all his enemies.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of the Discus," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[End of] the Section on Sacrifices. Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
The Ritual for Festivals. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence of festivals for the Lord of Gods.
Festivals are traditionally recorded as being of three types: those based on time, those based on faith, and those based on specific causes. 1.

If it is performed every year in whatever month may be chosen, that indeed would be a seasonal festival; but that which is performed with faith on a specific day in a specific month—[that is the true observance].
2. But that which is performed with faith on a specific day in a specific month... [is the true observance].
That, however, should be known as the Festival of Faith; therefore, the Festival of Time is superior.
When performed for the sake of pacifying causes that bring fear, such as drought and the like, it is remembered as the Festival of Omens.
If there is a festival at the beginning of the village, one should perform it in the proper sequence;
therefore, for the sake of pacifying portents, one should first perform the Kālī festival in due order,
followed by those of other fierce deities and the assembly of virtuous spirits.

Thereafter, for the sake of pacification, one should perform the festival of Śaṅkara as prescribed in the scriptures (verse 6). Furthermore, for the sake of pacifying the three groups of Viśas, one should again perform the festival of the Guru according to the gentle path, accompanied by the wheel and the army (verse 7).
For the sake of the peace of all the gods, of all the sages in every way,
of the ancestors, of the planets, and of all the wives as well,
and for the peace of the twice-born and of all the worlds in every way.
Thereafter, for the sake of prosperity, one should perform the festival of the house in due order;
otherwise, there will undoubtedly be the destruction of everyone.
Therefore, a wise person should avoid this, especially in villages and such places.

At the beginning of the solstices, during a solar transit (saṅkrānti), and especially during an eclipse— at these specific times it is a sacred occasion (tīrtha), and one should perform [the rite] even at night.
Bathing during an eclipse and at the solstices is most excellent, even at night.
Likewise, the authors of the Smṛtis have declared that the night is prohibited for [the performance of] rites.
Having completed the ritual at midday, if it is night, the wise man should pass that time in recreation and then perform the pilgrimage to that sacred site.
On the five days of Viṣṇu, on the day of the month's asterism, on the day of the installation,
on the sacrificer’s birth-asterism, or indeed on the king’s own birth-asterism—
having arranged the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) on these occasions, one should duly perform the festival.
Among those times, midday or the forenoon is auspicious for the commencement [of a rite].
When a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) spans two days, that day which has the greater portion of it is preferred;
likewise, other months and lunar mansions may mutually conflict within a single month.
When the beginning of the day has arrived, they know that bathing first at that [regular] sacred ford is not desired;
however, another [bath] is considered supreme and most excellent here among occasional rites,
as well as on a day when there is a conjunction of both the full moon and the lunar day.
In this case, for a sacred ford (tīrtha), it is specifically for that [deity], or else for other rites;
for a fortnight, or thirteen days, or eleven days in succession,
or nine days there, or seven days, or again five days.
For three days, two days, or even for one day; or again,
twenty-one days prior to the day of the pilgrimage (tīrtha),
having likewise hoisted the banner, one should perform the boat festival.
Or at the beginning of the festival day, one should cause the proclamation to be made according to the prescribed rite (verse 21).
Prior to the day of the proclamation, one should perform the ritual sowing of seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) using bamboo,
or a tree of noble species, or a *campaka*, or a *kramuka* (betel nut) tree (verse 22).
Or, having made a straight flagstaff from another auspicious tree, or even from the wood of others, it should be free from worms and hollows;
it may be equal in length to the vimāna, or one-quarter less, or likewise greater. 23.
The tip of the garland should be one and a half or even greater [in length], tapering gradually;
its circumference should be twenty-four finger-breadths, or as available, or measured here without regard for the depth of the pit, according to the dimensions of the staff of the twice-born.
Having made the staff-yoga or the separation straight and endowed with the proper characteristics,
one should take a well-beaten, very firm cotton cloth;
its width should be sixteen or twelve *bhāga-tālas* in length.
One should cause a banner (dhvaja) to be made according to the prescribed rite, with a length equal to the width of the base-section or equal to the inner door, or else half that width; then,
following the previously mentioned method, the wise man should draw the *vīśa* in the center.
Just as here, so too the wise knower of mantras, having sprinkled and taken up a well-painted banner that has ascended into the sky,
[should take] a bamboo staff twenty-one *tālas* in length. 29.
Taking [the cord] from the top down to this bottom, one should bind it with the mantra "iyame 'svastidā" (30).
One should then properly perform the installation of that banner; alternatively, having fashioned a staff from sacrificial trees, it should possess the proper characteristics (31).
The width should be half the length of the three-storey [structure], and having gradually increased the thickness,
one should join the supports for the staffs in a stable manner.
One should then join the bamboo pole, which exceeds the length of the staff, in due sequence.
Having fashioned a ring from copper and joined it gradually, the wise one [should prepare] a cord with a length twice that of the staff, having a width equal to the thumb and finger;
it may be made of triple-stranded thread or even of kuśa grass.
Having first joined it to the circle, one should wrap the garland of dots well; then, on the western side of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), in the center of the middle thread,
one should remove six *tālas* from that point, while the thickness is indeed five *tālas*.
Having washed the staff and placed gold within the pit at midday,
one should firmly install the staff while reciting the flag-mantra;
its length and width should be two cubits, and its height one cubit, in that order.
Having thus prepared the altar here with stone, brick, or even clay,
one should fashion at its base a lotus endowed with all characteristics, surrounded by eight petals and beautified at the foot of the flagpole.
Having constructed a pavilion, a gabled hall, or a water-shed in front of the temple, and having adorned it appropriately with canopies and other ornaments,
one should especially place [the image] in the central row to the east of that flagpole.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains measuring four *tālas* in length;
it should be two *tālas* in width and depth, and divided at the western end.
Having thus prepared the mound for the Wheel, one should likewise do so for the Peaceful deity to the north.
Likewise, one should cause a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be prepared to the east of that [mound] for the Khadādi-pati;
and having likewise prepared the aupāsana fire-pit on its northern side,
the wise man should perform the āghāra oblation to the west of the fire as previously described.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should place the banner facing east; then,
having purified it as is appropriate with fire circumambulation and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having recited "adabhyaḥ pvaḥ," one should perform the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma).
Having offered oblations of clarified butter with the Vaiṣṇava, Gāruḍa, and Dhvaja mantras (verse 45),
the wise one should then perform the "unveiling of the eyes" according to the prescribed ritual.
Having prepared the water-pot according to the rite, he should place it upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front [of the deity] (verse 46).
Having renounced [other thoughts], the knower of mantras, being composed, should meditate upon Garuḍa within the water-pot;
having invoked Garuḍa therein and worshipped him accordingly, he should sprinkle the *kautuka* cord and tie it along with that banner and the pot. 47.
Then, having taken that seed-syllable, having placed it in the heart and encircled it,
having taken the Śakti residing in the pitcher, one should likewise invoke her upon the head of the Lord of the Vīras with the Mūrti-mantra, worship her, and present the offerings. 48–49.
On the previously mentioned sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the wise one should subsequently place [the image] facing west;
behind that, the Discus (cakra) facing east; and in the north, the two Viśvāmitras well-established, facing south in succession. 50.
Having established the [deities] with the *mūrti-mantra* and having offered the *arghya*, the seat (*āsana*), and so forth,
he should worship them especially; then, after offering mung-bean rice to Garuḍa and pure rice to the other two, he should offer mouth-freshener (*mukhavāsaka*).
Having given [the gift] and offered salutation, he should also cause the previously mentioned *puṇyāha* (day of merit) to be proclaimed. Then,
the knower of mantras, having placed the image upon a pedestal of grain in the southeast,
should worship Bhūteśa and properly offer the oblation (*havis*).

Afterward, having strewn grass around the fire and offered oblations with the respective Vaiṣṇava mantras as before, the mantra-master, facing either east or north, performs the final oblation (antahoma) in the afternoon. 54–55.
Taking up a staff with the *praṇavas* while reciting "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ," and having struck him three times with the staff, he should thereafter again summon the son of a Śūdra woman (pāraśava),
duly adorned with a turban, garments, and other ornaments as before.
Taking up the kettledrum (*bherī*) accompanied by all musical instruments,
the knower of peace should likewise strike it before the discus according to the procedure prescribed in all the scriptures.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Festivals," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The Section on Sacrificial Authority. Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter: The Procedure for the Offering of Bali.
Furthermore, I shall explain separately the method for offering the bali-oblation;
specifically at evening, the sacrificer, being fully prepared,
[should offer] with *droṇas*, half-*droṇas*, or *āḍhakas* of rice.
Having cooked [the mixture] in a cauldron, one should pour it out as prescribed by the ritual rules.
Then, having taken mung beans, niṣpāva beans, sesame seeds, parched grain, and cakes,
and having placed them well in a golden vessel, the disciple should carry it upon his head.
Having first paid obeisance to the banner, one should take it— well-adorned and auspicious—
and place it upon a chariot, a palanquin, or a mechanical vehicle; then, taking offerings of oblations, flowers, and bali in a vessel, one should lead it back again.
Thereafter, he should not cause the wheel-turning kings to follow him;
rather, the preceptor should go in front, accompanied by all musical instruments,
surrounded by every kind of music for the sake of destroying the conduct of the low.

For the sake of protecting the preceptor, one should mentally perform the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*), and should cause him to recite the *Cakra*, the *Vīśa*, and the *Amita* [mantras]. Afterwards, one should proceed step by step toward the banner, which is adorned with all ornaments.
Having first offered the bali-oblation to the deities such as Brahmā and others residing in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) as before,
one should thereafter offer it again to the lords of the gates,
and then once more to the guardians of the temple (vimānapālas) and the world-protectors (lokapālas).
One should offer oblations (bali) under their respective names to others as well who do not fall into ruin;
then, having gone again to the lords of the city gates (gopureśas), one should be adorned with all ornaments. 10.
Having gone to the village and reached it, especially at every junction,
the mantra-practitioner should meditate upon and recognize the presiding deities, invoke them upon the ground as before,
worship them with offerings up to the *arghya*, and then present handfuls of food while reciting their names.
Taking that sand from the center, [he should offer it] in the east with "To the elements";
likewise in the south to the Yakṣas, in the west to the Rākṣasas, in the north to the Nāgas, and then in the upward direction in that same sequence.
Then the wise one again offered that water, as well as flowers and an oblation, to the Rākṣasas; he presented them in the presence of the Discus,
accompanied by incense, lamps, and the sounding of bells.
Accompanied by dance and song, as if releasing [offerings] in every direction;

in whichever direction the celestial chariot (vimāna) is located, one should perform a bali offering superior to that of Brahmā’s station, or otherwise cast a bali offering to the lords of those directions and so forth. 15–16.
If there are celestial palaces (vimānas) to the west and so forth belonging to Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Soma,
one should offer an oblation (bali) and then cast the others for Śambhu as before.
Alternatively, if the path of Brahmā (brahmavīthi) should be located in the middle of that village...
One should offer oblations beginning with Brahmā to the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas), as well as the bali-offering to the spirits (bhūtabali).

Otherwise, these [deities] are established in the path of the animals (tiryagvīthī) for Śambhu; indeed, there is a specific distinction in the offering for that which resides in the abode of the lord of the respective direction.
From the portion of Dhātṛ, one should offer the Brahmabali in the middle of that path;

having offered the oblation right there along with Indra, one should [worship] the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa). Or, here, even during the enclosure of the Brahma-sthāna, one should say "Salutation to the Brahmins."
Having first placed the offering for the deities all around, starting from the west as before in due order,
the wise preceptor should then place the bali-offering at the edge of the eastern sector and specifically around the path of the navel for the guardians of the directions.
Having offered the bali-oblation in the northeast, the wise preceptor should exit and enter the auspicious path at the entrance of the navel and soma;
having offered the bali-oblation to Indra (Purandara), he should offer it again to Agni (Pāvaka).
Especially on the Great Street (mahāvīthī) between two lords of the directions,
if there is a junction (sandhi), one should offer an oblation (bali) to the spirits (bhūta) there;
if, out of delusion, one should traverse a junction situated within a junction (sandhyantara).
If the eastern, western, or northern [alignment] is used for the site of the ritual action, harm will certainly arise; one should construct a single-path layout with a staff-like [axis],
and there, one should offer oblations with wheels and other implements starting from the west.
One should offer the *bali* offering to Varuṇa, Nirṛti, and Vāyu in the west (27).
One should cast the *bali* at the junctions and in the center to Dhātṛ, Yama, and Kubera; one should cast it in order at the eastern junctions to Indra, Pāvaka, and Rudra (28).
If there is a single street with an open space, one should offer the bali-oblation to Yama,
Nīla, and Anala from the south, either to the right or in the middle;
and one should offer the bali-oblation to Brahmā, Varuṇa, and Śakra from the north.
One should offer the bali-oblation in sequence to Kuberapavana and the other deities.
Alternatively, if there is a bali-mālā at the site (vāstu), one should offer the bali to Indra and the others;
likewise, in the case of Indra-iṣṭi, one should face northward at the front of the gateway (gopura) along the central path.

One should offer an oblation (bali) to Brahmā in every street, or equally in rivers and other such places; if it is a temple, one should do so around the enclosure wall. Having first cast the oblation there, the wise man should then [offer it] for each of those [deities].
Having recited the previously mentioned mantra,

the wise one should proclaim it with verses and prose in cities and other places; having praised it, he should recite that respective mantra in a low voice and proclaim it through drums and other instruments.

"May the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Hari, the sovereign of all gods, together with Brahmā and Śiva, be pleased through this festival. May all the gods, sages, ancestors, planets, and others likewise be propitiated. (35)
From Rudra [came] the Āptyas, the Apsarases, the Svaras, the Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts;
the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Vasus, Daityas, Dānavas, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, Nāgas, and the various Rākṣasas. (36–37)
May all the inhabitants of the worlds who have gone to the realm of Viṣṇu,
and all other deities together with their retinues, come respectfully to this sacrifice of Viṣṇu. 38.
"Taking the sacrificial offering and the bali, may they who bestow auspiciousness partake of them.
Having spoken thus, he should again proclaim this in the two drums facing the discus;
furthermore, the drummer should proclaim the *brahmadya* with his own rhythmic claps.
Having thus offered the bali-oblation and performed circumambulation,
one should again recite the Śakuna-sūkta and then enter the temple once more. (41) Furthermore, [one should offer] the remnants of the bali on the Bhūta-pīṭha with the mantra "asarvabhūtebhyaḥ."
Then, the wise one should throw the offering and the remaining water into the vicinity of the *cakra*.
Having performed the circumambulation of the temple with the banner and other items that lead to the fire, he should then re-establish the *cakra* in its own place. 42–43.
Having entered the place where the flagstaff stands, the knower of mantras should take hold of the flagstaff and bind it with a rope using the mantra "Svastidā" (Bestower of Well-being). Thereafter,
the wise practitioner, facing either eastward or northward, should fix it with the mechanical device.
Thereafter, one should attach the conch and the kāhala to the tip of the staff;
having fastened them securely and again recited the mantra "bhūrasī," one should consecrate the banner and subsequently worship the seat and other requisites. 45–46.

Afterwards, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made; having offered food to the flag and the Garuda situated upon it, one should present mouth-perfume and also cause a prostration to be performed.
(47) Here, one should offer food and the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) to the Garuda on the flag.
Women desiring virtuous sons should eat this with devotion.
They shall give birth to a true son who is long-lived, endowed with strength and health, equal to Śambhu, intelligent, and possessed of auspicious marks.
Until the descent of the banner, one should especially offer oblations properly with the twenty-six forms, either three times, twice, or even once a day. 50.

Having worshipped the banner, one should thereafter offer the *bhūtabali* at night. From the commencement of the flag-raising until the day before the festival begins, one should offer the oblation in the evening at the conclusion of the worship, just as prescribed for the raising of the banner.
Whether by the disciple or by the teacher, one should likewise always offer the *bhūtabali* in front of the *cakra*, especially at night;
the wise one should do so until dawn on all nights, up to the edge of the sacred site (*tīrtha*). 53.1–2.
One should likewise lead the chariot itself along the path for protection, as well as the sacrificial offering (bali).
From the hoisting of the flag until its descent, the learned preceptor especially shall not incur impurity (āśauca), whether it be that of birth (sūtaka) or death (pretaka). 54–55.

Likewise, for all those seeking the sacred sites, and for that sacrificer as well as his preceptor, it will not be otherwise than a festival; and until the conclusion of the pilgrimage, the residents of that village [shall likewise rejoice]. 56. Until the end of the pilgrimage, those dwelling in that village [shall remain there].
"Let people not go elsewhere; otherwise, there would be great danger.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Offering of Oblations and the Hoisting of the Banner," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha-saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Bhagavatas proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The Authority for Sacrifice.
Now begins the fortieth chapter: The Procession of the Festival.
Then, for the sake of the festival, one should especially collect the necessary materials; having had chariots, palanquins, mechanical swings,
and the like fashioned according to the instructions of the artisans' craft, and having taken up other lamps as well.
One should bring other musical instruments such as kettledrums, conchs, and trumpets;
palm-leaf fans, banners, umbrellas, yak-tail whisks, and peacock feathers;
and likewise dancers and singers, as previously described. 2–3.
Having adorned the inner sanctum (ālaya) and decorated it with archways and other ornaments,
one should summon the attendants and assign them their respective duties; furthermore,
all the pavilions and other structures should be prepared on every side.

One should have it constructed according to the treatises of the artisans for the purpose of assembly and for dancing. With the mantra "avadhūtā," pure Brahmins learned in the Vedas should especially purify the village streets so that they are pleasing to the mind.

Having uttered "Seven in the quarters," and having sprinkled auspiciously all around with scented water and smeared [the ground], one should scatter rice grains at each door with plantain trees, *kramuka* trees, jars, and other such items.
One should especially decorate the auspicious site with canopies and other ornaments.

All the inhabitants of that village, having adorned themselves and being intent on nothing else, should with devotion meditate on Hari in their minds, except for those performing the ritual duties. 8–9.

Within the boundaries of that village, a wise man should not perform occasional (naimittika) or optional (kāmya) rites— except for obligatory daily duties— until he has reached a sacred ford (tīrtha),
even when a festival of Viṣṇu is underway or during the construction of houses on an auspicious site.
If one does not perform another festival there, it perishes.
During this divine festival and sacrifice, especially regarding those sites, once the northern altar has been consecrated and the rite has commenced, one should not perform other [rites]. 11–12.
If one performs [the rite] on the *yaja* day, there will be total destruction; the performer and the sustainer both perish.
Therefore, a wise man should avoid those dwellings up to the end of the *tīrtha* days. Prior to the day of *utthāna* (the rising), on the seventh or the fifth day, [one should act].
Having offered the sprouts, the commencement of the previously mentioned festival for the purpose of the ritual bathing should take place specifically during the early part of the night;
at the conclusion of the evening worship, one should take the deity to the pavilion.
Having placed [the deity] upon a seat and worshipped it with the eight forms,
one should offer mouth-perfume and oil like a king, as before.
Taking the previously mentioned deity, one should install him again in the Āsura [direction].
One should bathe the Imperishable One again according to the path prescribed for the pure bath (śuddhasnāna). Having placed [the deity] upon the yoga-seat at the conclusion of the dance and song,
and having duly worshipped the seat and other items, one should offer the oblation together with the sacrificial food (samaṅga).
Having smeared the southern side of the *ālaya* with cow dung,
one should place grains upon it and collect the aforementioned [offerings] such as those born from eggs (*maṇḍaja*).
Having sprinkled water here, one should invoke the Lord of Gods together with the two goddesses and the Wind-god (*vāyu*).
Having placed [the image] upon it and worshipped it thoroughly, one should likewise bind the protective thread (kautuka).

Having laid [the deity] down there in the same manner, accompanied by dancing, singing, and so forth, as well as all types of stringed instruments (tatā) and the like, one should pass the remainder of the night in due order.
At dawn, having awakened the deity and offered oblations,
one should perform the midday bath according to the procedure prescribed for bathing. Then, having presented the sacrificial food (havis) to him, one should establish him in the sacrificial pavilion.

Alternatively, the wise one should worship the Imperishable [Lord] together with the discus and other [emblems] in the place of worship (arcāsthāna). If the wise one performs the *kautuka* sacrifice at the conclusion of the morning worship,
he should not take the two Goddesses [to the bathing area], though he may perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*).
Having bathed [the image], worshipped it thoroughly, and offered the oblation (*havis*) together with *saṃman*,
one should afterwards place it upon the altar for the purpose of worshipping during the evening twilight (*sandhyā*).
On the first day, in the evening, together with those measured by the lords of the circles (*cakravīśa*).
Having bathed and worshipped him thoroughly, one should properly offer the oblation (havis).

Taking the *pālikā* vessels and others, which are well-adorned with the discus and other symbols, and having mounted the attendants such as Vīśa upon the palanquin, accompanied by incense and lamps— 26–27.
The wise practitioner should go outside the village or similar settlement for the purpose of taking clay;
having gone toward the east, the northeast, or the north, together with the *cakra* and other implements, he should smear the pure and delightful spot with cow dung. (28)
There, the Guru should draw Pauṣṇī according to the measurement of nine tālas (29).
She is stretched out toward the southwest, with her feet [pointing] toward the northeast and her head [toward the northeast]; she has an upward face, two arms, and is adorned with all ornaments (30).

Having written [the mantra] here, having worshipped it thoroughly, and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should worship the peaceful wheel on the western ground and likewise [the wheel] in the north.
Having worshipped Viśa in the east, one should worship the remainder in the spade.

Having wrapped [the site] with nine layers of cloth and taken up a spade, the knower of mantras, standing facing north, should [dig] between the breasts, or on the arms, or on the head, with the mantra: "I dig you. (32-33)
Then, having dug it up with a spade and taken that earth, and having likewise carried it in a vessel upon his head by the other gods in turn,
they circumambulated the village and entered the temple.
Likewise, one should offer sprouts on the eastern and northern sides.

Having consecrated the discus and other implements, having properly offered the oblation, and having firmly established them each in their respective places, one should thereafter commence the sacrifice.
Or one may perform it facing the Ālaya fire, or in the south, or in a pleasing spot between the fires of Yama and Pāvaka, or in the fire of Pāvaka;
or in the northeast, or according to some, in the space between Soma and Īśāna.
One should construct the sacrificial hall according to the method described in the *Pratiṣṭhā* [section].
In the middle row thereof, one should have an altar (*vedi*) made according to the measurement of that row;
or, for the purpose of festivals and the like, it may be made with a height of one *tala*, and so on in sequence.
A wise man should arrange five fires during the highest festival, and likewise,

a learned man should arrange the three sacred fires (tretāgni) in sequence during the middle festival. If the assembly is of the lowest grade, the wise man should arrange them as previously described.

Where the arrangement of the three sacred fires (tretāgni) is performed, the Gārhapatya fire is the primary one; likewise, one should perform the Sabhya fire for the other two. Furthermore, one should purify everything everywhere according to the prescribed rule by means of the Bhūmi-yajña.
Having lifted up a new pitcher according to the previously stated procedure, the wise one, having recited "indraṃ naro na," should likewise wrap it with threads;
then, the knower of mantras, having spread the aforementioned grains upon the altar, [should proceed].
Having divided that [area] into nine parts, one should place the jars there in this sequence.
Having filled the jars with water, one should place auspicious items— such as bundles of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth— as well as weapons and gems, individually into each jar.
Having carefully placed [the vessels] in the central jar specifically with the Gāyatrī mantra,
one should likewise place the *sruk* and other implements, measuring two finger-breadths in size, having fashioned them out of gold, using the Viṣṇu-sūkta. 46.
Having covered each of them individually with a pair of garments,
one should first place Viśa facing west upon the eastern part of the altar below,
and afterwards place the Cakra facing north on the southern side.

One should place Paṅktīśa facing east upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and likewise place Śānta facing west, south, and north respectively; this is to be done in those various locations even if the images of Garuḍa and others are unavailable. 49.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the water-jars and meditated upon them in their midst, one should invoke [the deities] in due order.
As long as the conclusion of the holy bathing site has not been reached, the wise practitioner should especially worship the attendants (pārṣadas) within the jars in sequence at every twilight.
Having performed the two libations (āghāra) and the invocation according to the prescribed rule, and having indeed offered the *juṣṭākāra* and the *svāhākāra*,
one should carry out the sequence of the oblation (*homakrama*) as described in the Nirukta for both the middling and the superior [fires]. 52.
In that very manner, the wise one should cause it to be made; his path shall now be declared.
(53) Standing facing north, the Guru, to the south of the altar, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), should begin the meditation prescribed for the installation (pratiṣṭhā). (54)
In the center of the principal pitcher, the practitioner of mantras should invoke Viṣṇu and the goddesses, as well as the attendants, starting from the east and proceeding in due order:
Puruṣa, Kapila, Satya, Yajña, and Acyuta.
Then, having invoked Nārāyaṇa, followed by Aniruddha and Puṇya,
and likewise Ādi situated in the east, and having worshipped them with the eight forms and sprinkled the fire, one should subsequently offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava in the proper sequence.
On the sacrificial altar, or specifically to its west or in the northwest,
having prepared a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), one should spread out the birds and other [offerings] there;
then, accompanied by the patron, Garuḍa should bow down to the Lord.

Having cast the handful of flowers while reciting "pra tad viṣṇu," and having taken the Lord of Gods together with the two Goddesses, he should place Him facing east upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and worship Him with the eight forms.
In the absence of a festival image, or specifically during a ritual bathing,

or even in the absence of a ritual bathing, one should perform it during the consecration (*kautuka*). If, however, during the consecration, the two goddesses are not present, one should proceed in that manner without them.

One should not perform the constant deficiency in the rites of dismissal (visarga) and invocation (āvāhana); likewise, the wise one should perform the festival (utsava) or the daily worship (nityārcā) according to the proper sequence. If there is a constant deficiency, total destruction will certainly occur.
If a wise person performs the bathing at the midpoint of the festival, when the time for the sacrificial bath has arrived,
he should perform the bathing for the *kautuka* (the auspicious thread). At the conclusion of the bathing,
during the various stages of the image's bathing, and during the festival, one should perform the sacrificial bath.

One should perform that [rite] for those engaged in the highest and middle festivals (65). When possible, one should perform the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) here; however, in the case of the *kautuka* [consecration], one should perform it without the festival. A wise person should not practice the commingling of rituals for both [the festival and the consecration] (66).
If, while a festival is underway, a ceremonial bathing (snapana) should take place,
one should perform the rites in their proper sequence at the prescribed time;
for there is no fault whatsoever in this regard concerning an action already previously commenced.
If there is a desire for ritual curiosity (*kautuka*), then one may perform many rites in a single fire;
however, in the home, one should always maintain the three fires (*tretāgni*) except for the formal installation (*praṇayana* and *āropaṇa*).
Regarding the bathing and festival images, the *kautuka* [image] is used every day.

If the installation (āropaṇa) takes place on a fixed day, it should be preceded by the ritual action; likewise, one should invoke [the deity] at the end of the rites and dismiss [them] in the evening. The morning invocation is obligatory, especially at the beginning of the worship.
The dismissal (visarjana) should be performed at the end of the evening worship in whatever manner is appropriate for the specific ritual occasion (kautuka).

Likewise, if at the beginning of all initiations (dīkṣā) and so forth, the wise one has invoked [the deity] from the Dhruva-vessel, he should not perform the dismissal in the interim; rather, he should perform it at the conclusion of the sacred bathing (tīrtha). 71–72.

Having thus resolved regarding them all, and having established the Lord of Gods upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and worshipped him, one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Then, the golden marriage-thread (kautuka) should be placed upon the mound in a golden vessel.
Having performed the ritual renunciation as before, the wise one should bind [the thread] on the right hand (74).

Having properly bound the pitchers, the two goddesses, and the [deities of] the discus and so forth, he should worship them; then, having sprinkled water around the fire, he should thereafter recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta (75).
Having offered oblations to the Vaiṣṇava-sūkta, the Narasūkta, and likewise the Śrī-bhūsūkta, as well as to the deity presiding over that day, and having bowed to the Lord,
he entered the village together with the Cakravīśas, Amitas, and others.
Having offered the oblation as announced by the proclamation, he should enter the temple again (77).
Having placed the remainder of the oblation upon the *bhūtapīṭha* along with water,
the wise one [should do so] if it is within the precincts of the royal palace in the capital city (78).

Having divided that [remainder] into three parts and placed [the portion] ending with "namaḥ" in the middle together with the wives of the Lord of Śacī, the wise man should then specifically offer a bali-oblation to Śrī in the fifth part and to the Vasus all around.
The Śaṅkha and Padma treasures are at both sides of the entrance. Having entered the temple from behind and bowed to the God of gods,
one should adorn him with garments and other ornaments that are pleasing to the eyes and the mind.

Having placed [the image] upon the vehicle with the mantra "Vedāham," he should perform a circumambulation— whether joined or unjoined— with the deities along the path of the offering (balimārga) as before,
together with the devotees and adorned with all ornaments. 82.

Accompanied by royal insignia and preceded by a stream of water, [the procession] should proceed through the village to the south at the proper time; it should not go by any other path except the route for offerings. If it should go elsewhere, there will be an empty [result], and there will be fear of an enemy army.
Upon his entry into the house, the Brahmins residing in that village should rise up with haste and reverence, accompanied by lamps and other offerings.
Those people who serve the Lord of Gods are partakers of merit.
At every step they obtain the fruit of a sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
(86) Having performed the circumambulation properly, one should again enter the temple, having descended from the vehicle and seated the Lord of Gods upon his seat on the throne. (87)
Having established [the deity], worshipped it thoroughly, and bathed it with the waters from the ritual jars,
the wise one should release the protective thread and then bathe [the deity] as before;
then, taking the Lord of Gods from the pit and entering the sacrificial hall—
Having established [the deity] from the pitcher in the west, one should worship him along with the two goddesses (89).
One should also worship the other pitchers, the deities beginning with Cakra, and Janārdana;
having offered oblations of ghee, one should again perform the fire sacrifice for peace (90).
Having prostrated before the deity and taken him along with the two goddesses as before,
one should install him in the seat of the living soul (jīvasthāna), and having prostrated once more, one should lead him [into the inner sanctum].
If the marriage-thread (kautuka) is present at that time, one should place it upon the altar (vedi).
The Section on Sacrificial Authority. Now begins the forty-first chapter:
The Performance on the Second and Subsequent Days.
Starting from the second day, until the conclusion of the morning worship,
having worshipped the jars according to the rules, one should properly offer the oblation. Afterwards, the wise man should bow to the Lord of Gods and likewise to the two Goddesses.
Having placed [the image] upon a carriage or a palanquin, like a king, one should cause it to enter—
either into the assembly pavilion or into the bathing hall— together with all the devotees, as if he were a sovereign.
Right here, as before, the wise one should fashion four seats; having adorned them as previously described, he should place them again upon the ascetic.
There, indeed, he should perform all the preliminary rites prior to the bath.
One should likewise cause all the constituent parts of the ritual bath to be performed upon the seat;
then, having placed the Lord of Gods in due order upon the yoga-seat up to the end of the cloth for wiping, one should adorn Him with garments and other ornaments.
Having again performed worship up to the *arghya* offering with the previous mantras,
and having first worshipped unbroken rice, sprouts, and *dūrvā* grass along with water in that golden vessel, one should afterwards take hold of Soma.

The wise preceptor, having performed a circumambulation clockwise around the crown of the head— which is shaped like the syllable *praṇava*— according to the Vaiṣṇava rites, should then place [the flower] into the hand of the disciple,
specifically taking a handful of flowers together with unbroken grains (*akṣata*).

Having honored [the deity] above the crown, one should release [the offerings] toward the directions with circumambulation for the sake of satisfying even the Vedas, ending with "Namaḥ" and using the form of the Veda;
then, having performed protection with the mantra "Viṣṇustvām" and with unbroken grains (akṣata).
With the mantra "devasya tvā," he should again show him a mirror;
having given him an umbrella with that same [mantra], the wise man, having finally provided the attendants such as the fly-whisks, should have him study the Vedas in their proper order.
Having placed the Purāṇas, hymns, Sūtras, the Kalpas, and the ritual manuals at the forefront, along with songs and dances, he should cause others to proclaim them.
Taking two *prasthas* of rice and one *prastha* of sesame seeds in a vessel, [he should proceed].
Taking a handful of *prasthapāda* rice, ghee, and betel leaf (14),
and having separately gathered a handful of *dūrvā* grass in a vessel for the purpose of beholding the Lord, one should place them before the Lord in sequence (16).
Having worshipped the Ṛgveda with rice grains, the Yajurveda with sesame seeds, the Sāmaveda with ghee, and the Atharvaveda with betel leaves in due order,
one should then invite Brahmins who are learned in those respective Vedas to sit before Lord Hari.
One should present the maṇḍala in due order according to the method described for worship (verse 18).
Afterwards, O Brahmins, one should offer betel and the Purāṇas and so forth;
then, having offered praise, the Guru should cause the Lord of Gods to be prostrated before. (Verse 19)

Having then offered water for the feet and water for sipping, and likewise having smeared the mandala in front, one should offer abundant [offerings] as before; then, having bowed and obtained the deity’s permission, one should take [the deity] from the seat.
He should cause [the deity] to enter the sacrificial hall by circumambulating it once.
Then, having established the Lord of the Gods of gods upon a well-adorned seat on the western side of the altar, he should worship Him with the eight forms.
Having propitiated each respective pitcher and worshipped the various deities along with their attendants, having properly offered the oblation (havis) and given the mouth-freshener (mukhavāsaka),
one should approach the assembly hall (sabhya) and sprinkle it as before.
Having offered the previously mentioned mantra dedicated to the presiding deity of that day,
and having finally presented the bali offering together with the lords of the Cakras and the Immeasurables (Amitābhas), one should [place] the bali-image along with the other deities.
One should worship [the deity] adorned with all ornaments according to the prescribed rite;
one should offer a *bali* oblation to the assembly of beings beginning with Dhātṛ and ending with Bhūta.
Afterwards, having entered the village and performed the *bali* offering as before, [one should proceed].
Having entered the ālaya once more, one should perform the rites upon the *bhūtapīṭha*.

Having washed one's feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and prostrated before the God of gods, and having bathed the [deities] such as Cakra and the others, one should likewise place them in the hall. 27–28.
Having offered oblations to the fire and protected it well,
one should again take up the deity from the sacrificial site and properly install him within a beautiful pavilion or similar structure, adorned with various kinds of cloths. 29.

Having adorned the Lord of Devas in due order with necklaces and other ornaments, as well as flower garlands and the like, one should offer oblations here according to one's ability, just as for a king. 30–31.
The Guru should again rub the hands of the deity with sandalwood paste,
offer abundant mouth-freshener (*mukhavāsa*), and bow to the deity while surrounded by other devotees accompanied by songs of auspiciousness (*svasti*). 32.
Having placed [the deity] upon a royal palanquin, one should lead him once around the temple and then enter the village street; thereafter,
one should transfer the deity from that seat onto a palanquin or a chariot.
Having placed the deity upon either a horse or an elephant like a king,
and having prostrated and offered scented mouth-fresheners along with ornaments,
one should perform the circumambulation of the village, or even that of the temple alone.
If the Brahma-sthāna is located on the inner path (nābhivīthī), one should perform a circumambulation;
then, having performed a circumambulation of the Great Path (mahāvīthī) like a king by way of the bali-path, one should subsequently enter the temple. 36–37.
Having alighted from the vehicle, O Lord of Devas, and having performed a circumambulation of the temple from left to right,
the wise one should then place [the image] in its station as previously described;
and having prostrated like a king, he should then offer water for the feet at the [deity's] feet.
There, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and then offer mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa).

Having concealed [the deity] with a curtain, and having worshipped the Lord of Gods with everything from the foot-water (pādya) up to the respectful offering (arghya), one should then remove the curtain once again. 39–40.
Having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony as previously described with ease by female attendants, like a king,
the Guru should finally offer abundant mouth-fresheners (*mukhavāsa*) once again. Then, the Guru should have the devotees recite other stories concerning the ways of the world (*lokayātrā*).
The preceptor himself should cause him to hear the words spoken therein;
he himself should remember that those words and the actions prescribed were spoken by Viṣṇu, and all the learned ones should perform them.
Having prostrated, the wise preceptor should then take up the garlands and other offerings, worship Viṣvaksena with garments and other excellent items,
and again offer mouth-perfume while wearing a white cloth.
Having covered [the head] over the hair-tufts, one should scatter the ends of the hair;
having poured oil onto the head, one should comb it again like a king, then slowly binding those locks of hair, one should wrap them with a garland of flowers.
Having removed the cloth from his shoulder, he should slowly apply an ointment to his limbs;
having bowed to the Lord, he should then anoint him with sandalwood paste (47).
Having offered mouth-perfume and finally bowed again for the sake of bathing, he should proceed.
Having joined the two sandals together, he should then place them at the feet like a king; then,
taking the Lord with both hands, the wise one should install Him again upon the Asura, having offered water for the feet and water for sipping according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having bathed [the deity] with scented water, he should then wipe [it] with a cloth;
having placed [it] upon a yoga-seat and adorned it as before (verse 50),
he should properly offer the oblation at the conclusion of the singing and dancing.
If there is a great sacrificial offering (mahāhavis), having prepared it as previously described,
one should establish the immutable Lord on its western side and likewise offer the water for drinking and rinsing the mouth as stated before.
Having given [the offerings] from that [vessel], the wise man should take them and place them on the supreme seat—
various kinds of food such as cakes (apūpa) and other edibles—
along with many coconuts, while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
Afterwards, having offered the fragrant paste according to the prescribed ritual, and then as before offering the mouth-freshener (mukhavāsa), one should finally cause a prostration to be performed;
[this is done] with stories from the Purāṇas, with the Vedas, and especially with musical instruments.
Having caused the diversion to be performed, he should take the deity as before,
perform a single circumambulation clockwise, and cause him to enter the sacrificial hall;
having established him well in his former place and worshipped him thoroughly, he should offer the oblation.
Having offered other jars and likewise performed the fire-oblation (homa) once more,
he should take up one wheel, grasp the materials for the offering (bali), present the bali, and enter the previously mentioned temple. 57–58.
Having prostrated before the deity and adorned him with pleasing ornaments as previously described,
and having placed him upon a chariot or a palanquin as before,
one should perform the circumambulation of the village and enter the temple.
Having taken the Lord of Gods from the vehicle and performed the circumambulation of the temple,
the wise one should place Him upon the bathing altar, discard the previous garments and garlands, and offer water for the feet and water for sipping according to the previously mentioned ritual.
Having consecrated [the deity] with perfumed water and offered a cloth as before,
one should then take the Lord of Gods from there and especially install Him in the seat of the *jīva*, worshipping the Imperishable One together with the two goddesses.
Having properly offered the oblation, one should again present mouth-fresheners (mukhavāsa).
Having bowed to the God of gods with the words, "Forgive my transgression," the wise and learned practitioner should then place the discus and other emblems in their respective locations.
From the second day onwards, in this manner, every evening and every morning,
at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform double the worship.
If one is unable to do so, then the double worship should be performed as before.
Having performed the offering of oblations, the fire sacrifice, the worship of the Kumbha-deity, the presentation of bali-offerings— either twice daily or at the immutable [single] time—
and likewise at the evening hour, one should conduct the festival.
In times of fear from enemies, thieves, and the like, or likewise during the danger of great winds,
or during the danger of excessive rain, or even in the second enclosure (āvaraṇa), some say that one should cause the offering of oblations (bali) to be performed. 68.
"If destruction occurs immediately due to some other cause, that [destruction] is certain.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Festival from the Second Day Onward," within the Section on Sacrifices (*yajñādhikāra*) in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu. This concludes the Section on Sacrifices.
Now begins the forty-second chapter:
The Hunt Festival.
Now, prior to the day of the pilgrimage site, during the interval between the morning twilight prayers, [he performed his rites].

Having performed all the rites beginning with the fire-oblation (homa), one should likewise cause a festival to be celebrated. For the purpose of hunting, the Lord of Gods, either accompanied by the two Goddesses or without them, should be mounted upon a vehicle and adorned specifically with royal insignia.
One should lead the Lord to a grove, or by a river and the like, or to a delightful forest edge, or to another dwelling, or even outside the site of the temple—
provided it be a meritorious place within a distance of one yojana from there.
In whichever direction one intends to go specifically for the purpose of hunting,
one should first have beautiful water-stations (prapās) constructed there;
having again performed the previously mentioned purification at that very spot, [one should approach] the Lord.
Having brought [the deity] here, one should place the well-adorned Lord upon the seat,
together with the two goddesses, the attendants, and indeed Viṣvaksena. Afterwards, having prostrated before the Lord along with the two goddesses as previously described, [one should proceed].

Right here, the wise one should perform the ritual bath according to the method prescribed for the pure bath (śuddhasnāna). Having worshipped as previously described up to the offering of *arghya*, and having prostrated,
he should offer a great oblation (*mahāhavis*) or an abundant one, according to his capacity and according to his inclination.
Having offered [the offerings] to the Lord of Gods together with the two Goddesses as before,
one should again present mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa) for the pleasure of the God and the Goddesses; and here, one should especially offer it to Viṣvaksena along with his attendants.
