Having offered [the oblation] according to the ritual procedure, he should then, as before,
mount another seat for the sake of hunting, together with the two goddesses; having adorned himself for the hunt, he should likewise adorn all the Nandana groves on every side.
Having offered edible foods such as cakes along with coconut water, one should also cause the offering of mouth-perfumes and prostrations to be performed.
When the desired rites for horses and other mounts have been completed, [one attains] immortality through the yantra.
Having placed [the deity] back [on the seat], one should again present the divine weapons.
Having placed the two goddesses upon the vehicle, which is adorned with divine insignia,
they should follow behind the deity together with that immeasurable host.
Some were mounted on horses, some had elephants as their vehicles;
some were wielding bows, and others likewise were bearing swords.
Some were engaged in dancing, and others were engaged in singing.
Some were meritorious bearers of the gadā (mace), some were bearers of the dīpa (lamp) in succession;
others were endowed with all ornaments, [adorned] by means of the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
Having thus caused the hunt to be conducted like a king, he then— 16–17.
Afterwards, having led the Lord together with the two goddesses into the village and performed a circumambulation of the village, he should enter the temple again.
Having installed the Lord in His place along with the two goddesses as before, [he should proceed].
Then, having bathed and worshipped him, one should likewise perform the night festival (19).
Having bathed him again— either together with the two goddesses or without them— and having tied the protective cord (pratisara) as previously described, one should then lay him upon the bed (20).
At dawn, having raised the deity, one should not offer oblations; rather, one should worship the presiding deity of the day. O best of sages, listen as I now describe the deities of the days. 21
The first is declared to be Brāhma, the second likewise Ārṣaka; the third is said to be Skanda, and the fourth is Vāsava. The fifth has Soma as its deity, and the sixth is Vaiṣṇava.

The seventh is dedicated to all the deities, and the eighth belongs to Yama; the ninth belongs to Varuṇa. Therefore, O Lord of the Day, one should offer oblations according to the mantras of those lords of the day, and with the form-mantras (mūrti-mantras) of the gods, as prescribed by their etymological definitions.
Regarding the powder festival (cūrṇotsava):
on that day of the pilgrimage site, after the aforementioned floating festival, one should likewise install the Lord of Gods in the pavilion even without the sacrificial oblation (havir). 25.

The wise one should place Garuḍa at the front, the Discus (Cakra) to the south, and Amita upon a heap of grain to the north; having sprinkled them with water and worshipped them with the eight forms beginning with the water for the feet (pādya). 26.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains, two cubits in length and breadth, and having made it square and level, one should place the mortar and pestle upon it in front, starting from the edge, and enclose them with a cloth. 27–28.
A wise person should worship Brahmā and Īśa as the lords of those two respectively;
having worshipped Sinīvālī with turmeric and purified [the site],
the preceptor, facing eastward, should perform a slight threshing.
Having had a mortar prepared by courtesans and their attendants,
he should grind [the substance] into powder and gradually take that powder into water from a pitcher;
the wise man should fill one or two pitchers with it.
Having taken one āḍhaka of that oil which has been infused with fragrance, he should place it along with the two blades of kusa grass upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Covering it with a new cloth, he should worship it with the mantra "somaṃ te".
Then one should worship the Sanivālī, as well as the powder, the discus, and the other [emblems].
Thereafter, having worshipped the Lord, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made;
then, taking oil in both hands while reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra, [one should proceed].

Having poured that oil onto the head with the mantra "vedāham" and having sprinkled [the deity] with powder, one should likewise sprinkle the Lord and the discus and other [emblems]. A person who has been consecrated should wear that powder upon his head.
By recollecting the God of gods, one is liberated from all sins. (36) Then,
having placed the Lord of Gods, who is fully adorned, upon a vehicle along with the discus and other [emblems], and having likewise held a powder festival for that village— (37)

During the festival of the final ablution (avabhṛtha), if there should be a natural pool (devakhāta) facing the temple, a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) should be established there; it shall be divine and equal to the Ganges. 38.
Having installed the Lord of Gods along with his vehicle, the discus, and other emblems, and having entered the temple,
one should place him upon the throne; whether together with the two Goddesses or without them.
The wise practitioner should sequentially place the discus and other implements in their respective positions as before (verse 40).
Then, having prepared an altar in front and divided it into nine sections,
the learned one should fill the jars with substances and water from a river (verse 41).
Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra, one should place white mustard seeds in the center;
in the east, there should be water with unbroken rice (akṣata), and likewise water with fragrance in the south.
Then, in the west, water with kuśa grass, and likewise water for recitation (japya) in the north.
And one should place the secondary bathing waters (upasnāna) in the intermediate directions and in the center, in due order.
Then, having worshipped the presiding deities and caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha),
and having worshipped the Lord of Gods with the discus and other implements as before, [one should proceed].
Having bowed to the Lord of the gods of gods and taken up the water-pots, he sprinkled the Lord of gods, Sudarśana, with the remaining water while reciting the mantra; then,
having likewise consecrated the lamps, he bowed to the god as before.
Taking the deity with both hands, accompanied by the attendant deities,
the preceptor should enter that Devakhāta and worship Varuṇa there; he should also take the Discus to that sacred bathing place and cause it to be immersed.
Afterwards, having bathed [the image] in the place of the discus and other [emblems] in the presence of the deity, the knower of mantras, having wrapped it in a white cloth and washed its feet,
should likewise perform the *ācamana* rite and cause the previously mentioned prostrations to be made. 48.
Then, having dismissed the Vastrins and others, and having adorned the deity with other ornaments (49),
the wise one, having gathered the materials for the bath right there as before, should establish the deity upon the *āsura* [seat], but must not use oil at all (50).
Together with the two goddesses and the [deities] such as Cakra, one should bathe the Lord as before;

having likewise given him a cloth for drying, one should place him upon the appropriate seat (yaugika-āsana). One should perform the services prescribed for the seat, excluding the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Afterwards, having taken up the deity adorned with all ornaments,

and having performed a circumambulation of the temple, one should especially install [the deity] in the seat of life (jīvasthāna) together with the two goddesses, and likewise install the discus and other [emblems]. 52–53.
Having performed the worship as previously described, one should provide abundant offerings here; this is the option for the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*).
Alternatively, if there is a sacred bathing place (*puṇyatīrtha*) or a temple nearby, [one may perform it there]. 54.
At a time other than that of the sacred bathing (tīrtha), having taken the jar— which is wrapped with thread, free from other defects, and [prepared] with the permission of the preceptor—
reciting "aduhatāṃ divam," he should proceed as before.
Having taken up the Cakradeva and entered the sacred bathing place (puṇyatīrtha),
the disciple should go into water reaching up to the thighs, facing either east or north, and having worshipped the Lord of Waters (Toyeśa) in front of the Cakra.
Taking the pitcher with both hands while mentally recollecting Hari, and saying "I grasp the primordial one," he should run forward, grasp it, and then,
having closed it again with its lid, carry it thus upon his head.
Accompanied by conchs and *kāhala* drums, and endowed with the sound of auspicious verses,
one should cause the deity to enter properly along with the wheel and the pitcher onto the previously mentioned path at the conclusion of the powder festival, as before. 59–60.
Having bathed the Lord of Gods, who is seated upon his chariot and facing either the east or the north, with scented water together with the lords of the circles and their retinues,
and having adorned him with a new cloth, one should worship him with the eight forms.
Taking the water-pot (kumbha) to the front, one should place it upon that chariot (62).
The lords of the [planetary] cycles, Amita, and others should also proclaim the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha);
having invoked the sacred bathing-places (tīrtha) into that water of the pot and worshipped them as before (63).
At an auspicious moment, the Guru, having taken that very holy water from the jar with a bundle of kuśa grass, should sprinkle the immutable God;
then, with the remaining waters, he should consecrate the discus with its respective mantra.

The manner of the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) varies according to the specific site; apart from these distinct locations, it may likewise be performed elsewhere on a mountain peak, in a forest, on a riverbank, by the shore of the ocean, or in any other delightful place.
If one desires all the festivities, such as the proclamation of the *ālaya* in that [temple], during the first consecration and so forth, one should proceed as before.
However, if at the sacred site (*tīrtha*) where the *āraṇa* rite is performed there should be a sacred tree (*puṇyavṛkṣa*), [one should act accordingly]. 66–67.
Or, even if there are no such [natural] directions, one should perform the rite at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) within its shade;
provided that there is a natural pool (devakhāta) as previously described in front of the temple,
one should perform the sprinkling after first performing the ritual placement of the water-pot (kalaśanyāsa) within its shade.

In the same manner, one should immerse the wheel, either together with the deity, in water (69). It is taught that there are three types: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa; if such [an immersion] is not possible, then as before, one should take the sacred water (tīrtha) into the ritual jar (70).
One may perform the *tīrtha* rite while in a vehicle under the shade of a sacred tree;
there is indeed no fault in performing the *tīrtha* rite while seated in a vehicle,
for others know that to be *rājasa*, and some here say it applies even when one is seated on a throne.

A devotee who bears Cakratīrtha upon his head with devotion becomes thoroughly purified of sins by that act and goes to the world of Viṣṇu; there, he performs the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the ocean.
Alternatively, at the conclusion of the powder festival, one should go to a pure body of water such as the ocean;
within a distance of one yojana from that [temple], one should cause the chariot wheel to enter its shore. As long as the wheel remains submerged in the water, it shall remain on level ground.
Having led [the disciple] there in due order, one should perform the *rājasa* pilgrimage at this very site;
or else, having seated him on a seat upon the shore in the midst of the light,
one should establish him together with the discus and other [emblems], and then prepare the ritual jars.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) as previously described, one should sprinkle [the deity] with water from the ritual jar (*kalaśa*).

Then, having again consecrated the Lord of Gods and the Discus (*cakra*) with the remaining [water], one should take the Discus into its presence and immerse it in that sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).

Or else, one should immerse the Lord of Gods together with the two goddesses in water; thereafter, having taken up the deity, one should go to a delightful grove, or to the abode of Saumya, or to the temple of Pañcarātra. 75.
In a hall for the Brahma-yajña, or else in a temple of Rudra, or in a decorated pavilion, one should install the Lord together with his attendants; then,
having bathed him according to the procedure prescribed for the pure ritual bath, like a king, (verse 77).

Having adorned [the deity] as before, together with the lords of the Cakras and the Amitas, and having offered oblations even without a formal food offering (naivedya), one should bow, seek permission,
provide diversions, and then cast forth the handful of flowers (kusumāñjali).
Then, in the afternoon, at an auspicious moment when a favorable conjunction arises, having said "Mount the chariot" (*rathaṃ tara*), he should place the Lord of Gods upon the chariot as before,
perform a circumambulation of the village, and cause him to enter the temple.
Alternatively, O Lord, having bathed the deity with that water— especially at the conclusion of the ritual bath—
and having performed the circumambulation of the village, one should carefully place it upon the bathing altar;
and here, having performed the bathing according to the prescribed rite by the previously mentioned method.
Then, having wiped [the area] with the thread itself, one should properly deposit [the deity] in the seat of the Jīva (82).
Having worshipped [him] together with the two Goddesses and the lords of the wheels and the [other] immeasurables,
and having offered abundant great oblation (mahāhavis) here, one should bow down (83).
Having also worshipped the preceptor, one should recite the prayer-mantra: "May you forgive all that is deficient or excessive," thus [concluding] the relief of the people. 84.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Hunt-Procession," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
In the Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavat-śāstra of Bhārgava,
this is the forty-third chapter:
The Ritual Procedure for the Second and Subsequent Days.
Henceforth, I shall explain the ninefold sequence of festivals;
it is traditionally known as threefold—superior, middling, and likewise inferior.
By dividing each of those three again into three, the ninefold classification is described.
For a fortnight, thirteen days, or likewise ten or eleven; or nine days, then seven days, five days,
or likewise three days, two days, and similarly one day— in this sequence.
Thus, the festival day has been declared in nine ways according to the rules; I have described at length the festivals beginning with the fifth day and starting from the first day of the fortnight.
Furthermore, in the supplementary section (khila), I shall clearly explain those lasting three days and so forth, even as we speak now.
O best of the twice-born, this festival is for the sake of the weak and the devotee;
first, the wise man should determine the sacred ford (tīrtha) and the lunar mansion (ṛkṣa).

Therefore, on the day prior to that, one should plant the seed-sprouts under an auspicious constellation (nakṣatra). Having gathered the necessary materials, the wise practitioner should especially perform the protective rites and other preparations for the ritual bathing, as previously described.
At dawn, the preceptor should awaken the deity; likewise, he should perform the midday ablution, and in the afternoon, he should proceed with the collection of earth.
He should not raise the banner, especially on the first day of the third fortnight.
On the festival day, the wise one, having worshipped twice as much with the *cakra* and other implements,
and having tied the initiation-thread (*kaituka*) for the sake of initiation, the learned one should worship the Goddess and the others as before; then,
having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) and offered the sacrificial gift (*bali*) in the village and other places, the intelligent one should proceed likewise.
Having fully adorned the Lord of Gods, whether together with his two consorts or without them,
and likewise having placed him upon a vehicle endowed with a circle of light,
one should circumambulate the village while he is equipped with all ornaments.
Accompanied by all musical instruments and together with all the devotees and people, he should proceed along the path of the *bali* offering; for if he goes by another way, it causes defects.
Therefore, having led him around clockwise, he should enter the temple again.
Having installed the deity in the assembly pavilion and worshipped him as before,
and having likewise performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) and the protective rite (*rakṣā*), O wise ones,
Garuḍa should afterwards release the marriage-thread (*kautuka*) from the deity along with the Goddesses and the others.
Having bathed [the Lord] with the waters from the jars, or with pure water, some then bathe the Lord of Gods and likewise seat Him upon a yogic throne;
having worshipped the God, together with the Goddess and the others, up to the offering of oblations (havis).
Having performed the supreme diversion, one should then establish Hari along with the two goddesses in the seat of the Jīva and worship the Lord of Death (Yama) with sacrificial offerings.
Having consecrated the staff-limbed [deity], one should address Janārdana, saying, "Forgive me."
Then, having installed the wheels and other [emblems] in their respective places, he should thus pass the night. Then, at dawn, the righteous-souled one, at the conclusion of the morning worship,
should bow to the Lord, take Him [the image], and likewise install Him in the pavilion.

Furthermore, the wise knower of Dharma, having mentally resolved upon four seats there, should worship each of them in due order with the prescribed offerings for the seats and with their respective mantras.
Having worshipped the infinite lords of the *cakras*, one should again commence the *homa*.
After sprinkling water around the fire, one should then offer oblations to all the deities and all the attendants (*pārṣadas*) of Viṣṇu, each with their respective forms.
In that manner, one should offer oblations in sequence from Brahmā down to the various beings;
likewise, with the two forms of the bali and the anna, together with the lords of the cakras measured by the syllables [of the mantra].
Then the practitioner of mantra, having gone to the village accompanied by all musical instruments, should proceed in the same way.

Having offered the bali-oblation to the gods as before, and having entered the temple adorned with parasols, peacock feathers, and so forth, surrounded by devoted attendants, one should conclude the rite upon the *bhūta-pīṭha*.
Having bathed and worshipped the wheels and other [emblems] as well as the image of the deity as before,
and having installed them each in their respective places, one should properly present the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Having bowed again to the deity, [one should perform this] until it is pleasing to the eyes and the mind.
Having thus adorned the Lord together with the two goddesses as before,
and having placed the Lord [on the palanquin] in the evening, one should perform the circumambulation of the village and then enter the temple again, accompanied by ornaments.
Having worshipped him thus and seated him in his proper place, one should present the sacrificial oblation;
having likewise performed the *bali* offering and the *homa*, one should conduct the festival at night. Then, re-entering the temple and consecrating [the deity] with pure waters, one should proceed.

Having installed the deity in the pavilion while wearing the *kautuka* (wedding bracelet), one should present the offerings. Having performed the binding of the *kautuka*, one should likewise have the deity laid upon the bed.
In the morning, having lifted up the God of gods, one should do so without the sacrificial oblation (*havir*).
And at midday, one should perform for him the festival prescribed for the day; then,
having entered the temple, the knower of mantras should likewise place the deity in the assembly hall, after having prepared the powder of the God of gods as before.

In the same manner, one should apply oil and powder to Viṣṇu and to the members of the assembly (33). Then, having performed the powder festival, the mantra-knower should likewise cause the final ablution (abhṛtha) to be performed again as before, according to the prescribed rules, at a river or similar location (34).
At the conclusion of the bath, having taken up the deity preceded by a stream of water and adorned with all ornaments, one should cause him to enter the temple;
after bathing him with jars, one should likewise do so in another abode.
Having established [the deity] in the place of the vital breath (prāṇa) and having worshipped it thoroughly, one should offer [the oblation].
Having uttered the mantra of supplication, one should again perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, having offered the pacifying oblation (śānti-homa) into the fire, one should worship the Guru.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform the flower sacrifice according to his means;
this is the best [method] for the youngest [initiate], while the other, which is universal, is as before.
This is the procedure for two days.
If it takes two days, the wise one, having performed the previously mentioned offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*),
should not perform the taking of the clay, nor the bathing and so forth; thereafter,
he should fasten the *koṭuka* (sacred thread) together with the discus and other implements as before.
Having performed the *homa* and the *bali*, one should then conduct the night festival (40).
Having worshipped [the deity] in the pavilion in that same manner, one should likewise tie the *kautuka* (protective thread);
then, at dawn, having raised the deity, one should cause its festival to be celebrated (41).
Having likewise performed the powder festival (cūrṇotsava), one should perform the ritual bath at the sacred ford (tīrthasnāna);
having likewise performed the ceremonial lustration (svapana), one should then worship at the seat of the soul (jīvasthāna).
This is the specific distinction for the two-day festival; everything else is as before.
Regarding the method for a one-day festival:
"O wise ones, this [standard] festival is for the youngest [temple]; it should be considered intermediate for the middle [temple].
(43) One should perform the entire one-day festival as prescribed for the day of the *tīrtha*."
This [rite] for the youngest [son] should be the youngest; it bestows all fruits.
O Brahmin, during the three days [of the festival], it is dedicated to Brahmā and all the deities, and to Viṣṇu;
on two days of the festival, it is dedicated to Brahmā and to Viṣṇu as the lord of the day. 44–45.
On a single day, Hari and Īśa are indeed proclaimed by the wise;
one should perform it thus with devotion alone, for it bestows the fruit of all desires.
(46) This is the Śraddhotsava.

One should likewise perform the festival of devotion, having bowed with devotion to the God; [one may worship] the God either without the Discus and other emblems, or together with the two Goddesses (47).
Having taken [the deity] from the seat of the Jīva, one should install him upon the throne of the Maṇḍapa.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rules upon the previously mentioned seats (verse 48),
and having adorned the Lord of Gods and placed him upon the vehicle as before, one should perform a circumambulation of the village while he is fully equipped with all ornaments (verse 49).
Afterward, having caused [the deity] to enter the temple, bathed it, and offered oblations,
and having likewise established it in the seat of the life-force (jīvasthāna), one should bow down and then lead it forth.
At that time, the wise person who desires to perform the festival of the temple should perform the festival with devotion.
Whatever is performed with faith by devotees during the festival of the temple is called the *ālayotsava*.
One should not perform rites such as the offering of sprouts (*aṅkura-arpaṇa*) during the temple festival;
rather, having worshipped and offered oblations according to the prescribed path in the assembly hall (*āsthāna*), [the festival should proceed]. 51–52.
Whether accompanied by the two goddesses or alone, one should adorn the immutable Hari according to the prescribed path, making him beautiful and worthy of being seen; then,
having said "O Rathantara," one should place the immutable Hari upon the chariot.
The wise man should mount the horse with the mantra "Thou art a horse" (aśvo'si) or "Thou art a steed" (hayo'si);
the elephant with "Of Indra [thou art]" (indrasya tvā), or with the Gāyatrī;
and the parrot especially with "Pratadviṣṇuḥ stavate" when mounting a palanquin. 54–55.
Upon whichever patron the desire rests, one should have Hari installed there,
or one should cause a circumambulation to be performed according to the rules for a perpetual festival, accompanied by all musical instruments and provided with incense and lamps. 56.
One should cause each individual *cūlikā* to be circumambulated in a clockwise direction (57).
There is one circumambulation in the first enclosure and two in the second;
although there may be others, some say that one should not perform them (58).

If the *ālaya* is inferior and possesses many obstructions, one should circumambulate it three times clockwise and, as before, place it in its original location outside the assembly pavilion, provided that space is sufficiently wide. 59.
If [the area] should be extensive, [it may be placed] outside the assembly pavilion.
In the first enclosure, having performed each [circumambulation] as well as an additional one,
and having likewise completed the circumambulation while adorned with all ornaments, he should then enter within and especially perform worship upon the altar.
Then, having offered water for the feet, one should present mouth-fresheners;
having performed worship at midday and in the evening, one should conduct the festival.
Some, however, desire to perform the worship in the morning and the festival at midday.

Some wise men say that the worship for specific desires (*kāmyārcā*) should be performed at the time of the conclusion of the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), or between the two twilights (*sandhyā*). Thus,
one should cause the excellent [worship] to be performed in the temple according to the desire of the patron.

For nine days, or seven days, or five days, or three days, or likewise two days, or one day, one should have the marriage-thread (kautuka) and the bed prepared according to one's means, preceded by the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa). 65.
In this very manner, the wise man should have it performed on a single day and not on another;
he should especially provide entertainment during those days through Purāṇas, hymns, Sūtras, and the like, recounting the divine sports of Viṣṇu in their proper sequence. (66–67)
Especially on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) during the fortnight of the waxing moon in the month of Dhanus,
one should properly teach the Vedas along with songs, dances, and other arts;
and elsewhere as well, specifically without regard for [particular] times.
"The commencement [of the rite] is enjoined by rule under a lunar mansion favorable to the sacrificer.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the One-Day Utsava," within the section on Sacrifices (*yajñādhikāra*) in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium (*saṃhitā*) proclaimed by Bhṛgu. This concludes the section on Sacrifices.
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter:
Expiation regarding the examination of the ground.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedures for the examination of the ground and so forth.
O best of sages, listen now to the prescription for expiation:
through pacification, a fault becomes pacified, just as a hunter is cured by medicines;
therefore, one should perform expiation with every possible effort.
If one does not perform [the rite], there is no doubt that [the obstacles] will lead to destruction;
the obstruction caused by what is deficient or excessive is pacified by expiation (prāyaścitta).
If it should be devoid of the ritual substance, then there is a loss of the ritual substance.
If the ritual action (*kriyā*) is deficient, there is a loss of the ritual; if the mantra is deficient, it is emptiness.

The preceptor, the artisan, and the performer will certainly meet with ruin in due course if the mantra and ritual are immediately deficient, as will the sacrificial materials—of this there is no doubt. (4–5)
O wise one, if an obstacle should arise during the time of examining the ground or other such worldly rites,

one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava and Śānti mantras and then recite the Vaiśvānara mantra. Furthermore, in the event of an ill omen, an evil word, or the occurrence of quarrels and the like—
At that time, having offered the *śānti* oblation along with the Vaiṣṇava rites into the worldly fire (7),
and when the dust of the ground has subsided at the time of examining the site,
one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* and then recite the *Mahīsūkta* in due order (8).
If there is a deficiency in the characteristics of the plowshare and so forth, or likewise if the rope is broken,
the wise one should perform a fire-oblation for peace and then begin the plowing.
If, at that time, skulls, bones, husks, and the like are seen, [one should perform a rite].
Having removed each of those [impurities] for the sake of purification, one should likewise sprinkle [the area] with cow-products (gavya).
Having offered oblations according to the rules there to Viṣṇu and the deities of the earth,
one should worship the respective mantras in sequence if the worship of Amitābha and others has been deficient.
Then, having performed worship and made the offering, one should indeed undertake the ritual;
having fully honored the Vaiṣṇavas, preceded by the worship of the Guru. [However,] if the sowing of the seed is omitted, as is the non-offering to the cows—
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava and Śānti mantras, he should commence the ritual.
After spreading out loads of straw and offering them to the herds of cows,
the righteous-souled one, having worshipped the Guru, should undertake the remaining rites.

If the syllables of the names are deficient or reversed, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite; having offered oblations with those names, one should finally present the bali offering in the proper sequence.
The re-establishment [of the deity] is performed through the fire-oblation (homa), consisting of the rites of Brahma, Padma, and Avaṭa.
Therefore, even without that [initial rite], one should perform the Mahīsūkta oblation in sequence for the sake of peace.
At the time of installing the Śaṅku (the ritual peg), if it is broken, lost, or misplaced,
one should offer oblations to the deities of the directions and finally perform the demarcation of the quarters.

At the time of digging out the stakes and other elements, especially for the sake of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), one should perform the Vaiṣṇava oblation upon seeing [the site] and then commence the ritual work. When [the vessel] is turned face-down and agitated, one should perform the great pacification (mahāśānti) in due order.
Then, having taken up [the materials] and placed them [in the vessel], one should deposit jewels in the center;
if those jewels are lacking, or if gold is lacking, one should deposit [other materials] and perform the oblation accordingly. 19–20.
If the depositing of the embryo (*garbhanyāsa*) is omitted or if there is a transposition of the sites,

one should perform a propitiatory oblation (*śānti-homa*), take up [the image], and install it as prescribed by the rules. A wise man should then give the face-cloth (*paṭṭi*) of that group to a Brahmin.
One should properly fix the *garbha* (the central pillar) upon a long wooden beam (*uradhvapaṭṭikā*), especially so;
below that, one should establish the *garbha* as prescribed for the specific caste (*jāti*) at both [ends].
If it is otherwise, there will be misfortune; the builder and the patron shall perish.
The twice-born and the other classes were born respectively from the mouth, the arms, the thighs, and the feet;
such is the Śruti. Therefore, one should properly assign him to his respective class.
If the mantra-knower should assign him to the wrong class, he must quickly take him back.
Having performed the Mahāśānti rite for seven days, one should finally deposit [the materials] in due order.
Whether on the head [of the structure], on a brick, or on a stone, if there is another defect in the marking,
one should offer oblations into the fire as in the case of the first brick and deposit them properly in sequence.

Having performed the *śānti* oblation in that manner, the wise one should proceed when there is a reversal regarding the *sthūpikīla*, or when the prescribed tree is unavailable, by employing those suitable for sacrifice;
[he should recite] the Vaiṣṇava *śānti* mantra together with the *Śrībhūsūkta*.
Having offered oblations there according to the path, one should establish [the deity] as prescribed by the ritual rules (28).

When the celestial mansion (vimāna) is completed, if the rites beginning with the water-pot (kalaśa) have not been performed, then after offering the peace-oblation (śānti-homa) at the end, one should not act otherwise (29).
If the walls, gate-towers, and so forth are deficient, it will result in those very defects;
therefore, one should ensure they are beautifully adorned with great effort.
If the Vīśa is lacking, there will be an increase in the enemies of the builder.
If [the ritual] is devoid of the *śānti* [mantras], there will undoubtedly be the destruction of the performer's lineage;
if it is devoid of the *bhūta-pīṭha* and so forth, then total ruin occurs.
Therefore, one should cause all these to be performed together, as prescribed by the rule. 31–32.
If the installation of the golden [image] in the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) has been completed,
one should perform the *śānti* oblation according to the path and install it as prescribed by the ritual rules (33).
If it has not been installed, the *rākṣasas* will enter right there.
Therefore, one should properly perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the first brick as prescribed;
for if it remains incomplete, Hari departs and there is fault in every respect.
To destroy those cruel Asuras, [the architect] constructed their dwelling place.
In a multi-storied palace (bahubhūmivimāna), having firmly established [the foundation] floor by floor, one should subsequently raise the upper structure;
from the end of the roof-beams to the end of the floor, it should be done floor by floor.
Therefore, one should install [the deity] gradually on another, different ground;
such is my opinion regarding the installation along with the preliminary rites (*kautuka*).
Some, however, maintain that one should perform the installation only after having completed all the grounds (*bhūmi*). 37–38.
Having taken that particular limb and the *kautuka*, one should likewise install it;
one should not worship others there for as long as one’s own site remains.
The primary ground (*ādibhūmi*) is the most important among all grounds for the wise man. (39)
When the deity has entered the child-form (bāla), one should perform the festivals and so forth there;
all occasional rites (naimittika) are universal, with the exception of those pertaining to the child-abode.
Therefore, at the beginning, one should have the daily rites performed here according to the primary abode (mūladhāman). 40–41.
Just as the *gārhapatya* fire is the primary one among all fires in a certain house, so too is the ground of wisdom (*dhīmān*) the foremost in many places.
At the outset, it is said that for the first [type of practitioner], the trident is made of stone; likewise, for the other two, it is made of wood.

A trident made of wood or clay may be used for all [other] types [of temples]; however, one should never install a stone trident at the outset, as it brings misfortune even when used improperly. For temples other than those with three stories (tritala), one should certainly use a trident made of iron in some cases.
Specifically regarding a single level:

having established the first brick as the womb (*garbha*) in the first [layer], the *dhruva* in the second, and likewise the *mūrdheṣṭakā* in the third; then the *pratiṣṭhā* in the fifth, in due order above that.

Some authorities maintain that one should perform the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) prior to the laying of the crown-brick (*mūrdheṣṭakā*). However, the instruction is that if the patron is in haste, he should especially cause both the placement and the consecration to be performed at the conclusion of the *prastara* rite.
Having likewise consecrated the crown-brick and the pinnacle according to the prescribed rite,
and having performed the *kalabhakti* and other ceremonies at the end, one should install the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) in that manner.
(48) If, however, out of greed for wealth or through delusion, one does not act as prescribed, [the result is as follows].
One should perform the great propitiation (mahāśānti) for seven days by making oblations in the fire of lotuses in due order.
Having given the fee to the preceptor, having obtained his permission, and having honored him,
one should afterwards perform what has been prescribed, bowing down and saying, "Forgive me."
But if, at the time of installing the stone [image], it should be deficient in a limb—
whether it be a stone-liṅga or one made of metal— the wise man, having performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa),
should likewise have it joined together if it is suitable for rejoining.
Otherwise, if [the image] were not to be cast, one should instead procure another *bera*.

(52) Furthermore, if the great *bera* that has been installed should become deficient in its limbs, one should take up that *bera*, discard it, and quickly perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*). (53)
If an image is clearly afflicted by defects, the wise one should discard that image;
having procured another image, he should worship it together with the learned elders.
(54) Even so, if a defect should occur in the case of the two goddesses in a fixed image, [the same procedure applies].
On another occasion, having gathered [the materials], one should worship together with the two goddesses.
By that alone, there shall be no lack of power; it is equal in every respect.
Therefore, after due consideration, one should not dismiss a faultless image.
If one should, out of delusion or negligence, abandon a faultless image,
there will be the sins of killing a Brahmin and so forth, as well as the ruin caused by a foreign army.
(57) And if a great image has been installed, yet after a month has passed, it is abandoned through delusion...
Or, in the case of one devoid of sacraments (*saṃskāra*) or in the fire of a lotus-born child, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite of pacification (*śānti*).

It is said that for two months it is double [the duration], and for three months one should perform it triple; thus, up to the end of a year, the best among those who know mantras should increase [the rites]. 58–59.
Thus, having performed the rites beginning with the plowing and ending with the twelfth year, one should again perform that consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Atonement for Plowing and Other Rites," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The Authority for Sacrifice.
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter:
The Procedure for the Expiation of Consecration.

O wise ones, hereafter I shall explain the ritual for re-establishing the installation of this deity’s fire, for the sake of pacifying the faults of transgressions committed during its daily and occasional rites,
and so forth, regarding this embodied fire.

The wise one should cause [the rite] to be performed according to the rules, preceded by the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa). If it is devoid of the offering of sprouts, the ritual action becomes otherwise;
therefore, having performed the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma), one should perform it preceded by the offering of sprouts.
Having first performed the assembly of the seats and the opening of the eyes,
one should deposit gold even in the absence of jewels; however,
at the time of opening the eyes, if the ritual is deficient or inverted.

But if it is deficient in substances such as cow-products, one should perform the rite only after offering the *śānti* oblation. If the perfuming with cow-products is omitted, or if the perfuming with milk is omitted,
one should again offer oblations a hundred times with the mantra dedicated to each respective deity.

Having filled the jar with those substances, having worshipped it and consecrated it with water, one should then let that jar undergo the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) for one day or for seven days,
either in the sacrificial hall upon the altar or in another location if more space is available.

If the jar lacks the prescribed measurements, or is cracked and so forth, and if the grain, cloth, gems, and other items are deficient, then Hari indeed destroys the man. Therefore, having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) as prescribed, one should recite the Narasūkta, which belongs to Viṣṇu.
Having offered oblations with the Śrī Bhūsūkta and the Mahāśānti mantra, one should proceed accordingly;
likewise, if the consecrated pitcher should be broken through negligence,
the Guru should take another pitcher and install it as before.
If the image is touched by those who are untouchable, one should perform a ceremonial bath (snapana).
If the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) are touched, one should perform a ceremonial bath for the image;
thereafter, one should bathe the auspicious marks (kautuka) and other parts with seven jars.
One should likewise practice tranquility when there is perversion or deficiency;
also when there is a reversal regarding the bed or the place of stay, or a reversal involving eggs and the like,
or even when there is a lack of grain, or a reversal regarding the supporting pillow.

Having offered oblations into the Sabhya fire according to the Vaiṣṇava rite, dedicated to the respective deities, accompanied by the Śrī-būsūkta, and concluding with the Vyāhṛtis, one should perform the final rites according to the prescribed rule; however, at the time of the Hotṛ’s recitation, if there is a reversal or confusion, [one should act accordingly]. 14–15.
At the time of the final oblation (*nirvāpa*) of the offerings, having likewise performed the propitiatory oblations (*śānti-homa*), one should act accordingly;
and in the event of the Lord and the Goddess being awakened from sleep through negligence, the wise man should recite the *Śrīsūkta* and *Bhūsūkta* four times each and lay them down as before.

Likewise, when the study [of the scriptures] is deficient, or when the worship of the assembly and the deities is lacking, or when the dance, song, and so forth are absent, one should shake that respective mantra in due order. Furthermore,
at the time of the fivefold consecration (pañcapratiṣṭhā), during the ceremonial bathing, and also during festivals, [the same applies].
From the time of the offering of the seed-syllable (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) until the conclusion of the impurity period, the Guru shall not incur his own sin nor the sin of others in all ritual acts;
this applies to both the Guru and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) until the completion of the rite. (19)
If there should be a crow at the end, there is no fault; of this there is no doubt.
(20) Thus say the authors of the Smṛtis regarding the gathering of materials and so forth, specifically for the consecrators, the preceptor, and the officiating priests. (21)
If threats, beatings, and so forth should occur that do not cause destruction,
one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava, Viṣṇusūkta, Pauruṣasūkta, Brāhma, and Sārasvata hymns, and then honor him by bowing down.
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) undoubtedly destroys the performer.
Life itself is the fee for the sacrifice; therefore, a wise man should bestow it properly.
This is especially true when the altar of worship is devoid of the depositing of gems.

Having cast gold [into the fire], and having offered oblations even to Vaiṣṇava, one should perform the expiation and the Great Peace (mahāśānti) rite, and then procure fire churned from wood— especially so when the installation of the Nityāgni has been omitted and in the case of the Sabhyāgni. 25.
At the conclusion of the *āghāra* oblation, having likewise offered the *śānti*, the *vaiṣṇava*, and the *vyāhṛti* mantras (26),

and having performed the final offering while ensuring thorough protection, one should perform the daily homa; then, having invoked [the deity] from the *kumbha* into the *dhruva* vessel and subsequently into the *kautuka* and other vessels in their proper order (27).
The knower of mantras, having invoked [the deity] from the *dhruva* [image], should worship it; this brings no misfortune.

Then, for the *kautuka*, the installation, and subsequently the festival, the mantra-practitioner should likewise invoke [the deity] from that *dhruva* image in due order, and should perform the same for the *baliberam*.
Having thus worshipped and praised Janārdana with devotion,
the mantra-practitioner (mantrī) should likewise invoke the retinue and worship the jars.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Expiation in Consecration," within the section on Sacrifice in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium (*saṃhitā*) proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The Authority for Sacrifice.
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter:
Expiation for Daily Worship.
Now, I shall describe the expiation for the daily worship,
which serves for the peace of all and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. It must be performed before sunrise in the morning, at midday, and indeed at sunset.
If the opening of the door is hindered, one should then open it quickly;

having likewise offered salutations for peace, the wise man should offer oblations into the perpetual fire (nityāgni) to the Vaiṣṇava deity, to the presiding deities of each respective door, and to the Śrībhūsūkta.
If the removal of faded flowers is neglected, or likewise the sweeping and smearing [of the temple],
one should offer oblations in sequence with the Vaiṣṇava, Vāruṇa, and Viṣvaksena hymns.
But if the daily bath is omitted, one should likewise [offer] the Vaiṣṇava and Vāruṇa [hymns].

Or one should perform a sprinkling for the very purpose of purifying the image. If, out of delusion, one should worship the *kautuka* (sacred thread) without performing the ritual placement of flowers (*puṣpanyāsa*),
the wise person should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymns, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Gāyatrī.
Having performed the ritual placement of flowers (puṣpanyāsa), one should perform worship during the three junctions of the day;
otherwise, there will be destruction, especially for the worshipper.
Likewise, if one does not worship the retinue beginning with Dhātṛ and the others, [the same result follows].

Having offered oblations with that mantra, one should worship [the deity] at the end according to the prescribed rite. If the morning worship is omitted, one should perform it twice as much at midday;
likewise, if both the morning and midday worships are omitted, one should perform it three times as much in the evening.
On the second day, the wise one should perform it twice as long; on the third day, three times as long.
In this manner, he should increase it until the end of the twelfth day, accompanied by rites for pacification.
But when the twelve days have passed, especially in the case of the *sabhyāgni* fire—

Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Śrī-bhū-sūkta (verse 11), and having bathed [the deity] together with the attendants according to the prescribed method for bathing (verse 12a),
one should worship the permanent image (dhruvabera) with the mantra "aśanno devī" (verse 12b).
Having worshipped all the deities, one should properly offer the oblation; let there be a sacrifice lasting for a month, preceded by a hundred thousand recitations.
Then, having taken up the Sabhya fire, one should perform the rite of pacification for seven days.

Having bathed the deity with one hundred and eight jars and worshipped him, the knower of mantras should offer abundant food (naivedya) and address him, saying, "Forgive me. One should perform this in the same manner every month, and likewise double it every two months.

It is taught that for three months one should increase [the offerings] threefold until the end of the year; then, at the end of the year, one should perform the re-consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) according to the prescribed rules for consecration. Excluding the two rites of opening the eyes and the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), one should perform everything else.
If the offering of the oblation is deficient, one should perform the Kṣīrabhū-sūkta; having offered the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa [sūktas], one should present twice as much.
Thus the wise man should increase it, especially until the end of six months.

At the end of six months, all people will certainly perish in due course if the ritual of offering oblations to the deity's form (*mūrti-homa*) is omitted; however, the wise practitioner, having offered the Vaiṣṇava mantra of the deity's form twice as many times at the conclusion, should well protect the fire.

If the worshiper is always unable to maintain the perpetual fire (nityāgni), he should, at that time, consign it into himself; then, having performed the oblation at the conclusion of the night-offering, he may consign it even into a common (laukika) fire. 20–21.
A wise person should offer it again before sunset, as if out of curiosity, having placed it within himself;
if the cooked oblation with its side-dish is offered while still warm, he should offer it again after sunrise. If it has been offered and is still warm, he should offer it again after sunset.
If, out of delusion, betel-leaf contaminated by hair or other impurities is offered,
one should discard it, take another, perform the propitiatory rite (śānti),
and offer it after having previously performed the expiation according to the procedure for the daily festival.
In the Nirukta, the wise one should practice the expanded universal rite;
likewise, the ritual bathing is declared to be of three types—daily, occasional, and optional—in order for the protection of the twice-born and others. 25. Indeed, these exist for their safeguarding.

Those beginning with the equinoxes (viṣuva) are obligatory (nitya); those such as eclipses are occasional (nimittavat); and the remaining ones are optional (kāmya), according to the sequence of those who have mastered the Vedas. However, if the respective ablutions (snāna) are omitted, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava and Vāruṇa rites.
Having offered oblations with the Viṣṇu-sūkta at the conclusion, one should perform the respective ablutions. An excellent bathing hall should be constructed to the north or in front of the temple;
that in the northeast is said to be middling, and that in the south or southwest is inferior.
One should not perform the *ābhicārika* rite in other corners out of delusion.

Therefore, having offered the oblation for peace (*śānti*) as prescribed, one should perform it correctly, especially during the time of twilight (*saṃdhyākāla*) when there is great heat, at the time of bathing, and so forth. 29–30.

Having completed the *naimittika* [rites], one should thereafter perform the daily (*nitya*) rites; however, if from the time of sleeping during the first part of the night until the end of the night, one has performed no acts such as lying down [in sleep],
one should offer oblations in sequence with the *vaiṣṇava*, *narasūkta*, and *śrīsūkta*.
However, at that time, the wise one should first perform the *kautuka* (the marriage-thread ceremony) alone;

thereafter, the wise one should have the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) performed according to the rules. Even in the case of a single image (*ekabera*), the *kautuka* should indeed be performed prior to that time.
Having performed the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha), one should immediately perform the ritual bathing; however,
if the ritual bathing has not been performed after the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
then one should perform the bathing properly at the conclusion, after having likewise offered the peace-oblation (śānti).
Some authorities maintain that one should never perform the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) during the consecration of a portable image, nor specifically during the ritual bathing; likewise,
this should especially not be done in a pit that lacks the proper measurements or in a row of sacrificial posts (paṅktipāli).
Having offered oblations to Paṅktīśa, who is devoted to Viṣṇu, one should perform the rite correctly according to the rules.
However, if the materials such as clay are deficient, or if they are excessive, or if there is a reversal [of the proper order],
and if the twelve substances beginning with those derived from a cow are lacking, one should likewise offer oblations for the sake of pacification (śānti).
If the consecrated jar is broken through negligence,
one should remove it and, having taken another, worship it and perform the ritual honors in the proper sequence.
Even when the ritual substances have been prepared, if worms, insects, or the like should appear within them...

Having set aside other items and taken up [the necessary materials], one should perform the propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa) and proceed as prescribed; however, if [the full set] is not obtained, one should prepare eight or even four [items] and subsequently perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) according to the ritual rule.

If an oil massage has occurred due to delusion during the ritual bathing and so forth, that bathing would be in vain; know that such an act would be demonic (āsura). Therefore, having bathed [the deity] with pure water and honored it by saying "Forgive me," [one should proceed].

Having thus performed the great propitiatory offering (mahāśānti), one should then perform the ceremonial bath (snapana). If the two goddesses are present at the time of that bath, the bath should be performed together with them; otherwise, that bath becomes fruitless and brings about strife for the kingdom.
The two goddesses, Snāpanā and Snapanā, are the wise ones who perform the ritual bathing with the pitcher (kalaśasnāpana).
If one does not perform this out of delusion, people will be afflicted by diseases;
therefore, having offered the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) and having paid homage with the words "May you forgive me," [one should proceed]. 44-45.
Having bathed the God of Gods and offered abundant oblations, if the installation is performed together with the pedestal, then at the conclusion of the bathing, it should be done as before;
one should bathe the God and Goddess with pure waters, excluding the ritual jar.
Whatever has not been stated here, all that is detailed extensively in the *Parākṣila*.
Thus, the wise one should follow the path of ritual action and perform atonement (*prāyaścitta*).
This concludes the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Rule for Atonement in Worship," in the section on Sacrifice within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The Authority for Sacrifice.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter:
Expiation for Festivals.
Now, O ascetics rich in austerity, I shall declare the expiation for the festival;
whether it be through ignorance, lack of respect, greed for wealth, delusion, or negligence,
the expiation shall be proclaimed with reference to each respective fault.

One should perform a festival in villages and other places; first, there should be a festival for Rudra, and afterwards one should perform a festival for Viṣṇu for the prosperity of the village. If the festival for Rudra has been performed but the festival for Viṣṇu remains unperformed, [the village will suffer].
If there is destruction of that village due to epidemics, famine, thieves, and the like,
one should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the sake of pacifying those evils;
having performed a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*), one should finally conduct a festival for Viṣṇu.
If the time for the festival has passed, one should perform the previously mentioned fire-oblation (homa).
One should bathe the immutable Lord with twenty-five water-pots,
or present an abundant great sacrificial offering to the Lord of Gods.
Thereafter, one should perform the festival according to the procedure prescribed for festivals;
when one year has passed, however, one should accomplish the five fires in due order.
Having offered the *āghāra* oblation as before, the Vaiṣṇava oblation is then well-offered.
Having offered oblations with the Brāhma and Raudra hymns accompanied by the Viṣṇusūkta,
and having offered the Puruṣasūkta at each individual oblation, he should then offer in the Sabhyāgni fire with mantras dedicated to all the deities.

One should perform the ceremonial bathing of the deity with one hundred and eight jars in due order; on the sacrificial altar itself, one should offer the great oblation of food (mahāhavis) and the bali-offering to the great elements.
Afterwards, one should perform the festival of Viṣṇu, which increases the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
One should give the previously mentioned sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and the others.

In the second year, one should perform it with double the amount; in the third year, especially when [the ritual] is deficient, one should accomplish the five fires and perform the animal sacrifice and the Āghāra offering as before.
One should offer the Viṣṇusūkta in the east, the Puruṣasūkta in the south,
the Ekākṣara and other mantras in the west, and likewise the Durgāsūkta in the north;
having offered oblations to all the deities in the Sabhya fire, one should likewise perform the rite of pacification (śānti).
Then, having performed the ablution of the deity with one thousand and eight [offerings],
he should present a great oblation (*mahāhavis*) to the Lord of Gods;
and after giving a mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*), he should offer the *bali* to the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
One should feed the Brahmins there and give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests;
having performed this with diligence, one should conduct the festival of Viṣṇu for nine days,
seven days, or one day— thus it is remembered as being of three kinds.
The rites for a nine-day period are as previously stated, and likewise for a seven-day period. When the festival is reduced to a single day, the Mahāśānti is indeed offered;
one should then worship with the Vaiṣṇava hymns, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Narasūkta.
Having bathed [the deity] with one hundred and eight jars, one should offer abundant food;
having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), one should perform the re-consecration (punarutsarga).
If the festival is deficient by even a single sound, one should gradually satisfy the members of the assembly and others.

Having performed the Mahāśānti rite, one should perform the previously mentioned oblation (homa). One should perform the ablution of the God of gods with one hundred and eight jars; having offered the great sacrificial oblation (mahāhavis), the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is bestowed.
One should perform a double offering for the deities of that village,
and specifically at midnight, one should present the offering to the great elements (mahābhūta-bali).
Having made the proclamation as before, one should properly conduct the festival.
If a festival for Hari is performed without the proclamation [of the day],
one should offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire eight hundred times for each [deity] and bathe the immutable Lord with twenty-five jars.
On the sacrificial altar itself, one should offer the great oblation of the elements;
having made the proclamation as before, one should properly conduct the festival.
If, after the hoisting of the banner, the proclamation is made once again, [the festival should be performed].

An oblation is offered to Vaiṣṇava, whose deity is the banner, as well as to the discus and other emblems (26). Having performed the oblations for Indra and the other deities, one should perform the ceremonial bath of the Lord;
then, having removed that banner, one should prepare another banner (27).
Having performed the proclamation as previously described, one should carry out the hoisting of the banner.

During the festival, if the proclamation of the drum occurs, or if it falls and so forth, or if its hide is torn, or if at that time the staff and other parts likewise fall; 28. [In these cases, the rite must be repeated.]
Having offered oblations to the deities of the musical instruments upon the falling of the players,
and having likewise offered to Nāndīśa, the Śaiṣika oblation is well-performed; then, having prepared another drum, one should carry out the proclamation as previously described.

If the banner falls or breaks, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) at that very moment; having offered oblations to the deity of the banner, oblations are also made for the discus and other emblems (31),
and after offering to Indra and the other gods, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
One should perform the ceremonial bath of the Garuḍa and offer oblations of clarified butter (havis).
The wise one should then release that banner and prepare another banner;
having fashioned it according to the previously mentioned rite, he should perform the hoisting of the banner.
When the banner is raised, broken, or fallen, and likewise when the staff is damaged,
one should abandon that staff and that banner, take up another banner, and having grasped another staff, firmly establish it with great effort. (34)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations each to the Vaiṣṇava banner,

the wise man, having performed the ceremonial bath of the deity, should bathe Garuḍa; then, having performed the rites according to the previously mentioned procedure, he should carry out the hoisting of the banner.
If the flagstaff is devoid of worship, one should worship the Vaiṣṇava deity presiding over the flagstaff one hundred and eight times on the day prior to the festival and other such occasions;
the wise preceptor should then bathe Garuḍa with twenty-five water-pots.

Having worshipped the deity of the banner well, one should present abundant offerings. Having performed the daily worship with such diligence, one should always cast the *bali* offering at night according to the prescribed method of worship.
If there is only one offering for all the gods, one should first offer the *bali* at night; one should perform the *bali* twice as much.
Having thus increased the *bali*, one should perform it correctly. 40.
On that very day of the proclamation, when the daily offerings have been omitted, he should offer oblations to all the gods, recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymns,
and then perform the ceremonial bathing of the deity with one hundred and eight jars.
One should perform the proclamation and other rites according to the previously mentioned procedure for either nine days or seven days; thus, the festival is said to be of two kinds.
At the beginning of these two festivals, on the first night, the offering of the sacred water and the auspicious sprouts (tīrthāṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed.

For other festivals, however, except for the day of the festival itself, the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) should take place on the ninth day prior to the prescribed day of the holy site (tīrtha). If the offering of sprouts is omitted, [the rite] should be performed with the Brāhma and Saumya [muhūrtas]. 44–45.
Having offered oblations to Paṅktīśa and Śaiṣika, the Cakra is indeed well-offered;
likewise, the Vaiṣṇava is offered together with the names beginning with Jaya (Jaya, Abhyātāna, Rāṣṭrabhṛt).
If the previously mentioned day is missed, however, flowers and sprouts will appear immediately.
At one time, during an inferior festival, a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice is well-performed (47).
One should offer oblations to the gods accompanied by the Narasūkta; having offered the Brāhma and Raudra oblations, one should include those for the poor and the like (48).
Having offered oblations to Indra and the others, one should then offer well to the Cakra and the rest;
beginning the festival in the morning, one should subsequently perform the festival immediately. At evening, however, when the festival has concluded, an oblation to Viṣṇu is well offered.
One should bathe the immutable Lord with twenty-five water-pots.
On the following day, one should perform a festival that is double [the previous];
however, if it is deficient by even a single day, one should then perform the Mahāśānti rite.
Having offered oblations to all the deities for the assembly members according to the prescribed rite, one should bathe them with twenty-five [mantras] and present abundant offerings.
Having provided mouth-perfume, one should then perform the festival once again.
If the festival is deficient by two days, one should perform all the remaining rites.
One should perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) for the deficient festival according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having performed the festival again, the proclamation and other such acts should likewise take place.
When a festival has been completed at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) that was previously deficient,
one should perform the pacification (*śānti*) for that deficient festival according to the previously mentioned procedure;
thereafter, one should perform the proclamation and other rites of the festival and attend to the sacred site.

One should perform the festival of Bali-hīna and offer oblations to the Vaiṣṇava deity (56). Having offered the bali-oblation dedicated to the protective deity and the deity of the day at that time, one should again perform the festival (57).
If the *bali* and the *bhūtabali* fall upon the ground,
the wise practitioner should offer the *balirakṣa-kha-mantra* and the *cakrādi* [mantras], and then cast away that *bali* while fashioning another *bali*.
Having offered the bali as before, one should lead [the deity] along with the *cakra* and other implements (v.

59). One should perform the festival upon that image which is intended for the festival; if the festival is to be performed upon another image, one should perform the fire-offering (*homa*) for the pacification of the festival's obstacles (v. 60).
Having performed the propitiatory rite according to the prescribed rules, one should perform the festival once again;
indeed, one should carry out that entire festival during the festival itself. (61) When [the deity] has gone outside the temple for the sake of the festival of another temple...
Even if that festival has been omitted, or if it occurs due to fate,

or even when [the deity] has gone to his own abode, one should quickly perform a rite of pacification (śānti) and offer oblations with the mantra of the presiding deity of that day and with the Cakra-mantras and others.
Having offered oblations to Indra and the others, and having offered those associated with Brahmā and Rudra, as well as the Viṣṇu-sūkta, the Vaiṣṇava oblation is properly performed;
likewise, for Śrī and Bhūmi, and for the two Ṛṣis, each [oblation] is made ending with the Vyāhṛtis.
One should perform the ceremonial bath of the deity with forty-eight pitchers (65). Having offered the *bali* at that time, one should again conduct the festival;
likewise, one should perform it for the discus and other emblems, as well as for the *baliberas* (66).
One should not move the *kautuka* (sacred thread) for the sake of a festival at another temple;

rather, one should offer it during the three junctions of the day specifically for the purpose of the festival. One should perform the festival without deficiency according to the rules for daily festivals.
One should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) thereafter, and then again conduct a festival.
Or, one should place Lord Hari upon a palanquin with side-panels;
once the Lord has ascended the vehicle or the chariot, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for Garuḍa.
Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma,
and Raudra according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the festival once again.
[One should also offer] vehicles, umbrellas, chowries, and so forth, to other fierce deities.
One should never worship the Lord of Gods with flowers that have been worn as garments or ornaments (71).
If one should worship out of ignorance, one must perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*) of the deity;
and if the vehicle has fallen to the ground or is broken, one should perform the rites as previously prescribed (72).

Once the image has fallen from the vehicle, an oblation to Vaiṣṇava should indeed be well-offered; one should also offer the mantra of that day one hundred and eight times. One should bathe the deity with water-pitchers and consecrate him with water.
When the image has fallen to the ground, one should bathe it with one hundred and eight jars;
one should bathe the deity with water and perform the oblation of the Vaiṣṇava-sūkta,
the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Śrī-bhū-sūkta.
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas there and offer oblations to all the gods;
having performed the gift of food, one should again conduct a festival.
[One should also offer] the pedestal, the halo, the lotus, the conch, the discus, and the ornaments and weapons.
One should declare the head-wheel (*śiraścakra*) and the armor (*varman*) to be the subsidiary limbs (*upāṅga*).

Having joined [the mantra] even when it is devoid of the subsidiary limbs according to the prescribed rule, and having performed the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) as before, one should perform the rite once again in this manner. 77–78.
A wise person should not abandon a golden or silver image that has a missing limb; rather,
one should have that image restored using the same materials,
making it superior in those materials and performing the rites for the deficient part.

Having performed the installation as before, one should subsequently conduct the festival (utsava). One should likewise fashion the Cakravīśa, Amitābha, and the Bimba images; however, one must never have festive images made of stone or wood. 80–81.
If one should cause this to be done out of ignorance, it is considered malevolent magic;
therefore, to pacify this fault, one should perform an expiation (prāyaścitta).
Taking the Pauṇḍarīka fire, one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu a hundred times.
Having offered oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Vaiṣṇava hymns,
and having brought abundant sacrificial food (bali), he should present that offering in the village.
He should perform the ceremonial bathing of the deity and present a profusion of offerings.
If the image, or the cloth, ornaments, or vehicle are touched by fire,
the wise man should discard all of that and perform the bathing of the image;
he should bathe the Lord of the God of Gods once again with the prescribed fragrant substances.
The Vaiṣṇava, the Brāhma, and the Raudra oblations are duly offered (86).
Oblations are also offered to the two Goddesses, to the two Sages, and to the Discus and other [emblems] (87).
Having made offerings to Indra and the others, one should present milk-rice and other foods.
Having fed the Brahmins here, one should perform the festival again;
for those [deities] such as the Discus (Cakra) and others, their respective mantras should likewise be employed. (88) If the preceptor has died, the festival should not be performed without him.
Having performed the propitiatory rite (śānti) for an inferior festival, one should then perform the [proper] festival;
having taken his disciple, he should appoint him to the office of preceptor (ācāryatva),
and likewise, when the patron (yajamāna) has died, having performed the propitiatory rite, one should perform the festival.
Having gathered together, one should perform the festival for the king who is the sacrificer;
likewise upon the death of kings and upon the death of members of one's own kin.
Even when a festival is deficient, one should perform the "festival for the distressed" according to the prescribed rules.
During periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*pretaka*), and when the performer (*kartṛ*) and others have assembled,
one must not worship with those materials, excluding the deities and the Brahmins. Indeed,
one should carry out the festival itself by means of avoiding those very materials.
In the event of a deficient festival, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) and then conduct the festival again;
likewise, if the teacher is in a state of ritual impurity (āśauca) or if the festival is deficient, the disciple should perform it by the teacher's command. 94.
One should perform the previously mentioned propitiatory rite (śāntika) and again conduct a festival.
During the festival of Viṣṇu, if it coincides with the festival of another deity, one should perform both the Vaiṣṇava and the Raudra rites for a single day. 95–96.
In the event of such a confusion, one should first perform the festival of Rudra without fault,
and afterwards perform the festival of Viṣṇu, accompanied by all the [prescribed] rites throughout the year;
this is for the sake of removing that defect entirely from the festival of Viṣṇu.
During the festival of Viṣ� liquor, meat, and blood should be offered as a *bali* to Bhadrakālī; one should perform the *bali* for the sake of the gods and must not cast a *paiśāca-bali*. 98–99.
From the proclamation until the descent [of the deity], if there is a confusion of castes due to delusion or ignorance for even a single day, it is destroyed;
to remedy that fault, one should perform an expiation for the sake of the welfare of the community. 100.
Having purified every joint and smeared it with cow dung,
one should there cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and perform the Vāstu-homa sacrifice; having offered oblations to Viṣṇu, as well as those to Brahmā and Raudra.
Having offered the *śānti* oblation for the wheel and other [emblems], and having likewise offered the mantra of the Lord of the Day according to the ritual rule,
one should perform the ablution of the deity one hundred and eight times. 103.
Having performed the ritual bathing of the discus and other emblems, one should present them with sacrificial offerings (havis).
After offering milk-rice (pāyasa) and other foods, one should then conduct the festival.
This is the procedure if the festival of Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī is being performed.
But in the case of their commingling, one should perform atonement for the fault;
Bhadrakālī and Śāstā are for the commingling (verse 106),
and in the case of commingling with the Primordial Form, one should likewise perform pacification.
One should never perform singing or dancing by Caṇḍālas for the sake of the gods (107).
If one should cause such acts to be performed out of delusion or ignorance, he perishes;
to counteract that fault and for the sake of honor, he should quickly perform a propitiatory rite (108).
Whether in a village or in a monastery, one should perform the purification of the ground;
having offered the Vāstu-homa sacrifice, one should then recite the Puṇyāha formula in due order.
Furthermore, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) of the deity with eight auspicious jars.
One should perform the ritual bathing of the [Liṅga] with the discus and other implements, and then have the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited.
There, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and perform the study of the Veda. Furthermore, if there is contact with those who are untouchable, the ritual bathing of the deity must take place.
Having offered the Vaiṣṇava oblation, the Pauruṣa is well-offered;
the Vaiṣṇava joined with the Brāhma and the Raudra are also well-offered.
(112) If, through some negligence, the parasol, the peacock-feather fan, the canopy, or any other [item] [is damaged], [one should perform the following].
In the event of burning or falling, one should offer oblations there with the Āgneya and Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Furthermore, when chowries fall, break, or are defiled by fire,
one should offer oblations in sequence with the Māyā-saṃhlādinī mantra and the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
In the case of a dancer, a singer, or indeed among the temple-maidens (devadāsīs),
as well as when one has fallen [from grace], been burnt by fire, or subjected to verbal abuse or physical killing—
115— in those instances, having first offered the oblation to Agni, one should then offer the Vaiṣṇava oblation in due order.
Having offered the oblation with the mantra "śriye jāta," the *śaiṣika* oblation is then properly offered.

In the event of the falling of musicians or their instruments, or upon the death or cremation of a broken [vessel], and likewise upon the falling of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) or sages, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).

In the event of agitation involving the patron or the preceptor, one should perform the oblation for the sages; having offered the Vaiṣṇava oblation, the supplementary oblation (śaiṣika) is then properly performed.
[This applies] in the case of a conflict, the flow of blood, a firebrand, or when a person has died.
One should cause the purification of the ground to be performed both in the village and in the dwelling;
having offered the Vāstu-homa, one should then have the Puṇyāha recited.
Having offered the Vaiṣṇava oblation, the offerings for the discus and other emblems are properly sacrificed.

Having performed the ceremonial bath of the deity, one should subsequently conduct the festival; however, when a festival of the deities approaches for those who have recently menstruated and so forth, one should ensure the purification of the ground, whether in the village or at the temple. 121.
Having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited;
having performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, the oblations for the discus and other emblems are well-offered;
and having offered to Indra and the other deities, the ceremonial bathing of the deity shall take place.
Having performed the study of the Vedas, one should thereafter conduct the festival;
