singing, dancing, instrumental music, as well as incense and lamps— these they call the five essential substances, for without them there can be no festival.

If one should cause a festival to be performed out of delusion or even through ignorance, it is declared that an *abhicārika* (malevolent) rite has been undertaken; in that case, a propitiatory (*śānti*) oblation is offered into the fire.
Having performed the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) of the deity, one should thereafter conduct the festival.

If one should perform a festival without the fire-worship, one must perform the fire-worship first and only thereafter conduct the festival. (127) If the binding of the *pratisara* is omitted through negligence at dawn, [one must rectify it].
Having offered oblations to Viṣṇu and likewise to Soma and the deities, one should bind the protective amulet (pratisara) there; the remainder should be performed as before.
However, if the bed is lacking, an oblation to Viṣṇu is indeed offered.
Then, having offered oblations with the Śrī Bhūsūkta and likewise with the Śaiṣika hymns according to the previously prescribed rite, one should properly perform the preparation of the bed.
In the event that five beds are not available, one should spread a cloth upon each individual one.

If the head-pillow (mūrdhopadhāna) is deficient, one should offer oblations to the deity Nāgādhi. If the day designated for the pilgrimage (tīrtha) should coincide with another occasion, one should perform the pilgrimage on that day according to the procedure for a minor festival.
But if the officiating preceptor (kartṛ-ācārya) perishes during the festival, it shall become fruitless;
therefore, having performed the ritual bathing (snapana) of the deity, a propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa) should be well-offered.
[133] This applies whether the interval is more than one day or even if the festival lasts for only a single day.
On that day, one should perform the pilgrimage without fault;
even if one is deprived of an oil massage or a powder bath, or if the powder festival itself is omitted, one should nevertheless perform the powder bath. 134–135.
Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, and Raudra, and likewise having offered to the Discus and the other [emblems], one should thereafter perform the utsava.
The pilgrimage (tīrtha) should be undertaken only during the day; one should not perform the pilgrimage at night.
At night, however, one should perform the ritual at the time of the *tīrtha*; one should not perform the *tīrtha* during the day.
If, through delusion or ignorance, it should happen to be done in reverse, one should offer oblations with the *Brāhma*, *Raudra*, *Viṣṇusūkta*, and *Vaiṣṇava* mantras. (137–138)

One should recite the mantra of the presiding deity of that day and offer oblations to the wheels and other components; having prostrated before the Lord of Devas, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed there.
If the day is devoid of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one should perform this during the daytime or on that very day.

Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the rite at the sacred ford (tīrtha) at that time. If the bathing at the ford is omitted, or if the offering of oblations (bali) is omitted during the mounting ceremony, one should hold a festival for one day and bathe [the deity] with one hundred and eight [offerings].
One should offer a great oblation of the primary elements (mahābhūtabali) and present it in abundance;
however, if the lowering of the banner has been delayed for seven nights,
one should perform a single festival and bathe [the deity] with one hundred and eight [offerings].
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) and other foods, one should feed a hundred Brahmins;
having offered oblations to all the gods, one should present the bali-offering to the great elements.
Having performed the worship of the banner, one should then lower that banner.
In a festival that is deficient in mantras, and likewise deficient in ritual materials,
one should perform the rites for malevolent magic as prescribed and also perform all rites for pacification;
therefore, with every effort, one should carry out the rite provided it is complete in its materials.
The preceptor alone shall bestow the substance that has been consecrated with mantras;
it is ordained as the due of the preceptor, and one must not cause it to be given to the disciple.
[If done so], it would be fruitless and lead to the destruction of the performer; therefore, Hari should abandon that place. 146–147.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation during Festivals," in the section on Sacrifices within the *Vaikhānasa Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu. [End of] the Section on Sacrifices.
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter.
The Expiation for the Abode of the Child.
Now, I shall explain the expiation for the abode of the child; when the abode of the child is being worshipped according to the prescribed method, the wise [should act as follows].

Beyond twelve years from the end of the period of childhood, the Blessed One will no longer take delight in the abode of a child; for thereafter, he is indeed subject to the weakness of the agent. [He shall leave] that village, the sacrificer, the king, and even the subjects.
And having performed the oblation, Hari indeed proceeds toward the orb of the sun.
Therefore, at the time previously specified, one should carefully construct the root-shrine according to the prescribed characteristics and duly install the lamps with great effort.
At the time specified, it should become equal to the primary temple of the deity;
having performed the great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) for seven days, at the conclusion, the most skilled knower of mantras,
having especially constructed a new abode for the child [deity] in the northeast, [should proceed].
The wise one should worship there as before until the end of twelve years; or else, in that temple, year after year,
having performed the propitiatory fire-oblation for seven days each time, he should worship while saying, "Be patient."
In the beginning, however, the righteous one, having considered his own strength,
should quickly worship [the deity] within a temple if it is deemed unfavorable;
in whatever time that blameless celestial mansion is completed.
There would be no fault for that duration of time during worship in a gabled pavilion (kūṭāgāra).
Therefore, having caused [the image] to be made according to the rules of the treatises on architecture, whether of stone or brick, one should worship the Lord of Gods for the sake of all peace.
In the construction of a gabled roof (kūṭāgāra), one who knows the scriptures should perform all the mobile rites; and at the base of the brick interior, the first brick alone [is used].
Wherever there is a requirement for a head-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā), there too the first brick is required.

One should place the permanent image (dhruvabera) and the embryo (garbha) in the ground where it is appropriate; otherwise, there will be destruction for both the builder and the patron. If that occurs, one must remove the [image] and perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti).
The wise and intelligent one should construct the walls and other structures with bricks or stones, and he should fashion the inner sanctum (garbha) exactly as before;
furthermore, O Lord of Gods, the wise one should place the deity in the location of the *jīva* without the inclusion of a gem.
One should establish [the deity] in a movable zodiac sign, just as in the case of a temple for a young [deity].

If it possesses many stories, one should designate it as a "child's house" according to the rules stated for such structures on barren ground, and worship it daily, excluding the first and last forms (vigrahas). 15–16.
If one, out of delusion, joins together unmentioned metals and performs rites such as *kautuka* (auspicious marks), and then installs [the image], it becomes indeed malevolent (*ābhicārika*).
To pacify that defect, a wise person should likewise perform a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*).
Having performed the fire-oblation and having fashioned an image endowed with the proper characteristics, the wise man should install it.

He should arrange the standing, sitting, and reclining postures, as well as the festive decorations for the standing and sitting positions; however, he should never perform the reclining posture in reverse, for that would cause misfortune.

Even when a flawless image is being worshipped, especially during festive occasions and the like, one should not perform the ritual of "entering the weight of iron" (lohagaurava-saṃveśa); such is the injunction.
[This applies] to an image lacking the application of beeswax, which should be joined with the Vaiṣṇava and Brāhma mantras.
Having performed a *śānti* rite for the sacred abodes (*dhāman*), or even for the consecration of metal images;
if an image worshipped in another temple is installed in one's own temple through ignorance, ruin will ensue; therefore, one should perform a *śānti* rite. (21–22)
Having quickly abandoned that image, the wise one should likewise perform its installation in a former abode and worship it according to the prescribed rite.
This applies also in the event of the destruction of villages and the like, or the ruin of the temple.
Having collected those various earthen vessels,
one should perform worship in other beautiful temples as is appropriate, according to what is available;
if that [vessel] is indeed permanent, one should keep it protected after closing it up.
If the temple is afflicted by enemies, rivers, or other such obstacles,
the wise one should take the image along with its pedestal and,
for a valid reason, construct a temple in a delightful location as previously described.
Likewise, one should certainly perform the auspicious rite as prescribed by the ritual rules (27). With reference to the empty abode, another abode is to be constructed;
if the patron is weak, he may have it performed through a proxy (lākhava) (28).
If that [mind], which is joined with many obscurations and associated with many stages,
has been lost, one should subsequently practice by means of the secondary path (gauṇamārga).
In the same way, conceptualization is primarily [the primary path], while the other is specifically the secondary.
For the sake of worshipping the Lord, one should perform it with devotion according to one's capacity (30).
By that alone, there are no faults for us; even if the worship lasts only a moment, it is sufficient.
However, if the principal deity has perished, performing the rite there does not cause any fault (31).
If what was not lost remains deficient, or if what was lost is not deficient, it does not constitute a fault;
provided that the maker of both [the original and the copy] does not deceive himself.
(32) If the manuscript is a composite of many locations and is heavy due to weakness or looseness...
One should construct a gabled chamber, maintain it, and likewise worship it;
or else, even if one is weak, one may construct a single-story structure, firmly establishing it either standing or reclining as before. 33–34.

Having established the *koṭuka*—which possesses its characteristic marks—at the site of the *jīva* of the first stage, one should worship it; others, the worldly deities, one should worship daily by offering oblations (*havis*) in the *mukhamaṇḍapa*. 36.
Indeed, one should always worship them here together with their respective purposes.

One should perform the bathing festival and other rites in two ways through the act of bestowal (prādāna). Having taken up [the image] as far as the pinnacle and the trident, the knower of mantras should perform the placement of the bricks on the head; if he installs it in a second temple, it does not cause any fault.
If the first bricks, the inner sanctum, the doorposts, the pillars,
and all other stones used therein are found to be defective,
then everything that was gathered together where the deity was installed must be removed.
"If one desires [to perform] the rites for stone and other materials, it should not be done otherwise; rather, it must be performed according to the prescribed rule.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Expiation for a Young Temple," within the section on Sacrificial Rites (*yajñādhikāra*) in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu. This concludes the section on Sacrificial Rites.
Now begins the forty-ninth chapter:
The General Procedure for Expiation (Prāyaścitta) for the Teacher, the Priest, and the group of attendants.
But when there is mutual conflict, I shall declare the expiation:
when the teacher is angry or distressed, or has become agitated for some reason, and a conflict has arisen between those two— the teacher and the sacrificer.

The self-controlled practitioner should worship the Vaiṣṇava mantra, the one whose deity is the Sage (Brahmā), the Viṣvaksena mantra, and the Vāsanā mantra, as well as the Bārhaspatya mantra, one hundred and eight times.
Afterwards, he should propitiate the Guru; then the Guru, being pleased, will act without delay.
One should recite the *praṇava* one hundred and eight times with a concentrated mind; likewise,
one should worship the *vyāhṛtis* accompanied by the *praṇava* one hundred and eight times— in this manner, one should prescribe the expiation even for the worshipper.

If any one of these qualities has begun to manifest here, or if there is a cause for the loss of his life, he should be released with haste. Even if he is one who possesses an expiation, he should be released immediately upon being entreated on account of his virtue.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, eating ghee, consuming the five products of the cow,
subsisting on water, and fasting— each for one day respectively; then,
having bathed on the seventh day, likewise performing recitation and fire-offerings.

"By feeding Brahmins, one is indeed released from one's own sin; one should prescribe this same rite for whoever caused it to be committed. Otherwise, there is great fault—such is the teaching of the ancestors."
If one performs acts such as worship without first performing the expiation (prāyaścitta),
then at the conclusion of the expiation, one should worship the God of gods with devotion twice over and offer the oblation twice over.
If one, out of delusion, performs sweeping with a broom in a temple at midnight,
he swiftly destroys the Goddess Śrī who resides in that abode.
(12) One should worship [the deity] once in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice with a lotus smeared with ghee, accompanied by the Śrīsūkta.
When a village or even a district is agitated by the oppression of enemies,
one should conceal the images in the ground out of fear that they might be carried away;
or, having placed a tuft of grass or a piece of gold separately upon each pedestal.

Having invoked [the deity] at each junction of the day (pratisandhya) and having worshipped him, one should present the offering; therefore, after lifting the image when it is no longer crowded and when [the time] has become peaceful, one should quickly purify it with sour liquids and the like, and proclaim the "day of merit" (puṇyāha) and other auspicious rites. 15.
Having immediately performed the ritual offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and having constructed the pavilion for the sacrifice,
one should then prepare six sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), or five, or two, as well as a pit and an altar,
according to the prescribed rule at the conclusion of the night-long worship.
Having specifically superimposed the *śakti* from the *kūrca* onto the fixed image (*bimba*),
one should then invoke it into the water-jar (*kumbha*), meditate upon it, and worship it according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) once more according to the procedure stated for consecration.
In the event of the destruction of a village or the like, or the ruin of a temple,
one should quickly establish one's power (śakti) here in due order while remaining firm;
then, having entered the sacrificial hall, one should consign the fire into oneself through mantra.
Having led it to another well-protected place that is undisturbed, he should gradually settle it in the temple of a mild deity, or in a monastery, or in the house of householders,
or even in an eastern chamber, at the conclusion of the *puṇyāha* ceremony.
Having prepared the *aupāsana* fire-pit and having established his own sacred fire therein, he should install [the deity] according to his capacity, perform especially the *śānti* oblation,
and likewise install the Lord of Gods as before, facing toward the wide space.

One should worship according to the respective emblems by the very same path previously described; likewise, one should perform the daily procession offering (*nityayātrābali*) and the seasonal festival (*kālotsava*), except for the latter.
There, one should perform the retinue offering (*parivārabali*) as prescribed for the *āśraya*.
When the crowd has dispersed, one should again bring the image back to its former place of immersion (laya).
If a Caṇḍāla woman, a woman in her courses, an outcaste, or others enter the interior of the temple, or if death occurs within it, the site should be purified by cows after they have dwelt there.
Having fed one thousand and eight, or one hundred, or even fifty Brahmins, and having proclaimed an auspicious day,
one should perform the consecration again according to the previously mentioned procedure.
If one is unable to do this, one should conceal the images in the ground (28). Having projected their power into oneself at the conclusion of the daily fire-oblation,
and having meditated with devotion, one should worship them within oneself according to what is available (29).

O best of the twice-born, for as many days as there have been deficient in worship, one should offer oblations into the Pauṇḍarīka fire with that same number of Vaiṣṇava mantras; and having likewise offered the Śānti mantra into that very fire, one should do so year after year.
Then, having performed the great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) every month according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) once again;
if the fixed image (*dhruvabimba*) is made of metal, they also desire its [re-consecration] within that scope.
Some indeed declare that for an image made of stone, there is security;
having performed twice the previously mentioned propitiatory oblation (*śānti-homa*), one should perform the installation.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The General Procedure for Expiation," in the section on Sacrifice within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Vaikhānasas.
Fifty-first Chapter: Expiation for the Fixed Image.
Hereafter, I shall explain the expiation for the fixed image (dhruvabera).
The limbs (aṅga), the secondary limbs (upāṅga), the great limbs (mahāṅga), and the minor limbs (pratyaṅga) are each distinct from one another.
The crown, the head, the neck, the arms, the heart, the navel, the thighs, the knees, and the regions beginning with the feet are designated as the "great limbs" (mahāṅga). 1–2.
The wise man should specifically recollect these secondary limbs: the nose, ears, fingers, eyes, and the two equal ears;
as well as the head, the discus, the mace, and the conch, wheel, and lotus.
Having understood these and other such limbs, that supreme guide [should know] that nails, hair, beard, and teeth are called the minor limbs (pratyaṅga);
or alternatively, bracelets, garments, armlets, and necklaces [are so designated].
Furthermore, the Brahma-sūtra and so forth are designated as the minor limbs (pratyaṅga),
while the hands, feet, and palms are the Prabhā-pīṭha;
likewise, the two lips, the cheeks, the tongue, and the palate [are also part of it].
This is declared to be an auxiliary (upāṅga); it is now being stated by me in brief.
However, for each [deity] that is devoid of all auxiliaries, having performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) as previously described, one should worship correctly according to the prescribed rule.
Having prepared two sesame seeds and one *tilva*, and separately one *māṣa* and two *māṣas*,
and having likewise adjusted each deficient limb in its respective place,
one should sprinkle them with water according to the rule and worship them properly according to the ritual procedure.
One should avoid the state of a fool when the secondary and tertiary limbs are deficient;
specifically, one should avoid it where there are thirteen toes on the two feet and two hands, totaling eighteen [limbs] lacking. 10–11.
One should employ gold, silver, or even something else besides those there;
one should remove the portion for the child (the base), sprinkle it with water, and worship it.
[One should fashion] the head, the discus, the lotus, as well as the conch, the discus, and the mace.

If this [image] is devoid of its limbs, one should designate it as the station of a child (bālasthāna). Having consecrated the image that has been obtained according to the prescribed rite, one should worship it there;
thereafter, having carefully examined the deity, one should proceed together with the artisan.

Having carefully examined gold, silver, copper, clay, grass, and wood as either primary or secondary materials, one should employ the secondary where appropriate and the primary where required. One should never employ a secondary material when a primary one is available; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.

Having determined the preliminary form, one should have it fashioned from the primary material. Whether it be one *tāla* or two *tālas*, this is called the measurement (*unmāna*). Having established it according to the rule, one should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
The fourfold yoga consists of heroism (vīra), valor (viraha), enjoyment (bhoga), and liberation; each is designated according to whether one is standing, sitting, or lying down.
Having first established the path of heroism in the ancient state, it arises within the very occurrence of the decayed mantra.
Having caused the reconnection (sandhāna) below, one should likewise cause the separation (viraha).
Having established the separation at the top, if decay or the like occurs there,
one should again perform the yoga-path, having attained the enjoyment previously created.
In this very place, O Jīrṇasambhūta, according to the wish of the sacrificer, one should perform the union, the hero-posture, the separation, and the enjoyment, just as before; likewise,
one should act here while remaining on the bed or the seat.
Some authorities maintain that one should perform the rite exactly as prescribed before;
however, a stone image endowed with color should first be installed in a divine temple,
whereas if it is worn out or devoid of color, one should perform the bathing rites and other ceremonies.

In that very place, having set aside the festive rites, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rites; one should worship the Viṣṇusūkta and the Puruṣasūkta in succession. If, however, that [image] there should become worn out or damaged, [one should act accordingly].

One should worship that very deity and that very house which were desired in each respective community. Afterwards, having abandoned the image (bera), one is liberated by binding it with ropes made of cow-hair and concealing it in water outside the village.
Then, having prepared the abode for the child, and likewise during the festival and the ceremony, one should invoke the Śakti from the pitcher according to the rite, install her, and worship her.
The wise practitioner should fashion her form, substance, and dimensions as previously described.
One should install [the deity] in the primary temple; there is no need to wait for a specific time.
If the image (bera) used for the preliminary rite (kautuka) becomes worn out or damaged, one should observe everything as previously stated and install it again according to the prescribed ritual.
If the two goddesses are lost, having remained steadfast in resolve, one should have the two goddesses fashioned again;
the wise man, having offered libations as prescribed, should perform the rite of marriage.
First, having performed the ritual for Mahī, he should effect the grasping of the hand.

Having firmly established [the image] with steadfastness once the grasping of the hands has been performed, there is no fault whatsoever here if the two deities should stand together; however, if they are lost through lack of firmness, one should bring another image. || 31-32 ||
One should perform a secondary rite again after a primary one has been performed, but one should not perform a primary rite when a secondary one has already taken place;
having established the marriage according to the injunctions, one must never cause it to be annulled.
Where there is mutual confusion of these rites, no fault is found therein.
If the image of the Goddess is lost, one should procure another image.
The fault in its destruction should be understood as being like that caused by Nṛsiṃha;
for the Nṛsiṃha born from a pillar did not arise through Śrī. || 34-35 ||
Therefore, there is no marriage; it is exactly as before.
Thus, with every effort, one should perform what was left undone as if it were already done.
Furthermore, having performed the re-consecration and invoked the deities, one should worship the Goddess.
Thus, because [the ritual] has been contracted, the expiation for the permanent image (dhruvabera) has not been mentioned.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Fixed Image," within the section on the Temple Dwelling in the *Vaikhānasa Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu; this concludes the section on Sacrificial Rites.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter:
Expiation for the Mixing of Tantras.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for the mixing of tantras.
The Tantra of Viṣṇu is said to be twofold for the purpose of worship: the Vaidika and the Tāntrika. The first is gentle (saumya), while the other is fiery (āgneya).
According to the Vaikhānasa Sūtra, the rites beginning with conception (niṣeka) and so forth are performed by those [following the former].
That which is performed by Brāhmaṇas is considered gentle and Vedic;
however, the ritual rooted in the Vedas and accompanied by initiation (dīkṣā) is Tantric.
And that Tantric path is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as pure and mixed.
The Bhāgavata is declared to be pure, while the Pañcarātra is otherwise. That which is a pure Tantra composed by the Sūtas or the Sātvatas—
the bodily consecrations for those [followers] are proclaimed in their respective Tantras.
The Vedic boundary does not apply to those such as the Sūtas and others,
who have abandoned the rules of their own [caste] manuals and perceive the meaning of various other manuals;
that which is performed by those who are initiated is called "mixed" (miśra).
"Pure [devotion] grants only worldly enjoyment; mixed [devotion] is the sole means for liberation.
O elder, the gentle [path] bestows both enjoyment and liberation—this is the vision [derived from] the Vedas.
Nārada declared this gentle path to be the essence extracted from the Vedas. (7-8)
From him [Brahmā] came Virāṭ; from him, that very sage named Mukha;
from him, the four sages beginning with Asmadādi obtained the sacred rule (vidhi).
From them, the supreme scripture consisting of four parts appeared.
Those who know Brahman understand that which was formed by the merging of the Vedas before their decline is the Vaikhanasa Śākhā;
likewise, the Sūtra, which is the collective essence of that, was proclaimed by Vikhanas.
Furthermore, that [Veda], divided by the distinctions of the Ṛg and so forth, exists in its individualized form;
it became fourfold as the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan. That sūtra likewise became fourfold in its individualized form.
Ātreya, Bhārgava, Marīci, and Kāśyapi—these are the [four].
That which was declared by me as Bhārgava is considered to be elevenfold: Khila, Kriyādhikāra, and likewise Vāsādhikāraṇa. 14.
The section on pride, the etymological analysis, the miscellaneous section,
the qualification for worship, likewise the section on sacrifice,
the section on the social classes, and similarly the ancient tantra.
The essence of these [treatises] is the Tantra known as the Uttara;
this much alone is proclaimed as the Mārīca and the Ātreya.
The Kāśyapīya, according to the distinction of its subject matter, is fivefold. 16–17.
The *Mārīca* consists of one hundred thousand verses (*lakṣagrantha*), half of that was taught by Bhṛgu,
half of that was proclaimed by Atri, and half of that by Kāśyapa.
Furthermore, there is the *Khila*, the *Purātantrya*, and likewise the *Mānādhikaraṇa*.
The section on the qualification for worship consists of six thousand verses each;

the section on castes (varṇa), the section on legal authority (adhikaraṇa), the Virukta, and the Prakīrṇaka consist of two thousand, three thousand, and more than that [three thousand] verses respectively.
The fifty-first chapter is considered the section on Sacrifice (Yajñādhikaraṇa);
then there is the chapter named Vāsa, measuring four thousand [verses], and likewise the excellent section on Action (Kriyādhikāraṇa), consisting of one thousand [verses]. 21.
"O sages, listen to the Mārīca-śāstra, which is called the Bhārgava-śāstra. It consists of the Khila, the section on ritual action (kriyādhikāra), the ancient tantra known as Arcanā,
the sections on measurement (vānamāna) and authority (adhikāra), and likewise the section on sacrifice (yajñādhikaraṇa)."
In the *Prakīrṇanirukti*, there is likewise the *Varṇādhikaraṇa*;
each of these consists of eight thousand [verses] and is designated as "Uttara.
That which is the *Vimānārcanakalpa* is the tantra known as "Uttara."
This section on the installation of the image (arcādhikāra) consists of four thousand verses;
likewise, the section on the dwelling (vāsādhikaraṇa), the section on sacrifice (yajñādhikaraṇa),
and the supplementary section (khila) comprise five thousand verses, while the Nirukta consists of two thousand.
The remaining portion of the *Uttara-tantra* is known as the *Samūrtārcādika-rāga*;
in the *Kāśyapīya*, that which is called *Arcana* is said to consist of two thousand [verses].
Likewise, there is the *Vāsādhikaraṇa* and that which is designated as the *Khila*.

The section on ritual action (*kriyādhikaraṇa*) is said to consist of five hundred [verses] more than that; the remainder, concerning the worship of the Lord, is proclaimed as the subsequent section known as the *Kalpa*, which includes the procedure for the Viṣṇu-sacrifice. 28–29.
One should bring to completion with the same tantra-system by which one began;

if it is not stated therein, one should perform the remainder according to another tantra-system. Whatever is enjoined regarding the various offices that is contrary to the subsequent parts of the tantra [should be avoided].
"A wise man should never act [otherwise]," such is the view of the predecessors (pūrvaja).
It is stated in the *Yogottara-tantra* that one should act as prescribed for the qualified practitioner;
this applies to the preceptors (*ācārya*), the worshippers (*arcaka*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and the bearers of the sacrificial offerings (*balivāhaka*). 31–32.
Those who impart the mantras, those who cook, and those who serve—

Brāhmaṇas who have performed the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* and who know the reality of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*)— are the qualified persons.
Having performed the consecration and worship, the preceptor, together with the patron and knowing the mantras, shall appoint the officiants and others to their respective duties—
those who gather flowers as well as those who live by making garlands. (34–35)
Water-carriers, palanquin-bearers, and others— these,
if Vaikhānasas are not available, one should employ as those who bear the other thread;
one should accept those who bear the other thread whose arms are marked with the conch and discus.
One should indeed appoint Vaiṣṇavas from among the four castes as garden-keepers and food-preparers (37).

One should take those who possess the knowledge of the discus and conch, as well as others previously obtained and those from the north; furthermore, women skilled in dance and song should be taken for the purpose of dancing and singing (38).

In cases of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*pretaka*) among these, such as Brahmins and others, one should not observe a reduction in the period of impurity there, due to the weight of their virtues (39).
Wise men [should observe it] during festivals, at the time of a wedding, and during rites for peace (*śāntika*) and so forth.

For a guru who is engaged in ritual work, and especially for officiating priests (ṛtvij), impurity (āśauca) is prescribed at the conclusion of each respective rite; this applies particularly to a worshipper who is engaged in daily worship. 40–41.
At the conclusion of that twilight worship, however, that worshipper would become impure; therefore, one should by no means practice the mixing of roles with the preceptor, nor with the worshipper.
One should perform the mantras and the ritual services (upacāras) as prescribed in the subsequent section.
Names, forests, colors, syllables, and so forth are as described in the section on color (varṇa-adhikaraṇa); 43.

Fortifications, images, and so forth are as described in the section on residence (vāsa-adhikaraṇa); and the seers, meters, and presiding deities are as described in the section on ritual action (kriyā-adhikaraṇa). 44.
The daily worship is as described in the Nirukta, and the sacrifice and festival are proclaimed; one should perform the specific fire-rituals as stated in the Purāṇas and Tantras.
Whatever is not mentioned in the scriptures should be performed according to what is stated in the section on the *khila* (supplementary rites).
The measures of weight, capacity, and length, as well as the rules regarding weights, have been stated;
likewise, the ritual for the image and its furnishings, the procedure for anointing, and the remainder of the rites are explained everywhere according to the miscellaneous injunctions. 46–47.
The procedure for the qualification for worship shall be universal;
in the *Tantrottaras*, all procedures are considered universal.
(48) These include everything from the plowing [of the site] up to the installation, as well as the daily worship, the bathing, and other rites.
Expiation for all ritual acts consists in remedying deficiencies, excesses, and contradictions.

Furthermore, in the application of other mantras, the procedure of the *Tantrottaratantra* is prescribed; this includes the visualization of the names, syllables, and letters, as well as the various ritual services (*upacāra*). 49–50.

One should not cause a mutual confusion of rites; however, if one desires an *ābhicārika* (malevolent) rite, even if it involves such confusion, it does not result in fault. This *Vaikhānasa* scripture has been proclaimed to you in brief.
If the pure [rite] is devoid of worship, one should introduce the mixed [rite] there;
if the mixed [rite] is devoid of worship, one should introduce the gentle [rite] there,
performing the ritual from the purification of the ground up to the consecration according to the superior procedure.
Having performed [the rite], one should cause the primary [deity] to enter; otherwise, one should worship with purity.

If the primary is [already] present, the secondary should be performed again; however, when the primary is present, one should not perform the secondary. (54) If both are pure and auspicious, one should perform the consecration twice over.

If, while the worship is being performed, one desires the primary path, one should offer oblations for peace and worship quickly; no deliberation is required. If one desires the opposite, that is considered a fall from what has been ascended.
"A wise man should never practice [this]," O elder, such is the teaching;
it should not be told to one who is not a disciple, nor likewise to one who does not wish to listen (57),
nor to one who has not addressed the Lord of Gods, and especially not to one who lacks faith.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Expiation for the Intermingling of Tantras," in the section on Sacrificial Rites within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā* of the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*. Victory to Śrī Rāma, the Lord of the Self, who dwells in the city of the virtuous and is embraced by Sītā; he is the beloved guest of the palace of meditation, which is ever-awake for the Lord of the Soul. Salutations to the Great Guru, the venerable Vikhanas.
The Supplement on the Authority for Sacrifice.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the section on the Authority for Sacrifice within the Śrī Vaikhānasa, concerning festivals, expiations, and so forth, as well as the falling of the image.
Henceforth I shall proclaim the procedure for great portents; listen.
This applies to villages, cities, and likewise to towns, as well as in temples, sacred sites, and especially in royal capitals.
Likewise, when there is an earthquake, or when there is thunder in the sky,
during a great wind or a heavy rain, when lightning strikes everywhere, when the deities weep, and when there is incessant darkness; (2–3)
When that direction is agitated by the hurling of stones, when there is a rain of dust,
when it is entered by eruptions and the like, or when it is crowded with fevers, diseases, and so forth— even in all these cases, it may be either one or many.
This is declared to be a great portent, as well as one that produces [calamity] immediately.
When such a sign occurs at the beginning, one should anticipate misfortune for the king,
as well as agitation from fear of the enemy circles, disease, and famine.
In the absence of these eight, fever arises for all, and there is only suffering;
moreover, yakṣas, rākṣasas, paiśācas, gandharvas, and brahmarākṣasas enter every region and constantly bring about destruction.
With every effort, one should perform the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*).
Likewise, the wise man, avoiding the *tithis*, *vāras*, and *muhūrtas* [associated with malefic planets],
should perform it during all auspicious periods (*mānas*) within an interval of six months.

For a king who has been consecrated, when afflicted by a multitude of diseases such as wind-disorders (vāta), the [period of impurity] shall be one month, twenty days, two fortnights, sixteen, twelve, or else nine days, seven days, five days, or indeed the same [number of] days.
For the sake of pacifying diseases such as those caused by wind (vāta), for the removal of all misfortunes,
for the increase of long life, and for the sake of nourishment, one should perform [this rite].
A wise person should offer sprouts prior to the time of commencement.
After the offering of the sprouts, one should also collect the ritual materials either from within the village street or even from in front of the temple;
this should be performed in a Viṣṇu temple, and especially on the bank of a river.
Having constructed the sacrificial hall, one should prepare the bed-altar (śayyāvedi).
Having established the five fires around it, as well as the Pauṇḍarīka fire,
one should perform the Śrāmaṇaka rite in the northern pit for the sake of pacifying the site (vāstuśānti).
Equipped with four doors and adorned with various ornaments,
one should construct a single door at the far end of the water-channel; in the eight directions of that site, one should prepare the sacrificial fire-pits (kuṇḍa) for the domestic rites.
In all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should perform the *āghāra* libation (verse 17).

Having likewise performed the *vāstuhoma* and the circumambulation with fire (*paryagni*) in each respective place, one should worship the deities beginning with Indra in the eight pits dedicated to Indra and the others (verse 18).
With the mantras dedicated to each respective deity, using sacrificial fuel (samidh), food offerings (anna), and so forth, in sequence,
one should perform one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight [oblations];
and with the mantra containing the names of Indra and the other deities, one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (ājya).
Having completed the *srava* fires and entered the sacrificial hall,
one should then perform the *vāstuhoma* and carry out the *paryagnikaraṇa*.
Then, having offered the *brahmasūkta*, one should likewise offer the *rudrasūkta*.
Then, having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Viṣṇu-sūkta according to the Vaikhānasa Sūtra, accompanied by the rites of sprinkling and so forth,
one should first choose the preceptor (ācārya) together with the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Or else, one should have sixteen, twelve, or eight Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and masters of the mantras (23).
According to the procedure prescribed for rites for the gods, one should cause the germinating of seeds (*aṅkura*) and so forth to be performed;
afterwards, having dismissed the fire, one should perform the *āghāra* oblation again (24).
With the *triyambaka* mantra, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should offer oblations separately for each [deity] with the thought, "May death perish; may my life increase.
One should offer ten thousand oblations, or else one thousand and eight.
One should perform [the sacrifice] with sesame, clarified butter, oblation, or other substances.
(26) A wise man should increase the *āghāra* offering in the *gārhapatya* fire; once the fires have been led forth from the *gārhapatya*, he should perform the *āghāra* in those fires. (27)
Having arrived at the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice and having sprinkled the fire,
one should perform the Mahāśānti rite in sequence, employing the seven substances; then, having offered the Atiśānti, one should likewise perform the Sarvaśānti.
Having performed the *prabhūtaśānti*, one should perform only the *kevalaśānti*.
According to the method of ten thousand oblations (*āyutāhuti*), one should perform the *śrīśatāṣṭaka*;
thereafter, the *adbhutaśānti* is prescribed for each respective fire.
Thereafter, one should offer the *vasordhārā* oblation, especially in the *sabhyakuṇḍa*;
having performed the *mahāśānti* and other rites for seven days during the three daily sessions (of the *savanas*),
one should take a very firm pitcher and wrap it with thread.
One should perform the pouring from the pitcher with the mantra "śucī vo havyā.
Having spread six bhāras of rice grains, half that amount of husked rice, and sesame seeds upon the altar,
one should place the pitcher on top of the altar.
One should fumigate the interior of the jar with the mantra "bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ," and having recited "vārīścatasraḥ," one should fill it with scented water; then,
one should cover it with various kinds of lotuses and wrap it with a pair of garments.
Having adorned it with sprouts and other offerings while reciting the mantra *namassuloma*,
and having placed the nine gems therein, the wise one should deposit gold measured by ten *niṣkas* and fashion the form of Viṣṇu.

One should have it made of gold, measuring four finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width, with the auspicious earth [element] occupying half of that; having recited the respective mantra, one should cast it into the center of the pitcher.
The Śrīvatsa, the full water-jar, the kettle-drum, and likewise the mirror;
the pair of fish, the goad, the conch, and the eighth auspicious sign, the whirlpool;
the conch, the discus, the bow of Dāśārha, and the five weapons.

One should have the figures of Garuḍa, an elephant, and likewise a tortoise made, as well as clouds and streaks of lightning; these should be fashioned with colors and marks, weighing nine, eight, seven, or even five niṣkas. 40.
One should fashion separate images with gold of the highest purity (niṣkāhīna).
All the [auspicious marks] beginning with Śrīvatsa should be placed within the pitcher;
the water is situated within the pitcher, and the lotus is within the water. 41–42.

In the center of the lotus, one should meditate upon Hari Nārāyaṇa together with Śrī and Bhūmi; having meditated thus, one should worship him with the eight forms and offer all uncooked foods as well as betel leaf.
Having offered oblations for the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and likewise the Puruṣasūkta (44),
and then the Śrīsūkta, followed by the Bhūsūkta,
and thereafter the Ekākṣara and other hymns, one should recite the five pacifications (pañcaśānti) in their proper order (45).
Together with the officiating priests and the preceptor, he should recite the hymns with a concentrated mind;

then, according to the rules for the morning bath, he should perform the ritual ablution (snānakarma). Having gone to the temple of Viṣṇu and having paid homage to the Lord of Gods, [he should proceed].

One should bathe Viṣṇu with water-pots according to the extent of one's wealth (verse 47). Then the preceptor, holding the pitcher with both hands, should circumambulate the temple of Viṣṇu twice and place it within the inner sanctum (verse 48).
One should sprinkle the imperishable Viṣṇu with this very hymn mentioned previously;
having then sprinkled the ground with the water remaining from that,
one should thereafter summon the kings and offer blessings.
Having fed the Brahmins with benedictions preceding [the meal],

he should then perform the ten gifts (daśadāna) as well as the gazing at the clarified butter (ājyāvekṣaṇa); he should carry out everything, including the giving of fruits and so forth, according to the ritual manual.
Having taken hold of the preceptor and adorned him with garments, ornaments, earrings, golden sacred threads, and other such decorations,
[one should offer] one thousand and eight, or half that number, or even a single *niṣka*.
One should give four hundred cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor;
one-fourth of that to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
He who performs this with devotion shall indeed attain imperishable prosperity.
One desiring sons obtains sons; one seeking victory obtains victory;
one desiring a kingdom attains a kingdom, and there shall indeed be peace.
In this very world, he shall obtain wealth, prosperity, and long life.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Pacification of Great Calamities and Expiation for Faults such as Earthquakes," in the section on Sacrificial Authority within the Śrī Vaikhānasa.
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the Great Peace (mahāśānti),
which pacifies all defects, brings about the fruit of all sacrifices,
bestows all desired objects, is most excellent, and destroys all that is inauspicious.
It bestows long life and health upon the performer, and grants peace, prosperity, and happiness.
In all cases of great calamities, a Great Peace (mahāśānti) rite is prescribed; when facing an approaching danger, one should perform the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice according to its characteristics.
Then, having decorated the kitchen in the south or the southeast,
one should adorn it in the four directions with full water-jars, sprouts, and banners, as well as with plantain trees, *kramuka* trees, and hanging strings of pearls.
Having resolved upon a month, a fortnight, seven days, five days,
three days, or even a single day, and having understood the relative gravity or lightness of the faults, one should perform the oblations in sequence for a corresponding number of days.
At the conclusion of the *āghāra* oblations, the two hymns dedicated to Viṣṇu and Puruṣa should be well-offered; then, having offered the Rudra-hymn as well as the Viśvajit-hymn,
one should likewise offer the eighty-eight [syllables] beginning with the syllable *Iṃ*, which relate to the Supreme Self.
One should offer oblations with the Śrīsūkta, the Rātrisūkta, and likewise the Sārasvatasūkta; these are dedicated to all the deities and are joined with the five Varuṇa hymns.
Then, having offered the Mūlamantra oblation, one should offer the Dhātṛ-mantras and the others in their proper sequence.
Having uttered "Namo vāce" and recited "Śanno vāta," and likewise with "Nārāyaṇāya vidmahe" and the six Vaiṣṇava verses,
[one should offer oblations] with clarified butter, with *caru* mixed with clarified butter, and with fuel-sticks smeared with ghee.

Having bathed the deity with jars containing, respectively, parched grain flour, fried rice, sesame seeds, and cakes mixed with clarified butter, and having worshipped him, one should present the offerings.
The best oblation is performed at the three times of day; that which omits the night is middling.
One should offer oblations in sequence with clarified butter and clarified-butter-caru in the middle [rite];
in the lowest, one should offer only clarified butter. Then, at midday, one should perform the bath in the highest [rite], while in the middle, there is only worship.
"For the lowest [class], it is merely the fire-oblation (homa); such is the instruction of the ancestors.
One should maintain the fire without interruption until the conclusion of the rite;
when this sequence is completed, one should feed the Brahmins.
One should offer a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to those beginning with the preceptor in the presence of the deity,
while reciting the hymns beginning with "yad devā devahedyam" and "tad āyuṣṭe".
Having offered each of those respective hymns, it is traditionally taught that this constitutes "Excessive Pacification" (*atiśānti*).
Having performed the supreme *atiśānti* oblation, which brings about all prosperity (verse 17),
and having performed the oblation known as *adbhuta*, which pertains to the nine planets and presiding deities, it increases his sons, fortune, victory, longevity, and health (verse 18).
On the western side of the altar, one should prepare rice there;
having divided it into nine parts, one should worship Āditya and the other deities.
One should likewise offer milk-rice and the like, as well as betel-leaf and water for rinsing the mouth.
Thereafter, one should perform the oblation into the fires beginning with the Gārhapatya;
however, the wise man should worship the Moon and Venus in the Āhavanīya fire,
and subsequently, Rāhu and Mars in the Anvāhārya fire.
One should subsequently sacrifice to Ketu and Śanaiścara in the *gārhapatya* fire; likewise, having offered oblations in the *āvasathya* fire to Budha and Bṛhaspati,
one should sacrifice to Savitṛ in the *sabhya* fire with fuel-sticks, food, and other offerings in due order.
Or one hundred and eight, or twenty-seven; likewise,
sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) starting from those of the sun-god (arka) and ending with kuśa grass, in due order, for nine days, or seven days, or five days, or even three days.
One may perform [the rites] for a single day, but one should not perform a portentous rite (*adbhuta*) at night;
if a rite for the pacification of portents is performed, it removes even the most grievous suffering.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Pacification and the Pacification of Portents," in the section on Sacrifices in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa*.
The forty-fifth chapter:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme rite for universal pacification;
having strewn the sacrificial grass for the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice and having sprinkled water around the fire.
Having offered the Prājāpatya oblation, followed by the Svāṣṭakṛt and the Ṛddhi,
and having likewise offered these sixteen [oblations] as well as the Jayādi offerings,
one should offer the Viṣṇu-sūkta and worship in sequence up to the Vaiṣṇava deities.
With the eight-syllable mantra, the wise one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter into all the fire-pits;
thereafter, he should perform the *dvāriṣṭa* offering, which destroys all misfortune.
It bestows great-grandchildren, is excellent, and increases longevity;
it is called "Pacification of Beings" (bhūtaśānti) and is indeed Vaiṣṇava in every respect.
One should offer two oblations with the *nṛmedha* mantra, and likewise the *gāyatrī* mantra dedicated to Viṣṇu for those whose lineage has been severed.
Having offered oblations with the mantra "śanno mitra," and likewise with the "viṣṇornika" verses and others;
having performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice of one hundred oblations, one should worship in sequence at the Pauṇḍarīka rite.
By offering abundant oblations for peace, it shall become the performer of all pacification.
Then, having performed the general oblation specifically in the Sabhya-kuṇḍa,
one should likewise offer the oblations beginning with "hiraṇyaśṛṅga" and ending with "punaḥ," accompanied by twelve and eight syllables respectively, along with the Sahasra-huti.
The wise man should offer oblations with clarified butter, excluding parched grains, fried rice, and other such items. He who performs this with devotion, intent on the meditation of Viṣṇu,
attains his desired fruit by achieving perfect peace alone.
One should take a white lotus, ghee, and likewise the [milk] of a Kapila cow; having soaked them in *ālpu* water, one should offer them as oblations with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī.
In the absence of white lotuses, one may use a red lotus or a bilva leaf.

It is declared that one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight, oblations should indeed be offered; this is proclaimed as the peace of Śiva. Having then offered the Śrī-śānti oblation, one attains prosperity and nourishment.
Hereafter, I shall describe the abundant oblation (puṣkalāhuti) in due order:
having strewn the lotus-fire (padmāgni) and performed the sprinkling around (pariṣecana), one should offer it combined with sugar and clarified butter, and accompanied by honey and milk. 14.
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta,
as well as the Śrīsūkta, the Bhūsūkta, and the Ekākṣara-sūkta and others, the wise man, having meditated upon the goddess Viṣṇugāyatrī, should perform the oblation.
Having offered a bountiful oblation, the blessed Lord Hari, being well-pleased,
[bestows] upon him the glory of sons, victory, and the increase of longevity and health.
One should perform the Śrī-Śatāṣṭaka-Śānti rite as prescribed in the Khila section.
Having kindled the *sabhyakuṇḍa*, one should worship the *vasordhārā* in due order.

(18) Taking the *juhū* ladle in his hand and holding the previously mentioned clarified butter (*ājya*), the preceptor (*ācārya*), standing facing east, should perform the sacrifice with a continuous stream in the proper sequence. (19)
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta,
the Śrīsūkta, and the Bhūsūkta, one should then recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn beginning with "atodevā," as well as the Ekākṣara hymn and the Vaiṣṇavī Gāyatrī.
Let these seven hymns be offered by reciting each four times.
(21) If one is unable to perform the sacrifice in this manner, one should have it performed there once;
by performing the Vasordhārā sacrifice alone, one shall obtain the entire earth. (22)
For the certain pacification of everything, including the falling of thunderbolts,
one should perform rites for peace upon the earth, which bring about the prosperity of the king and the kingdom;
one should feed Brahmins daily until the completion of the ritual.
All acts such as worship, as well as food offerings (naivedya),
and likewise all acts such as bathing, one should perform the sprinkling upon the pedestal (pīṭha).
For one, two, or twelve years, this [practice] should be maintained in the presence of that which is described as the pedestal.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Śrī Vaikhānasa.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter:
Hereafter, I shall explain the secret [rites] for the protection of the wood and other materials.
During a conflict involving the shedding of blood, or when villages and kingdoms are in turmoil,
one should firmly bolt the doors everywhere, including those of the inner sanctums of temples;
or else, one should block them with stones or even bricks placed directly in front of the entrances.
The wise one should seal it without gaps and perform a plastering with lime;
as long as there is no danger, he should perform the worship. Once the auspicious time has come, having dismissed them, he should perform the opening of the door.
Then, having performed the purification, one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Beginning with the rite for averting portents, the wise one should perform oblations for seven days.
Afterwards, having completed the consecration, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
Thus, he who performs this with devotion shall attain union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu.
Hereafter, I shall explain the peace rite for the village which is now set forth.
If, having completely abandoned one month, another month has arrived;
Then, having performed the purification of the site (*vāstuśuddhi*), one should carry out the recitation of the Vedas (*vedapārāyaṇa*).
Having performed the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) for the deity, one should conduct a festival (*utsava*) for one day.
It is declared that for a two-month period it should be doubled, and for a three-month period it should be tripled.
In this very manner, however, the expiation is prescribed;
once a year has passed, the expiation is likewise prescribed.
Having constructed a water-shed in the middle of the village, one should also cause the proclamation of an auspicious day to be made.

Then, having performed the purification of the site (*vāstuśuddhi*), one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited. Let the mantras of the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*) be well-offered,
accompanied by a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) and joined with the supreme self (*paramātman*).
Having offered oblations to the gods and others, one should indeed offer the *īṅkāra* and so forth,
together with the Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, and Raudra mantras beginning with "viṣṇornuka. Having thus offered the oblations, one should cause the Vedas to be taught in the four directions in due order.
Having performed the ceremonial bath of the deity with one hundred and eight jars,
and having offered sacrificial oblations, one should present abundant bali offerings;
one should perform this daily for a fortnight or for seven days.
Others, however, having fed the Brahmins, should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor;
[this includes] the gift of gold, the gift of cows, and the gift of sesame seeds.
And one should increase it by the permission of the Brahmins;
for a two-year-old calf, double is prescribed, and for a three-year-old, one should perform triple.
Thus, after ten years,
in the assembly halls, the courtyards, the halls, and those temples of the gods, [the ground] was marked with three lines.
Having removed that [defect] from the *masūra* [grain],
the wise and learned one should have the deity fashioned; having bathed the deity, he should skillfully offer oblations to Brahman and Rudra.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter for each verse, ending with the *vyāhṛtis* respectively.
Then, the wise one, having bathed the deity with seven jars... 23.
Having worshipped the deity Haviṣmān, one should observe a festival for one day;

then, having sprinkled water around that fire, oblations are well-offered with fuel-sticks joined to Indra and Agni (aindrāgna), and likewise joined to Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya) for the sake of vigor (ojas). 24–25.
In this very manner, when great portents have arisen repeatedly for passionate women in villages and cities, [it should be addressed] by the practitioner. 26.
And by the seeker.
In a pond, a monastery, a well, or likewise in a storehouse (27),
one should cause a fire-pit to be made with sand or even with rice-grains, in a pit provided with three lines (28).
With *śvamatva*, *nanta*, *samī*, *nyagrodha*,
*plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, *apāmārga*, and excellent *dūrvā* grass (29),
along with sesame oil, lentils, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
The root-homa and others are offered as far as the five Vāruṇa offerings (30).
Having likewise offered to the gods and others, one offers with the syllable *Iṃ* and so forth, conjoined with the Supreme Self, the Brahma-mantra, and the Naravaiṣṇava-mantra (31).
Having taken up thirty-two [blades of] *darbha* grass for the pure gods and having strewn them around the fire,
the *Viṣṇu-sūkta* is properly offered with honey.
One should bathe the deity with water-pots accompanied by the *adhi-vāsana* rite;
having performed the sprinkling as before, one should then proceed. Having dug up that spot, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
And having filled it with sand, one should also have the auspicious day (puṇyāha) proclaimed.
Having performed the digging, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
this should be practiced for one day, two days, three days, or five days.
First, one should offer an oblation to the spirits (bhūtabali) mixed with sesame powder,
combined with parched grain and cakes, and consisting of five ingredients;
at every joint [of the ritual space], one should scatter two by two [the offerings] together with *kaṇṭhakāhala*.

In the quadrangles, in the triangles, and likewise in the hexagonal points (śṛṅgāṭa), one should offer the bali-oblation by their respective names: in the quadrangle to the Viṣṇu-bhūtas, in the triangle to the Raudra [bhūtas], and in the hexagonal point to the Brāhma-bhūtas. 39–40.
Having honored the teacher with garments, ornaments, and earrings,
and having likewise honored the disciples according to their merit in accordance with the prescribed rite, he proceeds into the center of the Śivāruta [temple]. 41.
If a monkey is seen at a sacred tree, in an assembly hall, or in temples, or at the crossroads of four carriage-roads, O King,
one should perform an immediate pacification rite after offering oblations.
Then, having performed the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi), one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
one should sprinkle all those various locations with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
As before, one should perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍasaṃskāra) and carry out the Āghāra oblation as previously described.

Let the Arṣa, Bhautika, Vaiṣṇava, and Brāhma [offerings] be well-offered together with the Pañcavāruṇa and ending with the Vyāhṛtis; having bathed the deity in due order with the seven jars (kalaśas). 45–46.
Having fed the Brahmins and given sacrificial fees according to one's ability,
let [the offering] be well-offered in the city, in the royal palace, in the temples of the gods, in the town, in the huts, and in the shrines. 47.
This is declared to be the *śāntihoma*; one should recite only [the following]:
the Vaiṣṇava, the Pauruṣa Sūkta, the Brāhma, the Aindra, and the Vāruṇa.
Twice it is declared to be peace (*śānti*). 48–49.
Henceforth, I shall describe the characteristics of women with red [complexions].
If such a one arises in the station of Brahmā, one should incur great fear. Furthermore, if a fierce crow is seen there, [one should act accordingly].
If it is seen in the southeast (Āgneyī), there will be prosperity from across [the sea];
if it should appear beautiful when planted in the southwest (Yama-sthāna), and if it is seen in the southwest (Nairṛtī), one should predict the destruction of the crops. 51–52.
Likewise, it would rain [only] occasionally; this is the certainty in all the scriptures.
When [the moon] arises in the western quarter (Vāruṇī), prosperity does not remain in that house.
And when it arises in the northwestern quarter (Vāyavī), the daughter [of the family] departs from that house.
If it is seen in the north (Saumya), the house will certainly become empty. If it is seen in the northeast (Aiśānya), a friend who has gone to a foreign land [will return].
If it is seen at the doorway, one abandons that house.
If those living beings are seen on the back of the jar of ghee,
O sage, there will be fear from fivefold cattle and even from thieves;
however, wherever they are seen in a state of devotion, there shall be happiness free from womanly influence.
If the lords of the bed and the seat are seen in the place of the bed,
and if living creatures are seen at the root of the grain-stalks,
she will herself become a housewife. 57–57.

For those things that have been lost, this single rite is prescribed; if the place where they were found is within the house, one should perform the *gṛhaśānti* (house-purification rite), and if it is elsewhere, one should perform the *svastyayana* (rite for well-being).
Thus, he who performs this with devotion goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
(61) Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Peace of the Village Extracted from the Secret [Text]," in the Śrī Vaikhānasa.
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter.
O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall specifically proclaim the Durgā-kalpa;
one should worship again during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa under the asterism Ārdrā,
either on the ninth or the seventh day prior to that [lunar] day.
Then, in the fifth [day], or thereafter on the third day, one should have an image of Durgā fashioned; having taken it up, one should cause it to enter the bathing altar,
bathe it with seven jars, and consecrate it with pure waters.
Having seated the Goddess upon the ritual seat and worshipped her with the eight forms, and having offered oblations to her, one should present mouth-perfume; then,
by this very same procedure, one should perform the commencement of the festival.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, he should enter his residence again.
Having seated the Goddess upon her throne, he should bathe her and worship her especially.
Then, taking two *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, not less than that amount—
Then, having mixed Marīcijīka ghee with coconut fruit and jaggery, one should place rice in front;
having offered that according to the prescribed method, one should present the oblation with water.
Having offered sandalwood with the *naya* mantra, one should present mouth-perfume (8).
Taking rice and other offerings, let them be given to his devotees, including the final portion (9).
On the day of completion, having worshipped the Goddess especially,
one should then worship the seven Mothers and offer [the gifts] to them. Into each of their hands, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of gold along with water.
Gold and mouth-perfume should be given to the Brāhmaṇas.
One should perform the Vāstugāna with great reverence for all the deities,
and thereafter, having offered to the Goddess with many offerings such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and other delicacies.

Having offered mouth-perfume to the Guru, one should present the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā); having established [the deity] in the seat of life (jīvasthāna), one should then perform the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
In the absence of a physical image, one should perform the rite according to the prescribed procedure upon a painted cloth (paṭa).
Having first performed the ritual bathing (snapana), one should carry out the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with consecrated waters.
Thus one should worship the Goddess; it shall bring peace to the land.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Durgā," in the Śrī Vaikhānasa [Dharma-sūtra].
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall describe the worship at the edge of the village,
as well as the festive rite (*kautuka*) and the ceremonial bath (*snapana*), both for the daily and occasional rites.
The instruction is that one should perform [the rites] before the second watch;
one should carry out the festive *baliberam* at the end of a *yojana*.
Whether through delusion or ignorance—

The kingdom and the realm will surely perish, and the destruction of the villages will follow. Therefore, having performed a propitiatory rite (*śānti*), one should once again carry out the ritual action,
especially when there is fear of an enemy army and turmoil in the kingdom and villages.
Having taken up the auspicious thread and other items, one should place them in a suitable location and worship them;
afterwards, at an auspicious time, one should re-establish the Lord of Gods in his former place for a fortnight or even for seven days, in order to remove that defect.
Having performed the marvelous rite of pacification (śānti), one should subsequently perform the installation (sthāpana).
One should perform it once in one month; in two months, it should be twofold;
in three months, it is said to be threefold; and in the fourth month, one should perform it four times.
At the end of the year, if it is an auspicious time, one should perform the *māsa-śānti* (monthly propitiation) and carry out all activities such as plowing once again; this is the instruction.
It brings about the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, and serves to ensure peace for the village.
Then, following the other treasuries, she was not fully satisfied.
